Medicine is an ever-changing science. As new research and clinical experience broaden our knowledge, changes in treatment and drug therapy are required. The editors and the publisher of this work have made every effort to ensure that the drug dosage schedules herein are accurate and in accord with the standards accepted at the time of publication. Readers are advised, however, to check the product information sheet included in the package of each drug they plan to administer to be certain that changes have not been made in the recommended dose or in the contraindications for administration. This recommendation is of particular importance in regard to new or infrequently used drugs.

###### PREFACE SSS 

Updates to accompany Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine? Why, what, and how often? The editors of Harrison’s have struggled, usually unsuccessfully, to keep each new edition from expanding. Despite admonitions to themselves and to the authors, these efforts have met with only limited success. At present, a new edition of Harrison’s appears every three or four years, but many advances occur in the interim. The ninth edition of Harrison’s is about 2200 pages in length, but scientific and medical progress continues unabated—fortunately —resulting in the need to describe new diseases, new disease mechanisms, and new modalities of diagnosis and treatment. Even the tried, true, and well-established clinical principles are hard to encompass and condense within one textbook without the book becoming unmanageable in sheer size and weight. 

What then might be done to make the ever-expanding medical data base available to the physician and student of medicine in a form which is current and comprehensive, with scientific facts presented accurately but in a simplified and lucid style and format? To this end the editors have decided to initiate a series of Updates, four of which will appear between the ninth and the tenth editions of Harrison’s. These Updates are intended to cover some of the new and important medical advances that, even since the preparation of the ninth edition, have become an integral part of medical knowledge (and will in all likelihood be included in the tenth edition of Har- 

rison’s, albeit in less detail). In addition, the Updates are intended to review clinical topics which, while important, either could not be comprehensively described in the textbook or had to be omitted altogether. It is the hope of the editors that Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine will be used as the core reference which, in conjunction with the Updates, will become the basis of what constitutes present-day knowledge of internal medicine. As physicians and students of medicine, we have witnessed the tremendously rapid rate at which scientific and clinical discoveries have been introduced into practice and the major impact that they have had on diagnosis and therapy. We have seen a major revolution in the diagnosis of numerous diseases through the use of imaging techniques such as ultrasound and CT scanning, which were unknown as recently as 10 years ago. Cell receptors and prostaglandins are no longer topics considered esoteric or of interest only in the laboratory. Derangements in cell receptors are influencing our thinking about disorders such as diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, and myasthenia gravis and about the treatment of breast cancer. Increased knowledge about thromboxanes and leukotrienes has enhanced our understanding of inflammation and coagulation and of the pathogenesis of asthma and peptic ulcer disease. New developments in immunology have had a pervasive impact on almost every facet of medicine. 

The clinical areas presented in this Update 

> Xx PREFACE 

and those that will be presented in the next three Updates have been carefully planned by the editors in an attempt to provide a balance of topics that represent new and important knowledge for the physician-internist or that could not be covered in depth in the ninth edition of the textbook because of space limitations. The contents demonstrate our attempt to cover selectively various clinical topics, ranging from such new areas as the role of glycosylated hemoglobins and the artificial pancreas in the management of diabetes mellitus to comprehensive and in-depth expositions of clinical problems such as newer infectious diarrheal syndromes, the diagnosis and treatment of biliary obstruction, mitral valve prolapse, and the neurological aspects of systemic tumors. 

With these Updates, we hope to bridge the “gap” between editions of Harrison’s and to 

provide a meaningful contribution to the effective and continuing education of medical students, graduate trainees, and physicians, whether they are generalists or specialists. To this end we have arranged that review of an Update can provide 25 category 1 CME credits to U.S. physicians. We have prepared a series of questions on each chapter that together constitute the CME examination in the back of this Update. Details about how credits may be earned by taking the examination are described in the introduction to the examination.

#### DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO 

###### MARK S. McPHEE and ROBERT H. SCHAPIRO 

The relatively recent introduction of a wide variety of innovative diagnostic and therapeutic procedures has revolutionized the clinician’s approach to the jaundiced patient. With the advent of this continually expanding technology has come some confusion on the part of the practitioner regarding the appropriate use of newer techniques in the diagnosis and management of patients with biliary obstruction. Experience has been sufficiently limited with some procedures that their risks, their potential benefits, and the clinical settings in which they might be put to best use have yet to be defined fully. This article is intended to clarify a few of the uncertainties about the proper role of these less familiar recently developed techniques for examination and manipulation of the biliary tree and to recommend some guidelines for the current approach to the diagnosis and treatment of patients with biliary obstruction. 

###### CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS AND DIAGNOSIS Differential diagnosis of jaundice 

The differential diagnosis of jaundice is complex, and the causative diseases or underlying conditions may be classified in accordance with a variety of methods. Since the first objective (and the major problem) in diagnosing the cause of jaundice involves making the distinction between intrahepatic (hepatocellular or medical) cholestasis and extrahepatic (obstructive or surgical) jaundice, classification methods based on these two basic categories appear to remain of greatest clinical use. The list of reported causes of cholestasis, both intra- and extrahepatic, grows longer 

as newer diagnostic techniques provide further definition of the hepatobiliary system in jaundiced patients. In particular, the availability of improved radiographic, endoscopic, and surgical investigative procedures has resulted in the identification of a number of unusual causes of extrahepatic biliary obstruction. Table 1 summarizes the common as well as the less frequent disorders to be considered in the differential diagnosis of extrahepatic cholestasis. 

###### Symptoms and signs 

Technological innovations, however sophisticated, to date have failed to provide any substitute for a carefully performed history and physical examination in the jaundiced patient. These are the foundations upon which subsequent tests and procedures will be selected from the often redundant array available. The first objective is the differentiation of intrahepatic from extrahepatic causes of biliary stasis, with a view toward embarking on an orderly workup which will maximize speed, safety, and precision of diagnosis, while minimizing expense and risk to the patient. In this light, data gained from the history and physical examination are of prime and often overriding clinical importance in establishing the direction of the diagnostic approach and in initiating therapy. 

###### The laboratory investigation of cholestasis 

Appropriate use of laboratory tests in the investigation of the jaundiced patient should be based largely on positive clinical findings. Biochemical, hematologic, and immunologic tests may give

substantial clues in differentiating intrahepatic and extrahepatic cholestasis and may provide specific diagnoses in some clinical situations. In general, information gained from standard liver function tests is not sufficient to distinguish intrafrom extrahepatic cholestasis; however, marked elevations of serum aminotransferases may suggest hepatocellular necrosis, whereas large increases in serum alkaline phosphatase or 5’nucleotidase suggest extrahepatic obstruction. In the setting of suspected hepatocellular necrosis, 

the finding of circulating hepatitis B surface antigen or of a rising antibody titer (especially of IgM type) against hepatitis A or cytomegalovirus may provide specific diagnoses. Serologic tests for certain bacterial or parasitic agents may also be specific or highly suggestive. Low albumin and high serum globulin levels and prolonged prothrombin times unresponsive to parenteral vitamin K administration suggest chronic liver disease or acute hepatic failure; the presence of a positive test for lupus erythematosus, antinuclear antibodies, and anti-smooth muscle antibodies may point toward chronic active hepatitis. A diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis is suggested by positive antimitochondrial antibodies, whereas marked elevation of alpha fetoprotein suggests underlying hepatocellular carcinoma. Appropriate iron studies may suggest hemochromatosis, and low levels of a,-antitrypsin or ceruloplasmin may direct investigative efforts toward diagnoses of a,-antitrypsin deficiency or Wilson’s disease. Noninvasive procedures in the diagnosis of jaundice The relatively recent introduction and increasingly widespread use of ultrasonography, computerized body tomography (CBT), and radioisotopic imaging of the biliary tree have altered considerably the noninvasive approach to the clinical diagnosis of biliary obstruction. These newer technical innovations have emerged as sophisticated, complementary procedures for hepatobiliary and pancreatic investigation, adding to or, in some cases, supplanting older procedures more familiar to the clinician, such as abdominal and chest films, oral cholecystography, the upper gastrointestinal series, and intravenous cholangiography. The clinical utility and limitations of some of the newer noninvasive diagnostic procedures are reviewed below. 

Oral cholecystogram (OCG) The familiar technique of OCG allows a correct diagnosis of cholelithiasis to be made in about 95 percent of affected patients. A fatty meal or an injection of cholecystokinin may be given during cholecystography to enhance the detection of small stones and to assess gallbladder contractility (though failure of the gallbladder to contract, as 

###### CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS AND DIAGNOSIS 

Radioisotope scanning Recently introduced radiopharmaceuticals such as 9™Tc-labeled N substitutions of iminodiacetic acid (HIDA, DIDA, PIPIDA, etc.) and pyridoxylideneamino acid compounds (PyG, PyL, PyA) are rapidly extracted from the blood, excreted into the biliary tree at high concentration, and have the capability of imaging the gallbladder, common bile duct, and even intrahepatic ducts despite the presence of moderate bilirubin elevations (6 to 12 mg per 100 ml of serum). Failure to image the gallbladder may indicate cystic duct obstruction, cholecystitis, or prior cholecystectomy. In the absence of extrahepatic biliary obstruction, activity should be seen in the common bile duct within 60 min. Failure to identify imaging of the entire length of the common bile duct may indicate complete biliary obstruction, and the delayed appearance of radioisotope in the duodenum may suggest partial obstruction. Poor hepatocellular function with diminished bile excretion may also be associated with diminished and delayed radioisotope activity in the gut. The diethylacetanilide IDA (DIDA) scan, in particular, represents a rapid and safe method of examining biliary patency. Its clinical value in identifying partial obstruction versus hepatocellular jaundice remains unclear, however, and the technique is not of much use in the deeply jaundiced patient. In the past, 'I-labeled rose bengal was used as an agent for the clinical investigation of biliary patency. The relatively high radiation dose delivered by !3'I has limited the amount that may be safety administered, and, as a result, the radioisotope images are usually of poor quality, with insufficient definition<sup>ofthebiliarytreein</sup> occur on a double-dose oral cholecystogram may inwith trast agent. most patients to distinguish reliably intrahepatic from extrahepatic obstruction. Rose bengal imaging is currently being replaced by the higherresolution technetium HIDA or DIDA scans. Liver scanning using 9°™Tc-labeled sulfur colloid may be of value in the diagnosis of hepatic metastases (with a reported accuracy of 75 to 86 percent), abscesses, cysts, or hematomas. False positives may result when the technique is used in patients with high-grade extrahepatic obstruction or severe hepatocellular dysfunction. Decreased activity in the porta hepatis may be seen in patients with obstructive jaundice, but the diagnostic specificity of this finding is low. Although the roles of liver scan, ultrasound, and CBT have not yet been completely established in patients with diffuse hepatic parenchymal disease, the “‘traditional’” liver scan has limited clinical value in the investigation of the jaundiced patient. Pancreatic scanning using [7°S]selenomethionine has proved even more disappointing clinically, since the test is time-consuming, difficult to interpret, and nonspecific when abnormal. Administration of [6’Ga]gallium citrate (gallium scanning) may be of some use in the identification of hepatocellular carcinomas and for the localization of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic abscess cavities; but gallium is concentrated to some extent in the normal liver and colon, and these scans are expensive, time-consuming, and of variable reliability. 

Ultrasonography The introduction of diagnostic scanners utilizing very short pulses of focused high-frequency sound to form a reflected image which varies in intensity with the acoustic impedance (density, elasticity) of the tissues scanned has caused a revolution in the investigation of jaundiced patients. Ultrasound techniques are rapid, painless, safe, relatively inexpensive, and quite accurate in the diagnosis of high-grade biliary obstruction. There are no real contraindications at the sound intensities employed. The utility of ultrasound in the detection of biliary obstruction is limited by the availability of experienced personnel to perform and interpret the scans and by the poor ability of ultrasound to penetrate gas—soft tissue and bonesoft tissue interfaces (with resultant limitations in patients with large amounts of bowel gas or with extreme obesity, massive ascites, very high dia- 

4 BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT 

phragms, or low ribs). The accuracy of diagnosis of biliary obstruction by the detection of a dilated ductal system has been reported to approach 95 percent in experienced hands. False-negative examinations may occur in partial or early obstruction, when the serum bilirubin level is below 6 mg per 100 ml and the ducts have not yet become detectably dilated. Identification of a dilated common bile duct in the ligamentum teres may precede dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts. Most ultrasonographers consider unequivocal ductal dilatation to be present when intrahepatic biliary radicles exceed 4 mm or the common bile duct exceeds a diameter of 7 to 10 mm. Oblique or transverse scans may permit identification of the level of obstruction (e.g., porta hepatis vs. distal common duct) in up to 70 to 80 percent of patients and a probable diagnosis for the underlying cause of obstruction in about 40 to 50 percent of cases. These figures are derived from centers having the most experience with the technique. Clinicians may, with justification, dispute the reliability of ‘firm’? diagnoses made by ultrasound alone. 

Ultrasound is most useful in the detection of ductal dilatation and, occasionally, in identifying ductal calculi (the more proximal the position of the stone in the biliary tree, the easier its identification by ultrasound). Ultrasound may also detect pancreatic carcinomas or phlegmons (larger than about 4 cm in diameter), pancreatic pseudocysts, liver metastases, enlarged nodes in the porta hepatis, cirrhosis, ascites, hepatic cysts, and choledochal cysts. In the jaundiced patient, ultrasonography has replaced the oral cholecystogram for identification of gallstones. Stones as small as 2 to 3 cm may be detected with about 80 to 95 percent accuracy, but false positives may occur in up to 5 to 15 percent of cases. In addition, ultrasound may aid in the demonstration of gallbladder size and emptying kinetics (following fatty meal or cholecystokinin administration), in the detection of thick, viscid bile or biliary sludge and in the diagnosis of a fibrotic or contracted gallbladder and fatty liver. Ultrasonography is most limited in detecting lesions of the distal common bile duct (calculi, ampullary, or pancreatic head carcinomas) since bowel gas frequently overlies this area. It has very limited usefulness in the diagnosis of cholangiocarcinomas (with periductal infiltra- 

tion), sclerosing cholangitis, or small tumors of the gallbladder or pancreas. The familiar technique of gray-scale ultrasonography, which allows amplification and processing of echos on a videoscan converter in 8 to 16 shades of gray, is currently being replaced, in many centers, by what is referred to as real-time ultrasound or sonofluoroscopy. Efficient real-time systems allow high-speed continuous viewing of the organs scanned. As resolution capabilities increase, sonofluoroscopy may prove the superior ultrasonographic technique for examination of the gallbladder and biliary tree and for guidance of needles used in localization, biopsy, or aspiration procedures. Whether the gray-scale or the real-time technique is used, it is evident that ultrasonography is the single most useful noninvasive procedure in the differentiation of intrahepatic cholestasis from extrahepatic obstruction. The clinical information gained from the ultrasound usually represents the basis for the selection of subsequent diagnostic tests. 

Computerized body tomography (CBT) The technique of CBT allows complex information from multiple fan-shaped x-ray beams transmitted through the body to be integrated into anatomic images in cross section. Current CBT systems permit identification of structures not visible on conventional radiographs along with their spatial interrelationships. The CBT scan is relatively rapid and noninvasive and is not limited by the presence of bowel gas, ascites, or massive obesity. Its evident value has been somewhat modified by availability, high expense, limitations of experience in performance and interpretation, and the technical necessity to minimize movement artifact. Newer generations of CBT scanners employ markedly reduced scanning times and have improved or nearly eliminated poor resolution from movement. The image of the solid abdominal organs obtained by CBT is superior to that from any other noninvasive technique, and, as the method used is based on different scanning principles, it may provide information not obtainable by ultrasound. When used in conjunction with oral and/or intravenous contrast enhancement, CBT appears to be most useful in the detection of carcinomas or phlegmons of the pancreas (espe-

cially of the body or tail, and with probable superiority over ultrasound for lesions of the pancreatic head), pancreatic pseudocysts or abscesses, dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, primary or metastatic liver neoplasms, fatty liver, enlarged nodes in the porta hepatis, and hepatic cysts or abscesses. As with ultrasound, it may be difficult or impossible to distinguish between malignant and inflammatory masses of the pancreas by CBT. The accuracy of body tomography in the identification of obstructive jaundice by detection of dilated ducts has been reported to be in the range of 90 percent and about 75 to 80 percent in correctly demonstrating the site or probable cause of obstruction. CBT scans may aid in the assessment of obstructing hepatic or pancreatic tumors for surgical resectability. The technique appears to be less useful in the identification of gallbladder disease or of calculi in the gallbladder or biliary tree and in the recognition of cirrhosis or other diffuse hepatic diseases. At present, CBT should probably be regarded as a relatively expensive technique which in most cases has little diagnostic advantage over ultrasound in the investigation of cholestasis. It may be most useful when technical difficulties 

limit ultrasonography and when additional diagnostic evidence is desired in patients with an “‘inconclusive” ultrasound examination. 

Table 2 compares the uses and limitations of CBT, ultrasonography, and radioisotope scans in the investigation of biliary obstruction. 

###### Cholangiography and invasive procedures 

Major advances in the diagnosis of the jaundiced patient have resulted from the recent use of invasive techniques such as percutaneous fineneedle transhepatic cholangiography (PTHC), endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), and percutaneously guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy. The ability to obtain rapid preoperative cholangiographic evidence of the site, degree, and cause of biliary obstruction has markedly altered the diagnostic approach to cholestasis, but the selection of the most appropriate series of diagnostic tests should be based on the availability of experienced personnel for performance and interpretation and will thus vary from center to center. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) Another major advance in the cholangiographic diagnosis of the jaundiced patient has occurred with the introduction and refinement of endoscopic retrograde study of the biliary and pancreatic ductal systems. In ERCP, a specially modified, flexible, fiberoptic, sideviewing duodenoscope is introduced into the second portion of the duodenum, the ampulla of Vater is identified, and the ampullary orifice is cannulated with a small catheter passed through the instrument channel of the scope. After successful cannulation, contrast material is injected into the biliary tree and the pancreatic duct under fluoroscopic guidance. Films are then obtained and the ductal anatomy defined. In experienced hands, cholangiograms may be obtained in about 75 to 90 percent of cases and pancreatograms in 85 to 95 percent. The overall complication rate for ERCP is about 2.0 to 3.5 percent, including a reported 1 to 1.3 percent risk of injection-induced pancreatitis and less frequent complications of pancreatic abscess or infected pseudocyst, cholangitic sepsis, perforation, or hemorrhage. ‘““Benign’’ asymptomatic hyperamylasemia occurs postinjection in up to 25 percent of cases. Some decrease in arterial oxygen saturation during and following the procedure is not unusual, although overt cardiopulmonary complications are rare. Obviously, success and com- 

plication rates of ERCP depend upon the experience of the cannulating endoscopist. Failure rates of up to 60 percent with complications in as many as 15 percent of procedures have been reported for less experienced endoscopists attempting ERCP. Prophylactic antibiotics are usually administered prior to retrograde cholangiography or are added to the injected contrast medium in patients suspected of having biliary obstruction. ERCP requires more technical skill and more time for completion (10 to 60 min) than PTHC, and is usually more expensive. When compared with transhepatic cholangiography, the anticipated success rate for ERCP may be somewhat lower in the patient with dilated ducts and somewhat higher when the ducts are not dilated: Performance of ERCP is relatively contraindicated in patients with acute pancreatitis, acute viral hepatitis or hepatitis B surface antigenemia (instrument contamination), recent myocardial infarction, or severe pulmonary disease. Care should be taken to minimize retrograde filling of pancreatic pseudocysts and overfilling of an obstructed biliary tree. ERCP may be impossible in patients with Roux-en-Y biliary-enteric anastomoses, gastroduodenal obstruction, or ducts opening into duodenal diverticula. In contrast to PTHC, retrograde studies are not contraindicated in the presence of coagulation defects, ascites, or liver abscess. Major advantages of ERCP include (1) the ability to diagnose the presence of neoplastic or inflammatory diseases of the gastroduodenum or ampulla under direct vision (with potential histologic confirmation by biopsy or brush cytology), (2) the addition of pancreatography to the cholangiogram (which may be of overriding clinical importance in the obstructed patient with underlying pancreatic disease), (3) the ability to outline the distal common bile duct and intrapancreatic portion of the common bile duct in cases where there is more proximal obstruction, (4) the capability of obtaining a good quality cholangiogram in patients with prior ampullary sphincterotomy and in most patients in whom PTHC has failed, (5) the ability to collect pure samples of pancreatic juice or bile for cytology, culture, or chemical analysis, and (6) the possibility of performing choledochal manometry, endoscopic papillotomy (with or without stone ex-

Duodenoscopy and_ retrograde pancreatography are most successful in the identification of duodenal diverticula, papillitis, papillary stenosis, periampullary carcinoma, chronic pancreatitis (including evaluation for possible surgical intervention), pancreatic pseudocysts, and pancreatic carcinoma (especially of the head). The retrograde cholangiogram may reveal benign or malignant stricturing of the distal common bile duct, common duct calculi, primary sclerosing cholangitis (where PTHC may be difficult or impossible), choledochal cysts, enlarged nodes in the porta hepatis, or biliary-enteric fistulae and anastomoses. The technique may also be useful in diagnosing gallstones, carcinoma of the gallbladder, and intrahepatic malignancy. ERCP is usually the cholangiographic method of choice in jaundiced patients without 

dilated ducts on ultrasound, in patients with dilated ducts and suspected gastroduodenal, ampullary, or pancreatic disease, and in patients in whom endoscopic papillotomy would probably represent the best form of treatment for choledocholithiasis if confirmed on cholangiogram. Table 3 compares ERCP, PTHC, and IVC in the cholangiographic investigation of biliary obstruction. 

Operative and postoperative cholangiography The biliary tree may be visualized intraoperatively by instillation of contrast medium into the cystic duct following cholecystectomy, through a choledochotomy in cases of common duct exploration, and, on occasion, through a cholecystostomy catheter. These techniques have been advocated as routine procedures during biliary surgery in order to assess indications for performance of common duct exploration at cholecystectomy, to determine the degree of 

###### CLINICAL PRESENTATIONS AND DIAGNOSIS 

Following common duct surgery, contrast may be injected through an indwelling T tube or cholecystostomy catheter. T-tube cholangiography has become routine in most centers in order to exclude the presence of retained stones and to ensure biliary patency before removal of the T tube. Cholangiograms are almost always obtained in postoperative patients whose jaundice shows delayed resolution, when T-tube clamping fails, or when cholangitis supervenes. The well-matured T-tube tract may be dilated after removal of the T tube and used for percutaneous extraction of retained stones or for fiberoptic cholangioscopy. Percutaneous guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy The ability to obtain a firm tissue diagnosis based on cytologic or histologic specimens obtained preoperatively in jaundiced patients has been remarkably improved by the introduction of new techniques for percutaneous fine-needle biopsy. When a suspicious lesion has been identified by ultrasound, CBT scan, or cholangiopancreatography, a thin, flexible needle may be guided directly into the lesion under fluoroscopic, ultrasonic, or CBT guidance and a tissue sample obtained by aspiration. A fine needle of the Chiba type (as used in PTHC) may yield samples suitable for cytology; a similar needle, modified to include a cutting tip and a beveled stylet, may be used to obtain a small tissue core which may be large enough for specific histologic diagnosis. Fine-needle biopsies offer the advantages of safety, the<sup>abilitytomakemultiple</sup> passes at one sitting,<sup>theabilitytobiopsyrou-</sup> tinely through bowel<sup>orotherorganswithout</sup> or absence of retained stones following exploration of the common duct. Operative cholangiography may detect overlooked stones, strictures, tients. Cholangioscopy and operative cholangiogdebris, blood clots, and tumor. cholangiography” has become an accepted part of the common duct exploration in most major biliary patency and to demonstrate the presence or malignancies in up to 2 to 15 percent of paraphy appear to be complementary procedures for detection of retained calculi since nonemptying of contrast material or filling defects on the cholangiogram may be easily assessed endoscopically with differentiation between stones, “Completion medical centers. 

undue complication in order to reach the target, the option of doing outpatient biopsies, and the ability to sample multiple targets. The fineneedle technique is probably of less potential value when the diagnosis requires larger cores of tissue for architectural or detailed histologic features as in diffuse hepatocellular disease or lymphoma. Larger-bore (16- to 18-gauge) rigid aspiration biopsy needles yield a thicker, longer tissue core that allows for such accurate histologic interpretation. Precise access to targets, however, is limited, complication rates (especially with hemorrhage) are substantially higher, and the operator is usually limited to one or two passes at a single target under less satisfactory guidance when these large, inflexible needles are used. Thin-needle biopsy is usually preferable for sharply defined lesions. 

In fine-needle biopsy, the guidance system may be individualized to the patient, although ultrasound is usually preferred if the target lesion is easily seen, since time and expense are comparatively small. The needle, however, may be more difficult to see by ultrasound, and accurate samples from small lesions are more difficult to obtain. The use of real-time ultrasound guidance may eventually offer some advantages over grayscale or current aspiration biopsy transducers, giving high resolution, a more “dimensional” image, and scanning obtained in temporal conjunction with the biopsy. Standard x-ray fluoroscopy may allow good needle visibility, familiarity, speed, and the ability to move the patient freely, but target definition in the abdomen is often poor. CBT guidance is best suited for precise sampling of small, deep-seated masses, some pancreatic lesions, and targets poorly visualized on ultrasound. In the jaundiced patient, thin-needle aspiration biopsy techniques have their greatest utility in two settings: (1) in the biopsy of localized or richly vascularized hepatic lesions and (2) in the evaluation of malignant-appearing obstructions of the biliary tree, since further diagnostic or therapeutic decisions may be influenced considerably by the histologic confirmation of malignancy. The major contraindications are similar to those for PTHC. 

The diagnostic accuracy of this new technique remains to be determined, but centers having the most experience with fine-needle aspiration 

10 BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT 

biopsy report diagnostic success rates of 70 to 80 percent for pancreatic carcinomas. Complications such as pneumothorax, pneumoperitoneum, bacteremia, hematoma formation, or metastatic implants in the needle tract appear to be infrequent. Percutaneous liver biopsy The standard percutaneous liver biopsy employs a rigid, 16- to 18gauge needle to obtain tissue core specimens by aspiration or by use of a split inner cannula. Liver biopsy is most useful in the jaundiced patient without dilated ducts to establish a diagnosis of intrahepatic cholestasis or acute or chronic hepatocellular disease. Although liver biopsy may be performed in patients with extrahepatic biliary obstruction (at somewhat higher risk), the diagnostic information obtained is usually quite limited when compared with other techniques now available, and the procedure is very rarely indicated in any patient having a demonstrably dilated biliary system. Contraindications include poor patient cooperation, uncorrectable coagulation defects, massive ascites, and the presence of infection in the potential path of the needle. Hemangiomas or other highly vascular neoplasms represent relative contraindications, and these lesions may be sampled better with fine-needle aspiration techniques. Complications are infrequent and include pain, pneumothorax, inadvertent biopsy of other abdominal organs, bile peritonitis, needle fracture, intrahepatic or subcapsular hematoma formation (about 7 percent), hemorrhage (0.2 percent), and, rarely, death. Percutaneous liver biopsy is of greatest clinical value in establishing a diagnosis of hepatocellular disease in jaundiced patients without evidence of mechanical biliary obstruction by ultrasound or cholangiography. 

Angiography The increasing use of several of the techniques described above has diminished the utility of selective angiography in the diagnosis of cholestasis. These procedures require highly trained personnel and sophisticated machinery, are time-consuming and expensive, and also involve the use of rather high doses of iodinated contrast material and radiation. Angiography tends to have a relatively low diagnostic yield in the elucidation of biliary tract obstruction in comparison with other techniques. Most 

biliary tract tumors are relatively hypovascular and are not readily detected by angiography. Selective or superselective angiographic studies may be useful in the diagnosis of space-occupying hepatic lesions—especially hepatocellular carcinoma and other primary liver neoplasms, hepatic metastases, cirrhosis and regenerative nodules, and cysts or abscesses of the liver. Angiography may also aid in determining the surgical resectability of pancreatic and hepatic tumors. The technique is usually contraindicated in patients with severe, uncontrollable coagulopathy and in those with hepatic and/or renal insufficiency. 

Intraarterial catheters may also be used for embolization therapy in hepatic hemorrhage or hemobilia, for embolic occlusion of the blood supply to hepatic tumors, and for selective delivery of chemotherapy in hepatic malignancy. Asa diagnostic tool in the investigation of cholestasis, angiography should probably be reserved for those patients in whom diagnoses of primary hepatic neoplasm or pancreatic carcinoma appear most likely, especially when the question of surgical resectability is raised. 

Laparoscopy (peritoneoscopy) Laparoscopy or peritoneoscopy is performed after air, carbon dioxide, or nitrous oxide insufflation of the abdomen. Under local or general anesthesia, a trocar is inserted through the anterior abdominal wall; then the peritoneoscope is introduced through the trocar sheath into the peritoneal cavity. The procedure is of greatest value in the evaluation of hepatic filling defects seen by scanning techniques, especially when it is combined with visually directed liver biopsy. The technique may also be useful in the detection of lymphoma or Hodgkin’s disease, in the evaluation of abdominal masses (excluding most pancreatic masses, which are difficult to visualize), and in the assessment of chronic liver disease. Cholangiography, by direct puncture of the gallbladder, has been performed through the peritoneoscope, but the risk of serious bile leakage has minimized this application. Relative contraindications include poor patient cooperation, massive obesity, tense ascites, uncorrectable coagulopathy, and prior abdominal surgery with extensive adhesions and scarring. In experienced hands, laparoscopy has a complication rate of

Biliary manometry Although still largely experimental, manometry of the common bile duct and Oddi sphincter shows promise as a diagnostic tool in the assessment of suspected papillary stenosis. Transpapillary manometry may be performed through the side-viewing duodenoscope as an adjunct to ERCP, using either an open-tip perfused system or a microsensor system. In the perfused system, the sensing catheter is used to cannulate the papilla of Vater and is then advanced into the bile duct, infused with water, and connected to a calibrated transducer-recorder. The choledochal and Oddi sphincter pressures are measured and compared with intraduodenal pressures obtained simultaneously by means of another catheter taped to the endoscope. Experience with the technique is so limited to date that its value to the clinician is not yet clear. Manometry has been advocated as potentially useful in the diagnosis of papillary stenosis and in evaluation of the adequacy of sphincterotomy. At present, however, endoscopic transpapillary pressure recording is probably best viewed as an experimental investigative technique. Similarly, intraoperative biliary manometry, biliary manometry in conjunction with PTHC, and manometry of the pancreatic duct are, for the most part, experimental. Choledochoscopy and_ cholangioscopy Operative choledochoscopy may be performed through a standard choledochotomy incision (usually without requiring concomitant duodenal mobilization) for intralumenal visualization of both the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts at the time of<sup>surgery.Arigidscopewith</sup> rod lens optics is less expensive and less fragile 

than more recently introduced flexible fiberoptic choledochoscopes; it also requires less skill to operate and probably gives endoscopic images of superior quality. This approach may be useful for the diagnosis of retained calculi in the common duct or intrahepatic biliary radicles and may permit extraction of stones under endoscopic visual control. Choledochoscopy may also allow identification of cholangitis, ampullary stenosis, biliary neoplasms (which may be biopsied and assessed for resectability), and parasites or foreign bodies lodged within the biliary tree. The major value of operative choledochoscopy is as an aid in the detection and removal of retained common duct stones at the time of initial surgery. The procedure may expedite routine common duct explorations and may obviate the need for subsequent duodenotomy or reoperation. Choledochoscopy is usually followed by operative cholangiography, the two procedures being complementary in the detection of biliary calculi. Postoperative fiberoptic cholangioscopy through a well-matured T-tube tract (currently experimental) may in the future prove to be a safe, rapid, accurate technique for detecting and aiding in the percutaneous extraction of retained biliary calculi. Endoscopic examination of the biliary tree has been performed in association with ERCP by passage of a thin fiberoptic cholangioscope (“‘babyscope’’) through the instrument channel of the side-viewing duodenoscope (‘‘motherscope’’) and into the common bile duct. Experience with retrograde cholangioscopy is extremely limited, and this experimental procedure has little practical value for clinical diagnosis at present. 

Diagnostic laparatomy Accurate, less invasive approaches to the investigation of cholestasis have steadily reduced the need for early surgical abdominal exploration as a purely diagnostic tool in the jaundiced patient. Given the appreciable risks of anesthesia and surgery in patients with advanced underlying hepatocellular damage, diagnostic laparotomy should rarely be necessary in jaundiced patients without mechanical biliary obstruction. However, laparotomy may be indicated in the presence of pronounced cholangitis, sepsis, perforation, or hemorrhage. Direct inspection of the underlying process at operation may save time, effort and expense in 

###### BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO 

patients requiring rapid, accurate diagnosis and therapy. Of course, laparotomy performed by an experienced surgeon may succeed diagnostically where all else has failed. Early surgical exploration may be the procedure of choice when mechanical obstruction has been identified, the clinical diagnosis seems probable or definite, and the therapeutic plan calls for operative intervention. Needless “stacking” of nonsurgical techniques should not be the goal in the jaundiced patient, nor should the clinician exhaust the available facilities (and the patient) indiscriminately and at great expense in order to avoid surgery. On the other hand, diagnostic laparotomy is usually reserved for patients with evidence of mechanical biliary obstruction in whom early surgical intervention is dictated by therapeutic considerations or by a lack of alternative options for diagnosis or therapy. DIAGNOSTIC STRATEGY IN THE JAUNDICED PATIENT 

The revolution in innovative technology that has occurred during the past 10 years has taken most of the guesswork out of the diagnosis of cholestasis, and has permitted expeditious diagnosis and early therapeutic intervention in the vast majority of patients presenting with jaundice. However, with the use of these new techniques it is possible to lose sight of the patient while threading the maze of available diagnostic alternatives. Needless selection of multiple diagnostic procedures providing redundant clinical information must be avoided. Moreover, the selection of optimal techniques may vary among institutions depending upon the availability of appropriate technology. The clinician should orchestrate the diagnostic strategy in order to reduce time, expense, and risk to the patient while obtaining the data that will permit the formulation of an educated therapeutic plan. In the patient with cholestasis, it is of primary importance to determine whether the cause of the jaundice is intrahepatic or extrahepatic. The first diagnostic question to be addressed, then, becomes “Is mechanical obstruction of the biliary tree present?” The diagnosis of severe hepatocellular inflammation or necrosis may become obvious at several points in the history, physical examination, or laboratory investiga- 

###### DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT 

tion, and it is usually confirmed by the presence of pronounced elevations of serum aminotransferase enzymes. In contrast, biochemical determinations indicating a primarily cholestatic process (elevations of serum alkaline phosphatase and/or 5'-nucleotidase without marked aminotransferase elevations) rarely allow confident differentiation between mechanical biliary obstruction and intrahepatic cholestasis. More diagnostic information is usually required to determine whether evidence for an obstructive process exists. The presence of dilated ducts indicative of mechanical biliary obstruction may be demonstrated by a number of noninvasive techniques, but ultrasonography probably represents the initial procedure of choice. If there are no demonstrably dilated ducts, percutaneous liver biopsy may then be indicated. However, when the clinical impression of biliary obstruction is firmly supported by the history, physical examination, or laboratory studies, the finding of nondilated ducts does not exclude the use of cholangiography as the next step. In fact, when the clinical diagnosis of obstruction seems obvious, a direct move to cholangiography rather than to ultrasonography may prove the most appropriate and expeditious way to make the diagnosis. Once the presence of mechanical biliary obstruction has been established, the next issue is to determine the site of the obstructive process. This requires a decision as to whether cholangiography is appropriate and, if so, which technique should be used. Cholangiograms, which provide an anatomic “‘road map” of the biliary tree, can be of considerable value in the subsequent formulation of a therapeutic plan for decompression and in deciding the best surgical approach should operative intervention be selected. In some patients with urgent indications for laparotomy (e.g., acute cholangitis with dilated ducts and calculi on ultrasound), and in occasional patients with clinically apparent diagnoses in whom surgical therapy may be selected at an early time (e.g., Courvoisier galibladder and obstruction secondary to obvious metastatic pancreatic cancer), cholangiography may not be necessary preoperatively. In most patients with mechanical biliary tract obstruction, however, accurate cholangiographic information about the site of the obstruction is of the utmost importance in making fur- 

DIAGNOSTIC STRATEGY IN THE JAUNDICED PATIENT /3 

ther diagnostic and therapeutic decisions. The increasing availability of fine-needle transhepatic cholangiography (PTHC) has led to the adoption of this technique in many centers as the cholangiographic method of choice in the jaundiced patient with dilated ducts. On the other hand, ERCP may be preferred (1) in patients without dilated ducts, (2) when there is clinically suspected gastroduodenal, ampullary, or pancreatic disease, (3) when PTHC is contraindicated or has failed, (4) in patients with prior 

biliary surgery, and (5) in those patients in whom endoscopic papillotomy for biliary calculi might be the prime therapeutic option. In some patients, especially when the site of obstruction is near the hilum of the liver, both PTHC and ERCP may be indicated. 

The third diagnostic issue is the need to establish the precise nature of the obstructing lesion localized by cholangiography. This involves a decision on whether further diagnostic data are necessary in order to formulate an appropriate

14 BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO DIAGNOS!S AND TREATMENT 

therapeutic plan. When nonsurgical intervention is areal therapeutic possibility, the clinician must gather sufficient information to decide between surgery and a nonsurgical alternative. An example would be a patient with obstruction at the level of the porta hepatis (a difficult candidate for surgical bypass) in whom the histologic demonstration of lymphoma or metastatic cancer in the hilar nodes by fine-needle or laparoscopic biopsy would make percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage together with radiation or chemotherapy attractive alternatives to operation. More extensive evaluation should also be made before deciding between attempted surgical resection and palliative bypass. For example, in a patient with biliary obstruction secondary to a mass in the head of the pancreas, histologic confirmation of malignancy (by ERCP, cytology, or percutaneous fine-needle aspiration biopsy) and evidence of probable resectability (by liver scan, CBT, ERCP, and/or angiography) may change the therapeutic plan from a palliative procedure to an attempt at surgical cure by subtotal or total pancreatectomy. 

In summary, the approach to diagnosis in the patient with cholestasis is based upon the selection of studies designed to answer three fundamental questions: (1) Is mechanical obstruction of the biliary tree present (usually best answered by ultrasound)? (2) If so, what is the site of obstruction (usually distinguished by transhepatic or endoscopic cholangiography)? (3) What is the cause and nature of the obstructing process (addressed preoperatively only if the answer is likely to substantially influence the therapeutic approach)? Figure 1 provides a clinical algorithm for the diagnostic approach to cholestatic jaundice. TREATMENT OF BILIARY OBSTRUCTION Nonsurgical techniques 

The introduction of innovative nonoperative techniques for manipulation of the biliary tree has substantially changed the clinical approach to the therapy of biliary obstruction when the risk of surgical intervention is unacceptably high or when the underlying obstructing process is unresectable malignancy or retained calculi fol- 

lowing biliary exploration. In the latter case, percutaneous T-tube stone extraction is an approach with a very low risk in comparison with reoperation for the removal of retained stones, which is associated with a relatively high morbidity rate. Endoscopic sphincterotomy and stone extraction may have substantial advantages over surgical intervention in several clinical settings. Percutaneous insertion of permanent or semipermanent transhepatic biliary drainage catheters may be indicated in some obstructed patients in order to obtain nonsurgical or preoperative palliation. Recent innovations in the radiotherapy and chemotherapy of neoplastic biliary obstructions have extended the palliative role of percutaneous drainage. The use of these and other nonsurgical techniques in the therapeutic approach to patients with mechanical obstruction of the biliary tract is discussed below. 

Antibiotics and general supportive measures Selection and timing of therapeutic interventions for the correction of biliary obstruction are usually dependent upon the clinical state of the patient. Careful attention to supportive care may be the determining factor in deciding whether to proceed with operative or nonsurgical intervention. Prophylactic antibiotics (usually ampicillin or an aminoglycoside plus ampicillin or chloromycetin plus ampicillin) should be routinely administered prior to any diagnostic or therapeutic manipulations of the obstructed biliary tract, since cholangitis or bacteremia represent major potential complications of most interventions. Once obstruction is identified, the condition should be managed promptly and vigorously with antibiotics, volume replacement, and either surgical or percutaneous transhepatic biliary decompression. Impairments of renal function and deficits of water and extracellular fluid volume should be diligently corrected, and appropriate electrolyte balance should be maintained. Adequate nutritional support is essential, and particular attention should be paid to patients with chronic externally draining fistulas or long-term external biliary drainage catheters. Special care and monitoring in the replacement of calories, water, and electrolytes may be required in this setting. Supplementation of the fat-soluble vitamins may be necessary; parenteral vitamin K administration may prove advis- 

###### TREATMENT OF BILIARY OBSTRUCTION 15 

Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage This technique requires passage of a large (15-cm-long, 18-gauge) cannula sheath under fluoroscopic guidance into the bile ducts following PTHC. A specially modified angiographic guidewire may then be introduced and maneuvered up to or through an area of ductal stricture followed by the insertion over the guidewire of a tapered tip catheter with multiple side holes into the obstructed system for decompression. The catheter tip is advanced through the ampulla of Vater if possible; the side holes are positioned above and below the stricture to allow internal stent drainage of bile into the duodenum. If the guidewire or catheter cannot be advanced through the obstruction, a shorter, larger-bore catheter may be positioned above the strictured area for external drainage. Smaller (22- to 23gauge) cannula sheaths may also be used for percutaneous transhepatic drainage, but the site, orientation, and caliber of the punctured duct may not allow favorable positioning of these catheters; the caliber of the small sheaths is usually inadequate to admit insertion of appropriately cited guidewires for convenient catheter exchange. The drainage catheter is sutured to the skin and allowed to drain externally to gravity for 3 to 4 days while there is monitoring for catheter patency and procedural complications. If an internally draining catheter has been placed, it may then be clamped so that bile flow is directed into the duodenum. Contraindications for this procedure are similar to those for PTHC. nasogastric tube, may be considered in patients able in an effort to correct coagulopathy. An attempt at bile refeeding, orally or through a on chronic external biliary drainage in order to replete bile salts and limit the severity of steatorrhea. 

The complication rate of this technique is appreciable, but relatively modest considering the condition of the patients in whom the procedure is usually employed and the size of the cannula sheath inserted. Major complications have been reported in about 5 percent of patients; the long-term complication rates are approximately 25 percent. Complications include cholangitis, hyponatremia or acidosis, hemorrhage, bile peritonitis, catheter occlusion or dislodgment, and retrograde drainage of duodenal contents (which 

in some instances may limit the use of the technique for internal drainage). Recurrent cholangitis occurs in about 15 to 25 percent of patients with long-term drainage, but many of the cholangitic complications are correctable by replacement of a displaced or occluded catheter. This exchange may be accomplished, in most cases, on an outpatient basis. Using the large cannula sheath technique, successful percutaneous catheter drainage has been reported in about 90 percent of cases. Percutaneous biliary drainage is probably of greatest value for short-term or long-term palliation of biliary stricture from inoperable malignancy or for palliation of failed billary-enteric anastomoses. It may also be useful for preoperative decompression of patients with suppurative cholangitis or pronounced cholestasis in whom early operative intervention is associated with an especially high risk. The technique allows performance of serial cholangiograms to assess results of radiation or chemotherapy in cases of malignancy; it also permits the sampling of bile for cytology and culture. In addition, the left hepatic ductal system may be drained separately or in conjunction with decompression of the right-sided biliary tree. Externally draining catheters have been advanced successfully into the duodenum for more satisfactory long-term internal drainage after a period of limited external decompression. In some instances, irradiation and chemotherapy may cause enough tumor regression to allow discontinuation of palliative catheter drainage. Rarely, the technique may be used to dilate benign postOperative strictures (using a balloon-type catheter) or to allow percutaneous stone extraction (after maturation and dilatation of the transparenchymal tract). Experience with percutaneous biliary drainage has not been extensive. At present,’ the technique should be limited to selected patients with inoperable malignancies or failed operative decompressions and to obstructed patients with suppurative cholangitis in whom the surgical risk dictates delay of operative intervention. 

Percutaneous stone extraction Five to six weeks or more after common duct exploration, the matured T-tube sinus tract may be used for percutaneous extraction of retained stones by 

16 BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT 

specially designed steerable catheters, extraction forceps, or basket catheters. After removal of the T tube, the remaining sinus tract may be progressively dilated over a guidewire in order to introduce the steerable biliary catheter. Contrast is then injected and the retained calculi are localized cholangiographically. Under fluoroscopic guidance, the steerable catheter is positioned so that its tip lies just distal to the stone to be extracted. The stone basket may then be introduced through this catheter system, guided to a point distal to the stone, and the basket opened as the catheter is slowly withdrawn in an effort to capture the stone and allow its extraction through the sinus tract. Large calculi measuring 1 cm or more usually require fragmentation by forceps, modified ultrasonic “‘drills,” or the basket itself. Piecemeal extraction of large remnants may then be attempted, with the hope that smaller fragments will pass into the duodenum. Calculi impacted at the most distal end of the common duct may require the use of tilt tables, balloon catheters, suction catheters, saline injections, or other maneuvers to bring them into a more favorable location for basket extraction. Calculi may also be extracted from major intrahepatic radicles, especially if they can be maneuvered into the extrahepatic biliary tree before removal is attempted. Percutaneous cholangioscopy has been performed through the matured T-tube sinus tract to aid in stone extraction, but experience with this technique is still limited. Recently reported experimental techniques include the use of matured, dilated percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage tracts for stone extraction, and even the basket crushing of calculi at the time of diagnostic transhepatic cholangiography. In centers with the most experience, the success rate for percutaneous stone extraction through the T-tube tract has approached 95 percent, with the remainder requiring endoscopic papillotomy or reoperation. The failure rate is increased when there has been operative placement of small-caliber T tubes (No. 12 French or smaller), when T tubes are brought out through midline incisions rather than through right flank stab wounds (the shortest possible extraction route), and when large or multiple calculi are present. In the absence of clinical indications for more rapid therapeutic intervention, however, 

multiple inpatient or outpatient sessions may be used over a period of weeks to achieve complete stone extraction with this technique. The major relative contraindication to percutaneous stone extraction is a T-tube tract which is “immature” or of inadequate caliber. Complications have been reported in about 5 percent of patients. The most frequent complications include fever, sepsis, pancreatitis, hemorrhage from the T-tube tract, vasovagal reactions, and perforation (of sinus tract or bile ducts). Complications requiring operative intervention for correction or resulting in death appear to be rare. This percutaneous extraction technique has emerged as the therapeutic procedure of choice in patients with retained calculi following common duct exploration who posses mature T-tube tracts that may be dilated to a diameter adequate for the stones to be extracted. The major disadvantage is the 5 to 6 week delay necessary for T- tube sinus tract maturation. Since endoscopic sphincterotomy (discussed below) may often be performed successfully in cases where early stone extraction is necessary or where the percutaneous technique has failed, it should be possible to avoid reoperation in the vast majority of patients with retained calculi after biliary surgery. 

Endoscopic sphincterotomy (papillotomy) Endoscopic sphincterotomy has become a therapeutic alternative to surgical intervention in three major clinical settings: (1) in patients with residual common bile duct stones after cholecystectomy, (2) in patients with choledocholithiasis (especially with complete biliary obstruction), in whom underlying diseases or complications make the risk of operative decompression unacceptably high, and (3) in patients with benign papillary stenosis, in whom successful papillotomy may be an alternative to surgical sphincteroplasty. Sphincterotomy is an option in patients with retained stones following common duct exploration in whom T-tube tract stone extraction is unavailable, contraindicated, or has failed. The papillotome may be used rarely to create permanent or semipermanent biliaryenteric fistulas as a palliative maneuver in poor risk or unresectable patients with ampullary carcinoma. Other relative contraindications are the same as those for ERCP. In experienced hands, endoscopic sphincterotomy has a success rate of about 90 percent (stones pass spontaneously after papillotomy in over 60 percent and may be successfully extracted by basket or balloon catheter in an additional 30 percent). Complications, including bleeding, cholangitis (prophylactic antibiotics should be administered in obstructed patients), pancreatitis, and perforation, occur in 7 to 9 percent of patients. A mortality rate of 1 percent is reported. Late complications and restenosis of the papilla are rare. 

Dissolution of biliary stones Solvent infusion through T tubes or biliary drainage catheters has been attempted with a variety of techniques in an effort to dissolve retained stones or promote their fragmentation. The nonspecific flushing action of the infusion may result in passage of smaller stones into the duodenum; in fact, saline infusions alone may be effective in up to 50 percent of cases with “gravel” or small retained stones. Nitrites, anticholinergics, bile salts, or other drugs have been given orally in association with the infusions in order to relax the sphincter of Oddi, promote choleresis, and facilitate stone passage. The efficacy of this pharmacologic approach is still unclear. To date, a variety of agents have been used in an effort to dissolve ductal stones, including solutions of ether, chloroform, bile salts (especially sodium cholate), heparinized saline, or medium-chain monoglycerides. Although some of these agents may indeed promote fragmentation or dissolution of cholesterol stones, much of their effectiveness may be secondary to nonspecific flushing. Major side effects for the various infusates have included abdominal pain, diarrhea (with bile salt infusion), cholangitis, sepsis, and pancreatitis. Biliary pressure should be continuously monitored during infusion and should not be allowed to exceed 25 to 30 cmH.,O because of the danger of producing cholangitis, bacteremia, and hepatocellular damage. The development of abdominal pain usually indicates flow obstruction or cholangitis, and the infusion should be stopped immediately if pain or fever supervene. In view of the potentially serious nature of the complications with use of current methods 

18 BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT 

for stone dissolution, this approach is still largely experimental. Solvent infusion should probably be attempted only if efforts at percutaneous and endoscopic stone extraction have failed in a poor-risk patient with retained calculi. In that setting, infusion of sterile solutions of 150 to 200 mM sodium cholate or of glyceryl-L-monooctanoate (monooctanoin) at rates of 3 to 30 ml/h may be attempted over a 1- to 3-week trial period with continuous biliary pressure monitoring and serial cholangiography. Although oral treatment with chenodeoxycholic or ursodeoxycholic acid over periods of 6 months or more may be effective for the dissolution of nonradiopaque gallstones, the use of these bile salts is not appropriate in the treatment of choledocholithiasis. 

Radiation and chemotherapy of malignancy Radiation and chemotherapy have permitted successful nonsurgical palliative therapy in patients with unresectable primary tumors of the bile ducts or liver and in some patients with cancer metastatic to the porta hepatis, in whom jaundice may result from involvement of strategically placed lymph nodes rather than from end-stage hepatic replacement by tumor. These therapeutic approaches have been successfully combined with ductal decompression by longterm internally or externally draining biliary stents. In the presence of obstruction secondary to lymphomatous involvement or metastatic disease in the porta hepatis, radiation and chemotherapy may be preferable to surgery, which may prove difficult or impossible. Carcinomas of the biliary tract have been demonstrated to have greater radioresponsiveness than previously believed, and intraoperative radiation or external beam delivery of high-dose shrinkage-field radiation to demarcated, unresectable lesions may allow good local control. Chemotherapeutic agents administered systematically or through indwelling highly selective intraarterial catheters appear to have greatest therapeutic efficacy in biliary obstruction secondary to Hodgkin’s disease, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, or metastatic carcinoma arising in the breast or occasionally in other sites. Chemotherapy is probably somewhat less effective in the control of obstructing hepatocellular, pancreatic, ampullary, duodenal, or metastatic colonic or squamous bronchogenic carcinomas. Although evidence supporting the 

routine use of combined radiotherapeutic and chemotherapeutic approaches is at present inconclusive, a palliative combined therapeutic trial in conjunction with percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage or surgical decompressive bypass should probably be considered as a treatment option in any patient with mechanical biliary obstruction from unresectable malignant disease. 

###### Newer surgical techniques 

Despite the increasing availability of nonsurgical procedures for biliary drainage, stone extraction, and antitumor therapy, the majority of patients presenting with biliary obstruction are still most appropriately treated with surgical decompression. A potential disadvantage of nonsurgical therapy in obstructed patients is the possibility that these interventions (or their complications) may make subsequent definitive surgical correction of the problem more difficult. This caveat applies especially to preoperative percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage, which may cause friability of the ducts and sufficient decrease in their caliber to make a subsequent intrahepatic biliary-enteric anastomosis quite difficult. An important objective is to plan definitive surgery asa one-stage rather than a two-stage procedure if possible. The “standard” techniques for correcting obstructions of the biliary tree at the level of the common bile duct (distal to the cystic duct takeoff) are listed in Table 4. The choice of the most appropriate biliary-enteric bypass procedure may vary with the nature and location of the obstructing process, the local anatomy, the effects of prior surgery, and the experience and/or preference of the operating surgeon. However, patients obstructed higher in the biliary tree, especially in the hepatic hilum, present more formidable problems in surgical management. The introduction of newer operative procedures for dealing with high bile duct strictures or tumors has allowed a more aggressive surgical approach to decompression, drainage, and resection of neoplasms in patients obstructed at this level. These newer surgical techniques are briefiy discussed below. 

Hepatocholangioenterostomy If the obstructing lesion lies too high in the biliary tree to 

TREATMENT OF BILIARY OBSTRUCTION /9 

allow enteric anastomosis with extrahepatic duct remnants, intrahepatic ducts of sufficient caliber for surgical anastomosis can often be found by entering the substance of the liver. A variety of techniques has been described, including (1) an infrahepatic approach with dissection along the hilum of the liver above the ductal bifurcation; (2) a transhepatic technique, in which the hilum is approached by splitting the liver vertically in the plane between its right and left lobes to reach the common hepatic duct and bifurcation; (3) the Longmire procedure, in which the left hepatic lobe is partially amputated and the dilated stump of the left hepatic duct is identified and anastomosed to a loop of jejunum; and (4) the Bismuth procedure, which involves the identification and anastomosis of the duct draining the anterior segment of the left hepatic lobe (segment III) toa Roux-en-Y jejunal loop. As a last resort, when alternative ducts cannot be located, hepatojejunostomy may be performed, in which an open-ended Roux loop is anastomosed directly to the region of the liver hilum. Mucosa-tomucosa biliary-enteric anastomoses are definitely preferred. If this is impossible to achieve, a mucosal grafting technique may be used, with a fine-gauge perforated balloon-tipped catheter passed through the liver substance so as to exit from a bile duct and then inserted through a puncture wound in a loop of jejunum. The balloon is inflated and the jejunal mucosal graft is drawn tightly up to the bile duct and held in place by traction on the balloon catheter, which is secured, and the anastomosis is accomplished without mucosa-to-mucosa suturing. The Bismuth cholangioenteric anastomosis has the advantage of being the easiest surgical procedure for palliation of obstructing hilar carcinomas, and although the segment III duct drains only approximately 30 percent of the liver, this is often sufficient for adequate palliation. If possible, the choice of operation should be made on the basis of prior cholangiography. At the time of surgical exploration, the largest available ducts are usually used to make the anastomosis with a view toward accurate mucosa-to-mucosa apposition, relief of tension on the anastomosis, and the possible use of a transanastomotic stent. Given the small caliber of duct used, any of these techniques may result in inadequate drainage despite a technically successful anastomosis. For this reason, the surgical approach to biliary ob-struction in or near the hilum must be compared with anticipated results from percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage. Hepatocholangioenterostomy is preferable to nonsurgical drainage in patients with benign disease and minimal scarring from secondary or primary biliary cirrhosis (so that intrahepatic ducts are well dilated) and in patients in whom surgical resectability or longterm palliation are possibilities. 

Operative biliary stents Transanastomotic catheters, placed at the time of operation, may prevent stricture formation or bile leakage at the anastomosis and allow convenient performance of postoperative cholangiography. The routine use of operative stents is particularly important in settings where mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis has proved impossible, as in the mucosal graft technique. Lengths of polyethylene, latex, or silastic tubing of appropriate caliber may be brought out through the jejunum and abdominal wall or transhepatically through tunnels in the liver parenchyma. Some biliary stents, such as 

20 BILIARY OBSTRUCTION: CURRENT APPROACHES TO DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT 

the U tube (where the proximal end of the stent is brought out through the liver and the distal end through jejunum and abdominal wall), permit convenient exchange with new tubes under fluoroscopic guidance and are suitable for longterm palliative drainage in patients with unresectable malignant obstructions in the liver hilum. This, however, is now equally true of percutaneous transhepatic catheters placed radiographically, which may be inserted and maintained with a lower morbidity rate than is the case with the U tube. Short unanchored internal stents may pass prematurely or may obstruct completely and have very little application in biliary surgery. Temporary stents are usually removed 2 to 6 weeks following surgery if cholangiography shows free flow across the anastomosis without leakage of contrast material. The decision when to remove the tube will vary depending on the indication for anastomosis, the size of the anastomosis, the presence or absence of infection, and the “reactivity” (tendency for scar formation) of the stent material employed. Both short- and long-term biliary drainage tubes require regular irrigation and careful attention to catheter care, but this may be accomplished successfully on an outpatient basis in most cases. Appropriate selection and management of operative biliary stents are important factors in the success or failure of a difficult cholangioenteric anastomosis. TREATMENT STRATEGY IN PATIENTS WITH BILIARY OBSTRUCTION 

When a diagnosis of jaundice secondary to obstruction of the biliary tree has been established, an appropriate course of action must be outlined for decompression and drainage of the obstructed system and, if possible, for specific treatment of the underlying obstructive process. In selecting a treatment plan, consideration should be given to the availability, risk, and expense of each therapeutic option, as well as to the existing expertise in the institution. If the patient risk is acceptable and appropriately experienced personnel are available, a single definitive procedure is usually preferred over multiple interventions. An “educated” approach, based 

upon firm diagnostic information, will usually lead to the most effective therapy. 

First, the clinician must determine the most appropriate therapeutic intervention for correction of the obstructing process. This usually involves a choice between a specific surgical technique and a nonsurgical alternative. Since most patients with obstructed bile ducts are best managed surgically, a decision against operative intervention should be based upon specific diagnostic information including the risks of surgical intervention. In patients with cholangiographic evidence of obstruction distal to the cystic duct takeoff, surgical correction with common duct exploration and stone removal, palliative biliaryenteric bypass, sphincteroplasty, or an alternative procedure is often technically feasible but is not always the therapeutic approach of choice. General supportive care, antibiotics, steroids, or specific medical drug therapy may prove sufficient in carefully selected patients with intermittent biliary obstruction. Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage may be appropriate for temporary preoperative decompression of obstructed patients at high surgical risk and for longer-term palliation of failed biliary-enteric bypass or inoperable malignancy. Currently, retained common duct stones following biliary surgery should be managed with endoscopic papillotomy or with percutaneous T-tube extraction. Endoscopic sphincterotomy can be the most appropriate and effective technique for stone extraction in the desperately ill or very elderly patient with choledocholithiasis and an_ intact gallbladder and occasionally in the treatment of suspected stenosis of the papilla of Vater. In the case of ampullary, pancreatic, or common duct malignancy, preoperative evaluation for specific diagnosis and estimation of surgical resectability may be appropriate, since ideally the patient would require special preparation for pancreatoduodenectomy or total pancreatectomy by a surgeon experienced with these techniques if resection for cure were attempted. Unresectable malignancies with obstruction below the cystic duct takeoff usually are best managed surgically, by use of one of the biliary-enteric anastomoses listed in Table 4. bile ducts in the region of the porta hepatis are The problems raised by obstruction of the 

TREATMENT STRATEGY IN PATIENTS WITH BILIARY OBSTRUCTION P| 

quite distinct. Obstruction at this level is usually a consequence of malignancy—lymphoma or carcinoma metastatic to hilar nodes, primary bile duct carcinoma, or hepatocellular carcinoma with spread down into the ducts. Occasionally, sclerosing cholangitis may give a similar picture of proximal obstruction. In such cases, a special effort to visualize the left hepatic ductal system by selective PTHC may be appropriate in order to evaluate the potential role of a Bismuth or a Longmire procedure, since conventional biliary bypass operations are usually not feasible. If possible, a biopsy diagnosis of the obstructing process should be obtained before deciding upon a therapeutic plan. Unresectable malignancy in this region, especially lymphoma or metastatic disease involving the hilar nodes, is often best managed nonsurgically with radiation and/or 

chemotherapy plus either percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage or surgical decompression. Hepatocholangioenteric anastomosis may be indicated in appropriate patients in whom resection of the obstructing process has been attempted or who require long-term palliation. Once a specific therapeutic approach has been selected, it is necessary to identify the optimal time of intervention. Poor-risk patients may be managed with antibiotics and temporary percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage prior to ‘“‘definitive” surgery. Delays in surgery may also be indicated in the face of acute pancreatitis, serious deficits in extracellular fluid volume, coagulation, nutrition, or electrolyte balance or other supervening severe medical problems. astomosis, pancreatoduodenectomy, total pancreatectomy, endoscopic sphincterotomy, or percutaneous stone removal), extensive diagnostic evaluation and preoperative transfer of the patient to an institution having more experience with these procedures may be in order. The timing of definitive therapy should depend on the clinical condition of the patient, the presence of sufficient diagnostic information to form a specific therapeutic plan, and the availability of the appropriate technical expertise to carry out that plan. 

In summary, treatment of the patient with biliary obstruction ideally involves a single, definitive procedure performed at an optimal time. In patients with obstruction at the level of the common bile duct, below the cystic duct takeoff, this procedure should most often be surgical, although nonsurgical alternatives may be preferred in special situations. Patients obstructed more proximally, at the level of the porta hepatis, usually have lesions that are less amenable to definitive surgical ‘correction and often require careful evaluation before an appropriate treatment plan can be selected. Figure 2 provides a clinical algorithm for the therapeutic approach to biliary obstruction.
