#### REFLUX DISEASE DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT OF GASTROESOPHAGEAL 

###### SIDNEY COHEN 

Gastroesophageal reflux disease is characterized by heartburn and the sequelae of esophagitis, esophageal ulceration, or stricture. It is the most common clinical esophageal disorder, but its prevalence cannot be determined exactly. Most persons have experienced heartburn at one time, and asymptomatic reflux has been observed. Physiologic reflux of acid is seen in most asymptomatic persons during prolonged pH recordings. In clinical practice, it is important to recognize the clinical conditions under which gastroesophageal reflux may occur, the sequelae of reflux, and the appropriate management of reflux and each of its associated complications. 

###### PATHOGENESIS 

Gastroesophageal reflux disease is due to an incompetence of the physiologic lower esophageal sphincter (LES). The etiology of LES incompetence varies according to the different conditions that cause gastroesophageal reflux. Table 1 lists the disorders in which LES incompetence and gastroesophageal reflux are seen. The pathogenesis of each disorder will be discussed separately. 

###### Idiopathic lower esophageal sphincter incompetence 

Idiopathic gastroesophageal reflux is the most common category of LES incompetence. It is considered to be a primary sphincteric abnormality. Initially, it was felt that idiopathic LES incompetence was due to the presence of a sliding hiatus hernia. However, several experimental and clinical observations indicate that hiatus her- 

nia does not cause gastroesophageal reflux. First, the presence of a hiatus hernia does not alter LES pressure. Second, there is a poor correlation between the presence of a hernia and the symptoms attributed to the hernia. Third, studies in laboratory animals show that gastroesophageal competence depends on the intrinsic tone of the LES and not on its location above or below the diaphragm. 

A reduced LES pressure has been found in most patients with clinical evidence of reflux or heartburn. Normal LES pressure is 15 to 30 mmHg; this pressure was reduced to below 10 mmHg in 80 to 100 percent of patients in various series. It is possible that the reduction of LES pressure is intermittent and not present at all times. Other mechanisms of gastroesophageal competence have been proposed but have not withstood critical evaluation. The LES in human beings is under complex neurohumoral regulation which varies extensively during any given 24-h period. Sphincter pressure is increased by the cholinergic and alpha-adrenergic neural system, as well as by serotonin, prostaglandin F,,, motilin, substance P, histamine, and pancreatic polypeptide. LES pressure is decreased by beta-adrenergic agents,

###### REFLUX DISEASE 

secretin, cholecystokinin, gastric inhibitory peptide, vasoactive intestinal peptide, dopamine, prostaglandin E, and E,, cyclic nucleotides, glucagon, and opiates. It is possible that these substances are involved in the spontaneous fluctuations in LES pressure and that these pressure fluctuations lead to episodic reflux. Gastroesophageal reflux appears to be closely controlled by LES pressure. The volume of the gastric contents acts as a stress or force tending to produce reflux at each pressure level. Patients with the lowest LES pressure will have reflux with small gastric volumes, whereas patients with higher LES pressures will reflux only with greater volumes of gastric contents. Some normal individuals may also reflux in association with high volumes. Thus, the presence of reflux symptoms is dependent upon (1) the LES pressure and (2) the stress (e.g., gastric volume of gastric acid load) placed on the sphincter. The sphincter is the barrier to reflux and is an accurate indicator of gastroesophageal competence when measured with an infused open-tipped catheter system. Three abnormalities in LES function have been observed: (1) basal LES incompetence, (2) diminished LES responsiveness to increases in intraabdominal pressure, and (3) decreased LES pressure changes during feeding. Basal LES incompetence has been attributed to an abnormality in the length-tension properties of LES circular muscle. The LES circular muscle has characteristic myogenic properties in vitro. It develops greater tension and force with lesser degrees of stretch than the adjacent esophagus. In patients with LES incompetence, the LES pressure in response to stretch is reduced. The cause of this abnormal myogenic function is not known, although it is generally accepted that the mechanical properties of LES muscle determine its basal sphincteric or tonic pressure characteristics. An abnormality in this function would thus lead to a decreased pressure. A decrease in excitatory factors or an increase in inhibitory factors acting on the LES may also lead to sphincter incompetence. Decreased fasting serum gastrin levels have been reported in patients with reflux, but this finding has not been consistent. In general, there is a poor correlation between serum gastrin levels and basal LES pressure. The role of gastrin in basal LES pres- 

sure and in LES incompetence is controversial, but most data suggest that it has some, although perhaps not a major, physiological role in LES pressure. Other inhibitory factors may be important but have not yet been measured. Recent work with animals suggests that prostaglandins released from the damaged esophageal mucosa in esophagitis may also contribute to LES incompetence. 

Regardless of the cause, an incompetent LES fails to respond normally to increased intraabdominal pressure. In healthy individuals, an increase in intraabdominal pressure leads to an even greater increase in LES pressure via a neural mechanism. When there is LES incompetence, the LES pressure response is less than the change in gastric pressure, leading to enhanced reflux. Thus this phenomenon leads to reflux in patients when they wear tight garments, perform physical activity, or experience gastric distention or gastric contraction. Patients with idiopathic LES incompetence show a reduced sphincter response to a meal stimulus, perhaps as a result of reduced release of gastrin. It is noteworthy that an incompetent LES retains its ability to respond to further inhibitory stimuli. Thus, cholecystokinin release following a fatty meal will further reduce pressure. 

It is evident that the LES is a dynamic muscular structure with intrinsic myogenic properties and is also responsive to numerous neural and humoral factors. The pressure fluctuates in response to these factors, leading to intermittent periods of reflux after the ingestion of certain foods or following other unexplained stresses. Reflux is therefore a dynamic disorder that must be viewed in relation to the unique physical and neurohumoral factors in each patient. Clinical episodes of reflux are most common (1) in the basal state when the patient is recumbent, (2) after the patient eats, when there is an increased gastric volume with an inadequate increase in LES pressure, and (3) following exercise or increased exertion, when intraabdominal pressure acts upon a poorly functioning LES. 

###### Pregnancy 

From 30 to 50 percent of pregnant women experience heartburn, usually during the third trimester. It was previously thought that the fetus and

Women taking sequential oral contraceptives have reduced LES tone, and such changes can also be induced in animals who are given estrogen and progesterone. In vitro studies on LES muscle strips indicate that estrogen, progesterone, or both impair LES responsiveness to neurohumoral stimuli. These data indicate that LES muscle changes during pregnancy probably reflect a generalized smooth-muscle response to female hormones. However, there is also an abnormal LES responsiveness to neurohumoral agents during pregnancy as early as the first trimester. is now recognized that women with heartburn during pregnancy have a reduced LES pressure its membranes produced an increase in intraabdominal pressure, causing reflux. However, it which returns to normal after delivery. This reversible LES incompetence is most likely due to changes in levels of female hormones acting on the esophageal smooth muscle. 

###### Chalasia of infancy 

Infants regurgitate easily and show appreciable gastroesophageal reflux. This reflux is believed to be developmental, and clinical observations of infants indicate that easy regurgitation gradually diminishes with growth. In normal infants, the LES pressure measurement has been shown to be within the broad range of normal adult levels. Reduced levels have been demonstrated only in infants with reflux. The LES in infants responds to cholinergic drugs, which are sometimes used as temporary therapy. Gastroesophageal reflux has been implicated in some cases of sudden infant death syndrome. Progressive systemic sclerosis and other collagen vascular diseases 

The esophagus is involved in about 75 percent of patients with systemic sclerosis. The characteristic manometric changes consist of marked diminution in peristaltic force in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus, together with a reduction in LES pressure. Initially<sup>theperistalticforcesare</sup> reduced, and then the<sup>changesprogressto a total</sup> loss of distal esophageal<sup>functionandamarkedly</sup> 

incompetent LES (pressures below 5 mmHg). The combination of severe gastroesophageal reflux and inability of the esophagus to propel refluxed material back into the stomach leads to progressive esophagitis. Thus, stricture formation occurs in about 40 percent of patients. The esophageal manometric changes and Raynaud’s phenomena may precede by several years the characteristic skin changes of systemic sclerosis. The manometric findings described above are rare in systemic lupus erythematosus, idiopathic Raynaud’s disease, and dermatomyositis. 

Esophageal dysfunction occurs in about 75 percent of patients with mixed connective tissue disease who demonstrate specific antibodies to an extractable nuclear antigen. It is noteworthy that virtually all patients with esophageal dysfunction associated with a collagen vascular disorder have Raynaud’s phenomena. The pathophysiology of esophageal disease has been studied only in systemic sclerosis. Portions of the esophagus with abnormal peristaltic or LES function may have histologically normal muscle when examined at autopsy. The prominent abnormality consists of patchy areas of smooth-muscle atrophy with fibrosis. The finding of abnormal motor function in areas of intact smooth muscle suggests that atrophy is probably a late stage of this disorder. Other studies support this concept. In the duodenum of patients with systemic sclerosis, intestinal slow waves (a function of smooth muscle) remain intact despite evidence of abnormal cholinergic reflexes of distention and gross dilation on x-ray. Other esophageal studies show that in patients with systemic sclerosis, the LES responsiveness to cholinergic drugs that act directly on the muscle remains intact. The responsiveness to cholinesterase inhibitors and gastrin is impaired in all patients. In advanced or long-standing disease, the response to cholinergic drugs is also lost, which suggests a later stage of smooth-muscle atrophy. These studies indicate a probably similar pathogenetic mechanism in the esophagus and other gastrointestinal smooth-muscle viscera. The lesion may be initially a neural, cholinergic disorder that later progresses to muscle atrophy and fibrosis. The latter changes possibly result from ischemia, since Raynaud’s phenomena and gastrointestinal dysfunction are so closely associated. 

26 DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT OF GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE 

###### Miscellaneous causes 

Gastroestophageal reflux occurs in association with several other clinical conditions. Drugs such as anticholinergics, nitrites, beta-adrenergic agents, and some tranquilizers reduce LES pressure. Postoperative reflux is common after esophagogastrectomy for malignancies and Heller myotomy for achalasia. Hypothyroidism results in a diminished LES pressure and peristaltic force due to direct effects on smooth muscle. 

###### CLINICAL SEQUELAE OF GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX 

In most individuals with gastroesophageal reflux, the presence of reflux itself does not lead to any serious sequelae. In a small number of patients with reflux, esophagitis with hemorrhage, peptic stricture, or ulcer develops as a serious complication. It is difficult to predict which patients will

Initially one finds morphologic alterations in the esophageal mucosa that consist of a thinning of the squamous epithelium surface and an increase in the basilar cell layer. These changes are felt to be diagnostic of reflux. They are not truly inflammatory and are usually not recognizable by endoscopic examination. The next change consists of polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration and mucosal edema with ulceration; this is associated with endoscopic evidence of friability, edema, and punctate mucosal ulceration. The ulcerations may then become linear, extending for several centimeters, and are associated with mucosal granularity and exudation. Finally, the mucosa becomes chronically ulcerated and has a pale grayish appearance. Esophagitis may be associated with bleeding and accounts for the cause of hemorrhage in about 3 to 5 percent of patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding. 

In some patients with reflux, a single large esophageal peptic ulcer may be present (Fig. 1). The ulcer is usually difficult to heal and may lead to stricture formation. In many cases, the ulcer occurs in an area of Barrett’s epithelium (discussed below) and is thus surrounded by relatively normal appearing mucosa. 

Peptic stricture of the esophagus is one of the most serious complications of reflux disease. It is generally seen in patients with long-standing disease who are older than patients who only have esophagitis. However, generalizations cannot be made since strictures may also develop rapidly in younger patients. Strictures are especially common in patients with underlying motility disorders, either nonspecific or secondary to collagen vascular disease. 

Nonspecific changes in esophageal peristalsis are seen in patients with reflux and esophagitis. These mobility changes, consisting of simulta-

A further complication of chronic reflux is the development of Barrett's epithelium—a transitional columnar type of epithelium that involves the distal and middle esophagus and represents a metaplastic response to inflammation (Fig. 2). Stratification of Barrett’s epithelium at various layers has been demonstrated. Most distally, the mucosa is gastric in type and contains parietal and chief cells, whereas proximally the cellular morphology more closely resembles that of the small intestine with mucus glands and a villiform surface. Barrett’s epithelium is precancerous, leading to adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. Barrett’s epithelium occurs in about 10 percent of patients with chronic reflux symptoms. Approximately 5 to 10 percent of this group will develop adenocarcinoma.

###### DIAGNOSIS 

The diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease has become a confusing and controversial area. Numerous tests have been devised to evaluate the reflux, either directly or indirectly. Many of these tests are accurate and sensitive and give valuable clinical information; others are either inaccurate, insensitive, or fail to give meaningful data. Certain tests of limited value have been utilized beyond their capabilities. 

Tests to assess gastroesophageal reflux disease must be considered in terms of the information that they can provide. They can be considered in four major categories. In Table 2, the tests are grouped according to their clinical indicators. Thus, it is important to consider the specific indication for a given study before determining its usefulness. A major error in discussing this field is the tendency to judge a test as good or bad without defining its specific purpose. For

###### Measurement of gastroesophageal reflux 

Specific tests have been designed to measure gastroesophageal reflux in order to establish the diagnosis. The most frequently used test is the PH study. A pH probe is placed in the esophagus, 5 cm above the LES. The study is performed under basal conditions and during the infusion of 300 ml 0.1 N HCl into the stomach. Under basal conditions, a decrease in pH below 3 indicates reflux of acid into the esophagus; in symptomatic patients, a positive result is found in only about 20 to 40 percent, with no false positives. After the placement of acid in the stomach, the yield is almost 100 percent, but there is an incidence of about 25 percent false positives. Smaller amounts of exogenous acid reduce the false-positive response. Prolonged 

PH recordings for 24 h provide a research tool for studying the temporal pattern of reflux. The radioisotopic scintiscan incorporates a radioisotope (such as technetium), which is measured in the esophagus after its ingestion. It is an accurate and sensitive test which has the advantage of not requiring any intubation. Barium x-rays and endoscopy have been shown to be poor means of assessing actual gastroesophageal reflux. Radiographic provocative tests for producing reflux have been especially misleading. 

Thus, if it is important to know whether a patient has gastroesophageal reflux, a pH reflux or radioisotopic scintiscan study should be performed. Assessment of lower esophageal sphincter (LES) competence 

Esophageal manometry is the only currently available test to measure directly the competence of the physiologic LES in humans. This measurement of sphincter pressure is considered by most investigators to be an accurate index of the sphincter’s ability to prevent reflux. In gen-

The LES pressure is the only direct measure of gastroesophageal competence. The major current value of esophageal manometry is in diagnosing LES incompetence and in assessing peristalsis in patients undergoing surgery. In most clinical laboratories, pH reflux, esophageal manometry, and the Bernstein test are performed at the same time. Gastroesophageal influx may lead to esophagitis, Stricture, esophageal ulcer, or Barrett’s epithelium. These sequelae have serious prognostic and therapeutic implications. The simplest and usually initial study is a barium swallow. As emphasized above, the barium swallow is performed neither to diagnose reflux nor to detect a hiatus hernia, but rather to diagnose the sequelae of reflux and to determine the presence of other complicating diseases. A barium swallow is an excellent means of diagnosing peptic stricture and esophageal ulcer. When an air contrast technique is used, the small ulcerations and granularity that are characteristic of esophagitis may also be seen. 

Endoscopy remains the major technique for assessing mucosal integrity. Esophagitis is seen at its earliest stages as minimal erythema. These changes progress to punctate ulcerations and small exudates and, finally, to more extensive linear ulcerations and exudation. The mucosa may become granular and grayish in appearance. A stricture is a symmetrical narrowing of the lumen that must be distinguished from a malignant stricture by biopsy and cytology. Esophageal biopsy, during endoscopy or by a suction capsule, has become widely utilized in gastroesophageal reflux. The biopsy has been 

used to diagnose gastroesophageal reflux in patients with minimum or no visible esophagitis. In virtually all reflux patients and 10 to 25 percent of asymptomatic controls, the biopsy shows thinning of the squamous epithelial surface and an increase in the height of the basilar cell layer. In cases of endoscopic ulceration, the biopsy shows an infiltrate of inflammatory cells and mucosal damage. The biopsy may show the typical mucosal changes of Barrett’s epithelium, as discussed earlier. 

Esophageal manometry is valuable in assessing esophageal peristaltic function, which may be impaired as a consequence of reflux. 

###### Provocative tests 

The major provocative study to assess reflux involves acid perfusion of the esophagus (Bernstein test). The Bernstein test determines the response of the patient during perfusion of the distal esophagus with either normal saline or 0.1 N HCI in a double-blind fashion. Production of pain with acid but not saline is a positive test result; it is found in about 90 percent of patients with reflux and about 10 percent of normals. The test reproduces the burning sensation typical of heartburn, but rarely provokes more severe angina-like pain. It is a valuable means of confirming the presence of gastroesophageal reflux, but is of little value (as a provocative test) in evaluating difficult cases of atypical chest pain. The acid-barium test was introduced in the hope of eliciting esophageal motility disorders in patients with esophagitis. It is, however, a highly subjective study, of little clinical value. 

In summary, the most useful tests to confirm or diagnose gastroesophageal reflux are the combination of the pH reflux study and esophageal manometry, together with either an esophageal biopsy or a Bernstein test. In assessing the possible complications of reflux, a barium swallow and endoscopy with biopsy are very helpful. 

###### TREATMENT 

The treatment of gastroesophageal reflux must be individualized on the basis of the severity of symptoms, presence of complications, and response to prior therapy. The treatment of gastroesophageal reflux can be viewed best in three specific stages, as outlined in Table 3.

Stage II: specific pharmacological therapy 7 Cimetidine 2 Bethanechol or metoclopramide Stage III: surgery 

Stage I involves the use of the simple therapeutic measures that are commonly recognized by most clinicians. However, several points deserve amplification. Certain substances, such as alcohol, high-fat-containing foods, and chocolates, will reduce LES pressure and thus increase reflux even further. Their ingestion should be restricted. Normally the LES pressure increases most markedly in response to protein; this response is impaired in patients with reflux. Foods that reduce LES pressure will have an adverse effect when they act on an already incompetent sphincter. Coffee, citrus juices, and spices may directly elicit esophageal pain, and their intake should be limited. Indeed, any food that elicits symptoms in a patient should be restricted. Smoking has also been shown to reduce LES competence and thus will enhance reflux. Raising the head of the bed is helpful in counteracting the gravitational effects which act to increase reflux. Also, weight reduction and attempts to decrease intraabdominal pressure (e.g., avoiding tight clothing) may also be helpful. Many of these therapeutic recommendations have been supported by physiological studies, but their clinical efficacy has not been proved in controlled trials. A major component in the stage I management of reflux disease is an effective program of non-calcium-containing antacids. Antacids should be given at a dosage and time similar to that used in peptic ulcer disease; this involves the ingestion of 15 to 30 ml of a potent antacid 1 h after meals and at bedtime. More frequent administration may be needed in some patients. The use of alginate is reported to give more localized neutralization of the esophageal mucosa, but its efficacy beyond that obtained with simple ant- 

acids has not been proved. In uncontrolled studies, antacids have been reported to improve esophageal symptoms in 60 to 70 percent of patients. Patients responding to an antacid program require no further evaluation and usually continue.to do quite well. 

Stage II therapy involves the use of two types of pharmacologic agents. Cimetidine reduces acid secretion without altering LES pressure in humans. On the other hand, bethanechol or metoclopramide increases LES pressure without altering acid secretion. Most studies with these agents have focused on symptomatic relief and reduction in antacid usage as indexes of clinical efficacy. In several studies bethanechol, metoclopramide, or cimetidine have been shown to relieve heartburn and to reduce antacid requirements. Pain relief is judged on both frequency and severity of pain. Studies with bethanecol or metoclopramide have shown no change in objective parameters, such as endoscopic evidence of esophagitis or mucosal changes on biopsy. Most studies with cimetidine showed evidence of endoscopic improvement that either represented a positive trend or was statistically significant. A review of the effectiveness of 4 to 8 weeks of cimetidine treatment in patients with reflux disease, including several trials in patients with progressive systemic sclerosis, indicates that cimetidine treatment will promote healing of esophagitis. There has been no evidence of healing strictures or of a reversal of the changes due to Barrett’s epithelium. 

Treatment with either cimetidine, bethanechol, or metoclopramide had led to clinical improvement in about 70 to 80 percent of patients. The recommended dosages for each drug are cimetidine, 300 mg; bethanechol, 25 mg; and metoclopramide, 10 or 15 mg. Each drug should be given 30 min before meals and at bedtime for at least 8 weeks. It is still not clear whether longterm treatment is required once patients with reflux are in remission, since no controlled trials addressing this point are available. However, from a review of the short-term trials, it is apparent that symptoms tend to return shortly after cessation of treatment. A nocturnal dose of cimetidine or antacid similar to that recommended for peptic ulcer disease would seem reasonable once remission has been achieved. About 95 percent of all patients with reflux will respond satisfac- 

###### TREATMENT 3/ 

torily to either stage I or stage II measures when initially treated. About 5 percent will subsequently require some form of antireflux surgery. The indications for surgery (stage III) are given in Table 4. Surgery is recommended in patients with serious complications of reflux disease (e.g., stricture, hemorrhage, peptic ulcer, Barrett’s epithelium) or intractable symptoms. Intractability includes the failure to respond to the stage II therapy. Obviously, the use of surgery is influenced by other factors such as concomitant medical conditions, the age of the patient, and the degree of response of the reflux complications to medical therapy. The newer surgical procedures incorporate a fundoplication around the distal esophagus. In general, these procedures give excellent symptomatic improvement and an objective reduction in reflux in about 90 percent of patients. In the past, simple hiatus hernia repair resulted in only a 50 to 60 percent symptomatic improvement; in most of these instances the indications for surgery were not clear from the outset. Fundoplication procedures improve LES function. The basal LES pressure is increased and the length-tension properties of the LES are restored. The LES response to intraabdominal pressure is improved but not restored to normal. The LES response to endogenous gastrin release is not altered, since gastrin levels are not changed. However, the LES response to exogenous gastrin and cholinergic drugs is restored. Several studies have shown an excellent correlation between clinical improvement and increase in LES pressure. Other studies suggest that decreased reflux may occur without marked improvement in LES pressure. Personal experience supports the former, i.e., there is a good correlation of improvement in clinical status and improvement in LES pressure. Postoperatively, reflux is unlikely to occur if LES pressure is above 15 mmHg. Surgical restoration of LES function produces objective changes in mucosal disease. Esophagitis, stricture, and Barrett’s epithelium may regress after successful repair. The Nissen fundoplication technique, a full 360° wrap of stomach around the distal esophagus, provides the most consistent improvement in LES and clinical function. The Hill procedure, a posterior gastropexy, appears to be the least reliable

Other proposed indications for surgery, which follow, are poorly documented in the literature: (1) hiatus hernia plus vague upper abdominal complaints, (2) hiatus hernia plus iron-deficiency anemia, (3) globus hystericus, (4) pulmonary disease without documented gastroesophageal reflux and aspiration. 

operation. In all reported series, the clinical and objective results from fundoplication are impressive. However, in clinical practice, the results are less impressive, and one finds that many patients may require several procedures. It seems evident that surgical expertise is essential if the excellent results reported in the literature are to be achieved. It is also evident that if only patients with advanced disease and complications are treated, the results will be less favorable. It should be noted that many initially successful fundoplication procedures appear to lose their effectiveness after several years. Long-term results of each fundoplication procedure are not available. Fundoplication procedures, especially the Nissen procedure, may be accompanied by postoperative complications. Two major complications have been noted—namely, the development of dysphagia and/or the inability to vomit or belch (‘‘gas-bloat syndrome’’). Dysphagia can be a major problem and seems to occur more frequently in patients with nonspecific motility. disorders or when there is esophageal dysfunction in association with collagen vascular disease. These patients should be approached cautiously and with a less aggressive operative tightening of the fundoplication. In a recent comparison of medical treatment versus surgery, the surgical approach resulted in a good clinical response in 73 percent of patients compared with 19 percent of patients treated with antacids. This finding should not cause the 

###### 32 DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT OF GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE 

clinician to recommend earlier surgery, but rather suggests that surgery is an effective alternative in patients who have the proper indications for this approach. Most patients will do very well on medical therapy, especially with the new histamine antagonist cimetidine. There is no evidence to suggest that acidreducing operations, such as vagotomy or antrectomy, have any place in the primary surgical approach to gastroesophageal reflux disease. Vagotomy is reasonable only if the patient has concomitant peptic ulcer disease. In conclusion, our understanding of the pathophysiology of LES incompetence has led to improvement in both medical and surgical therapy. In patients with gastroesophageal reflux, several specific etiologic factors are now recognized which determine to some degree the approach to clinical management. Therapy has become more specific, being directed toward preventing reflux and restoring sphincter competence. A number of critical issues remain, however. Thus, it is unclear which patients will develop serious sequelae of reflux and should have more aggres- 

sive initial management. Furthermore, we do not yet know the. long-term effectiveness of medical versus surgical therapy. Finally, the role of diet in the treatment of reflux disease has not been adequately evaluated.

#### H. FRANKLIN BUNN and GEORGE F. CAHILL, JR. GLYCOSYLATED HEMOGLOBINS: THEIR ROLE IN THE CONTROL AND COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES 

One of the most perplexing challenges in medical research is the pathogenesis of the complications of diabetes. In recent years, clinical and experimental studies have suggested that rigorous control of diabetes may retard the development of retinopathy or angiopathy. Correction of the diabetic state in experimental animals may prevent or reverse the specific pathology. Such information raises the question whether hyperglycemia per se contributes to diabetic complications. One possible mechanism is nonenzymatic glycosylation of proteins, a phenomenon that has received considerable attention lately. Ordinarily, glycosylation of proteins involves linkage of specific groups of sugars to certain residues such as serine, asparagine, and hydroxylysine, and is under strict enzymatic control. Enzymatic glycosylation may serve a wide variety of functions, such as facilitating secretion of a protein from its cell of origin, enhancing a protein’s survival in the circulation, providing a protective coat or barrier in certain tissues, and forming specific receptors for hormones and other humoral substances. In contrast, proteins can also combine nonenzymatically with sugars. This phenomenon, sometimes called the browning reaction, has been well known in the dairy industry for many years. Nonenzymatic glycosylation was considered to be dependent upon a high concentration of the free sugar as well as nonphysiologic incubation conditions of temperature, pH, or state of hydration. However, a number of recent observations have indicated that nonenzymatic glycosylation can also occur under physiologic conditions. Indeed this phenomenon accounts for the formation of Hb A,,, the most abundant minor hemoglobin component in normal red 

cells, as well as for the modification of several other proteins. In 1968, Rahbar screened a group of 1200 patients in Iran for hemoglobin abnormalities and found two with an apparently abnormal minor component. Both of these patients had diabetes mellitus. Subsequently he found this abnormality in 47 other diabetics. This electrophoretic abnormality proved to be due to a two- to threefold increase in Hb A,.. This minor hemoglobin component appeared to be a marker of the diabetic state. Accordingly, it was of considerable importance to work out the structure and biosynthesis of Hb A,. and determine its relationship to the diabetic state. 

###### GLYCOSYLATED HUMAN HEMOGLOBINS 

Human red cells contain one major hemoglobin component, Hb A, a tetramer consisting of two pairs of unlike polypeptide chains. Among the minor components of human red cells are Hb A, (a,6,) and Hb F (a,y.), which are the products of different globin chain genes, as indicated by the Greek letters in parentheses. In addition, several negatively charged hemoglobins can be isolated by chromatography and have been designated as Hb A,,, A;,, and A, according to their order of elution. Recently, Hb A,,, was found to be composed of two distinct hemoglobin components that have been designated Hb A,,, and Hb A,,,. The distribution of these hemoglobin components in normal red cells is shown in Fig. 1. ###### Biosynthesis of glycosylated hemoglobins 

Knowledge of the structure of these minor hemoglobin components raises obvious questions about their mode of synthesis: Is the glycosylation of hemoglobin under enzymatic control? At what stage in red cell development does the conversion take place? In vitro and in vivo studies have been designed to answer these questions. Incubation of human reticulocytes and bone marrow with *°Fe-labeled transferrin or with 14Clabeled amino acids resulted in significantly less incorporation of radioactivity into the glycosylated minor hemoglobins in comparison with the major component, Hb A,. These in vitro studies were consistent with Hb A,,, A;,, and A, being posttranslational modifications of Hb A,. Much better definition of the biosynthesis of the glycosylated hemoglobins was achieved by in vivo studies. Normal human volunteers were given an intravenous injection of *®Fe bound to transferrin. The specific radioactivity of major and minor hemoglobin components was determined over the next 3 months (Fig. 2). As expected, the specific activity of Hb A, reached a maximum level within 10 days following the injection of the iron pulse label and fell very slowly thereafter during the life span of this cohort of labeled red cells. In contrast, the specific activity of Hb A,,, Ay,, and A,, increased in a nearly linear fashion, crossing that of Hb A, by day 60, half the life span of the red cell. These findings indicate that glycosylation of hemoglobin takes place slowly and continuously throughout the 120-day life span of the red cell. In support of this conclusion is the fact that old red cells have significantly higher levels of Hb A,, than do young red cells and the concentration of Hb A,, is decreased in the red cells of patients with hemolytic anemia because of their short survival time. According to the reaction pathway shown above, it should be possible to synthesize Hb A,, in vitro. Fliickiger and Winterhalter incubated column-purified Hb A with ['4C]glucose and demonstrated the formation of a minor hemoglobin component that had the chromatographic behavior, structure, and functional properties of authentic Hb A,. Other laboratories have confirmed the synthesis of Hb A,, in vitro. Since the glycosylation of hemoglobin is nonenzyma-

The experiments summarized here indicate that the formation of Hb A,, in vivo is a function of two prime variables: the mean blood glucose concentration and the red cell life span. It follows that measurement of Hb A,, should provide an assessment of mean blood glucose concentration (see below). 

###### Functional behavior of glycosylated hemoglobins 

Since these minor hemoglobins are modified by specific sugars at specific sites, their functional properties are of particular interest. In the absence of organic phosphates, Hb A,, has an oxygen affinity very similar to that of Hb A, but, as shown in Fig. 3, the oxygenation of Hb A,, is less affected by the addition of 2,3-DPG, an important intracellular modifier of hemoglobin function. This observation provided initial evidence that the N terminus of the 8 chain is one of the sites involved in the binding of 2,3-DPG. Although nonenzymatic glycosylation has pronounced effects on the function of purified minor components, the oxygenation of intact red cells is probably not significantly affected by alterations in Hb A,, and the other minor components. GLYCOSYLATED HEMOGLOBIN AND DIABETES 

From the structural and biosynthetic studies presented above, it is clear that Hb A,, is formed slowly and irreversibly by the condensation of two very abundant reactants within the red cell: glucose and hemoglobin. Glucose in plasma readily traverses the human red cell membrane by facilitated diffusion. Accordingly, the percentage of Hb A,, in red cells should be a reflection of the cumulative mean concentration of plasma glucose. 

###### Animal models 

Observations in experimental animals have provided valuable information. Koenig and Cerami found that diabetic mice (C75BL/KsJ-db/db) had 

increased levels of a chromatographically distinct minor hemoglobin component, which, like human Hb A,., had borohydride-reducible linkages on the B chain. The proportion of this hemoglobin increased within several weeks after the onset of hyperglycemia. Like human Hb A,,, this minor hemoglobin component was shown to bea posttranslational modification of the major hemoglobin component. Furthermore its synthetic rate was greater in diabetic mice than in normal mice. The diabetes in this strain of mice is transient. As it regressed, the proportion of the minor hemoglobin component returned to normal. Koenig and his associates also found increased levels of this minor hemoglobin component in several strains of mice with chemically induced diabetes. 

###### Glycosylated hemoglobin and diabetic control 

The measurement of Hb A,. in diabetics provides a useful index of cumulative control of hyperglycemia during the 2 to 3 months immediately prior to the measurement. Such information is valuable to the clinician, since blood glucose determinations are subject to rather marked fluctuations, related not only to the severity of the diabetes but also to other variables such as prior ingestion of food or the administration of insulin or other hypoglycemia agents. Thus, the determination of Hb A,,. may be particularly useful in following the unstable diabetic who is difficult to control. Two approaches have been used to doc-

Nevertheless, Hb A,. measurement may still provide useful independent information in screening patients for diabetes. It would be of interest to investigate the natural history of patients who are grouped according to both OGTT and Hb A... 

Measurement of glycosylated hemoglobin in pregnant patients should be interpreted cautiously. When diabetic women become pregnant, there is a significant decrease in Hb A, by the third trimester. This finding may reflect better diabetic control. Alternatively, the decrease in Hb A,,. may be due to an influx of young red cells (low in glycosylated hemoglobin) because of the expansion in red cell mass which accompanies pregnancy. In accord with the latter explanation, there is a significant decrease in Hb A,, of nondiabetic women when they become pregnant as well as a slight decrease in blood glucose concentration from that of the nonpregnant state. Methodology for measuring glycosylated hemoglobin 

The increasing interest in using Hb A, measurement as a Clinical test demands the development of improved methodology. No technique has universal applicability. The standard column chromatography on Biorex-70 resin is time-consuming and cumbersome but must be considered the “‘gold standard” against which other methods should be compared. One should remember that column chromatography (as well as electrophoretic methods) measures Hb A,, or Hb A, but not glycosylated Hb A,. However, since the two species parallel one another, there is no additional benefit in measuring total glycosylated hemoglobin. 

Hb A,, can also be assayed with great speed and precision by automated high-pressure liquid chromatography. This technique is suitable only for clinics which process a relatively large number of specimens. In an attempt to accommodate clinics or physicians with smaller demands, several companies have been promoting kits containing convenient disposable columns, which 

measure the sum of the “‘fast hemoglobins,” i.e., Atay Atay» Am, Pre-Aje, and Aj, (hereafter designated as A,). The information obtained from ‘“‘microcolumns” generally correlates quite well with measurement of Hb A,, by standard chromatography. Glycosylated hemoglobins can be measured by other techniques that circumvent some of the problems inherent in column chromatography. Gel electrofocusing on polyacrylamide slabs is a high-resolution system which enables the clear separation of Hb A,, from Hb Ao. Alternatively, Fliickiger and Winterhalter have devised a colorimetric test for measurement of glycosylated hemoglobin. Upon acid hydrolysis, the glucose attached as a ketoamine forms a dehydrated sugar, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural, which can be readily detected after it is treated with thiobarbituric acid to make a colored product. This test, when carefully executed, provides a reliable assessment of glycosylated hemoglobin. Finally, a radioimmunoassay has been developed which should permit rapid determination of large numbers of specimens. Thus far there has been no published information on its clinical application. Ideally, the measurement of glycosylated hemoglobin should provide an integrated assessment of daily levels of blood glucose over the preceding 2 to 3 months. Hb A, will be proportionately reduced in patients who have decreased red cell life span. Column methods will also give erroneously low values in patients with common hemoglobin variants such as Hb S and Hb C, since the portions of these hemoglobins that are glycosylated are eluted less readily than Hb A,.. As noted in the introductory section, glycosylated hemoglobin exists in two forms, a precursor having a labile Schiff-base linkage (pre-A,,) and the stable end product, Hb A,.. Rapid chromatographic and electrophoretic systems fail to distinguish between these two forms. The proportion of the labile form fluctuates according to the patient’s recent blood glucose levels and can contribute up to 25 percent to the total fast hemoglobin. Only the stable ketoamine linkage (Hb A,.) provides an assessment of integrated blood sugar levels. Thus, the reliable interpretation of this test depends on an accurate measurement of Hb A, uncontaminated by the labile precursor. This can be achieved either by employing a more

###### NONENZYMATIC GLYCOSYLATION OF OTHER PROTEINS 

There is increasing evidence that nonenzymatic glycosylation can occur in vivo at sites other than the hemoglobin molecule. Logical candidates include proteins which have a long turnover time and are exposed to concentrations of glucose approaching that in plasma. The latter include all extracellular proteins and those intracellular proteins in which glucose entry is not limiting for glucose metabolism, except muscle and adipose tissue. Proteins in nonaqueous systems, such as central nervous system myelin, would probably be spared from significant glycosylation. Glucosyllysine has been detected in bovine collagen, proteins from human red cell membranes, albumin, basic protein from nerve myelin, and lens crystallins. These proteins fulfill the above criterion of prolonged exposure to high concentrations of glucose. An important question, although a difficult one to resolve, is whether nonenzymatic glycosylation has any effect on the function of the modified proteins. 

is a particularly likely candidate since it has a relatively prolonged survival (T,). = 14 days) and, unlike other plasma proteins, is not modified by enzymatic glycosylation. When normal human serum is incubated with [*H]glucose, a number of proteins incorporate radioactivity with albumin having the highest specific activity. Incorporation was linear with time during an 8-day incubation and was significantly reduced in the presence of aspirin. This drug is known to acetylate a particular lysine residue in albumin. It is likely that this residue is also preferentially glycosylated. About 6 to 15 percent of native albumin is glycosylated in vivo. Thus, albumin has a significantly higher reactivity with glucose than does hemoglobin since the two proteins are modified to a similar extent, but hemoglobin survival in the circulation is about five times longer. Glycosylation of albumin, like hemoglobin, is increased in diabetics (Fig. 6). It is unlikely that nonenzymatic glycosylation of albumin has any effect on its function. This modification has no effect on the survival of albumin in rats.

GLYCOSYLATED HEMOGLOBINS: THEIR ROLE IN THE CONTROL AND COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES 
didates for study not only because of their extreme longevity but also because of their susceptibility to structural and _ functional derangements, particularly opacifications, i.e., cataracts. Stevens and his colleagues have proposed that nonenzymatic glycosylation may predispose lens crystallins toward cataract formation. They incubated bovine nuclear crystallins with glucose and glucose-6-phosphate and found that,the protein solutions became opalescent coincident with the development of high-molecularweight aggregates. These alterations in solutions of crystallin could be partially prevented by maintaining anaerobic incubations and could be reversed by adding reducing agents such as mercaptoethanol to disrupt disulfide bonds. These results suggest that nonenzymatic glycosylation of a lens crystallin renders the protein more susceptible to oxidation of disulfide bonds and formation of high-molecular-weight aggregates. Similar changes may occur in the intact lens as cataract formation occurs. The relevance of these experimental observations to human beings is not clear. Recently, several investigators have demonstrated enhanced nonenzymatic glycosylation in lens crystallins of diabetic patients compared to normal controls. 

These observations provide a novel mechanism for the pathogenesis of diabetic cataracts. An alternative explanation implicates the accumulation of sorbitol in the diabetic lens, due to the reduction of intralenticular glucose by the enzyme aldose reductase. Aldose reductase inhibitors have been shown to prevent sugar cataracts in animals. Further experimental and clinical observations are needed to determine the major factors that are responsible for the development of cataracts in diabetic patients. 

###### NONENZYMATIC GLYCOSYLATION AND THE COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES 

Perhaps the most important issue concerning nonenzymatic glycosylation of proteins is whether this phenomenon contributes to the various Clinical manifestations of diabetes including some of the long-term complications. Spiro has stressed that those tissues that bear the brunt of diabetic complications do not require insulin for entry of glucose into cells. Thus, basement mem- 

brane proteins, lens crystallins, and nerve myelin protein are exposed<sup>tohighlevelsof glucosein</sup> diabetics, as, indeed,<sup>areallothercellsexcept</sup> muscle and adipose tissue. Saturation of the blood-brain-facilitated diffusion transport system also tends to protect the brain and spinal cord from marked degrees of hyperglycemia. Several centers are now conducting prospective studies that will relate the level of glycosylated hemoglobin to other clinical parameters in an attempt to ascertain whether the degree of hyperglycemia is connected with the development of complications. A number of investigators have examined the association between glycosylated hemoglobin and various clinical manifestations such as retinopathy, nerve conduction velocity, increased vascular permeability, decreased renal glomerular filtration, weight of babies born to diabetic mothers, coagulation assays, and serum lipid profiles. However, the establishment of a correlation does not imply causality. Some investigators are attempting to determine whether the observed abnormality is reversible with the establishment of tight control. The availability of pumps that can be programmed for the continuous subcutaneous administration of insulin should facilitate the execution of these studies. Considerably more information must be gathered before firm conclusions can be drawn on the extent to which complications of diabetes depend on control of hyperglycemia and on the extent to which longterm effects of hyperglycemia are mediated by nonenzymatic glycosylation.

#### THE ARTIFICIAL PANCREAS: FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF OPEN- AND CLOSED-LOOP SYSTEMS DIABETES MELLITUS 

###### A. M. ALBISSER 

Diabetes mellitus is characterized by a relative or absolute insulin deficiency. In the healthy pancreas, beta cells produce and store the quantities of this hormone needed for the control of many metabolic processes. When insulin secretion is abnormal, fuel homeostatis is deranged, upsetting the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Loss of control of the circulating plasma glucose level is the earliest manifestation of the disease. 

Despite expert clinical efforts to maintain blood glucose levels of diabetics in the normal range, it is the universal experience that degenerative complications of diabetes develop with increasing frequency as a function of the duration of the disease. Unfortunately, the available methods to treat hyperglycemia are less than ideal. Diet, exercise, and insulin are all important factors that can be manipulated, but normalization of glucose levels is rarely obtained even with multiple subcutaneous injections of carefully chosen mixtures of intermediate- and short-acting insulins. If improving the control of blood glucose can delay the development of the microvascular and neurological complications of the disease, then development of new and improved methods of insulin delivery that will more nearly mimic the activity of the normal pancreas will be of major benefit to the diabetic. 

The first external system that achieves this goal is a feedback-controlled instrument that regulates insulin delivery on a minute-by-minute basis according to measured blood glucose levels and their rates of change. Bedside instruments with glucose sensors are known as closed-loop 

systems Or artificial beta cells. Closed-loop systems have been developed in many laboratories, and with proper application the goal of ideal blood glucose control can be achieved. However, long-term application of the present generation of these instruments is precluded by their size and by the amount of blood required for continuous extracorporeal glucose sensing. 

More recently open-loop systems have been developed that differ from the closed-loop systems in their size and in their lack of an integral glucose sensor. Many such systems are portable. Open-loop systems sacrifice the precision and self-adaptation of the closed-loop instruments but do supply insulin at varying predetermined rates. The usual procedure is to infuse insulin at a uniform basal rate of delivery between meals and to give additional, timed pulses of insulin in anticipation of meals. Because these systems are portable, unrestrained subjects can participate in studies of longer duration. Clinical studies have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach to improve blood glucose control; the metabolic response to physical exercise is significantly improved, and the risk of hypoglycemia is minimized. Results of long-term studies in animals (up to 1 year) and humans (up to 6 months) have demonstrated that remarkable normalization of blood glucose can be obtained. The extension of these results to the treatment of insulin-dependent diabetics on a wider scale is potentially exciting. 

An overview of the methodology is presented here together with a discussion of the results that have been obtained to date with both systems.

The artificial beta cell is composed of a sensor, a computer, and a set of pumps. These components are connected in such a way as to form a closed loop with the subject, as shown in Fig. 1. By means of an indwelling dual-lumen catheter, venous blood is drawn into an analyzer modified for continuous blood glucose measurement. The computer receives the electrical signals generated by the glucose analyzer and interprets them in accordance with its internal algorithms. The computer then instructs a pump to deliver an appropriate amount of insulin, according to the level of the blood glucose and its rate of change. Similarly, glucose (or glucagon) can be administered by another pump in a counterregulatory manner should hypoglycemia occur. Instruments incorporating both insulin and a counterregulatory agent (glucose or glucagon) are often termed the artificial endocrine pancreas. Infusion into the patient is realized by means of a second indwelling venous catheter. This type of system is capable of regulating the level of blood glucose in diabetic subjects within normal limits and maintains normoglycemia in the presence of variable external stresses. 

###### Blood sampling 

Blood is withdrawn continuously by means of an indwelling double-lumen catheter in a superficial vein of the forearm. The double-lumen catheter

enables continuous withdrawal of whole blood from the subject because heparin is delivered through the outer lumen to the very tip of the device, where it mixes with the blood as it is being drawn into the inner lumen. Anticoagulant does not enter the circulation but prevents clotting in the conduit leading to the analyzer. The withdrawal of blood at a rate of 50 l/min is adequate to detect changes of | to 2 percent in blood glucose concentration. Because the blood used for analysis is not returned to the body, studies are limited to 24 h when continual glucose sensing is required. Patients participating in the studies with closed-loop artificial beta-cell instruments are usually confined to bed or to an armchair in the vicinity of the instrument. Continuous-flow analysis of glucose in whole blood The closed-loop control of glycemia requires that glucose be measured with minimum delay between sample withdrawal and computed response. Glucose analysis is therefore most expediently performed on whole blood. Practical methods for continuous blood sampling and glucose analysis at the bedside use standard laboratory analyzers adapted and modified for continuous-flow glucose analysis. Initially, the continuous-flow methods were sensitive to all reducing sugars, but enzymatic techniques are now used that produce interference-free assay of glucose alone. There is considerable interest in the development of electrochemical sensors that measure 

CLOSED-LOOP METHODS FOR BLOOD GLUCOSE CONTROL (THE ARTIFICIAL BETA CELL) 45 

the change in oxygen concentration or H,O, production when glucose reacts with oxygen in the presence of immobilized glucose oxidase. Alternatively, electron transport can be measured when glucose is oxidized at a platinum electrode. These devices, which are small enough to be portable or implantable, are still at an early stage of development. 

###### Nonlinear and linear computer algorithms for blood glucose control 

For the closed-loop regulation of the blood glucose in the diabetic, information from the glucose sensor must be translated into rates of delivery of two agents: insulin if blood glucose is too high and glucagon (or glucose) if it is too low. Early augmentation of insulin delivery in response to increasing levels of blood glucose even at normoglycemic levels (the derivative effect) is required to imitate the rapid release of insulin, in response to such an increase in blood glucose, which is characteristic of the healthy beta cell. Three relationships for the regulation of blood glucose are commonly used. Two relate insulin and glucagon (or glucose) delivery rates to the measured level of glycemia. The third depends on the rate of change of blood glucose to enhance insulin delivery at rising but still normoglycemic levels and to attenuate insulin delivery rates FIGURE 2 The closed-loop artificial pancreas apparatus in the Clinical Investigation Unit of the Toronto General Hospital. The glucose analyzer (pump, dialyzer, colorimeter, and chart recorder) are from Technicon Instruments. The control unit (pumps, keyboard, and computer) are from Life Science In\ struments.

when blood glucose concentrations begin to fall even if hyperglycemia is still present. Derivative feedback of this type improves the response of the system but at the expense of increasing sensitivity to system noise. 

To reduce the effects of such noise, filtering of some type is usually incorporated in such a way as to reduce to insignificance the effects of blood glucose changes less than +1 mg/dl/min. Many versions of this rate-dependent component have been described, the details of which are unimportant for this discussion. The critical point is that ideal control of blood glucose is obtained only if a rate-dependent component is included. 

###### Pump delivery systems 

The artificial beta cell delivers two substances under closed-loop control: insulin to correct for hyperglycemia and glucagon (or glucose) to correct for hypoglycemia. Usually, regular crystalline porcine zine insulin is used, diluted in normal saline to a final concentration of about 0.4 unit per milliliter. Glucagon is diluted as described by the manufacturer, and normal saline is added to give a final concentration of 100 pg/ml. The hormone solutions are connected through disposable intravenous tubing sets to two pumps. A third pump of the same type is used to deliver saline at a constant minimum 

###### 46 

###### THE ARTIFICIAL PANCREAS 

rate. The output of each pump flows through a separate tube, meeting remotely in a triple-input adaptor whose output is connected to the cannula in the patient. Flow rates of the insulin and glucagon (or glucose) solutions can be varied usually from 0 to 6 ml/min under the control of the computer. Saline delivery is adjusted manually and serves to maintain catheter patency and to flush the hormones into the circulation. By using the triple-input adaptor and the saline flush, significant delays in the delivery of the glucoregulatory hormones are avoided, particularly at the low flow rates usual in the postabsorptive period. A typical prototype closed-loop instrument in use at the bedside is shown in Fig. 2. More compact bedside instruments are now undergoing testing. OPEN-LOOP METHODS FOR BLOOD GLUCOSE CONTROL 

Because of the restrictions imposed by the present generation of closed-loop artificial pancreases, substantial effort has been directed to the development of open-loop systems (see Fig. 3). These systems include a reservoir filled with insulin, a pump, a regulated power supply, and a catheter delivery set, but they do not include a

Both electrical and chemical power sources have been used, and various approaches have been applied to the modulation of flow rates. Reagent reservoirs are constructed of titanium, silastic, or disposable plastic syringes. A variety of open-loop wave forms have been proposed for the control of glycemia using preprogrammed regimens of insulin delivery. These wave forms all involve low (basal) rates of insulin infusion in the fasting periods and more rapid rates (pulses) given for various periods either prior to or during meals. The pulses are activated manually by the subject or by the experimenter at mealtime, and the device executes the preprogrammed wave form without regard to the actual blood glucose levels. 

###### CLINICAL STUDIES WITH CLOSEDLOOP SYSTEMS Glycemic normalization in dogs given intravenous glucose 

Early applications of a closed-loop system in intact pancreatectomized dogs demonstrated that normalization of blood glucose can be accomplished. An example is shown in Fig. 4 where standardized uniform infusions of glucose were used to assess the performance of the device. Control that related insulin dosage only to the level of the circulating blood glucose without a rate-dependent component (Fig. 44) resulted ina response to the glucose load resembling mild maturity-onset diabetes, both in the high blood glucose rise of 130 mg/dl to glucose loading and in the large amount of insulin (32 units) required to effect a return to a normal blood glucose. In contrast, control that included a rate-dependent component (Fig. 4B) not only limited the glucose rise to 42 mg/dl but required only one-tenth of the insulin needed in the absence of this component. With the parameters used in Fig. 4B, this system responded like the normal pancreas, which lends support to the belief that the early secretory response to glucose challenge is essential to mimic glucose regulation in healthy subjects.

###### Clinical control of diabetes by the artificial pancreas 

Success in animal experiments encouraged the application of the closed-loop artificial pancreas to human subjects. The first clinical trials involved 2-day studies. On the first day the blood glucose profiles were monitored through the day, as shown in Fig. 5. The patients were given their usual doses of subcutaneous insulin and ate measured meals and snacks. On the second day insulin was administered intravenously by the artificial pancreas, in accordance with the momentto-moment changes in blood glucose resulting from the same meals as those of the previous day. Hypoglycemia was not encountered, and none of the patients experienced side effects during or after the trials. The mean glycemic excursion of seven such unstable diabetics is shown in 

Fig. 6A, and that of nine matched healthy controls is shown for comparison in Fig. 6B. Insulin levels in the diabetics were not measured because previous insulin treatment had resulted in the presence of circulating anti-insulin antibodies. Their presence does not appear to impair the operation of the closed-loop system. 

###### Glucagon as a counterregulatory agent 

Because insulin-dependent diabetics often respond poorly to hypoglycemia, the instrument has been programmed for exogenous glucagon delivery. Appropriate control parameters that successfully prevent hypoglycemia were derived. Glucagon delivery alone was sufficient to prevent hypoglycemia, thus obviating the need for glucose administration. 

48 THE ARTIFICIAL PANCREAS 

###### Controlled insulin delivery in the treatment of ketoacidosis 

The treatment of diabetic coma and ketoacidosis has also been explored. Return of blood glucose to the normal range is achieved more rapidly and with smaller quantities of insulin by the continuous intravenous infusion of insulin than by conventional regimens. As expected, the major amount of hormone is delivered by the apparatus early in treatment to correct for the hyperglycemia. Correction of hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis is usually possible in as little as 23 to 3 h. Whether this rapid correction is beneficial has not been determined. Rapid falls in blood glucose during treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis have been associated with the cerebral edema syndrome. Consequently, more studies are required 

before this system can be considered for routine use in diabetic ketoacidosis. 

###### Controlled insulin delivery and the oral glucose tolerance test 

The response to an oral glucose load in severe diabetics treated with the artificial pancreas has been examined (Fig. 7). Three diabetic patients received a 50-g oral glucose load after an overnight fast on each of three consecutive mornings. On the first and third days, each received the usual therapy prior to the test, but on the second day treatment was withheld and insulin was administered intranveously by the closed-loop system. The results are summarized in Fig. 7 and show that on conventional treatment the mean glucose tolerance is abnormal with fasting hy-

###### Peripheral or portal insulin delivery 

In the above studies insulin was always delivered into the peripheral venous circulation. Studies were undertaken in dogs to compare the consequences of insulin administration through the closed-loop system into the portal and the peripheral routes. Under general anesthesia, intraportal glucose was infused in normal and in pancreatectomized dogs, and insulin was administered either peripherally or into the portal vein. Normal glucose tolerance was restored by both routes of insulin delivery. No significant differences were found in blood glucose levels, insulin infusion patterns, peripheral immunoreactive insulin levels, or the total insulin requirements between the two routes. It was concluded that the more readily accessible peripheral route is an appropriate infusion site for an implantable or portable prosthesis for controlling blood glucose concentration. Notwithstanding the insignificance of the differences between the two groups, about 20 percent more insulin was required to achieve a given peripheral insulin level when the insulin was delivered intraportally. These findings may reflect the acute nature of the studies in anesthetized animals, and different results may be obtained in unrestrained animals given long-term intraportal insulin replacement. Controlled glucose infusion during pancreatic resection 

In addition to its application for the treatment of ketoacidosis the device has also been used to facilitate insulinoma resection. To this end the device was adapted to assist with the intraoperative localization of an insulin-secreting islet cell tumor. Glycemia was monitored continuously, and glucose was infused to maintain euglycemia, the apparatus being modified to exclude its usual insulin delivery capabilities. The glucose infusion rate was established in accordance with a 

control algorithm whose parameters were chosen to amplify changes in glucose delivery rate for small alterations in the measured baseline glucose concentration. The glucose infusion rate was about 100 mg/min initially. An area in the tail of the pancreas suspected of containing the insulinoma was excluded from the circulation by a noncrushing clamp. After 14 min the glucose infusion progressively decreased to 27 mg/min, reflecting a glycemia rise of only 15 mg/dl. These changes were taken to represent a fall in insulin activity. This was subsequently confirmed directly by the demonstration of a reduction in immunoreactive insulin and a progressive increase in plasma free fatty acid levels and in postoperative glucose intolerance. 

###### Remission of diabetes following closed-loop control 

The remission of diabetes has been assessed in nine recent acute-onset ketosis-prone juvenile diabetics after short-term control of blood glucose by the external artificial beta cell. The results were compared with those from a group of patients undergoing traditional treatment. In six of the first group persistent remissions were obtained but in only one in the latter group. Insulin infusion during the short application of the apparatus was accompanied by an increase in endogenous insulin secretion as assessed by urinary C-peptide excretion and a decrease in plasma glucagon values, leading to the conclusion that early, effective treatment by means of the closed-loop device may break the vicious cycle of hyperglycemia, insulin depletion, and hyperglycemia and result in remissions for varying periods. Verification of these findings by others has not been reported. 

###### Metabolic response to meals 

The metabolic response to control of the blood glucose was studied in diabetics on subcutaneous insulin and then during treatment with the artificial pancreas. The results were compared with a similar group of nondiabetic controls matched for age, sex, and weight. STUDIES WITH OPEN-LOOP SYSTEMS To circumvent the need for a sensor of blood glucose, several groups have developed programmable open-loop insulin delivery devices, and short-term studies have explored the effectiveness of such devices in controlling blood glucose using preprogrammed methods of insulin delivery. Open-loop systems can be made portable, enabling ambulatory subjects to participate in studies lasting longer than 1| or 2 days. In these systems insulin is given continuously at a basal rate that is enhanced either manually or automatically preceding and during meals. Specific patterns of insulin infusion must be determined individually. The application of these systems to animals is uniformly successful, not only in the short term but in the long term. Whether such open-loop systems can be programmed to provide to diabetic patients all the benefits of the closed-loop system remains to be established. ###### Unstable diabetics 

The regulation of brittle diabetics by a preplanned insulin-infusion program was_ subsequently attempted. Insulin in an amount corresponding to the previously optimized daily insulin requirement was infused in ambulatory patients at precalculated rates..Glucose homeostasis was improved during the infusion days, and the incidence of hypoglycemia was similar to that seen during ordinary insulin treatment. With this infusion program, better blood glucose control was achieved than with the combination of intermediate- and short-acting insulin injections administered four times daily, although the infusion program was not altered from patient to patient. Amelioration of aberrant blood glucose homeostasis was presumably achieved because the plasma insulin concentrations varied in a physiological manner as a result of the combination of insulin infusion rates used. 

Intravenous insulin may avoid the unpredictable absorption from subcutaneous depots. In another study with unstable diabetics, it was also demonstrated that the achievement of normal plasma glucose under ambulatory fed conditions can be achieved with pumped intravenous insulin. The best reproduction of the normal blood glucose and insulin patterns was obtained when 13 percent of the daily insulin dose was given at each meal in such a fashion that the insulin level in the circulation began its ascent within 15 min of the start of the meal. This resulted in correction to normal of the time of the glucose peak and to base-line recovery after the peak. In this study standardization in the experimental design was used, including identical meals taken at 6-h intervals. Exercise was programmed to follow each meal except that at 2 a.m. Interestingly, in this study the same amount of insulin given at each meal while the patient was ambulatory resulted in the same degree of blood glucose control, a finding contrary to the belief that more insulin is required in the morning. 

52 THE ARTIFICIAL PANCREAS 

###### Non-insulin-requiring adult diabetics 

Adult diabetic subjects who were previously not treated with insulin received, in addition to a basal infusion, a 5-h pulse of insulin with each meal, such that a normal diurnal pattern in plasma insulin was obtained. This form of treatment was carried out for 14 days, during which control of blood glucose was observed. On the first posttreatment day, plasma glucose remained significantly below pretreatment levels while the endogenous plasma insulin area increased significantly above pretreatment values. Several patients exhibited slight improvement in glucose tolerance for 7 days while on the diet but not on insulin treatment. Thus, insulin replacement coordinated with meals in a physiologic manner can return plasma glucose to normal even without feedback control of the delivery rate, and a transient remission of beta cell function may follow. Whether four subcutaneous injections per day of insulin would achieve similar results in such diabetics was not assessed. 

###### Subcutaneous insulin infusion 

Several studies have been performed to examine the feasibility of achieving long periods of nearnormal glycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus by giving a continuous subcutaneous infusion of insulin from a miniature battery-driven syringe pump. Thirty minutes before meals the basal infusion rate was increased, and the resulting blood glucose profile was closely monitored and compared with profiles on control days when the patients were managed with their usual subcutaneous insulin. Diet and exercise were standardized. In several patients the subcutaneous insulin infusion significantly lowered blood glucose without producing hypoglycemia. In some young diabetics abnormal levels of certain metabolites and counterregulatory hormones were normalized along with their response to exercise. With continuous intravenous infusion, most patients can be controlled on less than the usual 24h dose, but with the subcutaneous route requirements may be higher, possibly because of immobilization or destruction of some of the insulin at the subcutaneous site. Many patients developed blood glucose values of 40 to 50 mg/dl without experiencing hypoglycemic symptoms. The question whether such asymptomatic chemical 

hypoglycemia is harmful must be raised. Continuous subcutaneous infusion differs from ordinary depot injection treatment in that there is not much insulin within the patient at any given time. The absence of a depot may be beneficial in preventing the hypoglycemia that may accompany physical exercise in diabetics treated with intermediate-acting insulin. Certainly this is true when insulin is infused intravenously. Insulin requirements and exercise 

The question has been addressed of whether exercise makes necessary adjustments of the rate of insulin infusion by an open-loop system to prevent hypoglycemia. To this end, glucose turnover was measured. In normoglycemic, insulininfused diabetics, glucose production and disappearance increased synchronously in a fashion similar to that in normal controls. By contrast, moderate exercise of the legs was associated with a rapid fall in plasma glucose when subcutaneous insulin had been given in the exercising thigh. Plasma glucose in diabetics receiving insulin by constant intravenous infusion is unaffected by exercise. The responses of several other metabolites—lactate, pyruvate, fatty acids, and ketone bodies —were not brought back to normal. Thus, near-normal blood glucose in the context of exercise is not necessarily equivalent to a normal metabolic state. Complications of the open-loop methods 

All the above cited open-loop studies involved human subjects. Insulin was delivered into the peripheral circulation in the arm using an intravenous catheter, which generally led to local reactions after a few days. Thrombosis and phlebitis frequently occurred but disappeared after the removal of the intravenous catheters. Septicemia was not reported, and febrile reactions responded promptly to routine treatment. Central vein catheters which exit remotely by a subcutaneous tunnel are said to minimize these problems and can be left in place for extended periods of time. Tests in animals for up to 2 years and in diabetic patients for up to 9 months have indicated the feasibility of such techniques for experimental purposes. Similar catheters have been used therapeutically in humans for long- 

STUDIES WITH OPEN-LOOP SYSTEMS 53 

term total parenteral nutrition without major complication. 

###### Hyperinsulinemia 

Glycemic regulation using an open-loop insulin delivery system was examined in pancreatectomized dogs given glucose infusions. The animals were first studied as normal controls and then later following pancreatectomy. Glycemia was initially regulated by a closed-loop instrument to determine the details of the insulin requirements. The wave form was then resolved into three components: basal, priming, and sustaining waves. When this predetermined compound wave form was applied in the open-loop system, the glycemic response was similar to that in normal controls in the prechallenge and postchallenge periods and tended to be somewhat lower during the challenge (see Fig. 8).
