###### PROSPECTS FOR THE FUTURE 

Many clinical and research applications of the closed-loop insulin delivery system are now being explored. Usually these involve hospital studies such as during surgery, in labor and delivery, or for insulin dose determination in unstable diabetics. They are limited in duration to 1 or 2 days, because of the restrictions imposed by the size of the apparatus and a need for continuous blood withdrawal for glucose setting. The excellent control of blood glucose achieved by these devices is frequently associated with peripheral hyperinsulinemia. Whether hyperinsulinemia will prove to be undesirable remains to be established. Because of these and other limitations, much attention has been focused on openloop preprogrammed insulin delivery mechanisms. It is not yet known whether simple or complicated wave forms will prove superior or which route should be used for insulin infusion. 

###### Vascular access 

Long-term central venous access in animals is feasible using techniques that are similar to those that have been developed and applied for total parenteral nutrition. The use of these techniques in research protocols using open-loop systems in human subjects is gaining acceptance and is es- 

238) 

###### SUMMARY 

sential for such protocols because the usual methods for peripheral vascular access introduce undesirable complications that frequently limit to short periods of time the duration of studies. 

###### Route of insulin delivery 

Is the peripheral route of intravascular insulin delivery appropriate for the long-term treatment of diabetes using the new open- or closed-loop methods? In many of the studies reported using these devices, peripheral hyperinsulinemia accompanies the achievement of normal blood glucose when insulin is delivered peripherally but not when it is delivered portally. These findings may imply the desirability of the portal (natural) route of insulin delivery in the treatment of diabetes mellitus. Whether the achievement of long-term control of blood glucose by the administration of insulin will alter the course of any or all of the degenerative complications of diabetes mellitus remains to be established. The extent to which achievement of a normal metabolic state occurs with the peripheral intravenous route of insulin delivery is encouraging but by no means complete. Reports are now beginning to appear regarding the use of open-loop systems that deliver insulin subcutaneously. 

###### Pumps and sensors for implantation 

Implantable pumps suitable for the delivery of insulin have not been developed, although clinical trials have demonstrated the suitability of such a prototype device for the long-term delivery of heparin. The development of an _ intravascular indwelling or interstitial glucose sensor is being actively pursued. Sensing of intravascular blood glucose is a difficult technique, which is complicated by the complex nature of the indwelling device and the reaction of blood to foreign bodies. Vascular thrombosis and embolization are but two of the possible complications yet to be addressed with this form of indwelling device. Nor has it been established whether the extravascular tissue concentrations of glucose are measurable and sufficiently free of undesired rapid fluctuations to serve as the signal for a closed-loop system. Only with the solution of these problems and the development of suitable miniaturized pumps can implantable closed- 

loop systems for control of blood glucose be realized. In this regard open-loop devices are more promising because they demand only the design of a suitable pumping mechanism that can be preprogrammed to suit the fasting and fed insulin requirements of a given individual. Fortunately, in this regard exercise does not alter fasting insulin requirements. With the open-loop system a normal glucoregulatory response to postabsorptive physical exercise is observed, and the risk of hypoglycemia is apparently minimized. 

###### Properties of insulin 

The development of insulin delivery systems has been hampered by the propensity for insulin solutions to precipitate and gradually aggregate in the reservoirs of the devices. Such aggregates interfere with the flow of insulin and eventually result in poor control of blood glucose, regardless of the pH of the infusate. These appear to be fundamental limitations to the realization of new methods of insulin delivery. Recently, it has been suggested that the addition of small amounts of serum to the insulin may minimize this aggregation. 

###### SUMMARY 

New systems are being developed for continuous insulin infusion in patients with diabetes mellitus. Of these, the bedside closed-loop system (artificial beta cell) results in normal blood glucose in the fasting and fed states and favorably alters other fuel substrates and hormone levels in short-term studies of 1 to 2 days. More recently portable, external open-loop insulin delivery systems have been developed that achieve similar results in animals for periods up to 400 days and in humans for up to 300 days. This is accomplished without the need for continuous glucose sensing. The metabolic restoration is not compromised by physical exercise, and unacceptably low blood glucose levels are infrequent. Further development and application of these new systems will enable investigators to establish whether the achievement of ideal control of blood glucose in diabetes alters the course of the complications of the disease.

##### COMPLICATIONS OF THE BIRTH CONTROL PILL 

###### NORMAN M. KAPLAN 

Since their introduction in the early 1960s, oral contraceptives (i.e., the ‘‘pill’?) have been used by more than 20 million women in the United States and 200 million worldwide. The use of the pill has played a role in the decline in unplanned births among married women in the United States: in 1961, almost three out of four pregnancies were unplanned; today, two out of three are planned. The availability of oral contraceptives, used by a large fraction of fertile married women aged 15 to 29, is responsible for this freedom of choice. 

This review will focus on the problems accompanying the use of the pill and will conclude that, for some women, its dangers outweigh the benefits. But it is important to recognize that there remains a large, unmet need for the pill among unmarried teenagers. With an earlier menarche and a relaxation of social inhibitions, one in five females in the United States has had intercourse by age 16, two-thirds by age 19, and almost all before marriage. More than a third of these sexually active teenagers become pregnant before age 19, and the majority have never used any form of contraception. 

Married couples are increasingly utilizing permanent sterilization when they have had the number of children they desire; more than half of the couples in the United States are sterilized within 10 years after their last wanted pregnancy. But for the young unmarried woman, nonpermanent contraception is needed, and, for most, the pill is the best contraceptive now available. Therefore, it is important to be aware of the problems associated with the pill in the hope of recognizing them before serious trouble develops and, preferably, of preventing them altogether. 

The overall risks from oral contraceptive use will be reviewed first; then the specific problems will be considered. THE RISKS FROM ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE 

Three large prospective studies have recently been published, adding considerable evidence to the numerous retrospective studies on the hazards of the use of oral contraceptives: (1) the Royal College of General Practitioners (RCGP) study involving 23,000 users and 23,000 nonusers, (2) the Oxford Family Planning Association study involving 17,000 women, and (3) the Greater Boston questionnaire study of over 37,000 women. 

The overall mortality rate from diseases of the cardiovascular system was found to be increased in both British studies (Tables 1 and 2). Though the total number of excess deaths per 100,000 woman-years is little different between oral contraceptive users and nonusers in the two studies (58 vs. 41 and 50 vs. 42), the differences in cardiovascular deaths is significant. Moreover, the range of cardiovascular disorders associated with the pill was more extensive than that of the three disorders noted previously in retrospective studies: myocardial infarction, pulmonary ernbolism, and cerebrovascular disease. In particular, death from subarachnoid hemorrhage occurred in nine users and in none of the controls. The number of deaths is small, and, therefore, the ratios of excess mortality rates have wide margins of error.

As pointed out by Tietze, if the British findings of a fivefold increase in relative risk among oral contraceptive users were seen in American women, the decline in the overall cardiovascular mortality rate could only be accounted for by a 75 percent or greater decline in cardiovascular mortality rate for non-pill users, a decrease that is unlikely. 

But Beral and Kay defend the results of the Royal College study, denying the claims that their pill users were at higher cardiovascular risk for other reasons. They point out that pill users are less likely than non-pill users to have past histories of myocardial infarction, stroke, hypertension, rheumatic or congenital heart disease, diabetes, or other vascular disease; they are less obese and take fewer medications. Thus, there is no evidence to support the claim that the excess mortality rate among pill users may be accounted for by its selective use in sick women (as a safer alternative to pregnancy). Indeed, the reverse seems to be true; the comparisons in the RCGP study were adjusted for differences between the 

two groups in past health, smoking habits, age, parity, and social class. The fivefold increase in the cardiovascular mortality rate among pill users was found after these adjustments. 

###### SPECIFIC RISKS FROM ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE Cardiovascular diseases 

Before menopause, while exposed to higher levels of endogenous estrogens, women have less atherosclerotic vascular disease. After menopause the risk for cardiovascular disease increases. Yet exogenous estrogen increases cardiovascular risk. Moreover, exogenous estrogen increases plasma _ high-density lipoproteins (HDL), which is usually associated with lesser risk of myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular disease. A number of explanations for the toxic effects of exogenous estrogens have been offered: (1) the doses of exogenous estrogen used in oral contraceptives are beyond the physiologic range; (2) the type of estrogen, particularly the methylated esters, may be harmful; 

SPECIFIC RISKS FROM ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE 61 

disease. An editorial in the September 2, 1978, Lancet and (3) the lack of progestin may also be partly attempts to provide an explanation: responsible for development of cardiovascular 

One postulate that would resolve the conflict in the data is that oestrogens have opposing effects on different aspects of the atherogenic process. The disease can be broadly divided into two stages—an early stage, involving smoothmuscle cell proliferation and cholesterol-ester deposition; and a later complicated stage, characterized by fibrosis, platelet deposition, and mural thrombosis. The reciprocal changes induced by oestrogens in the plasma LDL and HDL concentrations, demonstrated by the Helsinki group and by others, would be expected to inhibit the development of early uncomplicated lesions by reducing the deposition of cholesterol (from LDL) and possibly also by enhancing its removal (via HDL). The progression of established complicated lesions, on the other hand, might be accelerated by oestrogens in view of their undoubted tendency to promote intravascular coagulation—manifest clinically, for example, by an increased incidence of venous thromboembolism in males participating in the Coronary Drug Project and in females taking oral contraceptives. Thus, the net effect of oestrogens and coronary atherosclerosis might be largely determined by the preexisting stage of the vessels, and therefore by the age of the subject. Increased endogenous oestrogen production from an early age, as in normal females, might protect against the development of the disease, whereas increased production or exogenous administration much later in life might predispose to thrombosis over existing complicated lesions. The pill may induce vascular disease for reasons beyond the increases in thrombosis, blood pressure, and metabolic derangements. Estrogens given to both men and women with abnormal stress tests cause the (ECG) derangements to become even more abnormal in most persons, which suggests an estrogen-induced increase in coronary artery smooth-muscle tone. Such a mechanism could explain the development of transmural myocardial infarctions in 

young women on the pill, who have normal coronary angiograms, and the four times greater rate of normal coronary angiograms in women than in men with ischemia on ECG. Another mechanism for pill-induced vascular damage may be proliferation in coronary vessels of fibroblasts and smooth-muscle cells similar to that demonstrable in uterine arteries and in tissue cultures exposed to serum from oral contraceptive users. 

###### Strokes 

The association between oral contraceptive use and strokes is strong: in a collaborative study of 598 women, aged 15 to 44, who had had a stroke, oral contraceptive users had a 9.5 times greater risk of thrombotic stroke and a 2.0 times greater risk of hemorrhagic stroke. In this study, oral contraceptive use alone was a significant risk factor for stroke, in the absence of smoking, hypertension, or migraine. Similar data have come from the Boston Collaborative Drug Surveillance Program and the Kaiser-Permanente Contraceptive Drug Study, where the risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage was 6.5 times greater for oral contraceptive users than for nonusers, and the risk appeared to increase with the duration of use of oral contraceptives. 

###### Thromboembolism 

An increased tendency for the blood to clot may also be an important mechanism by which the pill induces vascular disease, both directly within leg veins and various arteries and indirectly by obstructing blood flow to vital organs by embolization and thrombus formation. 

Most investigators have found an increased risk of both peripheral venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in oral contraceptive users, with the relative increase varying from two- to twelvefold. Various epidemiological techniques have been used to identify this increased risk: 

- 1 Retrospective case-control studies such as those from the Boston Collaborative Drug Surveillance Program (Table 6) and from Sartwell and coworkers show eleven- and fourfold increased risks, respectively. 

- 2 Review of mortality rate statistics has shown an increase in the mortality rate in oral contraceptive users.

- 3 Reports of adverse reactions, which likely underestimate the incidence, imply a definite increase in risk. 

- 4 Prospective trials, the largest of which is currently under way in England by the Royal College of General Practitioners, have found increased risk of deep leg vein thrombosis. 

The use of lower-dose estrogen pills seems to have decreased the risk by at least a fourth, but women taking pills containing only 30 to 50 ug estrogen continue to have more deep vein thrombosis. 

A number of possible mechanisms by which estrogens increase thrombus formation have been suggested: 

- 1 Enhancement of coagulation by decreasing the negative surface charge on vessel walls and blood ceils 

- 2 Decrease in the linear velocity of biood flow induced by the greater distensibility of peripheral veins 

- 3 Changes in the coagulation and fibrinolytic systems which favor clotting, including decreased plasma antithrombin III activity and reduced activated factor X inhibitory activity 

In addition, arteries may be thickened and roughened by structural changes induced by intimal proliferation or deposition of atheromas. Structural changes involving endothelial proliferation and intimal thickening were first reported in women who died suddenly from a_thromboembolic event while taking oral contraceptives. More recently, similar changes were found in arteries from uteri removed from living women. Atheroma deposition may be favored by 

increased serum triglycerides and decreased glucose tolerance. 

###### Other occlusive vascular disease 

Vessels other than myocardial and cerebral vessels have been involved in oral contraceptive users, including the retinal, mesenteric, pancreatic, renal, and aortoiliac vasculature. 

###### Hypertension 

Frequency of oral contraceptive-induced hypertension The RCGP study found a 2.6 times greater incidence of hypertension among contraceptive pill users than among non-pill users, resulting in an overall incidence of 5 percent after 5 years of pill use. Though other estimates vary from as low as zero to as high as 20 percent, the RCGP figure is likely to be close to the overall true incidence. 

Most, if not all, women who take estrogencontaining oral contraceptives have some rise in blood pressure (Fig. 1), though only a few go beyond the 140/90 level that defines hypertension. In a prospective study by Weir and coworkers in Glasgow of 186 women taking the pill for 2 years or more, systolic pressure rose in 164, and diastolic pressure rose in 150. Among their controls, 60 women using cervical diaphragms or IUDs, no significant change in blood pressure was recorded. Among these 186 women on the pill, 8 had rises in systolic pressure greater than 25 mmHg, and 2 had rises in diastolic pressure of 24 and 34 mmHg. 

Predisposing factors for hypertension Age over 35 and obesity appear to be associated with a higher incidence of pill-induced hypertension.

Beyond these two factors, there appears to be a small increased risk in women who have had pregnancy-induced hypertension or preexisting hypertension. Genetic factors may also be involved in the risk for development of hypertension. The dose of estrogen may also affect the frequency of hypertension. Briggs and Briggs found no significant effect on the blood pressure after use for 3 years of the 30-ug estrogen pill, whereas a Significant rise occurred in women taking a pill containing 50 wg estrogen. Weir reported that some women who developed hypertension while taking 50-ug estrogen pills had a significant fall in their blood pressures when they switched to 30-wg estrogen pills. However, other women had a return of hypertension with the lower-dose preparation. 

The mechanism for estrogen-induced hypertension The estrogen is almost certainly the culprit, since progestogen-only preparations rarely, if ever, cause hypertension. Estrogen induces an increase in the synthesis of several proteins in the liver. Among these is the renin substrate angiotensinogen. Since the formation of angiotensin follows first-order kinetics, an increase in the substrate causes an increase in angiotensin synthesis. Under normal conditions increase in angiotensin suppresses renin release, which returns the system to its preestrogen state at the expense of increased angiotensin levels (Fig. 2). The increase in angiotensin may induce hypertension by means of two mechanisms: vasoconstriction and increased aldosterone biosynthesis, which results in renal sodium retention. decrease in renal blood flow may contribute to the fluid retention. The validity of this model for estrogen-induced hypertension has not been established, but considerable inferential evidence supports this mechanism: (1) the plasma volume and cardiac output are increased; (2) sodium retention accompanies estrogen use and disappears when the estrogen is stopped; (3) treatment with an aldosterone antagonist often relieves the hypertension; and (4) blockade of angiotensin’s action by a competitive antagonist lowers the blood pressure. 

The consequences of estrogen-induced hypertension Hypertension predisposes _ to direct vascular damage and accelerates atherosclerosis. In a few individuals, the increase in blood pressure may occur so quickly and be so great as to provoke malignant hypertension and extensive renal vascular damage. In most, the blood pressure rise is less striking and less damaging. However, over many years, an elevated blood pressure may be involved in the increased occurrence of myocardial infarction, stroke, and other vascular accidents noted in women who take estrogens. 

A basic question remains unanswered: Does estrogen use cause hypertension de novo, or does it simply uncover at an earlier time hypertension that would have developed spontaneously? At least half of the women who stop taking the pill become normotensive, though it may take longer than 3 months for the pressure to fall. Data are inadequate to ascertain whether those who develop reversible pill hypertension subsequently develop spontaneous, idiopathic hypertension. 

Recommendations for prevention ‘The following guidelines seem appropriate to reduce the frequency of estrogen-induced hypertension: 

1 Provide other forms of contraceptive for women who are over age 35, obese, or already hypertensive. 

- 2 Use the smallest effective dose of estrogen. 3 Prescribe only a limited supply, enough for 3 months initially and for 6 months thereafter, with no refills permitted. Therefore, the recipient must return to a medical facility for monitoring of blood pressure. 

###### Recommendations for management 

- 1 If the pressure rises to above 140/90, stop the estrogen, provide other forms of contraception, and follow the patient every 1 to 2 months. No laboratory work is needed unless the patient remains hypertensive after 4 to 6 months, when workup appropriate for idiopathic hypertension should be performed. 

- 2 If the pressure is above 160/110, it may be helpful to treat the patient immediately, withdrawing therapy if the pressure falls after stopping the estrogen. 

- 3 If estrogens must be continued for contraception, the hypertension can probably be managed successfully with a combination of a thiazide diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist, though other antihypertensive agents may also be as effective. 

###### Hyperlipidemia 

The relationship between oral contraceptive use, lipids, and the occurrence of vascular disease is uncertain. Part of the confusion relates to the varying effects of the estrogen and the progestogen in various oral contraceptives and their differing doses. The relationship should be considered in the light of these facts: 

- ] Premenopausal women with higher endogenous estrogen and progesterone levels have less atherosclerosis than men. 

- 2 Premenopausal women have lower concentrations of serum LDL cholesterol and higher concentrations of HDL cholesterol (Fig. 3). 

- 3 Men who have myocardial infarction before age 40 have higher levels of endogenous estrogen and normal levels of testosterone. 

- 4 Increased levels of LDL cholesterol clearly increased cardiovascular risk; high levels of HDL cholesterol are associated with less coronary heart disease in people aged 40 or over, but a protective effect of high HDL cholesterol in younger people has not been established. 

- 5 Estrogens alone increase serum HDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels. The more estrogen, the higher the HDL and triglyceride levels.

- 6 The effect of progestogens depend upon the type: the estranes (e.g., norethynodrel) have little or no antiestrogenic action and tend to increase plasma HDL; the gonanes (e.g., norgestrel) have strong antiestrogenic effects, lower plasma HDL, and cause the least rise in triglycerides. The effects of various progestogens on lipid levels depend not only upon their degree of estrogenic or antiestrogenic action but also on their degree of androgenic, anabolic, and progestational action. Moreover, they have varying effects on the apolipoprotein components of HDL. 

Thus, the overall effect of a given oral contraceptive depends upon the type and amount of estrogen and progestogen. In the past, most attention was directed to the estrogen dose, since more thromboembolic disease occurred with the 

higher-dose estrogen (75 to 200 mg) preparations. Now most preparations contain 20 to 30 wg of ethinyl estradiol, though a fourth of oral contraceptives sold in the United States in 1978 contained more than 50 pg. 

###### Carbohydrate tolerance 

The oral contraceptive formula may also affect plasma carbohydrate metabolism in various ways. In Wynn’s study of 1628 women taking various oral contraceptives and 577 women not taking them, oral glucose tolerance tests (GTTs: 1 g/kg glucose load) were done measuring glucose and insulin at 30-min intervals. The area under the 3-h curve was used to derive indexes of carbohydrate tolerance. Oral glucose tolerance was impaired in women on all six types of oral contraceptives, though the fasting plasma glucose was lower. The high-estrogen oral contraceptive showed the greatest elevation of the oral GTT. Fasting and postglucose insulin levels were elevated in most oral contraceptive groups. Those oral contraceptives with 75 mg or more estrogen combined with an estrane progestogen caused the greatest loss of glucose tolerance and impaired insulin secretion. With less estrogen and the same progestogen, glucose tolerance was less impaired and insulin secretion was _ increased. With a gonane progestogen and low estrogen content, glucose tolerance was less impaired but insulin secretion was even higher. 

###### Neoplasia 

Benign and malignant growths in various organs have been reported to be more common in women who take oral contraceptives. But the overall risk seems small, and there is no clear evidence that oral contraceptives cause any form of cancer. However, it took 25 years to identify malignancies in the children of women who took stilbesterol during pregnancy and almost 15 years of oral contraceptive use for the first case of hepatic tumor in oral contraceptive users to be recognized. 

Breast Fibrocystic breast disease and fibroadenomas are less common in oral contraceptive users; breast cancer does not seem to be affected. 

66 COMPLICATIONS OF THE BIRTH CONTROL PILL 

Uterus Estrogens given to postmenopausal women increase the incidence of endometrial cancer, but a decreased risk has been found in younger women taking oral contraceptives. The progestogen may be protective. 

Cervix There may be a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer, but lesions that have been interpreted as possibly precancerous may reflect noninvasive histological changes and an increased surveillance among oral contraceptive users. Liver First recognized in 1973, benign liver tumors have been reported in over 200 oral contraceptive users. Most liver tumors are well differentiated, and the mortality rate stems from their rupture with intraabdominal bleeding. However, hepatocellular carcinomas have been reported in more than 20 users of birth control pills. 

Pituitary Sherman et al. reported 42 women with prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas, 74 percent of whom developed amenorrhea and/or galactorrhea in immediate association with the use or discontinuation of oral contraceptives or after pregnancy. They suggest that estrogen, known to modulate prolactin secretion in normals, can induce the growth and expression of some otherwise silent pituitary lesions that occur in 5 to 10 percent of the population. The portion that are potentially prolactin-secreting are those whose growth and function can be stimulated by 

estrogen. They conclude that estrogen-containing oral contraceptives provide an estrogenic stimulus greater than that of physiological endogenous estrogen secretion during mature reproductive life or even pregnancy and that longterm Use of oral contraceptives can result in the clinical expression of otherwise silent tumors. 

This association has been questioned by other investigators who believe that the apparent increase in the incidence rate (of pituitary adenomas) may be due primarily to improvements in endocrinological screening, advances in diagnostic radiology, and the development of safe and effective surgery rather than the use of the birth control pill. 

###### Miscellaneous 

Rheumatoid arthritis In the RCGP study, only half as many oral contraceptive users as nonusers developed rheumatoid arthritis. Migraine Along with various organic vascular syndromes, the incidence of migraine is increased among oral contraceptive users. 

Nonspecific symptoms Goldzieher _ performed a controlled study in women, a third of whom were given placebos (Table 7). Most complaints were seen about as commonly in women on the placebo and tended to decrease in frequency from month | to month 4 of the study both with placebo use and with oral contraceptive use.

#### THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

###### J. PHILIP KISTLER and ALLAN H. ROPPER 

As defined in Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, the term cerebral vascular disease refers to any disease implicating one or more of the blood vessels of the brain in a pathologic process. The process may be intrinsic to the vessel as in atherosclerosis, inflammation, dissection, or rupture; or it may arise from a remote site, as when an embolus lodges in an intracranial vessel or when there is inadequate blood flow through a vessel due to decreased perfusion pressure. A stroke is said to occur when any one of these pathologic processes results in either infarction or hemorrhage. Refinements of clinical analysis and neuroradiologic techniques have now reached the point where the type and location of strokes and their concomitant vascular lesions can be diagnosed with a high degree of accuracy. Once a stroke or transient spell of cerebral ischemia has occurred, the prelude to adequate preventive therapy is a precise diagnosis. In planning therapy, the characterization and localization of the pathologic process and knowledge of the vascular anatomy of the collateral circulation to the area of ischemia are of utmost importance (Fig. 1). Because brain tissue cannot regenerate and repairs itself only by forming fibrogliotic scar tissue at the site of infarction or hemorrhage, therapeutic efforts must be directed toward protecting the normal and ischemic brain from subsequent ischemia as well as from the secondary effects produced by the stroke itself. In its broadest sense, such preventive therapy 

has three aspects: first, prevention of the stroke by reducing the “risk factors,’ thus preventing the pathologic process from occurring; second, prevention of initial and recurrent strokes by eliminating or nullifying the pathologic process once it has developed, e.g., carotid endarterectomy or anticoagulant therapy in a patient with carotid transient ischemic attack; and, third, the prevention of further cerebral damage secondary to the effects of the acute stroke by maintaining adequate cerebral perfusion pressure and/or decreasing the mass effect of edema or hemorrhage. It should be noted at the outset that except for the elimination of risk factors, all these forms of therapy are controversial. A considerable literature has accumulated on the treatment of cerebrovascular disease. The conclusions have been inconsistent and difficult to interpret. Part of the difficulty has been that cases have not been selected with sufficient diagnostic accuracy. Strokes in the same vascular territory but caused by different mechanisms have been placed in the same diagnostic category. Another problem has been confusion of therapeutic objectives. Is the objective to restore function lost during a stroke, to survive the stroke, to prevent further strokes, or to lengthen the span of life by preventing heart attacks and other complications of hypertensive and atherosclerotic vascular disease? Finally, certain diagnostic measures and therapies carry their own risks, which vary from patient to patient and from institution to institution, and hence the

Lacking published proof of a given method, we will point out the present practice of many staff members of the neurology and neurosurgical services of the Massachusetts General 

Hospital. Our methods are largely empirical and are based on knowledge of the risks of diagnostic procedures and therapies at our institution. Readers must decide for themselves whether our methods are practicable in their hospitals and clinics.

Systolic blood pressure seems to be as important as diastolic blood pressure in causing both large and small vessel disease. Furthermore, effective long-term control of high blood pressure has been shown to decrease the incidence of both ischemic strokes and intracerebral hemorrhages. Smoking, obesity, and hyperlipidemia have also been strongly implicated as risk factors. Structural cardiac disease and arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation) have been associated with embolic strokes and are therefore regarded as major risk factors. 

###### CEREBRAL INFARCTION AND ISCHEMIA DUE TO THROMBOSIS AND ATHEROSCLEROSIS OF LARGE VESSELS 

###### Atherothrombotic disease of the internal carotid artery and its branches 

By and large, atherosclerosis in the internal carotid artery and its branches is confined to the artery’s origin, the siphon of the internal carotid artery (S-shaped portion of the internal carotid artery in the cavernous sinus), and the proximal 

###### 1 

###### THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

middle or anterior cerebral arteries. Symptoms produced by stenosis or occlusion (thrombotic or embolic) of these arteries depend on the adequacy of collateral circulation to the cerebral territory supplied by the vessel (Fig. 1). 

Atherothrombotic disease of the internal carotid artery origin PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Atherosclerotic narrowing usually occurs in the posterior portion of the proximal internal carotid artery, often extending into the common carotid artery (Fig. 2A). Stenosis at this site produces symptomatic hemodynamic changes when the vessel luminal area is narrowed by approximately 80 percent or when the residual lumen diameter is less than 2 mm. Such “low-flow” symptoms generally occur in the distal cerebral territory of the ipsilateral middle cerebral artery when collateral circulation around the circle of Willis is impaired. If the reduction in flow is severe enough, focal ‘“‘watershed”’ infarction will ensue. 

Atherosclerotic disruption of endothelium in the internal carotid artery allows tissue factors and collagen in the vessel wall to be exposed to blood and stimulates platelet aggregation and formation of mural thrombus. Occasionally, blood from the lumen dissects into an atheromatous plaque at the carotid bifurcation. This may be the 

###### FIGURE 2 

A. Angiogram showing atherosclerotic stenosis of the proximal internal carotid artery (arrow). B. Angiogram showing stenosis of the intracranial internal carotid artery just below the siphon section (arrow). 

mechanism for the formation of an ulcer crater, which then becomes a nidus for the production of mural thrombus. Less frequently, hemorrhage into an atheromatous plaque further narrows the lumen. In the majority of cases atheromatous narrowing of the lumen occurs in a conical fashion, with the length of maximal narrowing being only | to 2 mm. Mural thrombus may form at the narrowest point or proximal to it. Although an ulcerated plaque may be the only lesion found in symptomatic disease of the proximal internal carotid artery, more often a stenotic lesion with a residual lumen diameter of less than 2 to 3 mm is also found. Emboli arising from a lesion at the origin of the internal carotid artery may produce symptoms in the territory of the ipsilateral middle or anterior cerebral artery. The size of the embolus and laminar flow characteristics determine the vessels to be occluded. For example, platelet emboli may involve only the distal vessels of the eye, whereas larger emboli composed of platelet fibrin clots tend to occlude larger arteries, e.g., the middle cerebral artery or one of its branches. Once the internal carotid artery is totally occluded at its origin, the clot propagates upward. Embolic material may break off from the freshly formed occluding thrombus or from the distal stump of the propagating thrombus to lodge in the middle or anterior cerebral arteries or one of their branches. 

In many cases, prodromal symptoms or a minor stroke will herald the onset of impending or complete carotid occlusion prior to the onset of a devastating stroke. In this regard, several commonly used terms need to be mentioned. Stroke in evolution or progressive stroke refers to syndromes in which the neurological deficit is progressing or fluctuating while the patient is under observation. A completed stroke is one in which no further deterioration occurs. Unfortunately, there is often no straightforward way for clinicians to decide during initial contact with the patient whether a stroke is completed or if further deterioration is likely to occur. These terms therefore have limited value but are still used frequently in the literature. A variety of pathologic mechanisms have been suggested to explain stroke in evolution: for example, progressive narrowing of an artery by thrombus, secondary brain edema, thrombus propagation which oblit- 

Ue} 

###### CEREBRAL INFARCTION AND ISCHEMIA 

erates collateral branches to the ischemic brain, and systemic illness, to name a few. Although these factors may play a role in the acute stroke in the carotid territory, other possibilities seem more likely. (1) Cerebral emboli can cause a fluctuating deficit. In this setting it is suspected that the embolus is intermittently occluding the proximal middle cerebral artery, which produces fluctuating or progressive symptoms. (2) During acute carotid occlusion, fluctuations in collateral flow from the anterior or posterior circle of Willis or through the meningeal anastomoses may result in intermittent ischemia in the territory of the middle and anterior cerebral arteries or their branches. Because the incidence of the sudden onset of a major internal carotid stroke is low [80 percent present with a transient warning symptom or minor stroke (Fisher)], the physician usually has time to initiate therapy. The best and safest preventive therapy, however, may not always be obvious and often is controversial. The following offers general guidelines for evaluation and therapy of stroke caused by an atherothrombotic process at the origin of the internal carotid artery. 

EVALUATION AND THERAPY ° If the patient is seen in the first few hours after the stroke, the severity of the stroke is an important factor in choosing therapies. If there is involvement of the entire middle cerebral artery territory supplied by the internal carotid artery, as would be suggested if there was a complete hemiplegia associated with aphasia or apractagnosia, then for the moment prevention of further strokes in that region becomes meaningless. Anticoagulation or surgical therapy would appear to have no role. Careful attention to maintenance of an adequate blood pressure and prevention of cerebral edema as outlined below become important. If, on the other hand, significant improvement occurs or the deficit is small (minor stroke), there is potential for another stroke in the same arterial territory. It then becomes important to determine the exact pathologic process at the origin of the carotid artery and the availability of collateral circulation. Careful auscultation of the carotid bifurcation for a bruit is mandatory. Ophthalmodynamometry, once a_ preferred bed- 

side test, may indicate a hemodynamically significant lesion at the common carotid bifurcation. As suggested by Ackerman, noninvasive evaluation of extracranial carotid flow by Doppler examination and oculoplethysmography combined with direct estimation of the residual lumen diameter by quantitative phonoangiography and ultrasound imaging may implicate the internal carotid artery as the location of the pathologic process that caused the stroke. Selective common carotid angiography, however, remains the definitive test for the demonstration of carotid lesions. 

When suspicion arises that stenosis or recent occlusion at the carotid bifurcation has caused a minor stroke, the question of whether to use medical or surgical therapy or both arises. There is some evidence to suggest that anticoagulant therapy is beneficial in patients with minor strokes, especially if the deficit is acutely fluctuating or progressing, but there is little evidence in support of anticoagulant therapy once a thrombotic stroke is complete (Genton et al.). In many published studies the exact pathologic mechanism of the stroke was not documented adequately anda reliable assessment of the value of anticoagulant therapy was not obtained. It is our impression that acute anticoagulation in a patient with minor stroke from a tightly stenotic and/or ulcerated lesion at the origin of the internal carotid artery may be of value in preventing a second, possibly more devastating, event. Although deterioration from hemorrhage into an area of infarction is possible, this complication has not been a problem in our patients. 

Endarterectomy has also been recommended for patients with an ulcerated, tightly stenotic, or acutely occluded (hours), proximal internal carotid artery who have had a minor stroke in the territory distal to that lesion (Ojemann et al., Sundt et al., Robertson and Watridge). Although the risk of further neurological deterioration in such patients is not known, the risk of surgery in most patients is as low as 2 to 3 percent. Medical contraindications to surgery include congestive heart failure and recent myocardial infarction. Possible contraindications include severe pulmonary, renal, or hepatic disease, infection, and metastatic carcinoma. Although it has been suggested that hemorrhage into a cerebral infarct 

74 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

may follow carotid endarterectomy, this is probably rare. Careful control of blood pressure in the postoperative period minimizes the risks of hypertensive hemorrhage. In practical terms, when a patient presents with a minor ischemic stroke and a suspected atherothrombotic lesion at the carotid bifurcation, anticoagulation with heparin is instituted. Cerebral angiography is then planned if the patient is considered medically stable enough to undergo endarterectomy (Fig. 2A). Angiography is best accomplished by selective injection of both the ipsilateral and the contralateral common carotid arteries through a transfemoral approach. Both extra- and intracranial views are required to demonstrate the etiology of the stroke and the nature of the collateral circulation to the ischemic area. The risk of angiography has varied from 12 percent to less than 1 percent in different studies (Faught et al., Buonanno and Toole). Although risk may be greater in patients with tightly stenotic lesions at the carotid bifurcation, angiography is relatively safe provided an experienced angiographer performs the procedure. In any instance where surgery is considered, the morbidity rate of surgery should be less than 3 percent. If tight stenosis and/or a large ulcerative lesion is found and the patient is medically stable, then surgery may be recommended. In selected cases of acute carotid artery occlusion less than 12 h old with minor neurological deficits, surgery may also be considered (Ojemann et al.). When the contralateral carotid is tightly stenctic or occluded, endarterectomy of the ipsilateral carotid may be expected to have a higher morbidity rate, but it should still be less than 3 percent in experienced hands when there are no medical contraindications. It must be noted, however, that there are no valid studies comparing the natural history of such cases with surgical results. Nevertheless, common _ experience suggests that more than 3 percent of such cases develop further neurological deterioration after a minor stroke. If surgery is contraindicated or if the lesion is at a surgically inaccessible site such as the high cervical area, long-term medical therapy is recommended. If heparin has already been instituted, it is usually maintained for several days up to 2 weeks through a continuous intravenous infusion, keeping the partial thromboplastin time at 

50 to 70 s (normal 30 s), or it may be given asa bolus injection every 3 to 4 h. When embolic stroke from the carotid lesion is suspected, warfarin (Coumadin) therapy is subsequently instituted and maintained for as long as 6 months to several years, depending on the general medical and neurological status of the individual patient. The value of warfarin therapy beyond 6 months is unknown and must be weighed against the risk of bleeding complications. The risk of bleeding is greatly reduced by keeping the prothrombin time within 14 times that of control. The value of antiplatelet therapy in the setting of a tightly stenotic or totally occluded carotid bifurcation lesion which has produced a minor stroke is unknown. If anticoagulation therapy is medically contraindicated, administration of enough buffered aspirin to prolong the bleeding time may be considered an alternative form of therapy. 

Atherothrombotic disease of the carotic siphon: siphon stenosis The diagnosis of siphon stenosis distal to the ophthalmic artery as a source of embolic or low-flow stroke is made only by angiography (Fig. 2B). When siphon stenosis is encountered as the cause of a stroke, the residual lumen diameter is generally less than 2 mm. Surgical therapy consists of extracranial-intracranial bypass anastomosis, whereas medical therapy consists of either anticoagulants (warfarin) or antiplatelet drugs. Aspirin is the most commonly used antiplatelet agent. It is generally given as a 300-mg tablet once or twice a day, i.e., in sufficient quantities to prolong the bleeding time. To date there are no good guidelines on the relative value of surgical vs. medical therapy. This is currently the subject of a multicentered prospective randomized study (Barnett). In general, when siphon stenosis is suspected as the source of an embolus, anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy is recommended first. If further cerebrovascular symptoms occur, then extracranial-intracranial anastomosis is considered. 

Atherothrombotic disease of the middle cerebral artery: middle cerebral stem stenosis and occlusion Occlusion of the middle cerebral artery stem (the segment between the origin of the middle cerebral artery and the first bifurcation) is infrequently caused by atherothrombosis; 

###### CEREBRAL INFARCTION AND ISCHEMIA 

embolic occlusion is more frequent. When the occlusion causes a major neurological deficit, there is no role for emergency extracranial-intracranial artery bypass grafting, embolectomy, or acute anticoagulation. Management of the patient in these circumstances follows the general treatment for cerebral infarction. When atherosclerotic middle cerebral stem stenosis produces a limited infarct distal to the stenotic area, aggressive therapy is indicated, since it is ourexperience that total occlusion and major infarction may ensue. Hinton et al. (1979) reported that no strokes occurred following anticoagulation therapy (sodium warfarin) in 16 patients with mild stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) associated with atherosclerotic middle cerebral artery stem stenosis. As yet there are no data on the value of antiplatelet therapy in the setting of symptomatic middle cerebral artery stem stenosis. The value of extracranialintracranial bypass grafting versus medical therapy is currently currently under investigation in the same cooperative study that is investigating patients with carotid artery occlusion or siphon stenosis (Barnett). In symptomatic middle cerebral artery stem stenosis, anticoagulation is presently recommended, but antiplatelet therapy may be used. used. If further further symptoms occur, the patient may then be referred for extracranial-intracranial arterial anastomosis. 

When a lateral medullary infarction occurs, acute anticoagulant therapy with heparin may be used in an effort to prevent clot propagation into the proximal basilar artery, but the value of this therapy or long-term warfarin therapy is unknown. Before anticoagulation is used, a CT scan should be obtained to rule out unsuspected hemorrhage. The posterior inferior parts of the cerebellum are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and may also become infarcted if collateral circulation is not provided by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery. Rarely, edema formation in the infarcted cerebellum may cause pressure symptoms in the posterior fossa and result in progressive obtundation and death. Although cerebellar swelling can be treated initially with osmotic agents such as mannitol, surgical decompression may be necessary. A stable patient seen days or weeks after vertebral occlusion requires no therapy.

Occlusion of the distal vertebral artery or proximal posterior inferior cerebellar artery Occlusion of the distal vertebral artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery is most often caused by atherothrombosis. ###### Transient ischemic attack (TIA) 

In order to choose therapy for TIAs, a precise diagnosis of the nature and location of the caus- 

###### yo 

76 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

ative arterial lesions is necessary. When other conditions such as seizures and migraine are excluded, the ominous natural history of TIAs becomes clear (Duncan et al.). 

TIAs occur in three arterial territories: carotid, vertebral-basilar, and small penetrating vessels (lacunar TIA). There appear to be two principal mechanisms for TIAs: (1) recurrent embolism and (2) decreased blood flow distal to an atherothrombotic lesion (“low flow’’). However, precise information regarding the pathogenesis of these mechanisms is limited. After careful assessment of the patient’s history, physical examination, noninvasive evaluation of the extracranial circulation, and even angiography, the physician may still have difficulty in deciding what caused the TIA or which artery is involved. 

Appropriate therapy for TIAs remains controversial, and it is best to tailor therapy to the individual patient, carefully weighing the risk against the benefits. Therapeutic risks have varied in different institutions, and there is disagreement about potential benefits (Duncan etal., Easton and Sherman, Brust). Most physicians agree, however, that diagnosis and therapy are most successful when undertaken by a team of physicians and surgeons who share an extensive common experience in the field (Easton and Sherman). 

TIAs as a result of nonoccluding atherothrombotic disease of the proximal internal carotid artery PATHOPHYSIOLOGY TIAs in the territory of the internal carotid artery take two forms: transient monocular blindness (TMB) and transient hemispheric attack (THA). The two main theories of their pathogenesis are embolism and decreased blood flow in a specific vessel (low flow). Fisher coined the term local embolus to characterize an embolus arising from an atherosclerotic stenotic or ulcerated plaque at the origin of the internal carotid artery. Such an artery-to-artery embolus may progress rapidly through the distal carotid branches to produce TMB if the retinal vessels are involved or THA if the cerebral vessels are occluded. Although stereotyped, repeated, shortlived THAs have been attributed to emboli being carried to the same location by “laminar flow,” a more plausible explanation may be that such TIAs result from transiently decreased blood 

flow distal to an atherothrombotic stenotic or occlusive lesion, i.e., low flow. For example, recurrent stereotyped TIAs occur in patients with a tightly stenotic lesion or with total occlusion of the proximal internal carotid artery when collateral flow around the circle of Willis is compromised. Other mechanisms occasionally seen include cardiac arrhythmia (which, although often suspected, is rarely responsible), polycythemia, thrombocythemia, and orthostatic hypotension. 

In studies of the natural history of carotid TIAs, the incidence of stroke has varied from 2 to 50 percent (Duncan et al.). This wide discrepancy results from imprecise categorization of patients, variable length of follow-up, and lack of angiographic documentation. Obviously, the natural history of TIAs associated with emboli arising from the heart differs from the natural history of TIAs that occur in patients as a result of a tight carotid stenosis. Although it has been reported that approximately 5 to 8 percent of patients with TIAs will have a stroke per year of follow-up, only some of these TIAs are due to tightly stenotic or severely ulcerated lesions at the carotid bifurcation. As suggested by Ziegler and Hassanein, patients with TIAs associated with tightly stenotic lesions at the carotic bifurcation are probably in greater jeopardy of suffering a stroke. Caution should be used, however, in attributing the cause of TIAs to a smoothly stenotic lesion at the carotid bifurcation with residual lumen diameter of greater than 2 to 3 mm or to a mild irregularity in the lumen. Cardiac embolic events and lacunar TIAs can closely mimic TIAs caused by atherothrombotic disease at the origin of the internal carotid artery. 

THERAPY Anticoagulant therapy Studies on the effectiveness of anticoagulant therapy in preventing strokes or further TIAs in the territory of the carotid artery can be criticized for a number of reasons, such as lack of randomization, too few patients, and lack of uniformity in the diagnosis of the etiology of the TIA. There is some indirect evidence that the benefits of anticoagulants offset the risk of bleeding complications (Duncan et al., Millikan and McDowell, Genton et al.). We agree with the opinion that anticoagulation may be of benefit in patients with carotid TIAs who are not candidates for endarterectomy for medical reasons or because the 

Antiplatelet therapy Studies evaluating the effect of antiplatelet agents on the natural history of TIAs can be criticized for the same reasons as those concerned with anticoagulant therapy, i.e., lack of randomization, insufficient numbers to reach a conclusion, and lack of specific pathophysiologic diagnosis of the cause of the TIA. Despite shortcomings there is suggestive evidence from The Canadian Cooperative Study Group that aspirin is beneficial in preventing TIAs and stroke in male patients who are having TIAs or have had a small stroke. In another randomized prospective study by Fields et al. in which angiography was routinely performed, aspirin tended to benefit those patients who had TIAs associated with a lesion in the internal carotid artery and not those who had a single TIA and no carotid lesion, i.e., those suspected of having emboli from the heart. These two studies form the basis for aspirin therapy in TIAs, but they suffer from statistical problems that make their conclusions only tentative. 14 times the control cervical segment of the internal carotid artery. When sodium warfarin is used, the prothrombin time should not exceed value. Contraindications to anticoagulant thersion, uremia, hepatic failure, and poor patient compliance. lesions are surgically noncorrectable or inaccessible, e.g., in the carotid siphon or in the upper apy include bleeding ulcer, malignant hyperten- 

Recently, theoretical objections to too much aspirin therapy have been raised (Marcus). Aspirin inhibits formation of the platelet-aggregating, vasoconstricting prostaglandin, thromboxane A,, but it has the undesired effect of simultaneously inhibiting the formation of the antiaggregating vasodilating prostaglandin, prostacyclin. Because aspirin in low doses may have greater inhibiting effect on thromboxane A, production in platelets than on prostacyclin production in endothelial cells, it is currently recommended by some investigators that aspirin be used in small doses of 300 to 600 mg a day, Le., just enough to prolong the bleeding time. Dipyridamole (Persantin) is thought to act by inhibiting platelet phosphodiesterase, the enzyme that breaks down cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP). The resulting elevation of platelet cyclic AMP inhibits the aggregation of circulating platelets. If this is true, then low-dose dipyridamole, 25 mg four times a day, may be 

###### CEREBRAL INFARCTION AND ISCHEMIA 

useful as an adjunct to aspirin in an antiplatelet regimen. A clinical trial of this combination of antiplatelet therapy is in progress. Sulfinpyrazone (Anturane), a third antiplatelet agent that has been under investigation, is thought to inhibit the platelet release reaction and to interfere with platelet adhesion to subendothelial cells. Although it prolongs platelet survival in patients with prosthetic heart valves, it has not been more effective than aspirin alone in reducing the risk of recurrent TIA or stroke in patients with TIAs (The Canadian Cooperative Study Group). Surgical therapy Endarterectomy is the surgical measure of choice for TIAs due to carotid stenosis or an ulcerated plaque. Many studies have suggested that this procedure is safe and effective. It carries a morbidity rate of 1 to 2 percent in experienced hands (Ojemann et al., Sundt et al.), but may have a higher morbidity rate when performed infrequently (Easton and Sherman). Most patients who undergo endarterectomy have hypertensive arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease and peripheral vascular disease and require careful pre- and postoperative medical evaluation. Active coronary artery disease in the form of unstable angina or recent myocardial infarction (less than 6 months) and congestive heart failure are contraindications to surgery. Hypertension should be treated, but excessive lowering of the blood pressure should be avoided if there is a question of tight carotid artery stenosis. The combined complication rate of angiography and surgery should be less than 3 percent. If it is higher, the surgical risk approaches the risk of having the very stroke that the surgery is designed to prevent. 

Careful study of the collateral circulation to the ipsilateral carotid territory by selective extraand intracranial cerebral angiography is important in preoperative assessment. Patients with tightly stenotic lesions of one carotid and contralateral carotid occlusion or an inadequate circle of Willis are at somewhat higher risk of intraoperative stroke. In this regard, intraoperative electroencephalographic monitoring is useful in detecting cerebral ischemia during the operation so that the surgeon may take steps to improve circulation during the procedure. Although stenosis does recur after endarterectomy, this complication is rare. 

The management of bilateral severe proximal 

###### 77 

78 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

internal carotid stenosis is of special concern. It seems reasonable to operate.on the symptomatic side. In some of our cases, however, the tighter asymptomatic internal carotid artery has occluded after endarterectomy of the symptomatic carotid bifurcation. In these cases, it was suspected that collateral flow across the anterior circle of Willis raised the pressure in the asymptomatic distal internal carotid artery, thereby precipitating occlusion. Therefore, in this setting consideration could be given to operating on the tighter asymptomatic side first. 

Tandem lesions of the internal carotid artery, i.e., one at the carotid bifurcation and one at the carotid siphon, require special consideration. If the carotid stenosis is predominant and the siphon has a lumen diameter greater than 2 mm, carotid endarterectomy can be recommended. If the carotid siphon narrowing is more severe, the value of endarterectomy is uncertain, and consideration may be given to anticoagulant therapy Or extracranial-intracranial bypass surgery. There is no consensus as to the efficacy of either therapy in this setting. 

TIAS as a result of occlusion of the internal carotid artery, stenosis of the carotid siphon, or stenosis of the middle cerebral artery stem I[nall three of these situations uncertainty remains as to whether the TIA is due to a reduction in blood flow or to embolus. When TIAs occur in the setting of total internal carotid artery occlusion, emboli from the distal stump of the occluding thrombus have been suspected. Transient low flow to the distal territories of the middle cerebral artery due to poor collateral supply from the circle of Willis has also been implicated. Atheromatous narrowing of the carotid siphon is not expected to cause significant hemodynamic TIAs until the residual lumen diameter is less than 2 mm. In the same manner as occurs in the carotid artery, atheromatous narrowing in the middle cerebral artery stem may cause hemodynamic TIAs before thrombotic occlusion finally develops. 

Although the frequency of ischemic infarction following TIAs in each of these three settings is not known, it does occur. Therapeutic options include anticoagulation with sodium warfarin, antiplatelet therapy as described above, or extracranial-intracranial bypass surgery. In most instances antiplatelet therapy can be recommended 

initially (aspirin) in doses just sufficient to prolong the bleeding time. Should TIAs continue, warfarin anticoagulation or extracranial-intracranial bypass surgery should be considered. Occasionally, it is appropriate to use sodium warfarin therapy or bypass surgery first. Because the value of each of these forms of therapy is uncertain, a multicenter, randomized prospective study is in progress to compare surgical versus medical therapy (Barnett). In summary, therapy for each of these conditions should be tailored to the individual patient, particularly with regard to relative contraindications of anticoagulation and extracranial-intracranial bypass surgery. 

Vertebral-basilar TIAs It has long been recognized that basilar artery occlusion may be preceded by TIAs. The symptoms of TIAs in the vertebral-basilar artery territory are much more diverse than those of carotid TIAs because of the many different neuronal structures involved. They are sometimes confused with the symptoms of end organ disease, e.g., labyrinthine dizziness, which is inherently benign. Also, brainstem TIAs may be due to disease of the small branches of the basilar or vertebral artery rather than of the basilar artery itself. In general, small vessel disease is less threatening. There is some evidence to suggest that anticoagulation is useful in vertebral-basilar TIAs (Millikan and McDowell, Duncan et al., Genton et al.). If a patient is having repeated basilarderived spells, anticoagulation with intravenous heparin is instituted in an effort to prevent basilar occlusion. Once the patient is stable, angiography to document major-vessel basilar artery disease is justified prior to undertaking chronic anticoagulation. The effect of long-term use of anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents in treating TIAs from basilar branch disease has not been studied. 

Lacunar TIAs_ Lacunar strokes occasionally present as TIAs and are discussed below in the section on small vessel disease.

lumen diameter is greater than 2 mm and flow is not impaired or, conversely, when the residual lumen diameter is less than 1 mm and flow is greatly impaired. Quantitative phonoangiography, on the other hand, is most accurate when the bruit arises from a stenotic lesion with a residual lumen diameter between 0.9 and 2.5 mm. In experienced hands, these two types of methods compliment one another and can be used to follow progression of atheromatous disease at the carotid bifurcation (Ackerman). In the future, computerized intravenous angiography of the carotid bifurcation, combined with quantitative phonoangiography, may become the most reliable way to quantitate the degree of carotid narrowing and to follow the patient. Reliable guidelines for the management of the asymptomatic bruit have not been established (Fields, Heyman et al.). Careful studies correlating the underlying pathologic anatomy in the carotid bifurcation with the incidence and etiology of further stroke are lacking. Consequently, controversy exists concerning the value of antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy and the indications for surgical endarterectomy. It is important to identify those bruits that place the patient at high risk of stroke or TIA. It is our view, and that of others, that narrowing of the lumen to less than 2 mm places the patient at greater risk of developing future symptoms. The clinical examination and the above noninvasive methods allow the physician to follow patients and ascertain when this point is reached. Only when stenosis of this severity occurs would we seriously consider angiography and surgery. This recommendation includes those patients with asymptomatic bruits who are to undergo elective thoracic or abdominal surgery. The combined morbidity rates of angiography and surgery should be less than 3 percent to make such a recommendation reasonable. There is general agreement, however, that patients with atheromatous disease at the carotid bifurcation which is significant enough to produce a bruit usually have silent or symptomatic arteriosclerotic cardiovascular and peripheral vascular disease. The decision to perform an endarterectomy for the asymptomatic bruit must be considered with the knowledge of this high incidence of generalized atherosclerotic disease. In lieu of surgery, antiplatelet therapy has become a widespread current practice. 

###### 80 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

###### Other causes of primary largevessel occlusion 

Only a few cases of primary large-vessel occlusion are due to causes other than atherothrombosis. 

Dissection of the cervicocerebral arteries Dissection of the cervical carotid artery may be present without apparent cause or in relation to trauma or dissection of the aortic arch. It occurs in younger patients than does aiteriosclerotic carotid occlusion and may be more common than the literature has indicated. The presenting symptoms are usually headache or neck pain and TMB, THA, or stroke. The onset of a subjective bruit or oculosympathetic palsy (Horner’s syndrome) is an important diagnostic clue. Angiographic features that establish the diagnosis of carotid dissection lesions include a long narrowing “string sign,’ an out-pouching of the vessel (“telltale pouch’’), or a tapering occlusion of the artery. 

Dissection of the vertebral artery is less common and leads to symptoms and signs referable to the brainstem. Dissection of the middle or posterior cerebral arteries can cause transient or permanent neurological symptoms in their respective territories. 

The natural history of dissection lesions is uncertain, and questions of proper management cannot be answered reliably (Fisher et al., 1978). With regard to cervical carotid dissection, therapeutic options include surgical exploration and removal of the dissection, clot, and intima with a Fogarty catheter or medical treatment with anticoagulation or antiplatelet agents. When the patient has only oculosympathetic palsy, TIAs, or a minor stroke, anticoagulation with heparin is recommended except in the rare instance when there is an associated dissection of the aorta. Surgical exploration is generally reserved for patients with increasingly severe TIAs, a mild stroke that is worsening, or symptoms that continue in spite of anticoagulant therapy. Anticoagulation with sodium warfarin for 6 months to a year is recommended for patients not operated upon. Patients with symptomatic vertebral, middle cerebral, or posterior cerebral artery dissection may be managed in the acute stage with heparin and later on with warfarin. 

Fibromuscular dysplasia of the cervical vessels In this disease of young women, carotid and/or vertebral arteries show multiple rings of segmental narrowing alternating with dilatation. Occlusion is usually not complete. The process is generally asymptomatic but occasionally is associated with a bruit, TIA, and stroke. Hypertension, if present, may be the result of renal artery stenosis. The natural history of fibromuscular dysplasia is unknown. Caution should be used in attributing transient ischemic symptoms or an embolic stroke to this disease when the residual lumen diameter of the narrowed portion of the artery is greater than 2 mm. Surgical dilation of the cervical internal carotid artery has been utilized in selected cases. Anticoagulation may be used with TIAs of increasing severity, but there is a higher-than-normal incidence of associated cerebral aneurysms. 

Temporal arteritis and other arteritides of the intra- and extracranial arteries Temporal arteritis is an inflammatory process generally confined to branches of the external carotid artery and the central retinal artery; however, other extracranial and occasionally intracranial arteries may be affected. The value of steroids in preventing progression of the arteritis is undoubted. Prednisone, 40 to 60 mg, or an equivalent corticosteroid is administered as soon as the diagnosis is seriously considered. If a biopsy is confirmatory, steroids are continued and then tapered in several weeks. Systemic symptoms rapidly subside, whereas blindness is apt to be permanent. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) reflects disease activity and may be used as a guide in tapering the steroid dose. The ESR should be kept below 25 mm/h. The duration of therapy is difficult to predict. In some patients, steroids can be discontinued after several months, while in others symptoms recur and restoration of higher steroid doses is necessary. Anticoagulants may be of use in the rare case of internal carotid artery arteritis with fluctuating or intermittent symptoms. Necrotizing or granulomatous arteritis, occurring alone or in association with generalized polyarteritis nodosa or Wegener’s granulomatosis, involves the more distal branches (less than | mm) of the main intracranial arteries. The disease is relentlessly progressive. In some cases steroid therapy (prednisone, 40 to 60 mg per day)
