###### CEREBRAL EMBOLISM 

OCCLUSIVE DISEASE OF THE SMALL PENETRATING VESSELS AT THE BASE OF THE BRAIN: LACUNAR STROKES AND TIAs Granulomatous arteritis involving the great vessels arising from the aortic arch (Takayasu’s syndrome) is a rare cause of cerebral ischemia and infarction. There is no proven effective therapy, but steroids should be tried. Surgical reconstruction may be of value in selected cases. has been helpful; recently, immunosuppressive drugs have been added to the regimen with some reported success. 

Small penetrating nonanastomosing arteries arise from the proximal middle, anterior, or posterior cerebral arteries, basilar artery, arteries of the circle of Willis, and vertebral artery and supply the deep gray and white matter structures of the brain and the brainstem. They are subject to atheromatous narrowing at their origin or more commonly to lipohyalinotic thickening along their course (lipohyalinosis). Both processes are clearly related to hypertension. Occlusion of these vessels causes small 0.5- to 2-cm infarctions called /Jacunes. Frequently, the lacunar infarcts are preceded by transient ischemic symptoms — lacunar TIAs. Lacunar infarcts and TIAs have their own specific clinical syndromes, depending on the vessel involved. Although the value of heparin anticoagulation or antiplatelet agents in lacunar TIAs and fluctuating stroke is not known, such therapy may be considered in an effort to prevent infarction. Initially, care should be taken not to lower the blood pressure precipitously. Once the patient’s condition is stable, gentle lowering of the blood pressure may be accomplished safely. Chronic antihypertensive therapy is the cornerstone of treatment after lacunar infarction. 

###### CEREBRAL EMBOLISM 

Cerebral embolism is the single most common cause of stroke. Although the middle cerebral artery or one of its branches is the most commonly affected, emboli may lodge in any of the intracranial arteries (Kistler). The onset of the stroke is usually sudden with a maximal neurological deficit present at the beginning. Less often an embolus lodged in a large intracranial artery will 

give rise to a fluctuating deficit. Because in many cases the neurological deficit is small and improvement occurs, the most important aspect of therapy is identifying the source of an embolus in an effort to prevent recurrence. The two major sources of cerebral embolus are the diseased heart and, less frequently, disease of the great vessels, in particular at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery (see above). 

###### Cerebral embolism from the heart and great vessels 

Heart disease of any type may be the source of cerebral emboli. Except for congenital septal defects giving rise to paradoxical embolism, the unifying feature of embolic cardiac disease is the deposition of material on the endocardial surface, be it valvular or chamber. Vegetations of the aortic and mitral valves from bacterial or marantic endocarditis are commonly associated with systemic or cerebral embolism and may be diagnosed by physical examination or with appropriate tests. 

Atrial myxoma results in tumor emboli from the endocardial surface. Mitral valve prolapse with mural thrombus formation has been associated with cerebral embolism, but there are insufficient data on the natural history of this abnormality to ascertain the incidence of embolism. Mural thrombus formation with cerebral embolism occurs in arteriosclerotic heart disease associated with papillary muscle dysfunction, congestive heart failure, or ventricular aneurysm and recent or remote myocardial infarction. Cardioversion may present a special risk for subsequent emboli. Except for bacterial endocarditis, the optimal therapy to prevent further emboli in patients with structural cardiac disease is anticoagulation. In bacterial endocarditis, however, anticoagulation has been associated with intracerebral hemorrhage, probably from rupture of mycotic aneurysms. In selected cases with ventricular aneurysm and mural thrombus formation, surgical excision of the aneurysm may be of value. Although many cardiac arrhythmias have been associated with mural thrombus formation and cerebral emboli, the chronic sinoatrial disorder ‘‘sick sinus syndrome” and atrial fibrillation are most often implicated. Emboli occur as commonly in patients with atrial fibrillation from 

82 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

arteriosclerotic disease as they do from rheumatic valvular disease or other types of heart disease (Hinton et al., 1977). Although there is no satisfactorily controlled study proving the value of anticoagulants in preventing embolism, most physicians advocate their use in patients who have had a cerebral embolus in the setting of atrial fibrillation. There is no consensus regarding their use in patients with atrial fibrillation who have not yet embolized. Patients with valvular heart disease or those about to be cardioverted may benefit from prophylactic use of anticoagulants, but to date only clinical impression supports this hypothesis. 

The management of patients with cerebral emboli arising from the carotid artery is described above. Patients in whom no source for the embolus is found after careful evaluation may be managed with anticoagulant therapy or antiplatelet therapy as the clinical condition dictates, but no clear guidelines exist. If there are no contraindications, we prefer anticoagulation with sodium warfarin for 6 to 12 months in the event that there is no obvious source. Once an embolus has occurred and the CT scan has ruled out an unsuspected intracerebral hemorrhage, anticoagulation with heparin may be given to prevent further emboli. Because of the small possibility that embolic bland cerebral infarction will become hemorrhagic, some physicians wait 24 to 48 h before instituting heparin therapy. The proper duration for chronic anticoagulation with sodium warfarin is unknown, but it should be maintained for 6 months or longer, possibly indefinitely if no contraindication exists and the putative source of emboli remains. Again, great care should be taken to keep the prothrombin time approximately 13 times that of control. 

The general care of the patient with embolic stroke is discussed below, but mention should be made here of the tendency of these patients to develop cerebral edema. This is particularly important in patients with cerebellar infarction where swelling can compress the brainstem. Progressive dysarthria, stupor, and bifacial palsy with bilateral extensor-plantar reflexes usually precede respiratory arrest. The medical measures mentioned below to reduce edema may not be adequate in this setting, and consideration must be given to surgical decompression. 

###### Air embolism 

Cerebral air embolism is a rare complication of cardiothoracic or neurological surgery, trauma to the large thoracic veins, and hemodialysis. When a patient in one of these settings develops seizures, focal cerebral signs, or coma, the diagnosis should be suspected. Once air has entered the cerebral circulation, supportive therapy will allow most patients who are not comatose to recover with minimal deficit. Seizures should be treated acutely with anticonvulsants, and there is an occasional need for long-term therapy. Very early hyperbaric treatment has been employed successfully in a few cases. 

###### VENOUS THROMBOSIS 

Among the many causes of thrombosis of the dural sinuses are head trauma, hypercoagulable states, pregnancy, chronic wasting diseases, and infection. Sigmoid, cavernous, and transverse (lateral) sinus thromboses are commonly septic, whereas superior longitudinal sinus thrombosis is usually aseptic. Thrombosis of the lateral sinus usually causes headache and papilledema; cavernous sinus thrombosis is associated with chemosis, proptosis, and variable involvement of the third through sixth cranial nerves; and longitudinal sinus thrombosis gives rise to focal seizures, leg paresis, and headache. 

Thrombosis related to local infection is treated with appropriate antibiotics. Bland thrombosis is managed by treating underlying hypercoagulable states. Anticoagulants probably have no beneficial effect and may exaggerate adjacent hemorrhagic infarction, but their role and risk have not been settled by clinical studies. Intracranial hypertension may lead to papilledema and, finally, to optic atrophy. Steroids are useful because of their global brain-shrinking effect. If vision is threatened while steroids are being used, surgical shunting of cerebral spinal fluid to reduce intracranial pressure or subtemporal decompression may be beneficial. Cortical surface venous thrombosis is associated with the use of birth control pills, hypercoagulable states, meningitis, or trauma. Because the adjacent brain shows hemorrhagic infarction, some uncertainty exists about the use of an- 

###### INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE 83 

ticoagulants. Therapy consists of general measures in the management of cerebral infarction. 

###### GLOBAL CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA 

Cortical damage is a common sequel to cardiac arrest, protracted hypotension, or severe anoxia. Advanced life-support methods have left many of these patients with permanent neurological deficits. Several patterns of cerebral pathology have been described, including diffuse neuronal necrosis throughout the cortical mantle, borderzone infarction, basal ganglia damage, and delayed postanoxic leukoencephalopathy. Initial management consists of resuscitation, with mean blood pressure brought to at least 80 mmHg, and avoidance of hypercapnia, hypoxemia, and hemoconcentration. Other putative brain-oriented measures such as use of barbiturates or steroids, hypothermia, anticoagulation, and hyperosmolar dehydration with mannitol have been tried, but their value has not as yet been proved. Several of these treatments reduce brain swelling, but the severity of intracranial hypertension after global ischemia is variable, tending to be minor except after prolonged hypoxia such as that induced by carbon monoxide poisoning. If a lumbar puncture demonstrates high pressures, if the optic disks are swollen, or if CT scanning suggests diffuse cerebral swelling, barbiturate coma to reduce intracranial pressure should be considered (see below). 

###### INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE 

Two types of intracerebral hemorrhage should be distinguished. The first and most common is that which arises in the putamen, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum and occurs as a result of chronic hypertension (hypertensive hemorrhage). The second type is the hemorrhage that arises in the subcortical white matter of the cerebral hemisphere (lobar hemorrhages) (Ropper and Davis). The latter are not always directly related to hypertension, and<sup>withbettercontrolof blood</sup> pressure in the population,<sup>lobarhemorrhages</sup> may be becoming<sup>relativelymorefrequent.Both</sup> types of intracerebral<sup>hemorrhage,butespecially</sup> the lobar type, require<sup>differentiationfromcere-</sup> 

bral embolus. Vomiting, drowsiness, characteristic eye signs, and, in the case of cerebellar hemorrhage, headache and ataxia may suggest the diagnosis of intracerebral hemorrhage, but the CT scan is necessary for confirmation of the diagnosis. The initial symptoms and outcome depend on the size and location of the hemorrhage, both of which are easily ascertained by the CT scan. 

Immediate management of severely ill patients with a large intracerebral hemorrhage consists of ensuring adequate ventilation and oxygenation. Controlled hyperventilation to a Poy, of 25 to 30 mmHg may be used acutely to lower the intracranial pressure. Hypercapnia or hypoxia will worsen already increased intracranial pressure. Tissue-dehydrating agents such as mannitol or furosemide are effective in lowering the intracranial pressure further. The serum osmolarity may be used as a guide to dehydration with an optimal safe range of 300 to 310 mosmol per liter. Corticosteroids are used in high doses to minimize edema in surrounding brain tissue, though their beneficial effect has not been definitely established in hemorrhage. Fluid intake should be limited to 1500 ml or less and be given as intravenous solutions of normal saline. Direct measurement of intracranial pressure may be of value. Practical aspects of intracranial pressure control and their relation to cerebral perfusion pressure are discussed below. Patients with supratentorial intracerebral hemorrhages who deteriorate or have signs of progressive brainstem compression may be considered for emergency evacuation of the hemorrhage, but results are generally poor. Most neurosurgeons consider removing the hemorrhage only as a lifesaving procedure and are more inclined to operate on nondominant hemispheric lesions. Lobar, subcortical hemorrhages and putaminal hemorrhages that point laterally are more accessible to surgical evacuation. Intracerebral hemorrhages will be reabsorbed over time so that, if the mass effect is not severe enough to endanger further brain or brainstem structures, medical rather than surgical therapy is recommended. 

Cerebellar hemorrhages are a special exception. Surgical evacuation not only may be lifesaving but may offer the patient an opportunity for excellent neurological recovery. Small cerebellar 

###### 84 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

hemorrhages may be managed medically, but those that are large enough to produce Babinski signs, dysarthria, facial weakness, and stupor should undergo emergency evacuation. SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE Clinical presentation, evaluation, and management 

Initial clinical presentation Because of the seriousness of ruptured saccular aneurysm and the possibility of recurrent hemorrhage, the most important point in initial management is rapid diagnosis. Sudden severe headache, particularly if associated with loss of consciousness and/or vomiting, should be considered secondary to aneurysmal rupture until proved otherwise. Minor rupture, “warning leaks” prior to major rupture, occur ina significant number of patients. These usually present as sudden moderate headache on exertion without other symptoms. Once the diagnosis is established, careful documentation of the initial neurological status is of utmost importance, not only in initial management but also in identifying delayed neurological deficits. Initial neurological deficits occur for a variety of reasons. The aneurysm may rupture into the cerebral hemisphere or into the subdural or subarachnoid space and produce a localized mass effect. Unilateral hemispheric swelling may occur. It is possible that in such cases transient interruption of cerebral circulation is the cause of the initial swelling and focal deficits. At other times, such early focal deficits appear without obvious cause. 

Initial laboratory evaluation Because ruptured saccular aneurysms that give rise to subarachnoid hemorrhages are generally located at branch points on the large arteries at the base of the brain, blood is deposited in clots in the basal cisterns. The amount and location of clotted blood in these cisterns depend on the site and direction of aneurysmal rupture. Mycotic aneurysms arise from more distal branches of the cerebral arterial tree and generally do not give rise to large deposits of clotted blood in the basal cisterns. 

The initial evaluation is directed toward establishing the diagnosis and estimating the extent and location of subarachnoid blood in the basal 

cisterns and/or the brain. This is best done by a noncontrast CT examination. About 75 percent of cases will have evidence of subarachnoid blood on CT scan if the scan is obtained within 48 h of aneurysmal rupture. Furthermore, the size and location of globular clots or a thick layer of clotted blood in the fissures and cisterns of the subarachnoid space have a positive correlation with the later development and location of cerebral vasospasm serious enough to produce ischemic symptoms, i.e., symptomatic cerebral vasospasm (Fisher et al., 1980) (Fig. 3). After a plain CT scan is completed, a contrast-enhanced CT scan may be helpful in localizing the site of aneurysm or in demonstrating an unsuspected arteriovenous malformation. If the CT scan does not establish the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage and does not show a mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus, then lumbar puncture is indicated and may be done safely. After the diagnosis is established, angiography is generally avoided until the time of surgery. 

Initial therapy Care of the comatose patient with subarachnoid hemorrhage is similar to that of coma patients without subarachnoid hemorrhage. If the intracranial pressure is elevated, careful attention to maintenance of proper alveolar ventilation to prevent hypercapnia is of particular importance. Severe acute hydrocephalus may require surgical shunting. If the patient has a life-threatening intracerebral, subdural, or subarachnoid clot, consideration may be given to emergency surgery to remove the mass and, if possible, simultaneously to obliterate the aneurysm. 

All patients are placed at bedrest in a quiet room. If they are able to eat, stool softeners and laxatives are of value in preventing constipation. Sedation and analgesia with phenobarbital and acetaminophen (Tylenol) or meperidine (Demerol) may be necessary if the patient is distressed and in pain. Excessive sedation, however, is to be avoided, as it may obscure the recognition of the onset of delayed neurological deficits. Although careful control of the blood pressure is important, excessive lowering of the blood pressure should be avoided. Diphenylhydantoin (Dilantin) and phenobarbital may be given as prophylaxis for seizure, but seizures are not often a problem in subarachnoid hemorrhage. Loss of consciousness with stiffening or jerking

of the extremities is indicative of a sharp rise in intracranial pressure during aneurysmal rupture rather than of seizure. Steroids may be beneficial in reducing the head and neck pain caused by the irritating effect of subarachnoid blood, but there is no evidence that this medication helps prevent the cerebral edema sometimes seen in the acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. 

###### Delayed neurological deficits 

Deterioration in neurological status after the acute effect of the initial subarachnoid hemorrhage has stabilized is generally due to one of three factors: rebleeding, hydrocephalus, or symptomatic cerebral vasospasm with or without infarction. In each case, accurate knowledge of the initial deficit and the initial appearance of the subarachnoid blood and ventricular size on CT scan will aid in the detection of a clinical change and the establishment of the diagnosis of these three complications. 

Rebleeding If nothing is done surgically to obliterate the aneurysm, 40 to 50 percent of patients will rebleed within the first 3 months, with a 10 percent mortality rate. The incidence of rebleeding appears to be greatest in the first 3 weeks after the original subarachnoid hemorrhage. After 6 months, rebleeding occurs in approximately 2 to 3 percent of patients per year 

(Winn et al.). In 15 percent of cases of subarachnoid hemorrhage, no aneurysm is found even with four-vessel cerebral angiography. The incidence of rebleeding in these patients is quite low (Hayward). 

The antifibrinolytic agents, epsilonaminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid, although not yet officially approved in the United States, have been used in an effort to prevent aneurysmal clot lysis and resulting rebleeding. Some therapeutic trials have indicated a beneficial effect in the prevention of rebleeding, but the data are not conclusive (Peerless, Kaste and Ramsay). Thrombotic and other complications have been associated with the use of these drugs. Until such time that it is established unequivocally that these drugs have a net beneficial effect on the prevention of rebleeding, they cannot be included as established therapy. 

Because of the devastating effects of aneurysmal rerupture and the suggestive evidence that groups of patients have benefitted from antifibrinolytic therapy, we have been using epsilonaminocaproic acid in the first 3 weeks following aneurysmal rupture. It is best given continuously intravenously in doses of 30 to 35 g per day. Some physicians substitute oral therapy after the first week of intravenous therapy. In general, when antifibrinolytic therapy is used, it is maintained until such time as surgery is performed or for a maximum duration of 3 weeks, if 

86 THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

surgery is not feasible or an aneurysm is not shown on angiography. Hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure Although hydrocephalus may develop as an acute event following a subarachnoid hemorrhage, it generally occurs between days 4 and 20. There is dilation of the two lateral, the third, and the fourth ventricles, which implies that the obstruction of the cerebral spinal fluid flow is in the basal cisterns or arachnoid villi over the hemispheral convexity. The onset of hydrocephalus is often heralded by increasing stupor, incontinence, and inability to move the eyes upwards. CT scan with measurements of ventricular size is the single most helpful diagnostic procedure. Often the hydrocephalus is transient and may not require surgical intervention. Frequent lumbar punctures may be useful in lowering the intracranial pressure and may tide the patient over the critical period without ventricular-atrial shunting if there is no mass effect from hemorrhage or edema. There may, however, be a slight risk of rerupture during lumbar puncture because of pain, Valsalva’s maneuver, or rapid reduction in intracranial pressure. Aneurysms lying in the posterior fossa have been said to be particularly susceptible to such rerupture. If lumbar puncture does not control the intracranial pressure, then ventricular-atrial shunting may be required. 

Cerebral vasospasm In the setting of subarachnoid hemorrhage, the term cerebral vasospasm refers to the narrowing of the larger diameter intracranial arteries that lie in the subarachnoid space. Vasospasm occurs from 3 to 31 days after aneurysmal rupture (usually between 4 and 14 days), and if it is severe enough, it can cause symptoms of ischemia (symptomatic cerebral vasospasm) and lead to cerebral infarction (Fisher et al., 1977). Symptomatic cerebral vasospasm, which is an important cause of serious morbidity after subarachnoid hemorrhage, occurs in 30 to 50 percent of cases. The arteries most commonly involved are the distal internal carotid and the middle, anterior, and posterior cerebral, including their most proximal branches. When the initial neurological deficits and their clinical course are kept clearly in mind, it is usually possible to recognize the onset of 

delayed ischemic symptoms in the cerebral territory of these arteries. The amount and location of subarachnoid blood are related to the location and severity of the vasospasm (Fisher et al., 1980). An almost 100 percent incidence of symptomatic cerebral vasospasm has been found in patients with CT scan evidence of globular clots or layers of subarachnoid blood 1 mm or more in thickness in the basal cisterns or the frontal interhemispheric fissure. If this observation proves reliable, then blood localized in the subarachnoid space in sufficient amounts at specific sites is the most important etiologic factor in the development of symptomatic cerebral vasospasm. Other factors, such as increased intracranial pressure, become important when vasospasm is severe enough to reduce the vessel’s residual lumen diameter to less than 0.5 to 1 mm. Therapeutic efforts to prevent or treat symptomatic cerebral vasospasm have been universally disappointing. Reserpine and kanamycin reduce platelet and serum serotonin which has been implicated in precipitating vasospasm. Doses of reserpine at 0.2 mg every 6 h and of kanamycin at | g three times a day may reduce the occurrence of vasospasm following aneurysmal surgery (Zervas et al.), but the timing of surgery may be the most important factor in the development of postoperative vasospasm. This therapy would not be expected to prevent vasospasm resulting from the initial subarachnoid hemorrhage but may be beneficial if new bleeding occurs. Therapeutic agents theoretically designed to reduce symptomatic cerebral vasospasm once it has occurred have been equally disappointing. Isoproterenol has been used because of its ability to stimulate adenyl cyclase and increase cyclic AMP, which is a smooth-muscle relaxant. Aminophylline increases cyclic AMP by inhibiting the phosphodiesterase-mediated degradation. Once symptomatic vasospasm has occurred, neither of these medications has met with significant success. The direct smooth-muscle relaxant, sodium nitroprusside, has been effective in alleviating experimental cerebral vasospasm but has not convincingly been shown to be successful in patients. Sodium nitroprusside raises intracranial pressure and lowers mean atrial pressure, circulatory changes which lower cerebral perfusion 

###### ARTERIOVENOUS MALFORMATION 87 

pressure and may reduce flow to the ischemic brain. Sodium nitroprusside cannot be recommended for use in this setting. Currently, the most accepted form of therapy for symptomatic cerebral vasospasm involves increasing cerebral perfusion pressure by plasma volume expansion with intravenous fluids and albumin in order to raise mean arterial pressure. Pressor agents are resorted to if these measures fail to increase blood pressure and if ischemic symptoms persist. Pressor agents most often used are phenylephrine, up to 30 wg/min, and dopamine at 3 to 6 wg/kg/min. At higher doses of dopamine, decreased cerebral blood flow has been observed in laboratory animals. Although in some cases improvement in neurological signs has been noted with these efforts, the risk of rerupture is increased, particularly if the mean arterial pressure is above 170 or 180 mmHg. When hypertensive therapy is used, direct measurement of central venous pressure, arterial pressure and, in severe cases, pulmonary artery wedge pressure, and intracranial pressure can give critical information regarding cardiac output and cerebral perfusion pressure. Once infarction has occurred, cerebral edema may increase intracranial pressure to levels which reduce cerebral perfusion. Efforts to decrease cerebral edema by raising the plasma osmolarity with mannitol while maintaining an adequate intravascular volume and mean arterial pressure become critical. Barbiturate coma has been tried as a last resort when severely elevated intracranial pressure fails to respond to the above measures, but has met with little success. Timing of surgery 

With the advent of the operating microscope, microsurgical obliteration of a ruptured aneurysm has become a safe and effective means of preventing disastrous recurrent rupture. Proper timing of surgery, however, remains controversial. Because patients operated on in the first few days following aneurysmal rupture are still at risk of developing symptomatic cerebral vasospasm, most neurosurgeons recommend delaying surgery for 7 to 14 days. Recently, delay in operation has been challenged, especially in patients without neurological deficits. Prompt surgery offers the direct opportunity to prevent 

bleeding and avoid the risks of antifibrinolytic agents. In addition, in some cases it offers the opportunity of directly removing clotted blood from the basal cisterns (cisternal toilet), perhaps minimizing subsequent vasospasm. The timing of surgery must therefore be adapted to the individual patient. If, at the time of surgery potentially threatening localized blood clots in the subarachnoid space can be easily removed (this is not always technically feasible), there may be a place for early surgery. The answers to questions of the timing of early versus delayed surgery and of preventive therapy for vasospasm await further study. 

###### Future studies regarding prevention of vasospasm and timing of surgery 

If it can be ascertained by CT scan which patients are in danger of developing vasospasm, then it may be possible to recommend preventive therapy early in the course. Investigation of the effect of any new form of preventive therapy will be facilitated because patients not destined to develop symptomatic cerebral vasospasm will not be included in the therapy group. Early operation with removal of spasmogenic clot and prophylactic therapy with various vasodilators can be assessed more accurately. Caution should be used when considering the prophylactic use of any of these agents, because when the intracranial pressure is mildly elevated any of the vasodilators may dramatically raise it further. 

###### ARTERIOVENOUS MALFORMATION (AVM) 

AVMs are developmentally abnormal tangles of cerebral vessels with direct communication between arteries and veins. They produce symptoms that dictate management in three ways: 

- 1 Up to 50 percent of AVMs present with intracerebral hemorrhage. Unlike hemorrhage from a ruptured saccular aneurysm, which primarily leaks into the subarachnoid space, hemorrhage from an AVM tends to be primarily in the parenchyma of the brain with secondary leakage into the subarachnoid space. As a result, these patients are more likely to develop initial neurological deficits 

###### SS THERAPY OF CEREBROVASCULAR DISEASE 

related to the rupture and are much less likely to develop delayed ischemic deficits from arterial vasospasm. If rebleeding occurs, it is more likely to occur after a month rather than in the first 3 weeks as it does in ruptured saccular aneurysms. The use of antifibrinolytic agents is not advised. 

- 2 Seizures occur in about 40 percent of cases and may be controlled by antiepileptic medication. 

- 3 Larger AVMs may steal blood away from both near and distant normal brain, causing transient and occasionally progressive and permanent ischemic neurological deficits. Headaches may also be a prominent symptom, but their cause is not clear. 

Skilled microneurosurgical excision is currently the most effective form of therapy (Drake). It should be considered for all patients who have suffered a hemorrhage from an AVM and possibly for all patients with AVMs because of their future potential for hemorrhage. Surgical excision, however, carries a definite morbidity and mortality especially from intraoperative edema due to shifts in cerebral circulation. In addition, surgical excision in some cases is not technically feasible. Other forms of therapy must then be considered. These include embolization, conventional radiotherapy, and_ stereotactic Bragg Peak proton beam therapy. In all three of these forms of therapy, the AVM may shrink, and in some instances the lesion can then be handled surgically. We have had the most experience with focused proton beam therapy (Kjellberg et al.), which produces slowly progressive occlusion of the AVM, thereby eliminating the effect of acute, shifts in the cerebral circulation. Although the data are not complete, there is some suggestion that proton beam therapy reduces the incidence of rebleeding. GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF THE MANAGEMENT OF THE CRITICALLY ILL STROKE PATIENT 

When stroke occurs, cerebral blood flow is reduced in the territory of the occluded artery. The fundamental precept of acute stroke manage- 

ment is to restore blood flow and oxygenation to viable tissue as quickly as possible. An understanding of acute stroke therapy requires some familiarity with the physiology of the cerebral circulation. Regional cerebral blood flow is the quotient of perfusion pressure and local vascular resistance. Local metabolic demands, pH, and Peo, all influence regional blood flow by varying the caliber of resistance vessels. The vasoactive substances that link these factors to blood vessel smooth muscle are unknown, but it is likely that H+ has a central role. In ischemic areas, the normal parallel relationship between local metabolic requirements and blood flow is disordered in an unpredictable and heterogeneous way. 

The final result of several factors determines the extent of ischemia. First, small vessels adjacent to ischemic areas may effectively shunt blood to marginally perfused borders. Second, the fixed anatomy of vessels of the circle of Willis determines how large-vessel occlusion will affect blood flow in various regions. Third, cerebral blood vessels normally have the ability to keep local perfusion relatively constant by autoregulating their sizes to match varying perfusion pressures. Cerebral autoregulation maintains cerebral blood flow at approximately 75 and 30 ml/min per 100 g tissue in gray and white matter, respectively, over a range of mean blood pressure between 60 and 160 mmHg. In areas of ischemia or hemorrhage, however, autoregulation is disordered and leads to unpredictable changes in vascular resistance in response to alterations in blood pressure. In clinical practice few of the factors that determine blood flow can be effectively manipulated. Therapeutic hypertension has had a variable effect on infarct size. Hypertension cannot yet be recommended as a routine therapy in stroke. Inadvertent hypotension, however, should be assiduously avoided. Hypercapnia has a rationale in stroke therapy because poteniially it dilates cerebral vessels. Because vessels in the ischemic area do not consistently react in this way, however, hypercapnia has not been an effective means of limiting infarct size and may cause an undesirable increase in intracranial pressure. The major physiological parameter that can be altered therapeutically is intracranial pressure (ICP). In most ischemic strokes, brain swelling is

#### SYNDROME MICHAEL H. CRAWFORD and ROBERT A. O’ROURKE MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE 

Mitral valve prolapse refers to the posterior displacement of one or both mitral valve leaflets toward the left atrium during systole, which may result in mitral regurgitation. It has received considerable attention recently because of its prevalence and association with many other conditions. Although the etiology of mitral valve prolapse is unknown in most cases, it has been described in association with connective tissue disorders such as Marfan’s syndrome and with congenital heart diseases, especially atrial septal defect of the ostium secundum variety. Mitral valve prolapse has also been described in patients with rheumatic valvular disease, cardiomyopathies, and coronary artery disease. Furthermore, other cardiac conditions have been described in association with mitral valve prolapse, such as preexcitation syndromes, autonomic dysfunction, and coronary artery spasm. Thus, it is more appropriate to consider mitral valve prolapse as a syndrome than as a specific disease entity. 

The mitral valve prolapse syndrome is frequently found in young females, most of whom are asymptomatic. However, many present with chest pain, palpitation, dyspnea, and fatigue. The hallmark of the syndrome on physical examination is a midsystolic click, the timing of which can be altered by various hemodynamic manipulations and which is often followed by a late systolic murmur. These physical findings are due to the prolapse of one or both mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during systole, an event which can be documented by echocardiography or contrast cineangiography. The major clinical challenge is defining the prognosis in individual patients with this syndrome. There are many reports of complications 

occurring in patients with mitral valve prolapse. These include sudden death, rupture of chordae tendineae, infective endocarditis, chest pain, arrhythmias, and transient ischemic episodes. Since most patients with the syndrome are asymptomatic, it is difficult to define the exact incidence and outcome of these complications. However, various noninvasive diagnostic techniques are being used to identify patients at risk for various complications in an effort to prevent their development. The first purpose of this article is to present some of the newer information on the pathophysiology of this syndrome and place the many etiologic possibilities and associations into perspective; the second purpose is to review the general clinical features of the syndrome; and the third is to describe the complications of mitral valve prolapse and outline the steps in their prevention and management. 

###### PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGY 

The mitral valve apparatus is a complex structure composed of the mitral annulus, valve leaflets, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and the supporting left ventricular, left atrial, and aortic walls. Presumably, disease processes involving any one or combination of these components may result in dysfunction of the valvular apparatus and prolapse of the mitral leaflets toward the left atrium during systole, when left ventricular exceeds left atrial pressure. The complexity of the mitral valve apparatus provides an explanation for the presence of prolapse in the many conditions that affect one or more of the components of the apparatus. However, there is

###### c Cardiomyopathies 

considerable evidence that a primary disease of the mitral leaflets exists in which there are specific pathologic changes that lead to redundancy of the leaflets, allowing prolapse into the left atrium during systole (Tables 1 and 2). Therefore, the distinction between what is termed primary and secondary mitral valve prolapse is the presence of these pathologic changes in the leaflets in the former and evidence of another disease process affecting the mitral valve apparatus in the latter. 

The possibility must also be considered that the finding of mitral valve prolapse, which is a common entity, in patients with other commonly occurring conditions represents a chance association. However, there is now considerable evidence which indicates that other cardiac diseases can lead to secondary prolapse of the mitral valve. The case of ischemic heart disease is a good example because of its high prevalence in the general population. The combination of mitral valve prolapse and ischemic heart disease has been recognized for some time, but the exact pathophysiologic relationship was unclear, and at first it was considered to be merely the occurrence in the same patient of two common conditions. However, the authors have personally observed a patient without signs of mitral valve

prolapse on physical examination or left ventricular cineangiography, who sustained an acute myocardial infarction and subsequently developed the typical midsystolic click-late systolic murmur. Repeat left ventricular cineangiography also.demonstrated the development of mitral valve prolapse. There is also a recent report of two patients with clinical evidence of mitral valve prolapse and ischemic heart disease who had postmortem evidence of papillary muscle scarring without any pathologic changes in the mitral valve leaflets. Furthermore, there are numerous reports of mitral valve prolapse, as demonstrated by echocardiography and angiography, in patients with various types of congenital heart disease, who at operation or autopsy had no pathologic changes in the mitral valve leaflets. These observations support the concept that a number of disease states can disrupt the mitral valve apparatus by a variety of mechanisms, thereby leading to mitral valve prolapse. This concept does not exclude the possibility that primary pathologic changes in the mitral leaflets could coexist with other entities, but secondary involvement of the mitral apparatus seems the most likely explanation in many patients. 

###### Pathologic changes 

Perhaps of more importance is the growing body of information about specific pathologic changes in the mitral leaflets of patients with presumed primary mitral valve prolapse. The normal mitral valve leaflet consists of the fibrosa on the left ventricular aspect, where the chordae tendineae attach, and the spongiosa on the atrial aspect of the leaflet. The spongiosa component, which normally contains acid mucopolysaccharide, is increased in patients with mitral valve prolapse. In most other valvular diseases, it is the fibrosa which is increased and which is replaced by fibrous tissue. In contrast, the increased spongiosa in mitral valve prolapse encroaches on the fibrosa, and collagen dissolution is observed. The increase in acid mucopolysaccharides has led to the term myxomatous degeneration of the valve, but there is no evidence that the spongiosa is actually degenerated. The increased spongiosa and reduced fibrosa leads to a ““hooding”’ deformity of the valve with 

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGY 93 

redundant valve tissue which prolapses during systole (Fig. 1). A number of secondary lesions also occur. Thus, the atrial endocardium is thickened and platelet and fibrin deposits often occur on it. Collagen deposits are observed in the fibrosa, and calcium deposits occur throughout the leaflet. Friction lesions are produced where the elongated chordae rub against the left ventricular endocardium. This constellation of findings defines a specific valvular pathology that is distinct from those seen in other types of valve diseases. These pathologic changes are similar to those seen in Marfan’s syndrome and other related connective tissue disorders. Indeed, mitral valve prolapse has been described in these conditions and occurs in them even more commonly than does dilatation of the aorta. Also, increased spongiosa in the mitral leaflet has been described in apparently normal individuals in all age groups, but the changes are minor compared with the marked redundancy of the leaflets observed in patients with primary mitral valve prolapse. 

###### Other etiologic considerations 

Several observations have led to the speculation that the primary mitral valve prolapse syndrome represents a generalized disorder of connective tissue. In one report of patients with emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis, the incidence of mitral and tricuspid valve prolapse was inordinately high. Also, thoracic skeletal abnormalities such as straight thoracic spine and pectus excavatum are not uncommonly associated with this syndrome. It has been pointed out that the mitral valve undergoes differentiation between the thirty-fifth and forty-second days of fetal life, at the time when the vertebrae and thoracic cage are beginning chondrification and ossification. Any adverse factors in this period might affect both the mitral valve and the bony thorax. It is of interest that rats fed a diet containing large amounts of peas of the genus Lathyrus, which contain B-aminopropionitrile, develop both bony abnormalities and myxomatous changes in their valve leaflets. Therefore, one possibility, still unproven, is that the mitral valve prolapse syndrome is a connective tissue disorder, the result of fetal exposure to toxic agents during the early part of pregnancy. 

FIGURE | 

Autopsy specimen from a patient with primary mitral valve prolapse. AML, anterior mitral leaflet; Ao, aorta; Ch, chordae tendineae; LA, left atrium, PM, papillary muscle. 

Familial forms There are several reports of families with a high incidence of primary mitral valve prolapse which suggest a possible genetic basis. The data are consistent with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance, but with varying penetrance, since some family members are unaffected. Also, the clinical features are variable in affected members, and the disease may skip generations. Interestingly, Marfan’s syndrome also demonstrates an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. However, most patients with primary mitral valve prolapse do not appear to have afflicted family members, and systematic genetic studies are lacking in this syndrome. 

Autonomic dysfunction A recent report has suggested that there is generalized autonomic dysfunction in patients with primary mitral valve prolapse. A series of women with mitral valve prolapse studied by Gaffney and associates demonstrated a reduced reflex slowing of heart rate as a consequence of arterial pressure elevation with intravenous phenylephrine and of facial immersion in ice water (diving reflex) compared with a normal control group. Also, the responses of heart rate, arterial pressure, cardiac output, and forearm vascular resistance to lower body negative pressure were abnormal. These data suggested a defect in parasympathetic and alphaadrenergic tone and responsiveness. Furthermore, Leichtman and coworkers studied three patients with mitral valve prolapse and sinus 

94 MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE SYNDROME 

bradycardia, from a family with a high incidence of these abnormalities, who suffered episodic syncope. They had a normal response to phenylephrine, isoproterenol, and norepinephrine, but demonstrated impairment of atrioventricular conduction reversible by atropine, which suggested excess vagal tone. These studies of autonomic dysfunction are provocative because of recent reports of patients with coronary artery spasm and mitral valve prolapse. Also, some patients with mitral prolapse have QT-interval prolongation, an electrocardiographic finding which is associated with an increased incidence of ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Some of these patients with arrhythmias have been shown to have an imbalance of neural output from the stellate ganglia and have responded favorably to ablation of the left stellate ganglia. Therefore, autonomic dysfunction may account for the chest pain and arrhythmias seen in primary mitral valve prolapse. 

It is our contention that primary mitral valve prolapse is a connective tissue disorder with a variable spectrum ranging from an almost normal mitral valve to one which is severely affected. The tricuspid valve and other structures such as the thoracic skeleton may also be involved by this process. There appears to be a continuum from individuals who are clinically normal to those with a frank connective tissue disorder. Presumably, the primary mitral valve prolapse syndrome lies somewhere between these two extremes. One of the current major problems is to determine where the primary mitral valve prolapse syndrome ends and where a minor variant of normal begins. Indeed, there may be no exact dividing line. 

###### CLINICAL PRESENTATION 

The incidence of mitral valve prolapse in American females has been estimated to range from 6 to 21 percent depending on the specific population studied and the method used for identifying the disease. The incidence is thought to be lower in men. Since the majority of patients with this syndrome are asymptomatic, most studies on the incidence of mitral valve prolapse have been based on auscultatory or echocardiographic screening. However, the sensitivity and specificity of these techniques for detecting this syn- 

drome are unknown because of the lack of a suitable ‘‘gold standard” for comparison. Mitral valve prolapse is usually detected during a routine physical examination for other reasons. Some patients consult their physician because of one or more of the common complaints that occur in this syndrome. The most common presenting symptom is palpitation. The source of the palpitation is usually ventricular premature beats, but various supraventricular arrhythmias are also frequent, and the most common sustained tachycardia is paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Ventricular tachycardia has been observed in some patients, and others have had symptomatic bradyarrhythmias. Electrophysiologic studies in some patients have documented the presence of atrioventricular bypass tracts, usually originating in the left atrium, and the question of whether these are related to the mitral valve abnormalities has arisen. Patients with symptomatic bradyarrhythmias and tachyarrhythmias can present with syncope or cardiac arrest, but these conditions are rare. 

Chest pain This is a frequent complaint in patients with mitral valve prolapse. The pain is atypical in patients without concomitant ischemic heart disease and rarely resembles classic angina pectoris. Usually it is substernal, prolonged, and not related to exertion; and some patients have stabbing pains in addition to the sensation of prolonged pressure. Chest pain may occur frequently and can be incapacitating. Often it is severe for several weeks and then disappears entirely for variable periods. The major clinical problem is to distinguish this pain from that due to ischemic heart disease, especially since the latter can cause secondary mitral valve prolapse. The etiology of the chest pain is obscure. Some have speculated that it may represent true myocardial ischemia produced by abnormal tension on the papillary muscles and supporting ventricular wall by the prolapsing mitral leaflets. A study performed in our laboratory demonstrated that chest pain could be reproduced in some patients by elevating the systemic arterial pressure with intravenous phenylephrine. This study suggests that the pain is of cardiac origin, but it does not clarify the mechanism. Increased arterial pressure and the attendant eleva-

Dyspnea and fatigue These are not infrequent complaints in the mitral valve prolapse syndrome; although these symptoms may be related to significant mitral regurgitation, usually they are not. In fact, objective exercise testing often fails to show an impairment in exercise tolerance, and some patients exhibit distinct episodes of hyperventilation. These symptoms may be responsible for the neuropsychiatric complaints which are not uncommon in patients with mitral valve prolapse. Also, some patients have emotional lability and frank manic-depressive syndromes. The exact incidence of these emotional problems and their cause is unknown. Recently, it has been speculated that small platelet emboli from the mitral valve may lead to abnormal behavior secondary to central nervous system damage. The most recently described problem in patients with mitral valve prolapse is transient 

ischemic episodes. Reports of uniocular amaurosis fugax, homonymous field loss, and retinal artery occlusion have been described; occasionally the visual loss persists. Presumably, these neurologic findings are due to deposits of platelets and fibrin which have been observed on the atrial side of the mitral valve leaflets in pathologic specimens and which embolize to the ophthalmic artery or the posterior cerebral circulation. 

###### Physical examination 

The presence of thoracic skeletal abnormalities may suggest the diagnosis of mitral valve prolapse because of their frequent occurrence with this syndrome. The most common thoracic skeletal deformities are scoliosis, pectus excavatum, straightened thoracic spine, and narrowed anterior-posterior diameter of the chest. Some patients with mitral valve prolapse may show signs such as arachnodactyly, more typical of Marfan’s syndrome. However, none of these skeletal abnormalities is specific for mitral valve prolapse. 

Auscultatory features The principal auscultatory feature of this syndrome is the midsystolic click. This is a high-frequency sound of short duration which has been described as a clicking, snapping, or popping. Although it is the cardinal feature of the syndrome, it may vary considerably in its intensity and location in systole according to the hemodynamic conditions. The midsystolic click is thought to be generated by the sudden tensing of the mitral valve apparatus as the leaflets prolapse into the left atrium during systole. This timing has been confirmed by simultaneous recording of phonocardiograms with cineangiograms or echocardiograms. Some patients exhibit multiple systolic clicks; presumably these are generated by different portions of the mitral leaflet prolapsing at different times during systole. 

Systolic clicks are not specific for mitral valve prolapse and must be differentiated from other high-frequency sounds occurring during systole. In some cases, it may be difficult to distinguish clicks from early systolic ejection sounds produced by abnormal semilunar valves and dilated great vessels. An aneurysm of the ventricular 

###### 96 

###### MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE SYNDROME 

septum associated with a ventricular septal defect may produce a midsystolic click; and if a murmur due to a septal defect is present, it may be confused with mitral regurgitation. In addition, midsystolic sounds have been heard in patients with left-sided pneumothorax, adhesive pericarditis, atrial myxomas, malfunctioning heterograft valves, left ventricular aneurysms, and aneurysms of the atrial septum. Usually these conditions can be readily distinguished from mitral valve prolapse, but they may cause confusion in certain patients. The major differentiating feature of the midsystolic click of mitral valve prolapse is the ability to alter its timing during systole by maneuvers which vary the hemodynamic conditions (see below). The midsystolic click is frequently followed by a late systolic murmur, whose intensity peaks near the second heart sound, is usually medium to high frequency in pitch, and is most readily audible at the apex. Occasionally the murmur has a musical or honking quality. The character and intensity of the murmur also vary under certain conditions, from brief and almost inaudible to holosystolic and intense. studies have confirmed that the murmur is due to mitral regurgitation. The murmur of mitral valve prolapse must be distinguished from other apical systolic murmurs. Occasionally the murmur of coarctation of the aorta or severe aortic stenosis can be late in systole and cause some confusion. More important, papillary muscle dysfunction and other disruptions of the mitral valve apparatus can lead to late systolic murmurs which may be indistinguishable from those due to primary mitral valve prolapse. Often, these conditions are not associated with a midsystolic click. However, many patients with well-documented mitral valve prolapse have only a murmur and not a click, and it may be difficult by auscultation alone to distinguish those patients with mitral valve prolapse from those with papillary muscle dysfunction or other disorders of the mitral apparatus without prolapse. 

The intensity and timing of the click and murmur are highly variable from time to time and from beat to beat. This variability is the most important distinguishing feature of the auscultatory findings in primary mitral valve prolapse as compared with those of other diseases. It appears that there is a critical left ventricular volume below which the redundant mitral valve leaflets prolapse into the left atrium. The point in systole when this critical volume is reached is largely a function of the left ventricular volume at the onset of systole. However, other factors, such as the heart rate and the systemic vascular resistance, also determine the instant at which this critical volume is achieved during systole. 

Maneuvers for altering the click-murmur Figure 2 illustrates how changes in the left ventricular end-diastolic volume lead to changes in the timing of the midsystolic click and murmur. When end-diastolic volume is decreased, the critical volume is achieved earlier in systole and the click-murmur complex occurs shortly after the first heart sound. When end-diastolic volume is increased, the critical volume is achieved later in systole and the click-murmur complex occurs just before the second heart sound. Many bedside maneuvers have been proposed for altering the volume of the left ventricle in order to manipulate the timing and intensity of the click-murmur complex (Table 3). The most 

CLINICAL PRESENTATION 97 

useful maneuver is to request the patient to stand and to note that the click and murmur increase in intensity. Venous return is decreased in the standing position, and left ventricular enddiastolic volume is smaller and, therefore, closer to the critical volume at which prolapse commences. Also, the increase in sympathetic tone associated with standing increases the force of left ventricular contraction and intensifies the click. 

Many patients have increased adrenergic stimulation due to anxiety when consulting a physician; therefore, the click-murmur complex may already be near the first heart sound and standing will produce little further change in timing. In this case, it is useful to ask the patient to squat rapidly, a maneuver which elevates intraabdominal pressure, increases venous return, compresses the femoral arteries, and transiently raises central aortic pressure, thereby increasing the resistance to left ventricular ejection. The combination of these effects increases the left ventricular end-diastolic volume, delays the instant when the critical volume at which prolapse commences is reached, and moves the click-murmur complex toward the second heart sound. It is often useful to ask the patient to stand up rapidly from the squatting position to confirm the findings, since this produces a striking reduction in left ventricular diastolic volume and dramatic movement of the click-murmur complex to the first heart sound. 

In patients unable to stand or squat rapidly, other maneuvers can be carried out. There are several interventions that reduce left ventricular end-diastolic volume and move the complex toward the first heart sound. The Valsalva maneuver, in which the patient strains against a closed glottis, increases intrathoracic pressure during the straining phase; this reduces venous return and left ventricular volume, and as a consequence the click-murmur complex occurs earlier in systole and sometimes only a holosystolic murmur is audible. A submaximal isometric handgrip usually increases heart rate and left ventricular contractility sufficiently to decrease end-diastolic volume. As a result, the click-murmur complex is increased in intensity and occurs earlier in systole. However, a maximal handgrip may markedly increase systemic vascular resistance and arterial pressure, which counteracts

the changes brought about by augmentation of heart rate and contractility and leads to variable changes in the auscultatory complex. The response of click and murmur to the inhalation of amyl nitrite is more complex and often biphasic. Immediate vasodilation follows the inhalation of this volatile ester of nitrous acid, which reduces both arterial pressure and venous return. These changes facilitate left ventricular emptying and reduce end-diastolic volume, which moves the click and murmur closer to the first heart sound. However, the large reduction in arterial pressure decreases the propensity for mitral regurgitation and diminishes the intensity of the murmur. Later, a reflex tachycardia and increased contractility occur; these augment left ventricular contractility and may increase the intensity of the murmur. 

Other bedside maneuvers used to delay the systolic occurrence of the click-murmur complex include manipulations intended to increase left ventricular end-diastolic volume. In the bedridden patient, raising the legs to increase venous return or carotid sinus massage to slow the heart rate may delay the click and the onset of the murmur. However, intravenous phenylephrine is more reliable. This alpha-adrenergic agonist raises arterial pressure and causes a reflex bradycardia; both of these changes increase ventricular volume and delay the onset of the clickmurmur complex. One difficulty in evaluating the response of the click-murmur complex in mitral valve prolapse to these interventions is the variable changes in intensity of the sounds irrespective of change in 

98 MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE SYNDROME 

their timing. The intensity of the click is dependent on left ventricular contractility. Thus, with standing or handgrip exercise it becomes louder, and during the Valsalva strain or early after inhalation of amyl nitrite it is softer. 

The murmur of mitral valve prolapse varies in intensity as does that of mitral regurgitation secondary to rheumatic heart disease. Thus, raising systolic pressure with handgrip or phenylephrine increases the left ventricular—left atrial pressure gradient, augments the mitral regurgitation, and intensifies the murmur. Conversely, manipulations that reduce systolic blood pressure, such as occurs early after inhaling amy] nitrite, decrease the intensity of the murmur. The changes in the intensity of the click and murmur can obscure the changes in timing. For example, early after amyl nitrite inhalation, the decrease in intensity of the click and murmur may obscure their earlier onset. However, the characteristic feature of the click-murmur complex in mitral valve prolapse is the variability in its timing under different hemodynamic conditions; changes in intensity are nonspecific. The systolic murmur in idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis (IHSS) is usually late systolic and may be similar to that of mitral valve prolapse (Table 4). Many patients with IHSS have mitral regurgitation, but few have midsystolic clicks. The murmur secondary to obstruction of left ventricular outflow causes the confusion because it can peak late in systole. Also, it increases in intensity and duration with standing and diminishes during squatting. However, the murmur of IHSS increases markedly in

In addition, there is no early decrease in intensity of the murmur of [HSS after amyl nitrite is inhaled, as occurs with the murmur of mitral valve prolapse. Perhaps the most consistent difference between the murmurs in these two conditions is in the cardiac cycle following a premature ventricular beat: the murmur of IHSS increases markedly in intensity and duration due to augmented contractility, whereas the murmur of mitral valve prolapse is not changed because the larger left ventricular end-diastolic volume following the compensatory pause offsets the effects of increased contractility. 

###### Noninvasive tests 

Electrocardiogram The most common electrocardiographic abnormalities occurring in the mitral valve prolapse syndrome are ST-T wave changes in the inferior leads (II, III, and aV,). Some have. speculated that these changes reflect ischemia of the inferior wall due to traction on the posteromedial papillary muscle by the prolapsing mitral leaflets. However, these nonspecific ECG changes are seen in less than 15 percent of patients at rest. Occasionally, the changes may appear during interventions that induce earlier occurrence of mitral valve prolapse in systole. More unusual changes include prominent U waves, peaked T waves in the midprecordial leads, and prolongation of the QT interval. There are few data concerning the exercise electrocardiogram in patients with mitral valve prolapse, and there is a great deal of variability in the results reported. However, it appears that the mitral valve prolapse syndrome is a common cause of a false-positive exercise electrocardiogram in patients with normal coronary arteries, especially females. It is unknown whether some of these patients have true ischemia during exercise because of mitral valve prolapse and increased tension on the left ventricular wall. Therefore, the exercise electrocardiogram is of little value in differentiating between mitral valve prolapse and ischemic heart disease. Perfusion scintigraphy Because of the abovementioned problems with the exercise elec- 
###### CLINICAL PRESENTATION 

trocardiogram, exercise thallium 201 myocardial perfusion scintigraphy has been recommended as an adjunct to exercise electrocardiographic testing for detecting the patient with the physical findings of mitral valve prolapse who has ischemic heart disease. Very few patients with the mitral valve prolapse syndrome without demonstrable ischemic heart disease who have a positive exercise thallium scintigram have been described. However, it must be emphasized that this method will not detect global myocardial ischemia. Also, a small area of ischemia, for instance in a papillary muscle, may be beyond the resolution of the thallium scan. Therefore, a negative scintigram in these patients does not exclude ischemia as a basis for their chest pain, nor does it completely exclude coronary artery disease as the etiology. Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring Although arrhythmias may be seen on the resting electrocardiogram or during treadmill exercise, the most reliable way of detecting them is by continuous ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring. Several studies in patients with mitral valve prolapse have shown much more frequent occurrence of arrhythmias than in normal subjects. In fact, the incidence of arrhythmias ranges from 40 to 75 percent of patients with mitral valve prolapse. However, not all of the arrhythmias detected (such as atrial ectopic beats) are potentially hazardous. There is some evidence that patients with ST-T wave changes in inferior leads have a higher incidence of serious ventricular arrhythmias on ambulatory monitoring. Chest roentgenography Plain chest roentgenograms are useful for defining the extent of any thoracic skeletal abnormalities. Usually the cardiac silhouette is of normal size in patients with uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse, but if significant mitral regurgitation is present, left ventricular and left atrial enlargement may be noted. An enlarged cardiac outline in the posteroanterior projection may be the result of cardiac compression from a straightened spine and pectus excavatum. 

Echocardiography The most important noninvasive test for establishing the diagnosis of mi-

tral valve prolapse is the echocardiogram. Timemotion (M-mode) echocardiography has been very useful in this regard because of the ease with which the mitral valve can be imaged throughout the cardiac cycle. The most specific finding is a late systolic posterior buckling of the mitral valve leaflet (Fig. 3). The click usually occurs at the onset of this buckling motion followed by the late systolic murmur. However, this echocardiographic pattern can be observed in patients without auscultatory signs of mitral valve prolapse, and it can occur in patients with a pansystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation. Furthermore, the timing of the click and murmur may not coincide with the echocardiographic pattern. The explanation for these variations in the relationship between the auscultatory and echocardiographic events is that the single ultrasound beam can traverse only a portion of the mitral valve, and portions outside the beam may be responsible for the ausculatory features. In fact, by moving the echo beam, one can alter the echo pattern of mitral valve prolapse. Another common echocardiographic pattern is pansystolic ‘“‘hammocking”’ of the mitral valve 

100 MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE SYNDROME 

leaflet in systole. This finding is probably less specific for primary mitral valve prolapse than is late systolic buckling, and it may be a technical artifact. Abnormal posterior systolic motion of the mitral valve can be produced by too high a transducer position on the chest, so that the normal movement of the mitral valve apparatus toward the left ventricular apex during systole gives the false impression of posterior prolapse on the echocardiogram. Also, these echocardiographic findings are not specific for primary mitral valve prolapse and can occur with mitral valve prolapse due to other disease entities. 

The pathological changes of primary mitral valve prolapse are not readily identified by M- mode echocardiography. However, multiple layering of the mitral valve echoes is suggestive of the irregular hooding deformity of the valve and excessive motion in diastole is suggestive of redundant tissue. Patients with ruptured chordae tendineae have specific changes in mitral valve motion, and vegetations may be visualized in some patients with endocarditis. Also, alterations in left ventricular and left atrial size as a result of mitral regurgitation are readily detected by M-mode echocardiography.
