Occasionally the M-mode echocardiogram may be completely normal in patients with the classic auscultatory findings. The incidence of false-negative diagnoses has been estimated to be as high as 15 percent. Recently, two-dimensional echocardiography has been advocated as a more sensitive technique for detecting mitral valve prolapse. The advantage of this technique is its ability to image large segments of the heart in real time, which affords better spatial orientation because the actual anatomy is visualized. 

The most commonly used two-dimensional view of the heart for assessing mitral valve prolapse is the parasternal long-axis section, which is illustrated in Fig. 4. In this view, the entire mitral valve apparatus and its attachments to the mitral annulus and aorta can be visualized, and buckling of the leaflets back toward the left atrium is usually readily apparent. However, patients with auscultatory and left ventricular cineangiographic evidence of mitral valve prolapse have been described with normal two-dimensional echocardiograms. Some investigators believe that this incidence is lessened by using the apical four-chamber plane in which both atria and ventricles are imaged. 

###### Catheterization, angiography, and coronary arteriography 

Since the diagnosis can usually be established by auscultation and echocardiography, cardiac catheterization is used infrequently as a diagnostic technique in mitral valve prolapse. Also, it is not necessary to perform contrast cineangiography to determine the function of the left ventricle, since it can be determined by two-dimensional echocardiography or radionuclide angiography. However, contrast cineangiography is useful in assessing the severity of mitral regurgitation. Therefore, cardiac catheterization and angiography in mitral valve prolapse are most commonly used to exclude the possibility of coronary artery disease. Intracardiac pressures and cardiac output are usually normal in uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse. However, these measurements become progressively more abnormal as mitral regurgitation becomes more severe. In such patients, the findings are typical of mitral regurgitation from 

COMPLICATIONS /0/ 

any etiology and include elevated left ventricular end-diastolic, left atrial, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures, and occasionally pulmonary arterial and right ventricular hypertension. In the most severe cases, cardiac output may be reduced. 

Left ventricular cineangiography usually confirms the presence of prolapse of the mitral valve leaflets (Fig. 5). The right anterior oblique projection is best for observing prolapse of the three scallops of the posterior leaflet. The left anterior oblique view is necessary for the adequate evaluation of prolapse of the anterior leaflet. 

Left ventricular wall motion is usually normal in patients with primary mitral valve prolapse, but some patients show abnormal contraction patterns in the absence of coronary artery disease. These contraction abnormalities usually represent indentations of the left ventricle at the point of attachment of the papillary muscles that are thought to be due to abnormal traction on the papillary muscles and buckling of the ventricular wall. In support of this hypothesis, patients with the most severe prolapse more commonly exhibit misshapen ventricular cavities during systole, and several patients with wall motion abnormalities who had mitral valve replacement for severe regurgitation have been shown to have no wall motion abnormalities after operation. The significance of this systolic buckling is unclear, although it has been suggested that it may lead to arrhythmias and chest pain. Other observers have speculated that these wall motion abnormalities are the primary process and that they are responsible for prolapse of the mitral valve. However, the presence of specific pathologic abnormalities of the mitral valve in this syndrome would not support this thesis. One recent study has purported to show pathologic changes in the myocardium in patients with mitral valve prolapse, but it is unclear whether these changes are primary or secondary to chronic mitral regurgitation. Therefore, the issue of a myocardial component in this syndrome is not resolved. 

Coronary arteriography is usually normal in primary mitral valve prolapse, and no congenital anomalies of the coronary vessels have been found to be associated with this syndrome. Because of the great interest in coronary artery spasm and its possible relationship to atypical 

FIGURE 5 Systolic frame from a lateral left ventricular contrast cineangiogram in a patient with severe mitral valve prolapse. The dotted line partially outlines the prolapsing scallops of the leaflets. LV, left ventricle; Ao, aorta. 

chest pain syndromes, some investigators are now routinely giving ergonovine injections to symptomatic patients with mitral valve prolapse undergoing coronary arteriography. Presumably, ergonovine induces spasm in patients with variant angina but not in normal individuals. Some investigators have found an increased incidence of coronary artery spasm in patients with mitral valve prolapse, but others have not. Therefore, the prevalence of coronary artery spasm among the general population of patients with this syndrome is unknown, as is the extent to which this explains the chest pain and arrhythmias in some of these patients. 

###### COMPLICATIONS 

Sudden death This is the least common but obviously the most serious and feared complication of mitral valve prolapse. The actual incidence of this complication has been difficult to ascertain. In a long-term study by Mills and associates of 53 patients followed for 8 months to 22 years, there was one sudden death. In another study by Allen and coworkers of 62 patients with 

###### 102 

###### MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE SYNDROME 

auscultatory evidence of mitral valve prolapse followed for 9 to 22 years, no-episodes of sudden death occurred. The highest incidence of sudden death has been reported in the familial form of mitral valve prolapse. Some of these patients have been noted to have QT-interval prolongation, which would make them particularly vulnerable to the development of ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Also, patients with mitral valve prolapse with severe autonomic dysfunction and excessive vagotonia leading to bradyarrhythmias and asystole have been reported. Therefore, it is believed that arrhythmias are the usual cause of sudden death in patients with mitral valve prolapse. Of course, patients with Marfan’s syndrome may suffer from other complications, such as dissection of the aorta, which could lead to sudden death. 

It has been suggested that all patients with mitral valve prolapse should be evaluated for arrhythmias by continuous ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring. However, this would entail a great expenditure of money and resources for a rare complication. Furthermore, there is no evidence that the treatment of arrhythmias detected in this manner will prevent sudden death. Therefore, it seems prudent to try to limit evaluation to those patients at highest risk. Some observers believe that patients with electrocardiographic ST-T changes are more likely to have complex ventricular arrhythmias. Certainly, any patients with symptoms suggestive of arrhythmias or who have arrhythmias noted on physical examination or on the resting electrocardiogram should be evaluated further. However, at this time, we do not recommend screening all patients with mitral valve prolapse for arrhythmias by means of ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring, especially if they are asymptomatic and there are no arrhythmias detected by physical examination or on the resting electrocardiogram. 

Infective endocarditis Another serious complication of mitral valve prolapse whose exact incidence is unknown is infective endocarditis. In the study of Mills and associates, 3 of 53 patients developed endocarditis, whereas Allen and coworkers noted that 5 out of 62 patients developed this complication. Of the 8 patients with infective endocarditis reported in these two stud- 

ies 2 succumbed to the disease and 2 others developed chordal rupture and more severe mitral regurgitation. Some observers believe that infective endocarditis occurs more frequently in patients with murmurs than in those with isolated midsystolic clicks. However, there are reports of patients with isolated midsystolic clicks who developed infective endocarditis and then were discovered to have murmurs of mitral regurgitation. Some of these patients have required valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation. It appears that all patients with auscultatory evidence of the mitral valve prolapse syndrome are at risk of developing this complication, and it is recommended that these patients receive antibiotic prophylaxis for any dental or other surgical procedures. It is unclear whether or not patients with so-called silent mitral prolapse visualized on echocardiography without the accompanying auscultatory features of the syndrome should receive antibiotic prophylaxis. We are currently not recommending it. 

Progressive mitral regurgitation This complication can occur in the mitral valve prolapse syndrome as a result of endocarditis or chordal rupture. It may also occur as an insidious process over the years. The exact incidence of slowly progressive mitral regurgitation in patients with mitral valve prolapse is unknown. Studies of families have shown a preponderance of isolated clicks in young children, the click and murmur complex in young adults, and pansystolic murmurs in older individuals. This distribution of the auscultatory findings suggests that at least in some patients the lesion progresses slowly to more severe degrees of mitral regurgitation at older ages. Of the 53 patients followed by Mills and associates for up to 22 years, 5 developed progressive mitral regurgitation and 2 of these required mitral valve replacement. In the study of Allen and coworkers of 62 patients followed for up to 22 years, 1 patient, aged 75, died of progressive mitral regurgitation and 10 patients were felt to have increased mitral regurgitation. 

Cerebral emboli The reports describing young adults with mitral valve prolapse who presented with visual problems consistent with 

###### MANAGEMENT 103 

embolism in the ophthalmic or posterior cerebral circulation have stimulated interest in other potential central nervous system complications of the syndrome. A recent retrospective study of patients with cerebrovascular accidents of various types found a higher incidence of mitral valve prolapse in those under age 45 than would have been expected in a similar population without cerebrovascular accidents. Some of these patients with no obvious cause for their strokes, except for the mitral valve prolapse, had cerebral angiography performed, and most had arterial occlusions consistent with emboli. Therefore, it appears that cerebral emboli, especially to the ophthalmic artery and posterior cerebral circulation, should be included among the list of possible complications of mitral valve prolapse. The etiology of the cerebral emboli is currently unknown, but speculation has centered on the platelet and fibrin deposits seen on the myxomatous mitral valves in pathological examination. Also of note is a report of a left atrial thrombus visualized by two-dimensional echocardiography behind the posterior mitral leaflet of one patient with mitral valve prolapse and in another in whom it was seen at autopsy. Of interest are recent reports that platelet survival is reduced in patients with mitral valve prolapse, especially those who have had cerebral vascular events. Therefore, it has been recommended that antiplatelet drugs, such as aspirin and sulfinpyrazone, should be administered to patients with mitral valve prolapse and suspected central nervous system emboli. Whether or not such therapy is effective in preventing these cerebral events is not known, and because of the rarity of this complication it is not recommended that patients with mitral valve prolapse who have not suffered such complications receive this therapy. 

###### MANAGEMENT 

The asymptomatic patient The most frequent problem in the management of mitral valve prolapse is presented by the asymptomatic patient. Ideally, one would like to identify patients who are at a higher risk of future complications so that they may be carefully followed or treated prophylactically. No definitive guidelines exist, but it has been observed that patients with more 

severe mitral regurgitation with evidence of left ventricular and left atrial enlargement are at higher risk for all complications. Also, patients with the ST-T wave changes in inferior electrocardiographic leads may be at a higher risk for developing dangerous ventricular arrhythmias. The best policy would be to submit such patients to continuous ambulatory monitoring, a test which would not be recommended in the usual asymptomatic patient without such electrocardiographic changes. Our approach to the asymptomatic patient is to perform a careful physical examination and to have an echocardiogram made to document the presence of the syndrome and to assess chamber size and function. Patients who have arrhythmias detected during physical examination or on routine electrocardiography, and those with ST-T wave changes in inferior leads, would then undergo continuous ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring. Other patients would not be evaluated further unless symptoms arose. All patients with auscultatory evidence of mitral valve prolapse should receive antibiotic therapy for dental and surgical procedures in order to prevent infective endocarditis. Asymptomatic patients without evidence of complications are not restricted in their activities. However, patients who wish to engage in competitive athletics should have an exercise ECG test performed. 

The symptomatic patient First, let us consider the patient with chest pain. Patients younger than 35 to 40 years of age, especially if they are female, should have continuous ambulatory monitoring to detect ST-segment changes and arrhythmias during episodes of pain. For this purpose, a modified lead II as well as lead V,, should be recorded. This technique is useful in trying to exclude variant angina due to coronary artery spasm, but it may also reveal typical ischemic ST-segment depression or tachyarrhythmias during pain. Treadmill exercise also should be performed to establish the patient’s functional capacity and to try to provoke the chest pain. It must be realized that ST-T wave changes on the exercise electrocardiogram may be misleading in these patients. Therefore, exercise testing with thallium should be repeated in patients with positive ECG changes. If the exercise electrocardiogram and thallium scintigram

are negative and the pain is atypical for ischemia, the young patient is treated with propranolol. If this drug, in adequate beta-blocking doses, does not control the pain, then the patients are referred for coronary angiography. Patients with positive exercise electrocardiograms or thallium scintigrams, especially if their pain 1s typical of ischemia, should be referred for coronary arteriography to establish or exclude the diagnosis of coronary artery disease. 

The patient with chest pain who is older, especially if a male, should have coronary angiography recommended regardless of the results of the noninvasive workup. In this situation, ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring is performed to detect arrhythmias that may contribute to the symptoms, and a treadmill test is carried out to evaluate exercise tolerance. Therefore, the major goal in the older patient with chest pain is to exclude ischemic heart disease, which carries a different prognosis and may require other forms of therapy. 

Patients with fatigue and dyspnea should undergo treadmill exercise testing in order to assess their functional capacity. If there are signs of lung disease on physical examination, the patient also should have pulmonary function tests, including arterial blood gas determination. If no reduced cardiac or pulmonary function is detected by means of objective testing, the patient can be reassured and placed on an exercise program to build up his or her exercise capacity. Patients with significant cardiac limitation due to mitral regurgitation or left ventricular dysfunction are treated for heart failure; if troublesome symptoms persist, they should undergo cardiac catheterization and left ventricular angiography and be evaluated for mitral valve replacement. 

The indications for mitral valve replacement in mitral valve prolapse are similar to those for

mitral regurgitation of any etiology. Significant symptoms due to elevated pulmonary venous pressure despite medical management constitute the primary indication. A few patients have undergone this operation for medically intractable cardiac arrhythmias with variable results (see below). Theoretically, mitral valve replacement might be recommended in selected patients because of recurrent emboli that are unresponsive to anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents. 

Patients with palpitation should undergo continuous ambulatory monitoring to determine the presence and define the frequency and type of arrhythmias present. If palpitation occurs during exertion, treadmill testing may be useful to define the type of arrhythmia. Once the type of arrhythmia is determined, appropriate therapy can be planned. Most atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias associated with mitral valve prolapse respond well to propranolol therapy. Occasionally, a patient may require other agents such as quinidine or procainamide. In the patient with prolonged QT interval, diphenylhydantoin may be helpful, although propranolol usually is effective in this situation as well. 

Some patients with severe ventricular arrhythmias are refractory to all available antiarrhythmic agents. A few such patients, who were shown to have severe contraction abnormalities on left ventricular cineangiography, have responded to mitral valve replacement. Since both the contraction abnormalities and arrhythmias disappeared, it was suggested that tension on the papillary muscles and left ventricular wall due to the prolapsing leaflets was responsible for arrhythmias and contraction abnormalities. However, other patients in whom this procedure was ineffective have been described. Therefore, mitral valve replacement for severe refractory ventricular arrhythmias is controversial and proba- 

###### REFERENCES 105 

bly should not be undertaken unless the patient also has symptomatic mitral regurgitation. Although several serious complications of primary mitral valve prolapse have been described and the management of these problems can be vexing, the vast majority of patients with this syndrome not only are asymptomatic but will have a benign course (Fig. 6). Also, physicians should be careful not to overdiagnose the condition on inadequate evidence, such as questionable auscultatory findings and minor changes on the echocardiogram. In the asymptomatic patient with the primary mitral valve prolapse syndrome, reassurance and antibiotic prophylaxis for surgery are the most important aspects of management.

###### VARIANT ANGINA 

###### JAMES E. MULLER and EUGENE BRAUNWALD 

###### DEFINITION 

Variant angina is a clinical syndrome characterized by the presence of reversible ST-segment elevation in an electrocardiogram (ECG) recorded during an anginal attack (Fig. 1). It is now recognized that the disorder may occur with or without rest angina, with or without exertion-induced angina, and with or without significant fixed coronary atherosclerosis. Although the classic form of variant angina is rare, the condition has recently attracted intense interest because an effective new therapy has appeared. In addition, variant angina serves as a model for the possible role of coronary artery spasm in the more common conditions of classic angina pectoris and acute myocardial infarction. 

###### HISTORY 

In 1959 Prinzmetal et al. described a group of patients with ST-segment elevation during pain, angina at rest, and preservation of exercise capacity. Although this article was the first to clearly separate a distinct group of patients from the much larger group of patients with classic angina, Prinzmetal was careful to note contributions by his predecessors to the identification of these patients. He pointed out, for instance, that even in the original description of classic angina pectoris Heberden had described a patient in whom angina occurred at rest: “I have heard one, and only one person say, that he had known it attack him while he was up and standing still or sitting.” The ECG findings of Prinzmetal’s

###### (A) BEFORE PAIN 

###### 108 VARIANT ANGINA 

angina were first described in 1941 by Wilson, who reported changes similar to those of myocardial infarction occurring with attacks of angina pectoris. Although recognition of the characteristic history and ECG changes pre- 

###### FIGURE 2 

Angiograms provided by Dr. Philip Oliva which demonstrate (A) focal narrowing of the right coronary artery during an episode of chest pain and ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads. B. After the pain and ECG changes resolve the artery is patent. i = 

ceded Prinzmetal’s description of the condition, his papers crystallized the features of the disorder and led to concentration on the identification and treatment of this subgroup of patients with angina pectoris. 

Since this publication, several other features of the disorder have come to be appreciated. It has been found that in some patients the attacks of pain and ST-segment elevation may be provoked by exercise. In addition, it has been observed that certain patients who generally develop ST-segment elevation with their attacks of pain may, during other attacks, develop ST-segment depression. 

These new observations as well as the results of angiographic studies have led to great confusion in the use of the terms Prinzmetal’s angina and variant angina. It seems most useful to reserve the diagnosis of Prinzmetal’s angina for patients known to have reversible ST-segment elevation with angina at rest and preservation of exercise Capacity, i.e., to retain the exact criteria used by Prinzmetal. The term variant angina can be used to describe the larger group of patients with ST-segment elevation during pain who may or may not have rest angina, exertion-induced angina, and fixed coronary atherosclerosis. Such terminology preserves the traditional meaning of the term Prinzmetal’s angina and permits description of more recently discovered forms of the disease with the term variant angina. 

###### ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS 

The episodic anginal pain and ST-segment elevation which characterize variant angina are caused by transmural ischemia of a major portion of the myocardium. ST-segment depression, which is sometimes observed in these patients, can result from subendocardial ischemia of the anterior or inferior myocardium. In some cases, reciprocal anterior ST-segment depression can result from posterior transmural ischemia. 

The ischemia in these patients may result from one of two processes. In patients without significant coronary atherosclerosis, transient focal narrowing may occur, which is best termed spasm of a coronary artery (Fig. 2). The cause of such local spasm is unknown. It has been hypothesized that minor intimal damage caused by nonobstructive atherosclerosis may prompt local 

DIAGNOSIS AND EVALUATION /09 

strictor. Thromboxane A, is highly unstable and that the level of thromboxane B, in venous blood centrations of thromboxane A, which causes platelet aggregation and formation of thromboxane A,, an extremely potent coronary vasoconis rapidly transformed into the chemically stable but inactive thromboxane B,. It has been found of patients with variant angina is markedly elevated. The range of concentrations of thromboxane B, (10 to 100 pmol/ml) observed in patients with variant angina is similar to the range of concontractions of isolated coronary arteries in several species of animals. 

The coronary vessels are richly innervated with sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers which may also cause focal spasm. However, these fibers cannot be the only cause for the abnormal contraction, since coronary artery spasm has been found to occur in some patients with cardiac transplants whose hearts are totally denervated. 

In patients with significant coronary atherosclerosis, a normal increase in vasomotor tone may be sufficient to occlude the coronary lumen. Alternatively, platelet plugs may form on an atherosclerotic plaque and temporarily occlude an already narrowed lumen. 

Patients with no coronary atherosclerosis and those with severe atherosclerosis represent the ends of a spectrum. There are many patients in the middle of the spectrum in whom substantial amounts of fixed and variable obstruction combine to produce obstruction to coronary blood flow (Fig. 3). Even in a single patient, there may be one coronary vessel in which spasm predominates and another in which an increase in vasomotor tone of an already narrowed vessel causes occlusion of the lumen. Although the precise distribution of patients along this spectrum is not known, approximately 50 percent of patients with Prinzmetal’s angina have no fixed coronary stenosis exceeding 70 percent. 

###### DIAGNOSIS AND EVALUATION 

The single most important clinical clue to the identification of this life-threatening illness is the occurrence of angina at rest with preservation of exercise capacity. The patient will usually experience numerous brief unprovoked attacks of angina that resolve spontaneously or following

A diagram indicating that different mixtures of fixed and variable coronary obstruction may produce myocardial ischemia. The dashed line represents a case in which both spasm and fixed obstruction play significant roles in occluding a coronary artery. 

the use of sublingual nitroglycerin. The onset of the problem may be quite sudden. The illness may start on a single day with numerous attacks of severe transient chest pain. The attacks may be associated with syncopal episodes. In a few patients other disorders of smooth-muscle tone such as Raynaud’s phenomenon or esophageal spasm may be present. The disorder occurs with equal frequency in males and females; the average age of the patients is 5 to 10 years less than that of patients with classic angina. Recognition of the disease is of great importance because without therapy it is associated with a significant mortality rate, presumably from ischemia-induced arrhythmias. In patients who report such a history, every effort should be made to obtain an ECG during an attack of pain. If the chest pain is being caused by variant angina, the ECG during pain will show dramatic changes similar to those seen during the very early stages of an acute myocardial infarction. The ST segment rises above the base line, the R wave increases in height, and the S wave disappears. These ECG changes begin to resolve as the patient’s chest pain diminishes. Within minutes the QRS complexes and ST segment return to normal but, T-wave changes often persist for a longer period. These changes generally occur in several of the anterior or the inferior leads, reflecting events in the distribution of a 

###### 110 VARIANT ANGINA 

major coronary artery. Ventricular arrhythmias and AV conduction disturbances occur in over 30 percent of patients. There is no doubt that these ECG changes reflect the sudden onset and resolution of severe transmural myocardial ischemia. An identical sequence of ECG changes can be reproduced in the experimental animal by the temporary occlusion of a major coronary artery. 

Admission to acoronary care unit with continuous electrocardiographic monitoring is generally the best method to obtain an ECG during pain, if the attacks occur at the rate of at least one every 3 to 4 days. In patients with less frequent attacks, periodic Holter monitoring may reveal episodic elevation of the ST segment above the base line. Continuous electrocardiographic monitoring in either the coronary care unit or by Holter recorder will often reveal that ST-segment elevation may occur without chest pain. When the chest pain and ECG changes can both be observed, it will be found that the ECG changes generally precede the onset of chest pain. The patient should be evaluated for the presence of complete heart block or ventricular tachycardia. Holter monitoring and ECG recordings during pain are useful in determining if such arrhythmias are present. 

It is now the general practice to perform coronary arteriography in all patients with variant angina to determine the presence or absence of fixed coronary obstruction. This knowledge is of immediate value since coronary artery bypass grafting should be considered only for patients with fixed obstructive lesions. 

###### The ergonovine test 

The intravenous injection of ergonovine maleate produces focal spasm in the coronary arteries of patients with variant angina but causes only a diffuse narrowing in patients without the condition. The test has been used frequently in patients with chest pain syndromes to establish or exclude the diagnosis of Prinzmetal’s angina. The patient is given gradually increasing doses of ergonovine and observed for evidence of an attack. A coronary arteriogram is then obtained to determine the presence or absence of coronary spasm. 

At the present time there is a growing aware- 

ness that this test may be more dangerous than originally thought and that its use for clinical purposes should be more limited. Certainly patients known to have rest pain with documented reversible ST-segment elevation need not be subjected to ergonovine provocation. In patients in whom it is likely that the pain results from coronary artery spasm, a therapeutic trial of nitrites or nifedipine (an experimental calcium channel blocking agent which is remarkably effective in the therapy of variant angina) should be done to determine whether or not the patient’s symptoms can be controlled. If it is less certain that the patient’s symptoms are caused by coronary spasm, the ergonovine test may be of value. A negative response will prevent a patient from receiving needless therapy for coronary spasm. The test should be performed only during cardiac catheterization since intracoronary administration of nitroglycerin may be required if intense spasm develops. A calcium channel blocking agent should be ready for use, if available. The ergonovine test has been used for research purposes to study the course of patients with variant angina. It has been found that sensitivity to ergonovine, which presumably reflects the intensity of the tendency to spasm, varies markedly over time. These spontaneous variations in the course of the disease provide opportunities for characterization of its basic cause. 

###### MANAGEMENT 

The complications of variant angina determine the urgency of treatment and the degree of control which must be sought. If the attacks occur with great frequency or are associated with lifethreatening arrhythmias, rapid and complete control must be sought. Prolonged attacks of spasm may lead to myocardial infarction and should be treated aggressively. However, if the attacks occur rarely and terminate spontaneously without arrhythmia, attempts to control them need not be as vigorous. 

###### Sublingual nitroglycerin 

As a first step, the patient should be instructed to take one or two nitroglycerin tablets (0.45 mg) sublingually at the first sign of an attack. This maneuver may prevent spasm from becoming 

###### MANAGEMENT 111 

Long-acting nitrates severe and may accelerate the spontaneous resolution of an attack. 

Oral isosorbide dinitrate and nitroglycerin paste should be the primary agents used in the attempt to prevent attacks. Isosorbide dinitrate can be started in a dosage of 10 mg every 6h and gradually increased to 20 mg every 4h or to a higher dosage if attacks persist and side effects of significant hypotension and headache do not occur. Calcium channel blocking agents 

The most promising new development in the control of variant angina has been the development over the past 5 years of agents which block the slow calcium channel current. The smoothmuscle cells in walls of the coronary arteries, which produce vasoconstriction, are particularly sensitive to these blocking agents. This sensitivity results from the dependence of these cells on the slow calcium channel for the generation of their action potential and a relatively specific effect of the blocking agents on cells in this location. Among these agents, nifedipine has been the most widely used. It is a coronary vasodilator which can produce coronary flow equal to reactive hyperemia. Nifedipine was originally developed in 1971 as acoronary vasodilator for use in patients with classic angina pectoris. It has since been proved to be effective therapy for classic angina in numerous controlled studies conducted in Europe. Its effectiveness in these patients may result from its ability to diminish myocardial oxygen demand as well as its ability to dilate the coronary arteries. 

In preliminary observations it has also been found to be extremely useful in the management of variant angina. The collective experience in the United States with the use of nifedipine for variant angina has recently been summarized. Data were available from 127 patients. All patients had chest pains at rest with reversible STsegment elevation or coronary artery spasm visualized during catheterization. Most patients had failed conventional therapy with nitrates. The average number of attacks per week fell markedly from 16 per week prior to use of nifedipine to 2 per week after nifedipine was administered. Complete elimination of attacks was 

achieved in 63 percent of the patients, whereas only 7 percent showed less than a 10 percent decrease in the number of attacks. 

Only minor reversible side effects such as mild hypotension, flushing, and dysesthesias were noted. This lack of serious side effects is in accord with more extensive experience in Europe and Japan, where nifedipine has been widely used for several years in patients with classic angina. 

Verapamil is a similar agent which has also been useful in the treatment of variant angina but is more likely to produce atrioventricular block and depress myocardial contractility than is nifedipine. Diltiazem is the most recently developed calcium channel blocking agent. Although experience with diltiazem is limited, this agent appears to be as effective as nifedipine or verapamil for the treatment of variant angina. 

Thus, calcium channel blocking agents are of great value in the treatment of variant angina. At the present time, since they are not yet licensed for general use, they are administed only to patients who cannot be controlled with long-acting nitrates. In these patients nitrates are generally continued because the antispasmodic activity of nitrates and calcium channel blockers are additive.

###### Pi VARIANT ANGINA 

###### Beta-adrenergic blockade 

Agents such as propranolol are not as effective in patients with variant angina as in patients with classic angina. In patients with classic angina, propranolol is effective in suppressing the periodic increases in oxygen demand which cause pain; in variant angina, control of increases in oxygen demand has little effect since the primary problem is a periodic decrease in oxygen supply. Furthermore, it has been theorized that blockade of the beta-sympathetic receptors which dilate the coronary arteries could actually enhance spasm. It has been suggested that beta blockers may be most effective in patients with variant angina who have severe fixed obstructive disease. Many clinicians begin a therapeutic trial of a beta blocker in patients who have continued attacks when on maximal nitrate therapy. Beta blockers should definitely be avoided in patients whose attacks are complicated by heart block. 

###### Alpha-adrenergic blockade 

Since alpha-adrenergic stimuli are known to constrict the coronary arteries, alpha blockers such as phenoxybenzamine have been given to patients with variant angina. The response to these agents, however, has not been impressive. It is likely that the systemic effects of the drugs prevent attainment of adequate alpha-adrenergic blockade of the coronary arteries. 

###### Antiarrhythmic agents 

Many patients with variant angina are given antiarrhythmic agents such as quinidine or procainamide in attempts to control premature ventricular contractions or ventricular tachycardia which develop during attacks of chest pain. These arrhythmias differ from those in patients without variant angina in that they are often refractory to therapy, since they result from acute ischemia. Also, it is possible to treat the cause of the arrhythmias in variant angina rather than the arrhythmias themselves. The highest priority in the treatment of variant angina complicated by arrhythmia should be given to the prevention of coronary spasm and recurrent ischemia. Antiarrhythmic agents should be used only in the small percentage of patients with arrhythmias in 

whom prevention of attacks of ischemia cannot be accomplished. Coronary artery bypass grafting 

In most instances attempts to bypass areas of focal spasm in patients without significant coronary atherosclerosis have not led to relief of symptoms. Failure of such attempts apparently results from intrinsic abnormality of the entire artery. In one patient a major section of the epicardial portion of a coronary artery was seen to constrict into a cordlike structure at the time of thoracotomy. Vessels with such abnormal reactivity are likely to constrict at sites distal, as well as proximal, to the site of anastomosis of a saphenous vein bypass graft. 

Even in the case of severe fixed obstruction, bypass grafting is not as successful in patients with variant angina as in patients with classic angina. Bypass grafting is most likely to be successful in relieving symptoms in those patients in whom the transient ischemia results from normal changes in coronary vasomotor tone superimposed on a significant fixed lesion. Thus, surgery should be considered for patients with severe fixed stenosis and attacks of ischemia which cannot be controlled medically. The role of surgery in patients with stenosis who become asymptomatic on medical therapy is subject to the same uncertainties as the role of surgery in patients with classic angina who become asymptomatic with medical therapy. Duration of therapy 

With the use of long-acting nitrates and calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine, it is possible to prevent virtually all attacks of variant angina in the majority of patients. After patients are asymptomatic for 6 months or more, the issue of discontinuation of one or all of the medications arises. In principle, discontinuation may be justified because the natural history of the disorder includes spontaneous disappearance of the stimulus for spasm. The agents must be tapered off gradually, however, because the withdrawal of long-acting nitrates or nifedipine over a 48-h period has led to prolonged coronary artery spasm, which causes myocardial infarction. Withdrawal should therefore be done in gradual 

1b ies 

###### REFERENCES 

steps over a period of weeks rather than days. During this period, the patient should be instructed to take sublingual nitroglycerin at the first sign of an attack and to reinstitute the previous level of preventive therapy. Since patients frequently miss doses of medication while on chronic therapy, the physician may gain useful information by inquiring about the occurrence of attacks during the period without therapy. Patients who once had over 20 attacks of variant angina per day may be found to be completely free of attacks and off all medication a year later. 

###### THE RELATIONSHIP OF VARIANT ANGINA TO CLASSIC ANGINA PECTORIS AND ACUTE MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION 

The greatest importance of the rare disease of variant angina may be its role as a model for the mechanism by which ischemia is produced in the more widespread disorders of classic angina, both stable and unstable, and myocardial infarction. Extensive efforts are now underway to determine the role of spasm in these disorders. 

Patients with stable angina have been shown to have temporary, inappropriate increases in coronary artery resistance under certain circumstances. It has been demonstrated in patients with classic angina that immersion of the arm in ice water (the cold pressor challenge) increases coronary vascular resistance at a time when myocardial work actually increases as a consequence of increased pressure. In some patients the increase in coronary resistance is associated with production of lactate by the myocardium and the occurrence of angina pectoris. 

A study was conducted to determine if nifedipine could block this inappropriate coronary vasoconstriction in classic angina, since the agent had been found to be so effective against spasm in variant angina. Patients with classic angina pectoris were given the cold pressor challenge while coronary flow was being measured with a coronary sinus thermodilution catheter. With the cold pressor challenge, systemic arterial pressure increased, producing an increase in myocardial oxygen demand which could be met by a decrease in coronary vascular resistance. However, coronary vascular resistance actually increased (from 0.92 + 0.13 to 1.13 + 0.25 

resistance units). Half of the patients developed chest pain and lactate production. Following recovery from the first cold pressor challenge, the patients were given 10 mg nifedipine, which was chewed for buccal absorption. The cold pressor challenge was then repeated. In the presence of nifedipine, none of the patients developed an increase in coronary vascular resistance. The mean coronary resistance fell (from 0.92 + 0.04 to 0.82 + 0.05), as was appropriate for the increase in systemic arterial pressure. None of the patients developed angina pectoris or lactate production by the myocardium after treatment with nifedipine. These studies indicate that coronary vasoconstriction may play a role in the production of classic angina pectoris and that such vasoconstriction may be selectively blocked by nifedipine. 

It is also likely that coronary spasm, which is so clearly evident in Prinzmetal’s angina, may play a covert but much more significant role in the pathogenesis of ischemic heart disease by causing unstable angina and myocardial infarction in certain patients. The elegant studies by Maseri have clearly shown with angiography that some patients with unstable angina and even myocardial infarction have spasm as the pathophysiologic mechanism. Studies are currently underway to determine if nifedipine may be useful in the control of unstable angina or in the prevention of threatened myocardial infarction. The impetus for these studies arose from experience in patients with variant angina in whom the role of coronary spasm and its control with nifedipine are most apparent.

##### FOR PREMALIGNANT AND MALIGNANT DISEASE COLONIC CANCER: SCREENING 

###### SIDNEY J. WINAWER and PAUL SHERLOCK 

###### GENERAL SCREENING CONSIDERATIONS 

It is presumed that screening asymptomatic people at risk for a disease will be of benefit if effective screening methods are available. The question, however, is a complex one, and the answer is not easily obtained. The process of screening is the efficient application of relatively simple and inexpensive tests to a large number of people in order to identify those who are likely to have disease. Screening would appear to be of benefit if people with asymptomatic disease identified by positive screening tests lived longer than the average person presenting with symptomatic disease. However, bias could influence screening benefit. Patients may be diagnosed earlier than is usual in the natural history of the disease and have a seemingly improved survival but without any real prolongation of life. This has been called lead-time bias. Patients with biologically slowgrowing tumors will tend to be selected out by the screening process, and a survival advantage could be erroneously attributed to the screening. This has been called length bias. In order to properly evaluate the potential benefit of screening and cancel out possible bias, suitable longterm controlled trials must ask pertinent questions and provide critical data on which to base conclusions. 

The effectiveness of screening can be evaluated within the framework of controlled trials by measuring validity, predictiveness, yield in relation to cost, ease of administration, and patient compliance. Validity has been defined as the percentage frequency with which the result of the screening test was later confirmed by an acceptable diagnostic procedure, or the ability of the 

test to separate those who do have the disease from those who do not. Sensitivity is the ability of the test to give a positive finding when the person tested truly has the disease (“ruling in’). Specificity is the ability of the test to give a negative result when the person tested is free of disease (‘ruling out’). The predictive value of a test depends on the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease. 

An important question is whether or not to screen for colorectal cancer, or, more broadly, for colorectal cancer and antecedent premalignant states. This question falls into the framework of the larger area of prevention. Prevention can be divided into primary prevention—the identification and elimination of those factors in the environment related to carcinogenesis — and secondary prevention—the identification and control of premalignant states and the detection of colorectal cancer at an early asymptomatic stage, prior to the onset of more advanced clinical disease. Consideration of the question of screening for colorectal cancer requires addressing several component elements: the expected benefit, in terms of the survival of those with positive screening tests and the possible reduction of the mortality rate in the entire screened population; the ability to identify high-risk subgroups; the availability of effective screening tests; the availability of community health resources adequate to the diagnostic workup and treatment of persons with positive screening tests; cost; patient compliance; and the risk of screening. To this list must be added the factor of the physician. Without the physician’s orientation to this approach and awareness of current concepts and technology, screening will be of no value.

rate reduction was demonstrated in a group screened with proctosigmoidoscopy. Ongoing controlled trials that address this issue for the entire colon using fecal occult blood testing are too recent to have produced data on the mortality rate. The potential benefit of screening is related not only to the detection of cancers but also to the identification of premalignant states. One of these premalignant states is the colonic adenoma. In one study involving more than 100,000 proctoscopy examinations in approximately 18,000 people over a 25-year period, identification and removal of rectosigmoid polyps resulted in an 85 percent reduction in the number of cancers observed as compared with the number expected in the rectosigmoid. There is a considerable amount of information linking most, if not all, colorectal cancers to preexisting premalignant adenomas. Other premalignant states can be uncovered with greater or lesser degrees of effectiveness today. Screening of persons with a family history of familial polyposis will uncover affected individuals; screening of patients with ulcerative colitis will demonstrate a change of the mucosa to a potentially malignant phase; screening of patients in the general population who have genetic susceptibility will uncover individuals at risk for inherited colon cancer. The benefit of screening, therefore, is related to detecting colon cancer early, identifying adenomas for interruption of the adenoma-cancer sequence, and identifying high-risk persons for more intensive surveillance. 

###### POTENTIAL BENEFIT OF SCREENING 

It is justifiable to consider screening for colorectal cancer in the United States since this is a high-risk country by worldwide epidemiologic standards. More than 115,000 new cases occur per year in the United States, and the majority of patients do not survive 5 years. Cancer at this anatomic site ranks with lung and breast cancer as one of the top three cancers in this country in annual incidence. The potential benefit of earlier detection of colorectal cancer can only be inferred at this time. Traditionally, there has been a well-demonstrated correlation of survival with the pathologic stage documented at surgical resection. Patients with Dukes’ A and B cancers have an overall 10-year survival rate of 71 percent as compared with 41 percent in patients with Dukes’ C and distant metastases. In one study, asymptomatic patients who had primary rectosigmoid cancers detected on _ proctosigmoidoscopy had a 90 percent 15-year survival rate. There are no data available as yet on longterm survival in patients who had asymptomatic colon cancers detected. Early reports from screening programs using fecal occult blood testing indicate a higher percentage of cancers with an earlier Dukes’ stage. Based on the above statistics, one could expect an improved survival with early detection of colorectal cancers, especially in the asymptomatic patient. This is analogous to the gastric cancer problem in Japan. With aggressive endoscopic screening procedures, the Japanese have increased the percentage of gastric cancers coming to surgery at an early stage, with a concomitant improvement in patient survival. 

###### HIGH-RISK SUBGROUPS 

Before consideration of high-risk subgroups within the United States, it must first be restated that the entire country is at high risk for colorectal cancer by worldwide epidemiologic standards. Within the United States all males and females from age 40 to 50 and over are at risk for colorectal cancer and can be characterized as average-risk patients (see Table 1). Although there are some cases of colorectal cancer in individuals below age 40, the risk begins to increase significantly at this age and continues to increase more steeply beyond age 50, doubling with each decade, until it reaches a peak at age 75. The risk will be modulated by other risk factors that may 

However, a reduction in mortality rate for colorectal cancer in the screened group would better reflect the total impact of the screening program in the population screened and in the projected community at large. If screening were truly effective, a high percentage of prevalent cases initially and incidence cases later would be uncovered and treated early, with very few missed interval cases. Mortality rate reduction would be the best indication of benefit. Unfortunately, there is only one study available thus far that has addressed the mortality rate issue and provided data. In that study a small mortality

be operative as a function of the individual’s past personal history, family history, occupation, geographic residence, or ethnic background. Environmental factors operate in a broad epidemiologic sense and do not alter the age at which risk begins. Occupational factors operate in colorectal cancer in a very small group of patients and to a minor degree. 

###### Adenomas and prior colon cancer 

There is an overwhelming body of evidence that patients with adenomas of the colon are at increased risk for colorectal cancer. It has been stated that most, if not all, colon cancers arise from adenomas. On a worldwide epidemiologic basis, adenomas and colon cancer parallel each other in frequency of occurrence in different countries. Adenomas follow the same anatomic distribution as cancer in the colon. In high-risk groups such as persons with familial polyposis and inherited colon cancer, there is an association of adenomas and cancers. At St. Mark’s Hospital in London, 14 percent of the malignant tumors examined were interpreted as demonStrating evidence of contiguous benign tumor. The villous adenoma and the mixed type with both adenomatous and villous components (which together comprise about 25 percent of all the adenomas) carry a much higher risk for malignancy than the more common pure adenomatous polyps (75 percent of all colonic adenomas). The association of malignancy with polypoid adenomas is related not only to histology but also to size. The percentage of adenomas under | cm in diameter with malignancy is no greater than 1 percent; between | and 2 cm, approximately 10 percent; and over 2cm, approximately 46 percent. Only some 15 to 20 percent of all polypoid colonic adenomas exceed 2 cm in diameter, but of those that do, close to 90 percent are either villous adenomas or have a villous component. Removal of rectosigmoid polyps appears to reduce the risk of cancer developing in those segments. This was demonstrated in a 25-year study in which patients having periodic sigmoidoscopy had polyps removed whenever they were seen. The observed incidence of rectosigmoid cancer in this population proved to be only 15 percent of that expected, as indicated above.

The conclusions to be drawn from these data are that polypoid adenomas approaching 2 cm in diameter have a highly malignant potential and that this potential is related to the villous component of these adenomas. Since it is impossible to know reliably the histology without removing the lesion, it would appear to be wise, if feasible, to remove all colonic polypoid growths, especially those with a diameter greater than | cm. A past personal history of colorectal cancer that has been resected, or past personal history of adenomas of the colon, places an individual at higher risk for subsequent colorectal neoplasms, both adenomas and cancers. Patients with a colorectal adenoma that has been identified have a 40 to 50 percent chance of having an additional adenoma at the same time (synchronous lesion). If the colon has not been carefully viewed by colonoscopy as well as by radiologic methods, and all synchronous lesions removed, the patient will be at risk for possible continued growth of these lesions, which can then be transformed into cancer. This could occur within a few years of the identification of the index lesion. Patients who have had a colorectal cancer resected and who may be potentially cured of that cancer also have a 40 to 50 percent chance of having an additional synchronous adenoma and a 1.5 to 5 percent chance of having a second synchronous cancer. Either of these two types of synchronous lesions is a potential threat to these patients. 

118 COLONIC CANCER: SCREENING FOR PREMALIGNANT AND MALIGNANT DISEASE 

The patient with a prior colorectal cancer or adenoma also has a risk for subsequent (metachronous) neoplastic lesions. The true -metachronous rate of adenomas in these patients is not known, but it has been estimated to be on the order of 30 to 40 percent over a long period of time, perhaps as long as 25 to 30 years. The true metachronous rate for second cancers has also not been established, but it has been estimated to be between 5 and 10 percent over the same 25- to 30-year time span after cure of the index cancer. However, these estimates will have to be revised in future years after groups of patients who have had a thorough clearing of the colon of all neoplastic lesions on a periodic basis, by radiologic as well as endoscopic methods, have long-range observations made of new lesions that develop de novo. It is clear from all these observations and estimates that the patient with a single colorectal cancer or adenoma is at high risk for neoplasia. Cell proliferation studies have shown that the entire colonic mucosa is in a premalignant state in this setting. 

###### Genetic factors 

Genetic factors operate in a percentage of the patients in the general population to place them at high risk for colorectal cancer. The two major categories of genetically transmitted risk are the polyposis inherited colon cancer group and the nonpolyposis inherited colon cancer group. The polyposis inherited cancer group has been well established and includes familial polyposis and Gardner’s syndrome as the major types. Both of these are transmitted as autosomal dominant with a high degree of penetrance. In familial polyposis there is carpeting of the colon with hundreds or thousands of small adenomas. The adenomas are generally small and sessile, although larger and pedunculated types have been demonstrated. Within this group two distinct patterns have been described: one in which there are thousands of adenomas carpeting the colon, and another in which there are somewhere between 100 and 1000 adenomas. There is a group of patients seen in the general population who have fewer than 100 adenomas scattered throughout the colon. It is not always clear whether some of these patients are variants of 

the familial polyposis syndrome group or merely patients with multiple polyps without any genetic factors involved. It is our policy to consider these patients as variants of the polyposis syndrome with the same risk, providing many of these polyps have been biopsied and have been shown to be true adenomas. These polyps usually appear at puberty, although they can appear as early as 4 months of age or as late as 74 years. The average age for cancer in this group is 39, considerably lower than that seen in the general population, which is well over 50. If untreated, colorectal cancer will develop in 95 percent of affected persons. When the polyps appear, they appear in the rectum as well as in the rest of the colon, making detection easy once the family has been identified. In 1953, Gardner and Richards described a large family with familial polyposis and additional abnormalities. In Gardner’s syndrome, in addition to carpeting of the colon with adenomas, there are osteomas, fibromas, and desmoid tumors. The genetic pattern is the same as in familial polyposis, and the risk is the same for cancer. It is not clear whether Gardner’s syndrome is a separate entity or a fuller expression of familial polyposis. In both familial polyposis and Gardner’s syndrome one also often finds polyps in the stomach and the upper portion of the small bowel. The frequency of polyps at these other sites appears higher in countries such as Japan, where the risk for gastric cancer and gastric polyps is also higher than in the United States. However, the risk for cancer in the upper gastrointestinal tract is much lower than the risk for cancer of the colon. Cancer of the thyroid, adrenal, and ampulla of Vater have also been seen in this syndrome. A rare type of familial polyposis is Turcot syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder in which one finds carpeting of the colon with multiple polyps in association with central nervous system and spinal cord tumors. Within this group of polyposis-type inherited colon cancer one can include juvenile polyposis and the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Juvenile polyps are benign. However, there are a few families in which juvenile polyps coexist with a higher risk of adenomas and colorectal cancer among family members; thus, juvenile polyposis may be yet another marker of familial suscepti-

bility. Although the Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal-dominant syndrome that consists primarily of totally benign hematomatous polyps of the small intestine, true adenomas have been observed in the colon, stomach, and duodenum. Cancer of the colon, terminal ileum, and periampullary area of the duodenum have been reported. 

The second major type of colorectal cancer is the nonpolyposis inherited colon cancer group. It has been estimated that as many as 30 percent of the patients at risk for colorectal cancer may have the genetic factor predisposing to nonpolyposis inherited colon cancer. Two major types of nonpolyposis inherited colon cancer have been described, viz., (1) the site-specific colorectal cancer type and (2) the family cancer syndrome. In the site-specific colorectal cancer group there is autosomal-dominant vertical transmission only for colorectal cancer with no cancers at other anatomic sites. In the family cancer syndrome there is vertical transmission for colorectal cancer and for cancers in other organs, most commonly in female genital sites, especially endometrium. In the family cancer syndrome there is also a risk for cancers at other gastrointestinal sites, including stomach and pancreas; melanoma has also been reported. Within this category, various combinations have been reported. 

Multiple primary cancers occur in the families and in individuals. The cancers often present at an early age, and the colorectal cancers have a more proximal distribution. An autosomaldominant mode of inheritance has been described (see Fig. 1). Another type of rare family cancer syndrome is Muir’s (or Torre’s) syndrome. In this syndrome there are not only cancers at the above-mentioned anatomic sites but also epidermoid cancers of the vagina, skin, and esophagus; there may also be multiple sebaceous cysts of the skin. 

The nonpolyposis inherited colon cancer syndromes have become well established. A major question is to what degree individuals considered to be at average risk have genetic factors operative but may not have a striking family history. Patients who have one first-degree relative with colorectal cancer are at increased risk for colorectal cancer; with two first-degree relatives affected, the risk is even higher. It is often hard to discern a true family history of cancer when one is dealing with high-incidence cancers (e.g., breast and colon cancers) which may occur by chance within a family. In these patients there is no easily accessible biological marker (such as polyps in the rectum as in familial polyposis) to indicate that the individuals are affected by the risk. Their risk begins in the twenties, and the risk for colorectal cancer appears to be greater on the right side than on the left side of the colon. This shift to more proximal cancers in this group makes the cancer more difficult to detect. The usual distribution of 65 percent of colorectal cancers distal to the splenic flexure is reversed in this group with 65 percent of colorectal cancers occurring proximal to the splenic flexure. Although this group of patients is characterized as a nonpolyposis type of colorectal cancer on an inherited basis, the adenomas precede the development of cancer in this group, as is the case in familial polyposis and in the average-risk patient. This group is called nonpolyposis type because of the absence of carpeting of the colon with multiple polyps as in familial polyposis (see Tables 1 and 2). 

###### Ulcerative colitis 

There have been many attempts to estimate the risk of malignancy in ulcerative colitis. There have been difficulties in defining the population of patients at risk because the samples studied by different hospitals are influenced by variations in methods of selection. For example, the incidence of carcinoma in ulcerative colitis is lower in medically managed patients than in those treated surgically. Nevertheless, if ulcerative colitis is considered without reference to age of onset or duration of disease, there seems to be general agreement that the likelihood of developing carcinoma of the colon is between 3 and 5 percent of all cases (except in reports from Eastern Europe and Israel where increases have not been noted). This risk of malignant change is 5 to 10 times greater than in the general population. 

The increased risk of cancer begins to rise significantly after 8 years of chronic ulcerative colitis. The accumulative incidence of the first 8 years iS approximately 2 to 3 percent and increases 2 percent per year thereafter. The risk is highest for patients with universal colitis, lower for those with only left-sided involvement, and minimal for those with only distal colitis. The onset of ulcerative colitis at an early age, chronic continuous symptoms, and a Clinically severe first attack have been cited by some as significant risk factors, but this has been questioned by others. It has been estimated that the chance of a child with chronic ulcerative colitis dying of carcinoma of the colon is 500 times greater than that of a normal child. However, in comparison with the cancer risk in older colitis patients, early onset of colitis does not appear to exert any independent influence on cancer risk, except that it leads to a longer duration of disease. Relative freedom from the symptoms of ulcerative colitis (i.e., inactive disease) does not appear to protect the individual from colonic cancer. 

The average age at onset of cancer superimposed on ulcerative colitis is 40 to 42 years; this is about two decades earlier than in the general population. The cancers are more evenly distributed throughout the colon, a significant percentage involving the transverse and right colon. There is a higher incidence of high-grade, multiple, and colloid carcinomas as well as flat and infiltrating lesions than of cancers of the colon arising without preexisting colitis, a fact which perhaps accounts for the poor prognosis and rapid progress of the cancer. However, in series where lower grades of malignancy are present, 5- year survival has been as high as 75 percent. In many ways the characteristic flat and infiltrating 

###### SCREENING TESTS Al 

type of lesion with an ill-defined edge, which can be felt more easily than it can be seen, resembles the macroscopic pathology of carcinoma of the stomach rather than the usual carcinoma of the colon. Although the poorer prognosis could be related to the intrinsic nature of the cancer, it could also be related to diagnostic difficulties. The symptoms of cancer of the colon are quite similar to those of ulcerative colitis. Bleeding is the hallmark in ulcerative colitis and is also common in carcinoma of the colon. The only clinical features that distinguish cancer from colitis are an abdominal mass and obstruction, which are late complications. 

Radiologic findings are often difficult to evaluate in the presence of ulcerative colitis. Polypoid change may be adenomatous, inflammatory (pseudopolypoid), or malignant, and strictures or narrowing may be inflammatory or neoplastic. Radiologic and even endoscopic examination may not be conclusive. In one series almost half of the potentially diagnosable neoplastic lesions were missed radiographically because they were felt to be secondary to inflammatory change. 

###### Crohn’s disease 

Carcinoma of the colon occurs in granulomatous (Crohn’s) colitis, but much less frequently than in ulcerative colitis. Crohn’s disease may be associated with the development of adenocarcinoma in both the small and the large intestine. In general, carcinoma of the ileum is extremely rare. When carcinoma occurs in the small bowel, it often involves the ileum in the area of the inflammation. The age of onset is about 15 years earlier than in the general population. Carcinoma has also been observed in surgically bypassed segments of small intestine affected by Crohn’s disease. Carcinomas may also arise in the fistulous tracts associated with Crohn’s disease. 

###### SCREENING TESTS 

Screening tests can be grouped into those that primarily assess the distal bowel and those that assess the entire colon. Screening tests that assess the distal bowel include (1) digital rectal examination, (2) rigid<sup>proctoscopy,and(3)flexi-</sup> 

ble sigmoidoscopy. Those that assess the entire colon include (1) fecal occult blood testing, (2) barium enema, (3) colonoscopy, (4) tumor markers, and (5) tests for anemia. 

###### Digital rectal examination and proctosigmoidoscopy 

It has been estimated that approximately 15 percent of colorectal cancers can be detected by the rectal digital examination and that 50 percent of colorectal cancers and adenomas can be detected by rigid proctoscopy. The digital rectal examination and rigid proctoscopy have never developed into popular screening methods because of poor physician acceptance of these procedures and lack of interest by the general medical community in their application, probably because of the discomfort that the rigid instrument produces. It is not known how widely digital rectal examination is performed or how effective it is as a screening procedure. Rigid proctoscopy with a 25-cm instrument has the potential for evaluating the distal 25 cm of colon, in which approximately 50 percent of colorectal neoplastic lesions occur. However, with recent use of flexible instruments, it is evident that the rigid examination does not give consistent findings beyond 16 cm and that there are many false-negative findings from 16 cm to 25 cm. The rigid instrument should really be considered a rigid proctoscope because of its limited value in evaluation of the sigmoid colon. The rigid proctoscope has been of demonstrated value in the hands of experienced physicians and in some major screening centers. However, it has not evolved as a popular screening instrument for the average internist. In recent years, flexible sigmoidoscopes 60 cm in length have been demonstrated to have greater yield than the rigid proctoscopes in the hands of experienced gastroenterologists and rectum-colon surgeons. The use of 60-cm instruments requires considerable training and expertise; these are sophisticated and expensive instruments. Recently, prototype 30-cm flexible sigmoidoscopes have been developed as a substitute for the rigid proctoscope for use by the general physician. Preliminary studies to date indicate that with the use of this instrument family-practice physicians and nurse practitioners can consistently examine 30 cm of distal bowel with a minimum of training

and minimal patient discomfort (see Table 3 and Fig. 2). 

The value of sigmoidoscopy has been demonstrated in several studies. In a study of asymptomatic patients performed at the Strang Clinic— Preventive Medicine Institute, 58 cases of early rectosigmoid cancer were detected in approximately 26,000 patient examinations. In this group of patients, approximately 88 percent had Dukes’ A and B lesions; follow-up has shown 90 percent survival rates in 50 patients followed for 15 years. In another study, periodic sigmoidoscopy resulted in a mortality reduction for colorectal cancer for the screened group. At the University of Minnesota, it was demonstrated that over a 25-year period rectosigmoid surveillance by sigmoidoscopy followed by identification and removal of observed polyps reduced the incidence of rectosigmoid cancer expected in this group. It seems, therefore, that some type of sigmoidoscopy has potential value in screening of patients for cancer detection as well as for detection and removal of adenomas

###### Fecal occult blood testing 

Screening for colorectal cancer based on occult blood detection in the stool has become a focus of interest because of the development of better materials and methods. Prior tests such as the Hematest (orthotoluidine), benzidine test, and guaiac solutions, which utilize a single stool specimen from a patient on an uncontrolled diet, have been discarded because of unreliability and a high percentage of false negatives and false positives. There was a resurgence of interest in fecal occult blood testing with the impregnated guaiac slide test (Hemoccult! test, Fig. 3). Greegor has indicated the feasibility of screening asymptomatic patients at risk for colorectal cancer when they were placed on a high-fiber, meatfree diet when six fecal smears were obtained. In Greegor’s initial series, 5 percent of patients had positive tests. One of this group had a colon cancer, two had diverticulosis, and one had a polyp; in only one could no disease be found. His later personal experience indicated that the frequency of positive reactions decreased to approximately | percent. In a collaborative study involving over 100 physicians, 139 cancers were detected. Of all the patients who had colon cancer and who followed the instructions for the

In 47 cases considered to be silent, 85 percent were pathologically localized to the bowel wall; only 20 of these cancers were within reach of the rigid sigmoidoscope. These initial observations have been followed by many other uncontrolled studies around the world. They all support the potential value of this test. 

In 1974 a controlled clinical trial which utilized fecal occult blood testing was initiated at the Strang Clinic-Preventive Medicine Institute in collaboration with Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center. Asymptomatic men and women age 40 and older coming to the Preventive Medicine Institute received a comprehensive medical examination including a medical questionnaire and rigid proctoscopy; in addition, the study group was sent a fecal occult blood test kit to prepare at home. This initially consisted of the single Hemoccult slides, and later the Hemoccult II slide. Patients were asked to prepare six smears over 3 days ona meat-free, high-fiber diet with restriction of vitamins and medications. They were asked to perform this within 4 days of their examination and to bring the slides in for testing on their examination date. If the slides were positive, double-contrast barium enemas and colonoscopy were performed. If no colonic neoplasm was found, an upper gastrointestinal series was performed and, when indicated, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Approximately 22,000 patients have been enrolled in this study. The compliance for fecal occult blood testing in the different subgroups of the Memorial Hospital-Strang Clinic study for fecal occult blood testing ranged from 70 to 80 percent; 95 percent of all patients completed rigid proctoscopy. Positive slides were found in 2.5 percent of the patients, but this varied de- 

pending on the type of slides used, patient status, and age. With the single Hemoccult slides, the rate of positivity was 1 percent, with a predictive value for neoplastic lesions of 50 percent, including 12 percent for cancer and 28 percent for adenomas. With the Hemoccult II slides, the rate of positivity increased to 3.7 percent, with a predictive value of 44 percent. When the Hemoccult II slides were rehydrated, the rate of positivity increased to 5.4 percent, but the predictive value for neoplasia decreased sharply to 19 percent. There was an increase of slide positivity with age by decade. The majority of patients (85 percent) with significant neoplastic lesions had between one and three positive Hemoccult tests. Only 41 percent of neoplastic lesions would have been detected if only one smear per day rather than two smears had been examined. Preliminary data indicate that colorectal cancers detected by Hemoccult slides alone had a more favorable staging than did those cancers detected by either rigid proctoscopy or symptoms. In the Memorial Sloan-Kettering study, the double-contrast barium enema was sensitive for cancer detection but had a lower sensitivity for colorectal adenomas than did colonoscopy. Based on flexible endoscopic examinations performed, it was determined that there was a high false negativity for rigid proctoscopy, with most of the missed lesions 16 cm to 25 cm from the anal verge. The false negativity for adenomas within the rectosigmoid was 76 percent; this is known because all patients had rigid proctoscopy performed. The false negativity for cancers has not yet been determined, nor has the false negativity for adenomas above the rectosigmoid (Table 4). 

At the University of Minnesota a second control trial evaluating the Hemoccult slide in fecal occult blood testing as a screening test for colorectal cancer was initiated. Participants were divided randomly into one of three groups: (1) those who received Hemoccult slides annually, (2) those who received the slides every other year, and (3) acontrol group. Those with positive tests were requested to have diagnostic examinations, including x-rays and colonoscopy. The x- rays were of the single-column type rather than double contrast. Of those with positive tests and who had further diagnostic evaluation, approxi-
