mately 9 percent had colonic cancers, mostly Dukes’ A or B. It is of interest that only 39 percent of the colonic lesions were detected by barium enema, whereas 61 percent were found with only colonoscopy. The sensitivity of the barium enema in this particular study was low, but the enema consisted of the standard type of barium examination rather than a double-contrast (air contrast) examination. The data generated so far from this program suggest that fecal occult blood testing is a useful method for screening for colonic neoplasms. The highest yield appears to be in patients 63 years of age and over. 

In the reported studies, the impregnated guaiac slide test with stabilized reagent was used. This test is based on the peroxidase activity of substances in the stool which oxidize the guaiac compounds from their colorless phenolic to the blue quinone state. It is important to emphasize that a positive reaction is produced not only by 

the peroxidaselike activity of human hemoglobin, but also by the peroxidase activity of substances, such as nonhuman hemoglobin, bacteria, and vegetable peroxidases. 

It has become difficult to correlate and interpret the results of the various screening programs that utilize fecal occult blood testing. The problems include differences in the reporting of data as well as in the type of diets and the types of slides used. 

The reasons for false-negative findings by occult blood testing are still not clear, nor is the degree of false negativity known, except perhaps for lesions in the rectosigmoid from the study by the Strang Clinic-Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center. False negativity may relate to methodology but undoubtedly also relates to the intermittent nature of the bleeding from neoplastic lesions. Initially positive tests can become negative after 4 to 5 days, primarily when there is a low hemoglobin concentration in the stool. At- 

###### TUMOR MARKERS 1S 

tempts have been made to reverse this ‘“‘storage”’ false negativity by hydrating the slide with a few drops of water prior to adding the reagent. However, this hydration appears to result in an overly sensitive reaction, which leads to an increase in false positives. False positivity, of course, can result from vegetable peroxidases and dietary meat. There is clearly a need for a more specific slide test that will reduce the nonhemoglobin false positives. 

There has been considerable controversy as to whether a high-fiber, meat-free diet is necessary for cancer screening. Although this has never been adequately tested, it formed the basis for Greegor’s initial observations and for the subsequent controlled trials. 

In studies reported to date, short-term objectives have been achieved, including feasibility of the approach, yield, compliance, false positives, sensitivity and specificity of the diagnostic tests, and staging of detected cancers. Long-term objectives that need. to be achieved for acceptance of fecal blood testing as a valid screening approach are related not only to survival of the patients with a positive screening test who have demonstrated a favorable pathologic stage of cancer at surgery but also to the “‘mortality rate benefit” to the screened group. Such objectives may be forthcoming from ongoing clinical trials. 

###### TUMOR MARKERS 

###### Cytology and immunologic assays 

Additional screening tests have been under evaluation as potential indicators of the presence of malignancy or of phenotypic expression of a genetic trait. These have included studies of (1) skin fibroblasts from patients with familial polyposis and Gardner’s syndrome, (2) chromosomal tetraploidy in cultured skin cells from skin biop- 

sies of patients with Gardner’s syndrome, (3) defects in recognitive immunity in mixed leukocyte cultures from patients with inherited colon cancer, and (4) proliferative abnormalities in biopsies and colonic washings of patients with a variety of premalignant and malignant disorders, including genetic and nongenetic colon cancer. A cytologic technique of potential value involves DNA synthesis studies in short-term tissue culture. Cytologic washings obtained by a pulsatile lavage system are incubated with tritiated thymidine and studied with microautoradiography in the same manner as rectal biopsies. Normally only the lower two-thirds of the mucosal glands are involved in DNA synthesis, whereas well-differentiated surface cells have no DNA synthesis and, therefore, do not take up the tritiated thymidine. However, abnormal surface cells retain the ability to synthesize DNA and hence incorporate tritiated thymidine. This abnormal zone of tritiated thymidine incorporation has been detected in (1) ulcerative colitis, (2) the normal flat mucosa adjacent to isolated adenomas, (3) the mucosa between polyps in familial polyposis, and (4) patients with colorectal cancer. Many symptom-free relatives in polyposis families have similarly been shown to express this abnormal proliferative pattern. Recently, a proportion of Hemoccult-positive patients with no overt neoplasm were found to have abnormal surface-labeled epithelial cells without morphologic evidence of malignancy. The importance of this finding is now being studied with long-term follow-up of these patients (see Table 5): The markers developed in patients with polyposis are important for their potential value in standard-risk patients and patients with inherited colon cancer. Markers, per se, are less needed in the polyposis syndromes since there is good phenotypic expression of the affected state,

In addition, rising CEA levels appear to precede clinical or other biochemical parameters of recurrence that provide a possible “lead time” in those patients. The value of this lead time is questionable except, perhaps, when one is considering a timed ‘“‘second look”’ based on the rising CEA levels. The present data suggest that there is a 25 to 30 percent chance that a local resectable lesion will be found in patients reexplored for CEA values rising postoperatively. In the initial reports, the majority of reexplored patients had distant metastases, whereas in about 20 percent no tumor was found at the time of exploration. In some of the latter groups, a tumor was subsequently observed. The percentage of patients having locally resectable disease may be related to the interval between the detection of the CEA rise and reexploration. The long-term benefit of this approach remains to be determined. The morbidity and mortality rates and alteration in quality of life associated with reexploration will have to be carefully scrutinized in comparison with 5-year survival rates in operated and nonoperated patients. At present, it is difficult to accept the potential value of reexploration when it is considered that there appears to be a better correlation of high CEA titers with advanced disease than with early localized disease in patients originally screened with CEA measurements.

###### Biochemical tests 

Biochemical assays are also being studied in colonic biopsy and lavage specimens in an attempt to detect early changes of colon cancer in ulcerative colitis. These include various lysozomal enzymes, such as arylsulfatase and B- glucuronidase, and the isoenzymes of lactic dehydrogenase. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) has been studied extensively as a potential indicator of colorectal cancer. Unfortunately, it has not fulfilled its initial promise as a sensitive and specific biological marker for the detection of early colorectal cancer. Most patients with elevated values and colorectal cancer have had advanced disease. In addition, elevated values occur in a wide variety of benign diseases. Increased CEA levels have been found in about 30 percent of patients with inflammatory bowel disease during periods of clinically active disease. More severe disease, more extensive anatomic involvement, a younger age, and a shorter duration of disease are more likely to result in CEA elevations. There does not seem to be a consistent relationship between CEA elevation and known risk factors for the development of carcinoma. Unfortunately, since patients with inflammatory bowel disease may have variations in CEA levels during the course of their disease, the CEA level is not helpful as an indicator of early carcinoma. 

###### Dysplasia 

Another finding currently under investigation in a high-risk group is the appearance of dysplasia in colonic biopsy specimens in patients with ulcerative colitis. Morson and Pang in 1967 suggested the use of serial rectal biopsies to look for dysplasia or precancer. These biopsies were used in patients with ulcerative colitis to predict who had cancer elsewhere in the colon or in whom the colonic mucosa was at high risk for the development of cancer. The dysplastic change consists of (1) flattened rather than polypoid mucosa, (2) stratified, hyperchromatic, and irregular nuclei with multiple mitotic figures, (3) loss of mucin in the epithelial cells, (4) loss of parallelism, (5) distorted crypt architecture, and (6) lateral budding of the glands extending through the 

Recently, CEA has been studied to evaluate it as a possible indicator of prognosis in colorectal cancer. It appears that CEA levels that are elevated preoperatively and do not fall to normal postoperatively portend a poor prognosis. The interval between surgery and recurrence appears to be enhanced by coupling the CEA level with the staging of the cancer. Although there is generally a good correlation between serial CEA determination and clinical course, not infrequently the clinical course and the CEA levels do not parallel each other. The discordance seems to be most pronounced when there are pelvic or local 

TUMOR MARKERS 127 

muscularis mucosa. Occasionally, dysplasia can be present in a polypoid excrescence and resemble an adenoma. 

Dysplasia in ulcerative colitis consists primarily of cytologic changes comparable to those seen in malignant transformation in other organs such as the lung or cervix. Dysplasia may be graded as mild, moderate, or severe (see Fig. 4). In cases where colonic cancer has complicated ulcerative colitis, almost all specimens have dysplastic changes in areas distant from the cancer. The changes may be spotty in distribution throughout the colon and on occasion may even be confined to a localized area. It seems, therefore, that cancer of the colon develops in patients with ulcerative colitis in a setting of dysplasia. Dysplasia is present in over 80 percent of all colectomy specimens in which carcinoma is found. Not all pathologists agree on which mucosal epithelial changes constitute true dysplasia. Dysplasia may be graded as mild, moderate, or severe. It may be difficult to interpret in the presence of severe inflammation, and grading is still an imprecise process. Some pathologists use a mild-moderate-severe scale with only severe dysplasia being viewed as an indication for colectomy in ulcerative colitis. Others also consider moderate dysplasia as ominous. Most pathologists now equate severe dysplasia with car- 

cinoma in situ. Epithelial dysplasia is considered a neoplastic alteration comparable to atypical epithelium found in colon adenomas—the milder degrees of dysplasia are considered to be on the benign side of the neoplastic spectrum and the more severe forms closer to carcinoma. The finding of dysplasia at one colonic site raises suspicion about the status of the epithelium elsewhere in the colon. If dysplasia is to serve as an indication for colectomy, it should not be a transient event but should persist and probably be present at multiple colonic sites. 

Colonoscopy permits one to obtain biopsies at multiple colonic sites for evaluation of dysplasia. Since dysplastic changes may be patchy in distribution, the ability to identify mucosal abnormalities and biopsy them is advantageous. Biopsy of areas of severe inflammation should be avoided, and it is desirable to biopsy from the more proximal areas of the colon where inflammation may be less severe. A total of about 10 biopsies at regular intervals of 10 to 20 cm are taken from the various areas of the colon. Slightly irregular, slightly thickened areas that are plaquelike usually have the greatest yield of dysplastic change, although dysplasia can be found in normal-appearing mucosa. Given the present state of knowledge, when moderate to severe dysplasia is consistently found, colectomy should be considered seriously.

128 COLONIC CANCER: SCREENING FOR PREMALIGNANT AND MALIGNANT DISEASE 

The possible availability of indicators of early cancer is an exciting concept. However, for a marker to be clinically useful, it should be sensitive and have few false positives and a high degree of organ specificity. Very few biological markers have survived careful scrutiny of sensitivity and specificity. Neoplastic diseases in which biological markers have been used successfully include neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, carcinoid, choriocarcinoma, embryonal testicular tumors, multiple myeloma, hepatocellular carcinoma, osteogenic sarcoma, and other osteoblastic bone tumors. To date, no markers have become available for average-risk people for colonic carcinoma that provide an early diagnosis of the presence of cancer with a high degree of sensitivity and specificity except for the biochemical marker that indicates the presence of occult blood in the stool. Presently, only fecal occult blood testing seems to serve as a good screen for colon cancer detection. When it is performed in a prescribed manner, it provides a reasonably high predictive value for the presence of colorectal neoplasia in average-risk men and women. In ulcerative colitis the finding of severe mucosal dysplasia seems to be useful as a guide for the potential presence of superimposed colonic malignancy in this disorder. 

###### DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUES 

The barium enema and colonoscopy are superb diagnostic techniques to be used in asymptomatic patients who have had a positive screening test for colorectal cancer with the occult blood method or who have had a positive sigmoidoscopy or as a follow-up examination looking for synchronous and metachronous lesions. The accuracy of the barium enema is related to the thoroughness of patient preparation and to the type of examination performed. Thorough cleansing of the patient results in a higher yield of demonstrating neoplastic lesions, especially the smaller adenomas. In addition, the double-contrast barium enema which utilizes air as well as barium has a much higher yield of revealing neoplastic lesions. Where the barium enema has a high false negativity, it is complemented well by colonoscopy. In the region of the distal descending colon and upper sigmoid where one often finds overlapping loops of bowel, barium 

With colonoscopy one can reach the cecum in well over 90 percent of patients, and the sensitivity of colonoscopy is extremely high for neoplastic lesions. The false negativity for cancers has not been well established, but the false negativity for adenomas over 1 cm in size is only about 6 percent. Potential “blind areas” for missed lesions are around the flexures especially and the medial aspect of the ascending colon proximal to the ileocecal valve. The evaluation of patients at risk for colonic neoplasia cannot be considered to be complete without the use of colonoscopy. When neoplastic lesions are seen, tissue sampling can be obtained by biopsy or cytologic brushing. Cytologic brushing has been demonstrated to increase the yield of tissue sampling for a more accurate diagnosis of malignancy. Benign-appearing polyps should not be sampled but should be removed in toto. In addition to target biopsies and cytology of suspicious-appearing neoplastic lesions, biopsies can also be obtained from the flat mucosa for the assessment of dysplasia. Lavage cytology may be performed through the colonoscope in patients with longstanding ulcerative colitis to complement biopsies for dysplasia. In addition, lavage cytology can be used to evaluate inaccessible areas such as mass lesions in a fixed colon where the lesion cannot be reached. In this situation, the tip of the colonoscope may be positioned at a site distant from the lesion and lavage performed with collection of material for evaluation cytologically for the presence of malignant cells. Lavage cytology has also been performed through flexible sigmoidoscopes in retained rectal segments of patients with subtotal colectomy for familial polyposis in whom long-term surveillance of the rectal stump has been initiated. False-positive cytology can occur in the presence of considerable inflammation, as in diverticulitis or where the morphology has been changed by treatment, such as radiation or chemotherapy. Experienced cytotechnicians and cytologists usually have no significant problems with these factors (see Fig. 5). studies yield a higher degree of false negatives, and here colonoscopy can be of help. ###### PATIENT COMPLIANCE 

In ulcerative colitis, proctosigmoidoscopy with biopsy of suspicious lesions and barium enema are important diagnostic techniques to assess superimposed malignancy. However, because of the more uniform distribution of the cancers superimposed on ulcerative colitis, the 25-cm proctoscope does not detect the majority of cancers. With the fiberoptic colonoscope plus biopsy and brush cytology, it is now possible to clarify suspicious areas, particularly strictures that are beyond the reach of the standard proctoscope. Exfoliative cytology is a vastly underutilized technique that may be helpful in detecting in situ or early carcinoma of the colon in ulcerative colitis. Brush cytology and lavage cytology can be revealing in ulcerative colitis with its diffusely abnormal mucosa in which inflammatory and malignant lesions may appear grossly similar. and This aggressive apColonoscopy double-contrast barium tients with a positive screening test. In ulcerative colitis, the two most common problems requiring endoscopic resolution are strictures or a mass lesion. Although most strictures are benign, some may be malignant and carcinoma may spread submucosally, thereby narrowing the lumen circumference. Multiple biopsies may fail to reveal the presence of carcinoma within such a stricture. During colonoscopy most pseudopolyps need not be biopsied, since they have no malignant or premalignant potential. However, whenever multiple polypoid

Polyps in ulcerative colitis are usually biopsied when they are larger than 1 cm in diameter, have a color different from the adjacent pseudopolyp, or have an irregular surface configuration, which suggests that they are not pseudopolyps but rather adenomas or carcinomas. 

###### PATIENT COMPLIANCE 

Patient compliance is critical to successful screening for colon cancer. There is a tremendous spectrum of patient compliance with screening, ranging from 10 to 90 percent. The lowest compliance is in patients who have not been motivated or educated in this regard and in areas where the screening approach is in the form of an outreach into the community. A higher degree of compliance is found in control trials with a high degree of patient motivation and education and in situations in which the patients either come in voluntarily or have agreed to participate in such a program. In order to examine the factors in patient compliance, we have applied a health-belief model 

130 COLONIC CANCER: SCREENING FOR PREMALIGNANT AND MALIGNANT DISEASE 

which seeks to explain health behavior, including compliance, by relating the individual’s perceptions to the likelihood of taking action. The basis of this model is that a decision to undertake a health action will not be made unless the individual is psychologically ready to take such action. It tries to fit different factors related to health decision making into a sensible framework or model that summarizes items and explains compliance by highlighting the interactive or synergistic impact of the variables. The broad indexes commonly associated with the healthbelief model include (1) general health motivation (i.e., concern about one’s health) and a sense of efficacy about one’s capacity to improve it, (2) belief in the asymptomatic disease state, (3) past health practices, (4) perceived susceptibility to disease, (5) perceived severity of the disease being screened, (6) perceived health benefits from recommended health action, (7) confidence in physicians and medical care, and (8) perceived barriers of the individual to compliance. No single factor is considered to be predictive of compliance. Considerably more work is needed in order to understand patient motivation. One must be sensitive to the population’s understanding of cancer, which is viewed by many as a lifethreatening illness. The emotional reactions which cancer provokes may well be decisive in shaping beliefs. The health beliefs of the individuals in general, as well as psychological variables regarding cancer, will need to be probed for a better understanding of this area. COST In general, screening with fecal occult blood tests and with proctosigmoidoscopy has been estimated to be cost-effective. However, this is an exceedingly complex issue which involves not only the costs of the screening procedures themselves but also the cost of the diagnostic techniques, factors of false positivity and false negativity, cost of treatment, and indirect costs such as loss of work and other benefits. A comparison of these costs will have to be made in patients in whom an early diagnosis has been made with those in whom a late diagnosis has been made as a result of the usual presentation with symptoms. Such data may be forthcoming from ongoing 

screening programs. Elements from these programs can be incorporated into a computer simulation model to determine the outcomes of variously designed programs. It is very likely that the final decision regarding the type of program that should be initiated on a large scale will be based on the computer simulation model which has utilized elements from the ongoing programs. 

###### RISK 

It has been said that there is no risk from screening the patient with the fecal occult blood test and little risk from screening with proctoscopy. The screening with proctoscopy has a risk factor of 1:10,000 for perforation of the colon. However, to a large extent the risk occurs when a positive test leads to a subsequent series of diagnostic tests and possible treatment. The risk of an immediate perforation from a barium enema is exceedingly low, but the long-range radiation risk has not been clearly established. The risk of bleeding and perforation from colonoscopy is approximately 0.2 percent. No risk has as yet been established for the treatment of asymptomatic patients with colorectal adenomas and cancers. Preliminary observations within the framework of ongoing screening programs suggest that this risk is extremely iow. RECOMMENDED APPROACH AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS 

The approach to screening can be considered in terms of general and selective screening. The target of general screening is the majority of patients at standard risk; in selective screening the targets are the small subgroups at high risk. Screening methods for selective and general screening must be different. General screening, of course, can be initiated in different orders of magnitude. Individual screening can be performed by the physician in his or her practice. Group screening can be instituted within the framework of a workplace, school, or hospital. Finally, general screening can be performed on large populations, such as an entire community, State, or country. At present, screening of individuals and groups seems quite reasonable and

justified, but mass screening on a nationwide basis may still demand additional data, such as cost and mortality rates. 

###### Asymptomatic patients at average risk 

Annual fecal occult blood testing on a prescribed diet, coupled with flexible sigmoidoscopy every 3 to 5 years, may provide the most effective approach to screening this population. At present, sigmoidoscopy is largely performed with a rigid instrument, but in the near future, availability of 25- to 30-cm flexible sigmoidoscopes may make this approach more acceptable to patients and physicians. Screening in this group should begin between ages 40 and 50 (see Fig. 6). Any patient with a positive screening test should be investigated aggressively with double-contrast barium enema and/or colonoscopy. Asymptomatic patients at high risk These include patients with underlying diseases, such as long-standing ulcerative colitis; patients with familial polyposis; patients with family histories of family cancer syndrome and sitespecific colon cancer; patients with female gen- 

ital cancer or breast cancer; or patients with a past history of colon cancer or colon adenomas. Patients with a diagnosis of familial polyposis should have early surgery. If a rectosigmoid segment remains, the patient must have frequent endoscopic evaluation every few months, with cytologic lavage, as well as removal of new polyps, if possible. Patients with a history of female genital cancer or breast cancer can have fecal occult blood testing and sigmoidoscopy as screening procedures, but these must be started whenever the patients are identified rather than after they reach age 40, since the risk begins at age 20. Patients with site-specific colon cancer or family cancer syndrome must be screened with barium enema, and/or colonoscopy, since one cannot rely only on fecal occult blood testing in these patients. Such surveillance should begin at age 20. The appropriate screening interval is not known, but a reasonable approach would include fecal occult blood testing annually and x-ray or colonoscopy or both every 3 to 5 years (Fig. 7). The challenge in familial colon cancer syndromes is that the affected individuals and the even greater number at risk are in the community and are generally unrecognized. The number of patients with nonpolyposis syndromes or strong ‘sporadic family histories” is potentially large. Often the family history is incomplete or of ques-

tionable reliability. In addition, the lack of guidelines for physicians makes the information of limited value. Questionnaires to all hospitalized patients or their families that elicit detailed family histories are used in several institutions. The use of a family history of a common cancer asa criterion for defining a high-risk group, along with appropriate examination of individuals in such groups, is valuable. It can result in a diagnosis of cancers with a higher frequency at an earlier stage than without their use. Patients with prior history of adenoma or colon cancer must be screened directly with x- ray and/or colonoscopy. They should have their colons cleared of any synchronous lesions at some time before or after the index lesion is identified. Once the colons have been cleared of all synchronous lesions, one need not screen these patients more often than perhaps every 3 to 5 years, since the development of true metachronous lesions may take 10 to 15 years to evolve. However, it is not appropriate to remove the index lesion and not clear the colon of synchronous lesions, since this leaves this group exposed to a high risk of subsequent cancer (see Fig, 8): At present, there are insufficient data on the optimal time and manner to follow patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Cooperative studies are underway to determine the proper surveillance procedure for these high-risk groups.

However, interim operational guidelines can be outlined based on knowledge regarding risk factors. 

Since the occurrence of both precancer and carcinoma in ulcerative colitis increases after about 8 to 10 years from the onset of total colitis, surveillance should commence after 7 years of disease. Multiple biopsies of the rectum and colon by colonoscopic biopsy should be done and all histology specimens carefully studied for the presence of dysplasia. Colonoscopy should be performed when the inflammatory disease is relatively inactive. The frequency of repeat colonoscopy is not known. Various programs with intervals of 1, 2, and 3 years have been suggested. It is essential to have the histologic sections seen by a pathologist who is familiar with the dysplasia concept and the grades of dysplasia. If a skilled cytologist is available, colonic cytology can be obtained at each colonoscopy. On occasion an adenocarcinoma will be detected when the gross lesion was not evident on colonoscopy. Once definitive dysplasia is seen, even if not severe, frequent surveillance is needed; if there is no evidence of dysplasia, less frequent follow-up is required. The role of the barium enema in surveillance has not been established. 

Patients with only left-sided ulcerative colitis are at lowered risk for developing cancer. One should verify this by colonoscopy. Except for delaying the surveillance until after 15 years of left-sided disease, the surveillance procedure is similar. Patients with ulcerative proctitis, need only an occasional proctoscopy since these patients are not at increased risk of cancer. The risk of developing colonic carcinoma appears to be less in Crohn’s colitis than in ulcerative colitis, but the possibility of this development has to be considered. Although dysplasia has been observed in a few patients with granulomatous colitis, the association has not as yet been clearly or firmly established and at present cannot be used clinically. The signs and symptoms of carcinoma, such as weight loss, anorexia, abdomina! mass, obstruction, bleeding, and fistulization can be mimicked by Crohn’s disease, which makes early diagnosis difficult. Resection of the carcinoma at an early stage is curable. In most cases of carcinoma complicating Crohn’s disease, surgery has been required for diagnosis, but the use of 

###### REFERENCES 133: 

colonoscopy with biopsy and cytology to supplement radiologic studies may help in detecting carcinoma earlier in suspect patients, such as those with stricture and chronic fistulas. 

###### CONCLUDING COMMENTS 

Currently we have all the techniques and conceptual understanding to move forward in a more aggressive preventive approach to colorectal cancer. The high incidence of colorectal cancer and the low survival rate justifies such an aggressive approach. The target populations can be identified and we have screening and diagnostic techniques that can be applied to these populations. Rational positions propounded in this chapter must, of course, be tested in prospective trials for determination of benefit in terms of survival, mortality, and cost effectiveness. These positions can only be used as guidelines for individual and group screening until that time. The expectations are that, if used aggressively and judiciously in appropriate sequences, these techniques in conjunction with current conceptual understanding will lead to improved survival rates approaching 80 to 90 percent, and perhaps to a considerable saving in finances and resources. 

It is hoped that specific and sensitive tumor markers, preferably serological markers, will provide a basis for the early detection of cancer. When this occurs, techniques for localization and tissue confirmation of the neoplastic lesions will still be needed. Until primary prevention becomes a reality, secondary preventive approaches can be developed into programs that potentially could have an impact on saving lives and resources. These approaches will require a greater effort directed toward public education about colon cancer and an increased awareness among patients and physicians of the benefits of preventive medicine.

### BONE MARROW AND FUTURE EXPECTATIONS TRANSPLANTATION: PRESENT STATUS 

###### E. DONNALL THOMAS 

The development of the atomic bomb 30 years ago altered human existence and evoked widespread interest in radiation research for both military and medical purposes. A laboratory experiment carried out by Leon Jacobson and colleagues showed that if a mouse spleen was exteriorized and shielded during irradiation and then replaced into the abdomen, the mouse could survive otherwise lethal irradiation. Soon it was found that the same effect could be achieved by the administration of bone marrow cells from a mouse of the same strain. These observations set the stage for a large number of laboratory and clinical studies, covering many different disciplines, which led to the application of marrow transplantation to patients with otherwise lethal diseases. At first, the result of the radiation protection experiment cited above was thought to be due to humoral factors arising in the spleen or bone marrow. However, by 1955 studies using blood genetic markers or cytogenetics had demonstrated clearly that the radiation protection was due to the presence of “‘seed”’ cells which could repopulate the marrow spaces of the irradiated host. The potential clinical applications were apparent immediately, and by the late 1950s several efforts to transplant marrow in humans had been undertaken. These efforts were largely unsuccessful except in a few patients with leukemia who were given supralethal total-body irradiation followed by a marrow transplant from an identical twin. These patients showed hematologic recovery, which demonstrates that human beings could survive otherwise lethal irradiation, although the patients died of recurrent leukemia after a few months. 

During the 1960s few human marrow transplants were carried out, but intensive laboratory work continued. It was demonstrated, first in mice and then in dogs, that the outcome of the marrow graft was strongly influenced by histocompatibility similarities or differences between donor and recipient. In the 1970s marrow transplant research was stimulated by the steadily advancing field of human kidney transplantation, and that decade witnessed a rapid advance in the understanding of the major histocompatibility complex in humans, known as histocompatibility leukocyte antigens (HLA). In the outbred model, the dog, it was shown that when the donor-recipient pairs were selected from littermates matched for the major histocompatibility complex approximately 90 percent of the recipients were long-term healthy survivors. The feasibility of similar human marrow transplants carried out between HLA-identical siblings was obvious. These observations, coupled with rapid advances in the supportive care for patients lacking bone marrow function, set the stage for a rational renewal of marrow transplantation in human beings. 

In the 1970s there was a steadily increasing number of long-term healthy human recipients of bone marrow transplants, a continued improvement in the overall survival rate, and the application of marrow transplantation to an increasing number of diseases. 

Much of the current interest in marrow transplantation focuses, for obvious reasons, on the application of this approach to patients with an otherwise lethal disease. However, the significance of marrow transplantation, both practical and theoretical, is far broader. Marrow trans- 
BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION: PRESENT STATUS AND FUTURE EXPECTATIONS 

plantation involves the basic disciplines of radiation biology, oncology, hematology, immunology, transplantation biology, and cell biology. 

Patients undergoing marrow transplantation present a wide array of clinical challenges which involve all aspects of internal medicine. Most successful marrow transplants have been carried out by teams of individuals whose expertise encompasses broad areas of clinical medicine and basic science. Furthermore, since marrow transplantation represents only a beginning phase in the development of a medical therapy, it is essential to continue research so that improvements in long-term therapy for the patient will continue to be made. 

###### BONE MARROW TRANSPLANT PROCEDURES Selection of the patient 

Marrow transplantation is a rational therapeutic option only if the patient’s disease involves the bone marrow and, therefore, might be improved by substitution of a new marrow, or if damage to the normal marrow is the limiting factor in the aggressive treatment of the disease. A marrow transplant involves a transplant not only of the donor myeloid system but also of the donor lymphoid and macrophage systems. Application of marrow grafting to various diseases will be discussed later, but the underlying philosophy is illustrated by the three types of diseases for which marrow transplantation has been utilized most widely: 

- 1 Immunologic deficiency diseases. Here, the objective is to utilize marrow grafting to replace the recipient’s genetically defective lymphoid system with the normal lymphoid system of the donor. 

- 2 Aplastic anemia. In this case, the disease process, regardless of etiology, has resulted in loss of the marrow, and the objective is to replace the defective organ with a normal functioning organ. 

- 3 Acute leukemia. In this disease the objective is the complete destruction of the leukemic cell population and, unavoidably, the normal marrow cells by intensive chemoradiotherapy, fol- 

lowed by restoration of normal marrow function with the transplanted marrow. 

###### Selection of the donor 

The donor must be in good health, and the donor, or an appropriate advocate of the donor, must be capable of giving informed consent for the marrow transplant. Beyond these ethical considerations, selection of the donor is largely determined by histocompatibility testing, since the donor must share with the recipient all or part of the major histocompatibility complex, HLA. Before discussing histocompatibility, some basic definitions are in order. An autologous marrow graft refers to the removal of a patient’s marrow and administration of chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, followed by retransplantation of the patient’s own marrow. A syngeneic graft is a graft that is genetically identical to the marrow of the recipient, from an identical twin donor. In the case of an allogeneic graft, donor and recipient are of different genetic origin. A chimera is an individual whose body contains living and proliferating cells of a different genetic origin. 

The HLA region is composed of a series of closely linked genetic loci on chromosome 6.! The array of antigens encoded by this region on one chromosome is known as a haplotype. Each individual has two haplotypes, one inherited from the mother and the other from the father. The antigens located at HLA-A, -B, and -C are detected by serological techniques in a microcytoxicity assay and that at HLA-D by the mixed leukocyte culture. A locus that is either identical with or closely related to HLA-D, called DR, can now be recognized serologically by typing of B lymphocytes. These genetic loci, each with a large number of known alleles, make the HLA region by far the most complex genetic polymorphism yet described in humans. 

Despite this complexity, within a family there can be only four haplotypes and, therefore, for a given patient each sibling has one chance in four of being HLA-identical with the patient. Transplants between HLA-identical siblings, the most compatible form of allogeneic transplant, have 

' A schematic diagram of the HLA chromosomal region is shown on p. 361 of Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 9th ed. 

###### BONE MARROW TRANSPLANT PROCEDURES 137 

been most widely used for marrow transplantation. 

An identical twin is a special example of an HLA-identical sibling who is matched, not only for HLA, but for all genetic loci. Although only a small fraction of patients have identical twins, transplants between identical twins have been most effective therapeutically and most informative scientifically because the twin provides marrow that is like the patient’s own marrow except that it is free of disease. Marrow transplantation from a twin, therefore, is like a perfect autologous Marrow transplant. 

###### Preparation of the patient 

Infants with severe combined immunologic deficiency are conditioned by the nature of their disease to accepta transplant. All other patients are immunologically competent, to a greater or lesser degree, and therefore will reject the marrow transplant unless prepared with some form of immunosuppressive therapy. For example, an immunosuppressive regimen commonly used for patients with aplastic anemia consists of large doses of the drug cyclophosphamide, an anticancer drug which is also a potent immunosuppressive agent. Preparation of the patient with leukemia involves the administration of high-dose chemoradiotherapy designed to kill as many leukemic cells as possible. A commonly used regimen involves the administration of cyclophosphamide followed by 1000 rads of totalbody irradiation. A radiation exposure of this magnitude, approximately 23 times the lethal dose (LD,.,) for humans, is in itself sufficiently immunosuppressive to permit engraftment of marrow. Aspiration and infusion of the marrow 

As a single organ, the marrow is somewhat larger in volume than the liver. However, it is widely dispersed throughout the marrow cavities of the bones of the central skeleton. The pelvic bones are the most readily accessible, although marrow may be obtained from the sternum, the ribs, or, in children, the tibia. 

The marrow donor is taken to the operating room, and, under general or spinal anesthesia, multiple marrow aspirations are performed on 

the anterior and posterior iliac crests. In order to avoid excessive dilution with blood, the point of the aspirating needle must be placed in as many different locations as possible. Usually, some 100 to 150 aspirations are carried out, and the volume of the mixture of blood and marrow cells is from 500 to 800 ml. As each aspiration is performed, the marrow is mixed with heparin and tissue culture medium. When the collection is completed, the marrow is passed through stainless steel screens (300 and then 200 mm?) in order to break up the marrow particles. It is then transferred to a blood transfusion bag, taken to the patient’s room, and administered by intravenous infusion. The marrow stem cells pass through the lungs, and subsequent growth and reconstitution of the myeloid marrow is confined almost exclusively to the medullary cavities. Other routes of marrow administration have been utilized, such as intraperitoneal and intraarterial, but extensive studies in animals and now in humans have shown the intravenous route to be the preferred method. Support for the patient without marrow function 

Following marrow transplantation, the stem cells must reach the marrow cavities, proliferate, and undergo the normal maturation process. It is usually 2 to4 weeks, and sometimes longer, before the transplanted marrow starts to be functionally effective in producing the critical formed elements of the peripheral blood, particularly granulocytes and platelets. Supportive care is crucial for survival and is similar to that for the management of acute human radiation injury.2 Supportive care consists of efforts to protect the patient from exogenous or endogenous sources of infection, appropriate treatment of established infection, transfusions of red blood cells, platelets, and/or granulocytes, maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance, and maintenance of a satisfactory nutritional state. Minimal protection against infection involves mask and contact isolation, although a randomized study to demonstrate the effectiveness of this regimen has not been reported. Ultraisolation techniques involve complete isolation in a 

2 Described on p. 943 of Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 9th ed. 

13S BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION: PRESENT STATUS 

###### AND FUTURE EXPECTATIONS 

laminar airflow room with skin sterilization, a sterile diet, and oral nonabsorbable antibiotics for gut sterilization. Ultraisolation has been demonstrated, in a randomized study, to be superior to mask and contact isolation in preventing infection. However, ultraisolation techniques are not essential since many successful marrow transplants have been carried out with routine hospital isolation. 

Virtually all marrow transplant recipients will require platelet transfusions. Platelet transfusions should be given to maintain the platelet count above 20,000 per cubic millimeter until the engrafted marrow can sustain that level. Some patients will be refractory to random donor platelets when subjected to marrow grafting, and others will become refractory after grafting. When this occurs, HLA-matched platelets may become necessary. We have found that many patients who are refractory to random donor platelets can be supported by platelets from haploidentical family members. The haploidentical donor is one who shares one genetically identical haplotype with the patient but differs for the other haplotype. Not infrequently, the HLAidentical marrow donor must be used for platelet transfusions. Granulocyte transfusions may be of value in preventing infection in patients when the granulocyte count falls below 200 per cubic millimeter. Granulocyte transfusions given for prophylactic reasons should be given daily and continued until the marrow graft functions well enough to keep the granulocyte count above 200 per cubic millimeter. Therapeutic granulocyte transfusions are indicated for any significant infection in granulocytopenic patients. Packed red blood cells should be given as needed to avoid signs and symptoms of anemia, which usually appear when the hematocrit is below 25 percent. All blood products should be given 1500 rads in vitro in order to inactivate lymphocytes that might subsequently produce a graft-versus-host reaction in the immunosuppressed patient. Despite isolation and other measures, infection is an ever-present danger in the immunocompromised granulocytopenic _ patient. The appearance of fever, especially in association with any other clinical sign of bacteremia, is an indication for initiating systemic antibacterial 

therapy even though cultures have failed to disclose a significant organism. Initial therapy should include an aminoglycoside and carbenicillin, and the use of other antibiotics should be dictated by the results of cultures. If cultures are negative and fever persists, antifungal therapy with amphotericin may be instituted. A combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole is indicated to prevent Pneumocystis carinii infection and may be of value in preventing bacterial infections. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy initiated during periods of granulocytopenia should not be discontinued until the granulocyte count rises to above 200 per cubic millimeter. Many patients coming to marrow transplantation may have had inadequate nutrition because of their disease or the efforts to treat it. In any event, the preparation for marrow grafting results in nausea and vomiting and the mucositis associated with therapy and granulocytopenia will result in poor oral intake for at least several weeks and sometimes longer. In order to ensure adequate nutrition, the Seattle marrow transplant team has for several years routinely installed a Hickman modification of the Broviac catheter upon admission for marrow transplantation. The catheter is inserted usually in the cephalic vein, with the tip at the level of the upper margin of the right atrium, and it is tunneled out under the skin on the chest. The catheter makes it possible to administer hyperalimentation in whatever quantity is necessary to maintain adequate nutrition. In addition, the catheter can be used for drawing blood samples and for intravenous administration of almost all therapeutic agents. Although some catheters are removed because of infection or suspected infection, about 90 percent of the patients have the catheter in place for approximately 3 months, the usual period of time it is needed. Engraftment and proof of engraftment 

After a period of profound granulocytopenia, engraftment is usually signaled by a rise in granulocytes and platelets and reappearance of reticulocytes. Figure | depicts the peripheral blood counts in a successful marrow transplant. The median time required to reach a granulocyte count of 100 is 16 days and to reach a count of 

CLINICAL RESULTS OF BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION 139 

1000, 26 days. The rise in platelet count usually lags a week or two behind the rise in granulocyte count. 

Proof of engraftment depends upon the use of cytogenetics and/or blood genetic markers in order to confirm that the regenerating marrow is of donor origin. Cytogenetic evidence of engraftment is most easily demonstrated when donor and recipient are of the opposite sex, although banding techniques frequently permit distinction between cells of a donor and recipient of the same sex. A variety of red blood cell and isoenzyme differences can be demonstrated if they are not obscured by recent blood transfusions. Patients with leukemia prepared for engraftment with cyclophosphamide and total-body irradiation have invariably been found to have a regenerating marrow entirely of the host type. Patients with aplastic anemia prepared with cyclophosphamide occasionally show persistence of some host cells for a period of a few weeks. A few of these patients have an increasing number of host cells, so that the graft is eventually lost and the marrow is repopulated by host cells. 

###### Complications following engraftment 

The complications that may follow successful marrow engraftment and are discussed in greater detail below are as follows: (1) graft rejection, a problem primarily occurring in patients with aplastic anemia, (2) infection, including early bacterial infections or later opportunistic infections such as cytomegalovirus, (3) acute graftversus-host disease, (4) chronic graft-versus-host disease, (5) recurrence of leukemia, and (6) miscellaneous complications such as hemorrhagic cystitis, cardiomyopathy, cataract formation, leukoencephalopathy, and sterility. 

###### CLINICAL RESULTS OF BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION 

###### Immunodeficiency diseases 

Studies of marrow transplantation for the treatment of infants with severe combined immunodeficiency syndromes have provided important basic information, despite the rarity of these disorders. These patients are unique in that immunosuppressive therapy is not necessary to

One of these patients was the first to receive a transplant from an HLA-identical sibling, and some 50 similar patients have been reconstituted successfully in the intervening 10 years. According to the International Bone Marrow Transplant Registry, 63 percent of these patients given identical sibling marrow are alive 6 months after grafting and, presumably, cured. 

###### Aplastic anemia® 

Aplastic anemia is the term used to describe the syndrome of profound marrow hypoplasia and pancytopenia. It is a form of organ failure and, like failure of the liver or kidney, may be due toa variety of etiologies and may have a number of 

3 See pp. 1525-1529 of Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 9th ed. 

###### 140 

###### BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION: PRESENT STATUS AND FUTURE EXPECTATIONS 

tion, graft-versus-host disease, opportunistic infections in the first few months after grafting, and chronic graft-versus-host disease. A rare patient has been lost because of bleeding related to refractoriness to platelet transfusions or because of cardiac toxicity related to cyclophosphamide. More recently, a cooperative study was carried out by 28 medical centers in order to compare, prospectively, the results of marrow transplantation from HLA-identical siblings to those of conventional therapy with steroids and androgens. The results of this study showed that patients treated by marrow transplantation had a 2-year survival rate of 60 percent, whereas those treated by conventional methods had a 2-year survival rate of 25 percent. Most patients in this study were in the first three decades of life. The results of the study showed clearly that if a suitable donor is available, marrow transplantation is superior to conventional management, at least in younger patients. Although these results were encouraging, there was obviously much room for improvement. Studies of marrow transplantation in the canine model had shown that blood transfusions could sensitize an intended marrow transplant recipient, which would result in subsequent rejection of the marrow graft. It seemed likely, therefore, that marrow graft rejection by the human patient might be due to sensitization to minor transplantation antigens by prior transfusions. Accordingly, the Seattle marrow transplant team undertook to identify patients with severe aplastic anemia early in the course of the disease and to carry out marrow transplantation before blood transfusions had been given. In the initial series of 30 such patients, graft failure was observed in only 3, and the actuarial long-term survival rate was 75 percent. Twenty of the 25 long-term survivors are entirely well, and 5 have mild-to-moderate graft-versus-host disease. It is clear, therefore, that patients with severe aplastic anemia and their families should have tissue typing performed as soon as the diagnosis is made. If a suitable donor can be identified, marrow transplantation should be carried out promptly before transfusions become necessary. Despite these encouraging results, however, many patients with severe aplastic anemia present to the physician with bleeding and/or infection, and transfusions must be given as a mat- 

pathogenic mechanisms. Whatever the cause of the aplasia, marrow transplantation offers the attractive possibility of replacing the diseased organ with a normal one. At the time of initial diagnosis, the spectrum of aplastic anemia may range from mild to severe. The course is difficult to predict because some mild cases rapidly become severe, and some severe cases may recover spontaneously. Severe aplastic anemia is characterized by the finding of a hypoplastic marrow with at least two of the following three characteristics: a granulocyte count of less than 500, a platelet count of less than 20,000, and reticulocytes fewer than 50,000 per cubic millimeter in the presence of anemia. About 50 percent of the patients with severe aplastic anemia are dead 4 months following the diagnosis, and only approximately 10 percent are alive and well 2 years after diagnosis. Because of the poor prognosis with conventional therapy, these patients are logical candidates for marrow transplantation. Transplantation for severe aplastic anemia using HLA-identical sibling donors Patients with severe aplastic anemia must be prepared for engraftment with immunosuppressive therapy, and the most widely used regimen has been cyclophosphamide, 50 mg/kg, on each of 4 days, followed 36h later by the intravenous infusion of donor bone marrow. The first two successful transplants of this type were reported in 1972, and these recipients are alive and well now, 9 years after transplantation. 

For ethical reasons the initial marrow transplants had to be carried out in patients who had clearly failed to benefit from conventional therapy. As a consequence, these end-stage patients had already received multiple transfusions of blood and platelets, and many were severely infected at the time of marrow transplantation. By 1976 the Seattle marrow transplant team had reported a series of 73 patients treated by marrow transplantation. Of these patients, 30 were alive 5 or more years after grafting, for a longterm survival rate of 41 percent. Several other marrow transplant teams have reported longterm survival rates of 40 to 50 percent for this type of patient. The causes of failure, to be described in greater detail below, have been related to early bacterial infection, graft rejec- 

###### CLINICAL RESULTS OF BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION 14] 

ter of urgent medical necessity. Therefore, marrow transplant teams have investigated other preparative regimens in an effort to improve survival rates for these patients. A more intensive immunosuppressive regimen consisting of procarbazine and antithymocyte globulin administered before the standard cyclophosphamide regimen was studied in Seattle and was found not to be effective in preventing graft rejection. However, investigators in Boston found a low incidence of graft rejection using this regimen. The Seattle team prepared some patients with cyclophosphamide or procarbazine and antithymocyte globulin followed by 1000 rads of total-body irradiation. This regimen was successful in preventing graft rejection but was toxic and the overall survival was not improved. The transplant team at the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA) is studying a regimen of cyclophosphamide followed by 300 rads of total-body irradiation. The graft rejection rate seems to be decreased, but it is too early to evaluate the effect on long-term survival. In Paris and Baltimore investigators are studying the cyclophosphamide regimen followed by 800 rads of totalbody irradiation while shielding the lung to 400 rads in an attempt to reduce the incidence of interstitial pneumonia. The results of these studies cannot be evaluated as yet. The Minneapolis team has explored the use of cyclophosphamide followed by 750 rads of total-nodal irradiation. In the initial series of nine previously transfused patients, no patient suffered graft rejection and seven of the nine survived. A proportional hazard regression analysis of the first 73 patients with severe aplastic anemia transplanted in Seattle disclosed the fact that the number of marrow cells transplanted was inversely related to the probability of graft rejection. Since it was not practical to attempt to get more bone marrow cells from the donor, attention was turned to peripheral blood mononuclear cells as an added source of donor cells. Peripheral blood cells and thoracic duct lymphoid cells have been shown to enhance allogeneic engraftment in mice and dogs and to increase erythropoiesis in vitro in dogs and humans. Initial studies were carried out in patients who, on the basis of in vitro tests indicating sensitization, were thought to be at high risk for graft rejection. The standard cyclophosphamide regimen was administered, 

and was followed by the marrow transplant. Then, on each of 3 to 5 days following marrow transplantation, buffy coat white blood cells were collected from 4 units of donor blood by a leukopheresis technique and administered intravenously to the recipient without in vitro irradiation. Among sensitized patients given only bone marrow, 13 of 16 rejected the graft, whereas only 3 of 23 patients given marrow plus buffy coat cells had rejections. Survival in the two groups was 25 and 71 percent, respectively. In summary, early transplantation before transfusions are given or, for patients who have been transfused, modified preparative regimens largely have solved the problem of graft rejection. The result has been an overall improvement in long-term survival to approximately 75 percent. Transplantation for severe aplastic anemia using identical twin donors Aplastic anemia is not a common disease, and finding a patient with this disease who has an identical twin is even more uncommon. Nevertheless, at least 13 transplants have been carried out for severe aplastic anemia using an identical twin as the marrow donor. In 10 patients simple intravenous infusion of marrow without any type of immunosuppressive treatment resulted in recovery. These results reinforce the concept that aplastic anemia is due to an acquired abnormality of the stem cell which can be corrected by transplantation of normal syngeneic stem cells. However, two patients did not recover following simple intravenous marrow infusion. These two patients were subsequently treated with the cyclophosphamide regimen and given a second infusion of bone marrow from the donor, which resulted in complete hematopoietic reconstitution. Although the number of cases is small, the results suggest that about 80 percent of the cases are likely to be due to acellular defect correctable by stem cell replacement, but 20 percent may be due to immune suppression or abnormal regulators of cell growth. Whatever the mechanism, the physician should be alert for the rare patient with aplastic anemia who has a genetically identical twin. In this fortunate setting, marrow transplantation is virtually without risk and some 90 percent of the patients can be cured.

###### Acute leukemia‘ 

Acute leukemia has served as a prototype malignant disease of the marrow for treatment by intensive chemoradiotherapy and marrow transplantation. In this situation the objectives of the therapeutic approach are, first, to destroy the malignant disease and, second, to replace the destroyed marrow by transplantation of a normal marrow. The problems encountered are those described above for aplastic anemia and, in addition, the recurrence of leukemia subsequent to marrow transplantation. 

Almost all regimens used for preparing the leukemic patient for marrow transplantation have employed supralethal total-body irradiation. This has been done for several reasons: (1) much of the laboratory experience with marrow transplantation in animals has been carried out with supralethal total-body irradiation; (2) irradiation is known to be an effective means of eradicating leukemic cells, but its clinical usefulness is limited because of destruction of normal marrow as well; and (3) irradiation penetrates to the so-called “‘privileged” sites where leukemic cells may not be readily accessible to chemotherapeutic agents. 

Transplantation for acute leukemia in relapse using HLA-identical sibling donors For obvious ethical reasons, marrow _transplantation was initially attempted in patients with acute leukemia in relapse after “conventional” chemotherapy had failed. These end-stage patients were poor candidates for any therapeutic procedure because they usually presented with a heavy body burden of leukemic cells, were usually granulocytopenic and thrombocytopenic, and often were already infected with antibioticresistant bacteria and fungi. Nevertheless, the eventual demonstration that some of these patients could be cured of the disease was impressive and encouraged renewed efforts to improve the results. 

In the initial series of 10 patients in Seattle, 1000 rads of total-body irradiation (midline exposure at 5 to 8 rads/min from opposing ®Co sources) was given in preparation for grafting. 

4See pp. 1620-1630 of Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 9th ed. 

Four patients with acute myelogenous leukemia seemed to be engrafted successfully but died too early to be evaluated. Six patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia were engrafted successfully, but five suffered a relapse of leukemia 2 to 5 months later. Two of these relapses were subsequently shown to be in donor-type cells. One patient is alive, 10 years later, in remission with a marrow graft. 

Because of the: high relapse rate, a decision was made to attempt to kill more leukemic cells by giving cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg on each of 2 days) afew days before the administration of total-body irradiation and the marrow transplant. One hundred patients with acute leukemia in relapse (46 with acute lymphoblastic leukemia and 54 with acute nonlymphoblastic leukemia) were treated with this regimen 43 or more years ago. Approximately one-half of the patients died in the first 3 months of causes related to advanced illness at the time of transplantation, graft-versus-host disease, or opportunistic infections, principally interstitial pneumonia. Recurrence of leukemia was observed in 31 patients and occurred throughout the first 2 years after transplantation. After 2 years, however, no more recurrences of leukemia were observed. Thirteen of these patients became long-term survivors. One patient who had cardiomyopathy due to daunomycin at the time of transplantation died of congestive heart failure 45 years after transplantation. Of the other 12 survivors, 3 suffer from chronic graft-versus-host disease and 9 are living normal lives in remission now 5 to 8 years after transplantation. Figure 2 shows that these longterm survivors are very far out on a plateau, which indicates that these patients, on no maintenance chemotherapy, are probably cured of their disease. 

Because recurrence of leukemia following marrow transplantation has been a major problem for patients transplanted in relapse, several marrow transplant teams have attempted to achieve a greater antileukemic effect by administering other intensive chemotherapy regimens before total-body irradiation and marrow transplantation. The UCLA team has recently reviewed these attempts and has found that almost all teams described long-term survival of approximately 10 to 15 percent regardless of the regimen. Six patients with CGL in blast crisis were transplanted using an identical twin donor, and one of these patients continues in remission with disappearance of the Philadelphia chromosome now 52 months after transplantation. 

In an effort to improve the results in patients with CGL, the Seattle team initiated a study of marrow transplantation during the chronic phase of the disease for patients with an identical twin to serve as marrow donor. The objective was to use supralethal chemoradiotherapy and twin marrow transplantation in an effort to eradicate the Philadelphia chromosome positive clone and, thus, to prevent the transformation into blast crisis and to cure the disease. An initial group of four patients was treated with dimethylbusulfan, 

cyclophosphamide, and total-body irradiation followed by twin marrow infusion. The twin donors, of course, were examined and found to be clinically and hematologically normal without the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome. A complete hematologic and cytogenetic remission was induced in all four patients. One patient relapsed cytogenetically and hematologically 30 months after transplantation and is now back in the original state of chronic CGL. The other three patients are clinically, hematologically, and cytogenetically normal 35, 38, and 43 months after marrow transplantation. It appears that the Philadelphia chromosome positive clone has been eradicated in these patients. Obviously, a longer follow-up of these three patients and of the seven similar patients transplanted since the initial report is in order. 

The term chronic is inappropriate in describing the clinical course of patients with CGL. The conversion to blast crisis, and death, occurs ata fairly constant rate, and the median survival in most series of patients is approximately 30 to 36 months.® Although a small fraction of patients may live for a long time in the chronic phase, it is clear that the outlook for most patients with this disease is quite grim. The results of syngeneic marrow transplantation, cited above, which indicate that the Philadelphia chromosome positive leukemic clone can be eliminated, suggest that it may be reasonable to carry out marrow transplantation in the chronic phase of the disease by utilizing allogeneic donors. Although a protocol for this purpose has been initiated, it is still too early to begin to evaluate the results. 

Marrow transplantation for patients with acute leukemia using donors other than HLA-identical siblings The general experience in the United States has been that approximately one-third of the patients with acute leukemia will be found to have an HLA-identical sibling. Thus, the majority of patients will not have an HLA-identical sibling, and, therefore, a cautious exploration of the use of nonidentical donors has been initiated by several marrow transplant teams. Application of allogeneic transplants to blood genetic diseases In theory, any blood genetic disorder could be eradicated by intensive chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, with restoration of normal marrow function by an allogeneic marrow graft. Target diseases would include thalassemia major, sickle-cell disease, hemolytic anemia, and disorders of granulocyte function. Only a very few such transplants have been carried out because many of these patients can survive for years with supportive therapy. As the safety of the marrow transplant procedure is improved, application to these genetic disorders will undoubtedly be increased. Autologous marrow transplantation The technique for procuring and cryopreserving marrow has been established for 20 years. It is possible to remove the patient’s own marrow, set it aside during intensive chemoradiotherapy, and then return the marrow to the patient in order to avoid subsequent lethal marrow aplasia. The following points are pertinent in considering autologous marrow transplantation: (1) The patient’s marrow should not be contaminated with malignant cells. (2) Autologous marrow is of value only in protecting the patient against lethal toxicity to the hematopoietic system. If the regimen of chemoradiotherapy involves lethal toxicity to other organ systems, autologous marrow will not be of benefit. (3) The tumor being treated must show a dose-response curve such that supralethal chemoradiotherapy can be expected to result in a significantly enhanced antitumor response. Unfortunately, with currently available agents, only a few tumors appear to fall into this category. (4) The protocol must be designed in such a way that the role of autologous marrow can be demonstrated. In animal systems it is 

recipient pairs in which one of the HLA haplotypes was genetically identical and the other haplotype was phenotypically identical for one or more of the HLA loci. For example, the marrow donor might be a parent, in which case the patient’s haplotype inherited from that parent would be HLA identical. The haplotype inherited from the other parent might, by chance, be phenotypically similar to the donor’s other haplotype. Similarly, a sibling might be haploidentical with the patient. The results of these transplants carried out to the end of 1979 are as follows: eight patients with ALL in relapse, one survivor at 36 months; five patients with ALL in remission, three survivors at 8, 10, and 12 months; seven patients with ANL in relapse, three survivors at 5, 9, and 12 months; seven patients with ANL in remission, five survivors at 9, 10, 11, 17, and 29 months. It is apparent that the outcome for these patients is largely a function of the stage of the disease in which the transplant was carried out. The incidence of acute graftversus-host disease and the cause of death was not significantly different from the results described utilizing HIA-identical donor-recipient sibling pairs. There are as yet too few patients to permit an analysis according to the family relationship of the donor or according to the HLA locus involved in the mismatch.

One of the patients with severe combined immunodeficiency disease, transplanted by the Sloan-Kettering team, is the first long-term survivor of an unrelated graft. At last report, 2 years after grafting, the patient has suffered moderately severe chronic graft-versushost disease. 

The Seattle team has now transplanted a patient with ALL in second remission who received allogeneic marrow from an HLA-A, -B, -D, and -DR phenotypically identical unrelated donor.
