Nevertheless, the potential use of autologous marrow is the subject of a new wave of interest, and some results are encouraging. The tumors that might be expected to show a significant improvement in response to high-dose chemoradiotherapy include the leukemias, Hodgkin’s disease, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, — small-cell cancer of the lung, testicular tumors, and ovarian tumors. Several transplant centers are conducting studies of the utility of stored autologous marrow, and all have reported successful hematopoietic reconstitution in most patients. It is, as yet, too early to evaluate the clinical impact of these studies on the course of the tumor. IMMUNOLOGIC ASPECTS OF MARROW TRANSPLANTATION Marrow graft rejection 

Marrow graft rejection is a phenomenon in which the transplanted marrow graft functions briefly, but, after a few days or weeks, the peripheral blood counts suddenly drop and marrow biopsy shows the marrow to be devoid of myeloid elements. In some instances, the graft may be rejected so quickly that graft function is never clearly established. Marrow graft rejection is a common problem in patients with aplastic anemia, and the clinical problem is described in the above section on aplastic anemia. Marrow graft rejection is very uncommon in patients with leukemia, which may be due to several factors: (1) Transfusions are usually given to leukemic patients while they are receiving antileukemic chemotherapy, which is also immunosuppressive. This chemotherapy may prevent sensitization to transplantation antigens contained in blood products. (2) Leukemia involves the lymphoid system so that the disease process itself may interfere with sensitization. (3) Leukemic 

patients receive a more intensive immunosuppressive regimen before grafting and are thus less likely to reject the graft. Marrow graft rejection is a form of marrow graft failure, which may be due to causes other than graft rejection. With a solid organ, such as the kidney, histological proof of graft rejection is easily obtained, but histological proof cannot usually be obtained with a marrow graft, since the myeloid marrow simply disappears. Other possible mechanisms of graft failure include (1) defective or inadequate numbers of stem cells in the donor marrow, (2) allogeneic resistance not associated with HLA, and (3) susceptibility of the donor marrow to the same etiologic mechanism(s) responsible for the original disease process. In addition, inadequate immunosuppressive therapy before grafting may facilitate marrow graft rejection either by failing to overcome sensitization of the host or by failing to overcome allogeneic resistance. Acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) A “wasting disease” or “runt disease”’ was described many years ago in newborn mice or in rodents exposed to lethal total-body irradiation and given infusions of allogeneic hematopoietic cells. Over subsequent years these observations were confirmed for other species including humans and were recognized to be the consequence of an immunologic reaction of engrafted lymphoid cells, presumably T cells, against the tissues of the host. This graft-versus-host reaction and its consequences are now referred to as GVHD, which is one of the major complications of marrow transplantation in humans. In Seattle, a series of 262 patients was given a marrow graft from an HLA-identical sibling, and after the graft they received methotrexate, which was designed to prevent GVHD. Nevertheless, 116 (44 percent) developed moderate-to-severe GVHD. GVHD in animals and in humans usually involves the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and/or liver. A skin rash is usually the first sign of GVHD. Intestinal involvement results in diarrhea and may progress to abdominal pain and ileus. Liver disease is characterized by rises in bilirubin, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase, and alkaline phosphatase. Severe im- 

###### 148 

###### BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION: PRESENT STATUS AND FUTURE EXPECTATIONS 

new approaches in preventing or treating GVHD must be found. One such. new approach currently under investigation involves an agent with unique immunosuppressive properties, cyclosporin A. Cyclosporin A is a fungal metabolite that suppresses most immunologic reactions in vitro. In vivo it prolongs allografts of skin, heart, and kidney in several animal species. The Johns Hopkins team has reported that in marrowgrafted rats suppressor cells may emerge and maintain a stable chimeric state. The Seattle team has reported that cyclosporin A prevented or delayed GVHD in dogs given marrow grafts from DLA-identical littermate donors. The Royal Marsden team has reported preliminary data of the use of cyclosporin A in clinical marrow grafting. More studies are needed to determine the role of cyclosporin A in the prevention and treatment of human GVHD. Other experiments underway are designed to eliminate from the marrow inoculum the immune competent cells that are responsible for GVHD while retaining hematopoietic stem cells. Efforts to achieve a physical separation using albumin gradient separation have been reported. Other efforts involve treatment of the marrow inoculum with heterologous or xenogeneic antiserums in an effort to destroy the T cells thought to be responsible for the development of GVHD. The recent development of monoclonal antibodies that react with human T cells or subsets of T cells points the way to greatly improved methods of in vitro treatment of marrow. These attractive approaches for the prevention of GVHD require further study for application in human marrow transplantation. 

munologic deficiency accompanies GVHD, frequently ending in death from infection. The distinction between illness due to an active immunologic assault against host tissues — the graftversus-host reaction—and the consequences of this assault — deranged organ function and infection—is subtle and, therefore, both are considered to be a part of GVHD. 

Since GVHD is immunologically mediated, efforts to prevent the development of GVHD have involved the use of immunosuppressive therapy. In animal systems it was found that treatment with immunosuppressive agents must be started before GVHD becomes apparent. Of the many agents studied, methotrexate and cyclophosphamide were found to be useful. Methotrexate was found to ameliorate GVHD in mice, dogs, and monkeys, and for this reason the Seattle team has routinely employed it in the postgrafting period. The standard regimen consists of methotrexate 15 mg/m2 on day | post grafting and 10 mg/m? on days 3, 6, 11, 18, and weekly thereafter through day 102. For leukemic patients, in an effort to prevent relapse in the central nervous system, this regimen was modified so that the weekly methotrexate was given intrathecally, 12 mg every other week beginning on day 32. The Johns Hopkins team has used cyclophosphamide, 7.5 mg/kg for five doses on alternate days, beginning on the first day after marrow grafting, followed by additional doses at irregular intervals. Controlled clinical trials of these regimens have not been carried out in human beings, and, despite these regimens, GVHD remains a serious problem. A number of studies have been carried out in animals and in humans in an effort to treat GVHD once it becomes established. Most of these efforts have been disappointing. The Seattle team treated GVHD in human recipients of HLA-identical marrow with rabbit or goat antithymocyte globulin, and improvement was observed in some patients. In a clinical trial, without untreated controls because of ethical considerations, prednisone and _ horse antithymocyte globulin gave equivalent results in the treatment of established human GVHD. Despite these efforts, about one-third of the patients who develop moderate to severe GVHD will die with this complication. In general, the treatment of acute GVHD is unsatisfactory and 

###### Chronic GVHD 

Chronic GVHD occurs in approximately onefourth of the long-term recipients of marrow from an HLA-identical sibling. It may range from mild to severe and may develop as an extension of acute GVHD or de novo after a period of well-being. The manifestations include skin disease, keratoconjunctivitis, buccal mucositis, esophageal strictures, small and large intestinal involvement, pulmonary _ insufficiency, chronic liver disease, and generalized wasting. Histologically, the disease resembles the sys- 

###### IMMUNOLOGIC ASPECTS OF MARROW TRANSPLANTATION 149 

Initial efforts to treat chronic GVHD with short courses of antithymocyte globulin or prolonged treatment with prednisone were ineffective. More recently, the Seattle team treated a series of 21 patients with combinations of prednisone and either procarbazine, cyclophosphamide, or azathioprine. Of the 21 patients, 4 died with chronic GVHD, 11 are alive and leading almost normal lives on treatment, and 6 have recovered completely and treatment has been discontinued. It appears that combination therapy can modify the course of chronic GVHD, but new approaches must be sought to treat or prevent this disorder. Recovery of immunologic function Almost all patients given a marrow transplant from an HLA-identical sibling develop a functional graft with adequate levels of circulating granulocytes and platelets. Nevertheless, particularly in the first 3 months after grafting, these patients are susceptible to a wide variety of opportunistic infections. Approximately one-third of patients develop an interstitial pneumonia, and cytomegalovirus can be demonstrated in approximately one-half of these pneumonias. The mortality rate, especially in association with GVHD, is high. The high incidence of infection is the result of a very slow return of immunologic function which may be made worse by GVHD and by efforts to prevent or treat GVHD. The Seattle team reported a study of immune function in 56 long-term survivors after marrow grafting from HLA-identical siblings. All patients had pronounced impairment of most immunologic parameters studied during the first 3 to 4 months post grafting. Antibody responses to bacteriophage @X174 or keyhole limpet hemocyanin returned to the normal range within the first year in patients without GVHD, whereas patients with chronic GVHD continued to show profoundly deficient antibody responses. Patients without GVHD showed return of positive skin test responsiveness to dinitrochlorobenzene and keyhole limpet hemocyanin, whereas patients with chronic GVHD showed little or no erythematosus profundus. temic collagen vascular diseases, especially morphea and Chronic GVHD may be associated with recurrent and occasionally fatal bacterial infections. lupus 

return. Despite the poor in vivo immune reactivity during the first months post transplantation, many in vitro parameters of immunity rapidly returned to the normal range. Total lymphocyte counts and the number of T and B cells in the peripheral blood were normal within 3 months. Cells involved in natural killing, antibody-dependent killing, or lectin-dependent killing were generally normal within 1 month. Lymphocytes from most patients showed good responsiveness in mixed leukocyte culture and to various mitogens within | to 2 months after grafting. Fortunately, by the end of the first year after grafting most patients have recovered immunologically and are able to lead normal lives without an increased incidence of infection. Tolerance The long-term healthy human recipients of allogeneic marrow transplants are true chimeras. Their myeloid system, lymphoid system, and monocyte-macrophage system are made up entirely of cells of donor origin. Clearly, these donor cells in the recipient are ‘“‘tolerant”’ of the host’s tissues. The nature of this tolerance has been studied for years in experimental animal chimeras. These studies constitute a fascinating story in immunobiology, but a clear understanding of the state of tolerance has not emerged. At least three mechanisms may be operative, including classic central tolerance, tolerance maintained by “blocking factors,” and tolerance related to the presence of “suppressor” cells. The Seattle team has studied the phenomena of cellular inhibition and serum blocking factors in human patients given marrow grafts from HLAidentical siblings. Only occasionally did chimera serum block the inhibition of the proliferation of host fibroblasts by the chimera lymphocytes (of donor origin). It was concluded that maintenance of stable graft-host tolerance did not depend on the presence of serum blocking factors. The Boston transplant team and the Seattle transplant team have described the presence of nonspecific suppressor cells in patients with chronic GVHD, but these cells could be demonstrated only occasionally in healthy chimeras. On the other hand, the Seattle team, using cryopreserved trinitrophenol-modified host lymphocytes, demon- 

###### 150 

###### BONE MARROW TRANSPLANTATION: PRESENT STATUS AND FUTURE EXPECTATIONS 

relapse following marrow transplantation. In the vast majority of patients, the recurrent leukemia is in host-type cells. However, four cases have now been reported in whom the recurrent leukemic cells were shown to be of donor origin. One explanation for the recurrence in donortype cells might be the existence of a leukemogenic virus in the host, perhaps induced by the total-body irradiation. Despite extensive study, there is at present no evidence for the existence of leukemogenic viruses in humans. In the laboratory, recent observations indicate that both viral and nonviral transforming genes can be transferred to and expressed in certain types of recipient cells following transfection with free DNA, chromatin, or both. An alternative possibility, therefore, is that cellular genes responsible for malignant transformation may have been transferred to donor cells. These cellular genes might arise from the large mass of leukemic cells undergoing rapid disintegration after the preparative regimen. It seems likely that further study of the phenomenon of recurrence in donor-type cells will provide insight into the origin of leukemia. 

strated that specific suppressor cells regularly could be found in healthy chimeras but not in patients with chronic GVHD. Many more studies must be done since it is clear that we do not, as yet, have a good understanding of the immunologic mechanism(s) of the stable tolerant state. 

###### STUDIES OF RECURRENT LEUKEMIA AFTER GRAFTING 

###### Frequency of recurrence of leukemia 

For patients with leukemia who are transplanted in relapse, a Kaplan-Meier plot of the probability that the patient will be in remission at any given time after grafting shows a rather constant rate of recurrence of leukemia in the first year, a decreasing rate in the second year, and no recurrences thereafter. This analysis shows that if there were no other causes of death, approximately 35 percent of the patients would be cured and 65 percent would relapse. For patients with ALL who are transplanted in the second or subsequent remission, the actuarial analysis predicts relapse in 55 percent of the patients. Most impressive, and rather unexpected, was the finding that only 1 of 19 patients with ANL transplanted in first remission subsequently relapsed. In contrast, of 20 patients with ANL transplanted in the second remission, 7 (35 percent) subsequently relapsed. It is evident that recurrent leukemia after grafting is a major problem for patients transplanted in relapse or in the second or subsequent remission. Recurrent leukemia is only a minor problem for those patients transplanted in the first remission, which may be explained by the fact that only a very small number of residual leukemic cells are present, by the possibility that the leukemic cells of patients in the first remission may not yet have acquired resistance to therapeutic agents, or both of these factors. 

###### Efforts to prevent recurrence of leukemia after grafting 

As mentioned in the clinical results section above, several marrow transplant teams have attempted to reduce the incidence of recurrence of leukemia after grafting by administering more intensive chemoradiotherapy regimens, but these efforts have been discouraging in that recurrence of leukemia has continued to be a major problem. One explanation may be that most patients had already been exposed to the most effective antileukemic agents, and the likelihood of leukemic cell resistance to these agents would be expected to be high. A more extensive range of agents is needed, especially agents whose mechanism of action is entirely different from that of chemoradiotherapy. Examples of such new therapeutic modalities include the use of interferon and of monoclonal antibodies that react specifically with leukemic cells. The efficacy of such agents might be most apparent when applied in the postmarrow-graft setting when the number of leukemic cells is minimal. 

###### Nature of recurrent leukemia 

Blood genetic markers and cytogenetic techniques can be used to identify the donor or host origin of the leukemic cells in those patients who 

###### REFERENCES lal 

###### Graft-versus-leukemia 

A graft-versus-leukemia effect has been demonstrated in murine systems in several laboratories. In human recipients of allogeneic bone marrow grafts, evidence supporting the existence of a graft-versus-leukemia effect has been difficult to obtain because of the large number of deaths from other causes among patients with severe GVHD. The Seattle team has utilized sophisticated statistical methods to account for differing intervals and competing causes of risk in order to analyze the rate of leukemic relapse in 46 recipients of syngeneic marrow, 117 recipients of allogeneic marrow with no or minimal GVHD, and 79 recipients of allogeneic marrow with moderate to severe acute or chronic GVHD. The relative relapse rate of leukemia was 2.5 times greater in recipients without GVHD than in recipients with GVHD. Thus, from studies in murine systems and in humans, it appears that the graft-versus-host reaction does have a significant antileukemic effect, which suggests that a therapeutic advantage might be achieved by utilizing this effect. The problem with this kind of therapeutic approach, particularly in outbred species such as dogs and humans, is the fact that the graft-versus-host reaction cannot be predictably initiated and, once initiated, is extremely difficult to control. In fact, as indicated above, with DLA- or HLA-matched donor-recipient pairs, the graft-versus-host reaction is quite often lethal. As advances are made in the management of acute and chronic GVHD, it may be appropriate to explore the therapeutic potential of the graft-versus-leukemia reaction. 

###### CONCLUSION 

Because of the complexity of the marrow grafting procedure, transplantation should be undertaken only by teams with all the resources needed to ensure an optimal result. The number of such teams has increased rapidly over the past few years, and in general the clinical results are comparable to those described above. Two major concerns have delayed a more general application of marrow transplantation. The first is cost. Marrow<sup>transplantationis obviously</sup> an expensive undertaking, but cost has been re- 

duced appreciably by transplantation earlier in the course of the disease, when the patient is in relatively good condition. Three centers (UCLA, Children’s Orthopedic Medical Center of Seattle, and the Royal Marsden, unpublished observations) have carried out cost analyses comparing marrow transplantation with conventional therapy and have found marrow transplantation to be less expensive. 

The second major concern has been that marrow transplantation has been regarded as an experimental procedure. As for all experimental procedures, the ethical problems of submitting a patient and donor to the marrow transplant regimen have limited its use. However, the demonstration of better long-term survival with marrow transplantation than with conventional therapy for younger patients with severe aplastic anemia and for patients with acute leukemia (excepting children with good risk ALL) should remove the ethical concern. In fact, it may be unethical to fail to transplant a patient with one of these diseases who has a suitable donor. Extension of this form of therapy to other malignant diseases and to blood genetic disorders is experimental at present, but the current rapid rate of progress may soon make a much broader application of marrow grafting a reality.

#### SYSTEMIC TUMORS FRED HOCHBERG NEUROLOGICAL ASPECTS OF 

Carcinomas and tumors of blood cells and lymph nodes are frequent and serious diseases in all periods of life. Although surgical excision is the primary therapy for many of the solid tumors, all too often dispersion of tumor cells into many organs precludes this mode of treatment, and of course leukemias and lymphomas never fall within the purview of surgery. Such patients become the primary responsibility of pediatricians, internists, and family physicians, usually after initial therapy has been instituted by oncologists. 

Many tumors involve the nervous system ina variety of ways. They may metastasize to the meninges, the substance of the brain and spinal cord, or the surrounding cranial and vertebral bones. The tumor or, more frequently, its treatment may predispose to certain opportunistic infections or vascular lesion of the nervous system. Or the tumor cells may induce a metabolic or endocrine disorder which secondarily deranges the function of the nervous system. 

The proper care of patients with systemic tumors requires that the attending physician have sufficient knowledge of these neuromedical complications to recognize them at their earliest stages, to know what laboratory procedures are available for confirmation of clinical diagnosis, and to be familiar with the different modes of therapy and their chances of success in relieving distressing symptoms and prolonging life. The exposition of this subject will be developed around the following four topics: 

1 Common syndromes resulting from systemic tumors metastatic to the brain, meninges, cranial bones, spinal cord, and vertebrae 

2 Vascular and infectious diseases of the 

nervous system associated with systemic tumors 

###### 3 Unclassifiable paraneoplastic diseases of the nervous system 4 Metabolic and endocrine encephalopathies induced by systemic tumors COMMON SYNDROMES RESULTING FROM NEUROMETASTASES: PATTERNS OF METASTASES TO THE CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM AND THEIR RELATIVE FREQUENCY 

Of all the neurological complications of a systemic tumor, metastases to the brain and spinal cord or their meningeal and osseous coverings are the most dreaded. Though such metastases were formerly regarded as a terminal event beyond medical control, newer methods for early diagnosis and new modes of treatment are making the outlook less dismal. 

Prior to 1948, not more than 10 percent of all brain and spinal cord tumors brought to the attention of neurologists and neurosurgeons were metastatic, and such tumors were most often diagnosed at autopsy. Today, in the same hospitals, metastatic tumors comprise two-thirds of all brain and spinal cord tumors. The increasing frequency with which metastatic tumors are being diagnosed during life results from the increased use of chemotherapy in systemic cancer, which prolongs survival, the wide use of computerized tomography (CT) scanning, and the greater awareness of the metastatic patterns of each type of tumor.

Most often the metastases of melanoma to the CNS occur in patients in the more advanced stages of disease who may have responded to chemotherapy or immunotherapy. Although lymphoma may spread in the nervous system, it is most often located in the subarachnoid space and involves the meninges. Most of these tumors are of the non-Hodgkin’s type. The total number of all carcinomas of the ovary, colon, cervix, pancreas, or thyroid that metastasize to the nervous system is relatively small (less than 5S percent). At the present time, 22 percent of patients with systemic tumors have autopsy evidence of metastasis to the nervous system. Of this 22 percent, 14 percent are to the brain, 2 percent to the spinal cord, 2 percent to the brain and spinal cord, 2 percent to cranial dura, and 2 percent to the meaninges. In addition, 1 percent of all systemic 

tumors have one of the remote complications described below under “‘Unclassifiable Paraneoplastic Inflammatory Diseases” and ‘‘Metabolic and Endocrine Disorders Sometimes Associated with Systemic Tumors.” Tumors of the lung, breast, and melanoma of the skin raise some of the most vexing neurologic problems. There is an interesting though unexplained relationship between the histologic type of cell and the interval between the diagnosis or primary tumor and its metastasess to the CNS. In most of the patients who develop CNS metastases from lung cancer, the spread to the brain becomes evident within 3 months of the diagnosis of primary tumor. In contrast, most breast cancers are observed to extend to the brain at least a year after the diagnosis of the primary tumor. This difference explains the fact that the first symptoms of a lung tumor may be caused by the brain metastasis, whereas most of the cerebral metastases of breast tumor occur in women known to have the primary tumor. The same is true of most cerebral metastases of gastrointestinal tumors. Moreover, in slow-growing tumors and in those of any organ where survival has been prolonged by modern therapy (ovarian carcinoma, hypernephroma, neuroblastoma, leukemia, and lymphoma) the interval between the time of the diagnosis of the “primary” cancer and the cerebral metastases increases in proportion to the length of survival. Table 1 shows these relationships. 

The spread of cancer to the nervous system follows several patterns: 

- I Hematogenous via small, clinically unrecognizable tumor emboli. This pathway is the one by which tumors of the lung spread. Primary and secondary lung tumors together account for 75 percent of all parenchymatous brain metastases in the large series of Weiss et al. Presumably masses of tumor cells enter the pulmonary veins and are carried into the carotid and vertebral arteries to the brain. 

- 2 Direct extension through cranial and intervertebral foramens. This is the most frequent pathway of the spread of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Schmincke’s tumor, lymphoepithelioma, and transitional cell carcinoma), sarcoma of cranial bones and the middle ear, 

COMMON SYNDROMES RESULTING FROM NEUROMETASTASES P55 

retinoblastoma, and adenocystic carcinoma of the parotid gland. 

- 3 Hematogenous deposits in cranial bone and vertebral bodies with direct extension to the dura (and rarely adjacent brain tissue) or to the spinal epidural space with compression of nerve roots and spinal cord. This is the pathway of spread of most of the tumors that metastasize to bone, such as carcinomas of the prostate and breast. Tumors with a predilection for bone rarely spread by the hematogenous route to the brain or meninges. Tumors infiltrating the cranial dura may be associated with subdural effusions.

Once the tumor cells reach the brain, they may grow as solitary or multiple discrete masses or they may invade the cerebrospinal fluid pathways. In some instances of meningeal carcinomatosis, virtually all the tumor tissue invading neural tissues appears to have extended through the pia and ependyma.

###### NEUROLOGICAL ASPECTS OF SYSTEMIC TUMORS 

cancer are solitary at the time of the first CT scan. In deciding on the number of metastases by CT scan, a double dose of iodine (80 g) with overlapping levels of scan should be used, but even then small lesions may be overlooked. 

Metastatic tumors, even relatively small ones, vary in appearance from a ring toa solid mass of increased uptake of the enhancing medium. A radiopaque mass in a nonenhanced CT scan means the presence of hemorrhage, either into the tumor or into adjacent brain tissue. Hemorrhages occur most frequently in metastases from melanoma, lung carcinoma, renal carcinoma, and choriocarcinoma. The ringlike appearance of tumor tissue is caused by necrosis of the central parts as the tumor outgrows its blood supply. There is often a zone of low density around the tumor caused by edema. These lesions may deform the ventricles. Tumors in the cerebellum and basal meninges may induce obstructive hvdrocephalus, which is also demonstrable by the CT scan. 

Clinical manifestations Table 2 shows the mode of presentation of the last 102 patients with central nervous system metastases found at autopsy at the Massachusetts General Hospital. Noteworthy is the high percentage with a clinical diagnosis of brain tumor in whom there had been no clinical signs of a primary extracranial tumor. There were also a considerable number of patients with a systemic tumor who had had no clinical signs of brain involvement. This may reflect in part the failure to make careful neurologic assessments of patients with terminal cancer. 

Headache, seizures, slurred speech (pseudobulbar palsy), mental dullness, and torpor were the most frequent signs of multiple metastases. Fully 50 percent of the patients complained first of early morning headache. Papilledema eventually developed. Single metastases were heralded

Neurologic symptoms in setting of diagnosed systemic cancer 60% Neurologic symptoms without known systemic cancer 20% Asymptomatic neurologic metastases 20% 

by seizures and focal signs such as hemiparesis, homonymous hemianopsia, cerebellar ataxia, or signs of brainstem disease — diplopia, dizziness, facial weakness, dysarthria, or dysphagia, depending on the location of the lesion. Usually the symptoms developed and progressed over a period of several weeks. Most patients had symptoms for 2 months before they consulted a physician. However, in about 20 percent of the patients the neurologic disorder developed over a period of a few days, and in 20 percent a convulsion was the initial symptom. Rarely, the onset of neurological symptoms was so rapid that it simulated a stroke. This was most likely in choriocarcinoma, melanotic carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and bronchogenic carcinoma. In some instances the abrupt onset was explained by a hemorrhage into the tumor, which rapidly increased its bulk and pressed on brain tissue. 

Decisions regarding therapy must be based on information concerning the type of primary tumor, the involvement of various organs and tissues, and the number and location of metastases in the brain. As a rule, the clinical examination does not provide such data and laboratory tests must be used to answer these questions. The search for the primary tumor and metastatic lesions in other organs should include x-rays of the chest (sometimes tomograms), radionuclide bone and liver scans, liver function studies, and xeromammograms in females. Of less value are intravenous pyelography, gastrointestinal barium studies, and abdominal and pelvic ultrasound or body CT scan. To determine the number of cerebral metastases, CT scan with contract enhancement of the brain is the single most important test. if meningeal invasion is suspected, cytology of the CSF after centrifugation is necessary. These laboratory and x-ray studies usually will show whether or not other organs, as well as the cerebrum, are also involved. These other sites of involvement by cancer are represented in Fig. 3, derived from our experience as well as from the reports of Globus and Meltzer and of Halpert et al. In 20 percent of patients with brain metastases, no involvement of other organs is found. The CT scan accurately identifies over 90 percent of supratentorial and 75 percent of infratentorial metastases. The most difficult tumors to visualize are those at the base of the brain near 

COMMON SYNDROMES RESULTING FROM NEUROMETASTASES 1/57 

bony structures, including the hypothalamus, lower brainstem, and cerebellum. Scans using photon-emitting radiopharmaceuticals which cross the blood-brain barrier are positive in 70 to 90 percent of metastatic lesions. Sodium [°°"Tc]pertechnetate (with a half-life of 65 h) and !™JIn (with a half-life of 100 min) are most widely used for intracranial imaging. Comparative studies indicate that radionuclide scanning is as effective as arteriography and pneumoencephalography. When CT scanning apparatus is not available, the combination of radionuclide scan and electroencephalogram will reveal 95 percent of supratentorial metastases. AS an initial test for identification and localization of metastases, the electroencephalogram is much less valuable and is abnormal in only 5 to 15 percent of cases with solid supratentorial mass lesions. As would be expected, rapidly growing, multiple, and diffuse metastatic tumors show the highest degree of abnormality. 

Regional x-rays, bone x-rays, bone scans, and serum acid phosphatase determinations provide useful information concerning bone involvement. These examinations and also myelography, are of particular importance in the diagnosis of metastatic involvement of the vertebral column with spinal cord and spinal roots compression. 

Therapy The therapeutic plan should be governed by the clinical status of the patient. Advanced, widespread systemic cancer is beyond the reach of all useful therapeutic measures; the comfort of the patient is the only consideration. However, in most instances the patient with cerebral symptoms is relatively healthy when he or she comes to medical attention. 

Once the diagnosis of cerebral metastatic disease is established, three methods of treatment are available: x-ray irradiation, antitumor drugs, and surgical excision. Since metastatic tumor of the brain is usually fatal within a few months (only exceptionally do patients survive for a year or more), a realistic estimate of the possible success, discomfort, and expense of the methods must be made in consultation with experts in oncology as well as the family as soon as possible. The expenditure of large sums of money on neurosurgical operations, long-term x-ray therapy, and expensive drugs with the prospect of prolonging the patient’s painful and anguished 

FIGURE 3 

Other organs involved with tumor metastases to the brain. (Partially based upon data of Globus and Meltzer and of Halpert et al.) 

existence for only a few months is hardly a mark of prudent medical judgment. 

Radiation is the most widely used therapy, and its effectiveness varies with the type of tumor. Some tumors such as the reticulum cell sarcoma are sensitive; others such as the melanoma are resistant. Yet some degree of response should be expected in nearly every patient, and the response is substantial in 75 percent of cases. 

The National Radiation Therapy and Oncology Group in the United States has proposed a schedule of whole-brain radiation up to 3000 rads (300 rads in each of 10 fractions) as the treatment of choice for single and multiple brain metastases. Although this radiation dose is considered to be palliative rather than curative, prolonged improvement in the neurological state and CT images can be achieved. One-fifth of the patients prove to be so ill that they fail to complete radiation therapy and survive less than 3 months. In many such patients with widespread

For those who complete the course of radiation, the survival period is 6 months (30 percent), but 9 to 20 percent live for a year, particularly those with primary tumors in the breast (25 percent), the lung (15 percent), and with melanoma (10 percent). Usually after a period of improvement for several months, the condition of the patient gradually worsens. Onethird will die of neurological disease caused by the tumor, and the remainder will succumb to its systemic effects. 

Prophylactic radiation of the whole brain is being performed in certain tumors such as childhood leukemia and oat-cell carcinoma of the lung. Preliminary results show a reduction in later cerebral involvement from 45 to less than 10 percent. 

###### Chemotherapy is the most promising addition to the therapeutic armamentarium. Certain drugs, highly effective in systemic cancer, may be of value in the treatment of brain metastases of particular tumor cell types, for example: Testicular carcinoma cis-Platinum Nasopharyngeal carcinoma cis-Platinum Methotrexate Bleomycin Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma High-dose methotrexate Chorionepithelioma and High-dose Wilms’s tumor methotrexate Estrogen-sensitive breast Tamoxifen carcinoma 

The majority of metastatic tumors of the brain are not responsive to presently available drugs. 

Potential new approaches include the use of high doses of chemotherapy with autologous bone marrow rescue or intraarterial or intrathecal chemotherapy. Surgical resection of cerebral tumors is now being practiced in many medical centers, providing the patient meets certain criteria, such as a solitary intracranial deposit that is accessible, as judged by clinical examination, but mainly by CT scan; no involvement of other viscera or, if they are involved, a good response to therapy; and reasonable life expectancy. 

The patient who is to be subjected to intracranial surgery should be prepared by the administration of dexamethasone (16 mg per day in divided doses of 4 mg every 6 h). Postoperative corticosteroid therapy and radiation are usuaily necessary. 

In fully 75 percent of patients neurological states are improved after operation. However, the average survival is only about 6 months; 15 to 34 percent live for | year and 6 to 12 percent for 2 years. Rare postoperative recovery and survival up to 3 years have occurred after the resection of solitary neurometastases in cancers of breast, melanoma, bronchogenic carcinoma, and renal cell carcinoma. 

The control of intracranial pressure is a problem in many cases of secondary tumor in the brain. The elevated pressure may be due to one or several masses of tumor and surrounding edema, to obstructive hydrocephalus, or to both. If the patient is critically ill, intravenous mannitol (20 g over 30 min) in combination with 16 to 48 mg dexamethasone per day is given. These drugs must be given cautiously in the face of congestive heart failure, and careful attention must be paid to urine flow. If the patient is stuporous and intubated, forced hyperventilation reduces brain swelling. For long-term control of intracranial pressure, various combinations of corticosteroids and hyperosmolar agents such as glycerol (1.0 to 1.5 g/kg, every 3 to 4h) will keep many patients comfortable. These measures tide the patient over this critical phase in the illness but seldom increase life expectancy. Since approximately one-third of the patients have convulsions, they should be maintained on anticonvulsant therapy. The usual medication is 300 to 400 mg diphenylhydantoin and 50 to 100 mg phenobarbital at bedtime. It is evident that these newer therapeutic

###### Meningeal carcinomatosis 

Widespread dissemination of tumor through the cerebrospinal fluid spaces, i.e., the leptomeninges and ventricles, is the second major pattern of neurologic metastases. It occurs in approximately 4 percent of all cases of systemic tumor at the Massachusetts General Hospital. In an analysis of 100 successive cases of this type this complication was due to adenocarcinoma in 60 percent (40 percent breast and 20 percent lung), melanoma in 10 percent, gastrointestinal carcinoma in 10 percent, and other carcinomas and leukemias in the remainder. The syndrome of meningeal neoplasia also occurs, though rarely, with gliomas, pinealomas, and nasopharyngeal tumors. Clinical manifestations The most frequent symptoms are listed in Table 4. The frequency of headache and pain in the back, some of which is radicular, and the high incidence of cranial nerve root involvement (facial weakness, facial numbness, and extraocular weakness) and of spinal nerve palsies is noteworthy. In this series of cases 37 percent also had metastases to the lung, 29 percent to the liver, and 29 percent involvement of lymph nodes. Evidence of one or more mass lesions in the brain occurred in approximately 40 percent of cases, and often they were 

responsible for headache and impairment of mentation. Enhancement of the cerebral cortex was seen in CT scans in some cases, but this was not a reliable finding. Others had only obstructive hydrocephalus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) abnormalities provided important clues to the diagnosis. Tumor cells were found in approximately 50 percent of our cases, providing the fluid was cytocentrifuged or filtered on a millipore filter. Hemocytometer count and a differential analysis of cells in the counting chamber are unreliable. Cytocentrifugation of a few milliliters of fluid will often yield several hundred cells even when the hemocytometer count is zero. The other CSF findings are shown in Table S. Often on the initial examination CSF abnormalities are not striking, and examinations must be repeated. Even then, as many as one-half of the cases will continue to show negative findings. Since the CSF pressure was elevated in many cases, the lumbar puncture must be performed cautiously. In fact, it is advisable to do the lumbar puncture only after beginning dexamethasone therapy.

Therapy The treatment of meningeal carcinomatosis involves the combination of radiation and chemotherapy. Radiation may be given to the entire neuraxis (brain and spinal cord). 

To facilitate medical therapy in some centers, a catheter has been inserted into the lateral ventricle and connected to a subcutaneous (Ommaya) reservoir. Through this system, chemical agents can then be injected into the ventricular fluid and the latter may be sampled from time to time. Initially, methotrexate, 7 mg/m? (diluted in lactated Ringer’s solution to a 10-ml volume), is instilled twice a week. Rescue from systemic toxicity can be achieved by using oral or intramuscular calcium leucovorin (5 mg), which is given 8 and 12 h after intrathecal therapy. Four weeks of methotrexate therapy (twice a week) is given with qualitative and quantitative analyses of ventricular or lumbar CSF once a week. The addition of cytosine arabinoside (Ara-C), 30 mg/m? twice a week, should be considered if residual cells are present at this time. Additional intrathecal agents that have not been fully tested include thiotepa and bleomycin. Progression of signs of radicular or spinal cord involvement may necessitate myelography and/or spinal irradiation. 

Methotrexate infusion is sometimes associated with reversible facial paresthesias and numbness and rarely with necrotizing lesions of the white matter of the brain and spinal cord, especially if it is administered concurrently with radiation therapy. Without treatment, 80 percent of patients will die as a result of meningeal disease within 3 months of diagnosis and within 6 months of the onset of their symptoms. Using the

They survive for a median time of 3 months, and 10 percent live for 1 year. This prolongation of life has been achieved most often in patients whose active systemic disease has been controlled. The long-term value of such intense therapy remains under critical study. 

###### Vertebral metastases and spinal cord nerve root compression 

The spinal epidural space may be invaded by secondary tumor without bone involvement; this presumably takes place by hematogenous spread to epidural tissues. Alternatively, it may result from vertebral involvement and extension to the epidural space; and lesions in the extravertebral tissues may reach the spinal epidural space by means of the intervertebral foramina. As the tumor enlarges in the spinal canal, it compresses the spinal cord and/or spinal roots. A combination of backache followed by radicular pain is a common clinical sequence in vertebral metastases. Bony metastases are usually located in the richly vascular vertebral body which attracts secondary tumor deposits more regularly than do the less vascular pedicles and spinous processes. Approximately 75 percent of the vertebral lesions occur in the thoracic spine, and the remainder are equally divided between cervical and lumbar areas. The sources of spinal metastases are shown in Table 6. 

Clinica! manifestations Pain is the initial symptom of spinal metastases. Then, after an interval of time as brief as a few days, but more often after some weeks, an asymmetric paralysis of the lower extremities, involving both motor and sensory functions, appears. The weakness becomes severe and bilateral and the function of bladder and bowel fails; there is incontinence of sphincters and, if the paralysis is acute, urinary retention and obstipation. Girdle sensations of tightness and pressure around the trunk and limbs are common. Radicular pain is localized to the level of the lesion. X-rays of the spine and bone scans reveal the lesion in 75 percent of cases, but contrast myelography is the definitive diagnostic procedure, if the spinal cord is involved.

Ovariectomy and pituitary ablation have also led to remissions in some cases. VASCULAR AND INFECTIOUS DISEASES OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM ASSOCIATED WITH SYSTEMIC TUMORS 

Laboratory confirmation of such lesions depends on tomography, bone scan, and serum acid phosphatase, calcium, and phosphorus determinations. Usually the CSF is normal, and CT scans rarely show a lesion in the substance of the brain. Multiple myeloma and prostatic cancer, which commonly produce these syndromes, virtually never extend by the hematogenous route to the substance of the brain. 

Therapy For spinal epidural tumors with cord compression, the two methods of treatment are surgery and radiation. In the opinion of most neurosurgeons and many neurologists, tumors that are unresponsive or poorly responsive to radiation, such as carcinomas, are best treated by surgical decompression, preferably as soon as possible after spinal cord symptoms develop. Others feel that radiation should be the primary therapy for all spinal metastases. Once complete 

###### Vascular disease in cancer patients 

Although in general cerebral vascular lesions occur with equal frequency in elderly cancer and noncancer patients, those who harbor a malignancy are predisposed to certain special types of strokes, regardless of age. In the cancer patient the strokes are mainly caused by a hemorrhagic tendency and septic or marantic emboli. Some of the thrombotic infarcts in cancer patients occur

###### VASCULAR AND INFECTIOUS DISEASES OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM 

with leukemia or lymphoma, and in one-quarter of patients with solid tumors. Several factors are responsible for this high infection rate: (1) granulocytopenia (500 neutrophils per cubic millimeter of blood), which occurs occasionally as a result of marrow invasion by tumor and more frequently in the wake of chemotherapy and radiation; (2) impaired cellular immunity, accompanying lymphoma and some carcinomas, which allows growth of intracellular organisms; and (3) depressed production of immunoglobulin, particularly in lymphatic leukemia and myeloma, which predisposes to specific bacterial infections and unusual viral infections of the CNS. The 10 percent rate of herpes zoster infection in patients with leukemia and lymphoma may be related to this abnormality. The CNS is frequently involved in these paraneoplastic infections because the bloodbrain and blood-CSF barriers isolate infective agents, once they reach the nervous system, from the action of certain natural immunologic mechanisms. Operative resection and ventricular shunting may also allow entry of unusual organisms into parameningeal structures. Continued use of antibiotics and/or corticosteroids predisposes to disseminated nosocomial fungal infection. Aspergillus, Nocardia, or Candida, localized to nonnervous tissue in normal individuals, may spread to the nervous system in the setting of leukemia or lymphoma. The appearance of systemic pulmonary, gastrointestinal, or bloodborne infection with fungi in these patients should alert the clinician to the increased risk of involvement of the meninges, the formation of brain abscess, or the occlusion of major intracranial blood vessels. 

tem occur in patients with systemic tumors, they usually present as meningitis. Brain abscesses with gram-negative organisms (Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas, Proteus) occasionally occur in many leukemic patients. Most patients with bacterial or fungal infections of the nervous system present with fever, headache, and altered mentation. Often the initial difficulties go unnoticed ina setting of immunosuppression or systemic infection without CNS involvement. Nuchal rigidity may not be present. Seizures, stupor, or coma focus attention on the neurologic problem and should suggest the presence of a brain abscess. CT scanning is usually performed to exclude intracerebral metastatic lesions but should permit differentiation of the larger infective abscesses. CT scan should be followed by lumbar puncture. The spinal fluid should be examined for cell count and samples studied in Gram stain, acidfast, and carefully filtered India ink preparations. Additional studies should include cultures for bacterial and fungal organisms, cytocentrifuge or millipore filter preparations for cancer cells and cryptococci, and glucose, protein, and cryptococcal antigen determinations. Viral cultures may be useful in some instances. 

The search for offending organisms can be aided by attention to the following simple principles: 

- 1 Patients with normal white blood counts are most likely to harbor infections with Listeria, Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, or Cryptococcus, Whereas leukopenic patients are more likely to have gram-negative infections. 

- 2 Patients with slowly evolving meningeal illnesses, especially in the setting of lymphoma and chronic corticosteroid or antibiotic therapy, must be suspected of having CNS fungal infections—even in the absence of CSF pleocytosis. Patients with Aspergillus, Candida, and Cryptococcus CNS infections are likely to have associated pulmonary lesions. 

Chernik and coworkers noted CNS infection in less than 1 percent of hospitalized cancer patients and in 3 percent of autopsy examinations of cancer patients. The vast majority of these infections were in patients with lymphomas, leukemia, and cancer of the head, neck, and spine. The majority of bacterial infections were due to Listeria (lymphoma patients), Staphylococcus aureus, and Klebsiella (head and neck cancer patients). Gram-negative organisms did not involve the CNS with regularity, despite their frequent occurrence as the cause of systemic infections in cancer patients. 

- 3 Patients with indwelling CSF catheters, craniotomy wounds, or parameningeal head and neck cancer are at high risk for Staph. aureus and gram-negative infections. 

In all situations of suspected bacterial meningitis, treatment should begin before definitive identification of the offending organism, provid- 

When bacterial infections of the nervous sys- 

###### 163 

164 NEUROLOGICAL ASPECTS OF SYSTEMIC TUMORS 

ing appropriate material has been obtained for culture and for visualizing organisms in Gram stain preparations. Presumptive Listeria meningitis should be treated with ampicillin and other gram-positive organisms with penicillin G; patients with gram-negative meningitis should receive carbenicillin and/or chloramphenicol. Intraventricular therapy (with aminoglycosides for gram-negative organisms) can be introduced through an Ommaya reservoir; this is especially important in patients with white blood cell counts of less than 1000 per cubic millimeter who have a poor prognosis at best. A similar reservoir may be used for the administration of amphotericin B to patients with cryptococcal and other forms of mycotic meningitis. 

Usually, severe or prolonged viral infections are most likely to develop in patients with Hodgkin’s disease, chronic lymphatic leukemia, and non-Hodgkin’s lymphosarcoma in adults and the acute leukemias of childhood. Encephalitis has followed systemic measles and herpes simplex infections in the latter population. 

Adult patients are susceptible to acute and subacute encephalitis from herpes simplex and to the more slowly progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) related to the oncogenic JC virus and papovaviruses. At least 200 cases of PML have been described. Most of them have occurred in conjunction with lymphoma or chronic lymphatic leukemia. These patients present with progressive difficulties in intellectual function, motor weakness, hemisensory loss, hemianopia, aphasia, and parietal lobe syndromes. The CSF is unremarkable; EEG abnormalities are uniformly present and tend to be focal; and CT scans show hypodense white matter lesions. Brain biopsy may lead to therapy with antiviral agents, such as cytosine arabinoside or acycloguanosine, which appear to be effective in some cases of acute herpes simplex encephalitis. 

###### UNCLASSIFIABLE PARANEOPLASTIC DISEASES 

In addition to these identifiable types of CNS infections, there are other remote effects of systemic tumors of a more obscure nature. In some lesions inflammatory reactions suggest an infec- 

tive origin. Included here are spinocerebellar degeneration, chronic polyneuritis and polymyositis. These diseases, like those described in the preceding sections, are associated with a number of different neoplasms in remote parts of the body. They usually occur in patients with carcinoma of the lung, particularly the oat-cell tumor (which is the most frequent), carcinoma of the ovary, and gastric carcinoma. Actually these paraneoplastic diseases are not esoteric rarities that are encountered only in neurologic institutes. Croft and Wilkinson at the London Hospital found one or more of them in 6.6 percent of cancer patients with solid tumors and 2.2 percent of patients with hematologic and lymphoid tumors, particularly multiple myeloma and Hodgkin’s disease. Table 8 is a listing of the several diseases of this category, along with some of their most prominent features. Limitations of space permit descriptions of only a few of these syndromes. More complete descriptions will be found in Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. 

###### Limbic encephalitis 

There have been reports of approximately 50 cases of a subacute encephalopathic process presenting as aconfusional state and followed by a defect in retentive memory. This combination of neurological findings is reminiscent of the clinical picture incurred by herpes simplex encephalitis, but, as a rule, the onset and clinical course have been more gradual and there has been no rise in neutralizing antibodies to this or other known viruses. The CSF is abnormal (increased protein and pleocytosis) in some cases. Descriptions of the neuropathology are to be found in the articles of Corsellis et al. and of Forno. Neuronal loss occurs mainly in the medial parts of the temporal lobes and is attended by perivascular and mild meningeal infiltrates of lymphocytes and mononuclear cells and microglial and astrocytic reactions. In two of our patients, dying after a long interval of time (years), only neuronal loss and gliosis remained. Similar, but less severe, changes were found in the cerebellum in approximately half of the cases. No effective treatment has been found. Other less definitive encephalitic diseases arising in conjunction with systemic tumors are

Subacute or chronic cerebellar degeneration, sometimes associated with intellectual impair- 

ment, is a rare effect of tumors. First described in connection with ovarian carcinoma, its linkage has since been established with carcinomas of lung, breast, uterus, gastrointestinal tract, and with lymphoma. The ataxia involves the legs and arms, deranges gait, and may alter speech. The CSF is usually normal except for slightly elevated levels of protein. A diffuse degeneration of 

###### 166 

###### NEUROLOGICAL ASPECTS OF SYSTEMIC TUMORS 

Purkinje cells and, to a lesser extent, of granular cells has been reported. Infiltrations of lymphocytes, present in some cases, are completely absent in others. 

A special syndrome of opsoclonus (“dancing eyes’’), myclonus of limbs, and cerebellar ataxia has also been observed in a number of our own cases, but its pathological basis is not settled. It resembles the myoclonic syndrome associated with some cases of neuroblastoma in children. There is no known therapy; corticosteroids may have helped a few patients. 

###### Subacute and chronic myelitis 

It is still a matter of controversy whether a form of pure degeneration of motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord is ever a remote effect of cancer. There is no doubt, however, as to the existence of a rare chronic poliomyelitis that progresses for several months or a year. In one of our cases of Hodgkin’s disease it caused a pure, atrophic, areflexic motor paralysis spreading from limb to limb, and in another patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus the same signs, plus a syringomyelic analgesia of shoulders and arms, occurred. The anterior horn cell degeneration was accompanied by microglial neuronophagia, gliosis, and lymphocytic infiltrates. A virus could not be seen under the electron microscope. Mancall and Rosales have described both an acute and subacute transverse necrotizing myelopathy with cancer. 

###### Polyneuropathies 

Denny-Brown in 1948 described a subacute to chronic sensory polyneuropathy with disabling ataxia in two patients with carcinoma of the lung. Similar cases have since been reported. More frequent, however, has been a subacute or chronic sensorimotor polyneuropathy with increased CSF protein in patients with lung and other tumors (ovary, stomach, breast, colon) and with multiple myeloma. Also, isolated cases of typical acute Landry-Guillain-Barré syndrome have been observed in tumor patients from time to time. These chronic polyneuropathies may precede or accompany the primary tumor, but their course does not parallel that of the tumor. The 

Neuropathies in cancer patients must not be confused with some of the neuropathies induced by antitumor therapy, e.g., vincristine or isoniazid. moved, and there may be a response of a polycular reaction. ###### Polymyopathies 

Approximately 15 percent of cases of polymyositis and dermatomyositis are related to occult tumors. About two-thirds of all cases of the Eaton-Lambert syndrome of inverse myasthenia have accompanied lung cancer (oat-cell carcinoma). See Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine for descriptions of these syndromes and their therapy. 

###### METABOLIC AND ENDOCRINE DISORDERS SOMETIMES ASSOCIATED WITH SYSTEMIC TUMORS 

One of the most intriguing and least understood aspects of systemic tumors is why tumors of certain types are capable of engendering an endocrine or metabolic disorder, often with striking functional derangement of the nervous system, which may simulate metastatic brain disease. The central issue is how a tumor cell in a nonendocrine organ can become an ectopic source of a hormone. Sherwood, who discusses this topic in the ninth edition of Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, advances two hypotheses: (1) the tumor cell, by dedifferentiating, acquires the capacity to synthesize the same proteins as the primitive embryonic cells of an endocrine organ, and (2) the tumor cells that produce the hormone are actually pluripotential cells derived from the neural crest. ###### CONCLUSION 

The paraneoplastic complications noted in this chapter give little indication of the complexity of the clinical states presented by patients with 

###### 168 NEUROLOGICAL ASPECTS OF SYSTEMIC TUMORS 

neoplastic diseases. In the listless, drowsy patient, disinterested in family members, confused as to whereabouts, wasted, and disheveled, there are at play varying degrees of organ malfunction from tumor invasion, cachexia and malnutrition, depression of mood, a complex of metabolic derangements of cerebral neurons, and the effects of drugs. The natural inclination of the physician is to shun the patient. The written histories tend to be brief and uninformative. There is a tendency to postulate metastatic disease of the brain, which more often than not is unconfirmed at autopsy. 

This is a rich and unexplored field of neurology and psychiatry. The main point of this chapter is to call attention to the complexity of these clinical states and to the many nonmetastatic processes to which the nervous system is subject. Finally, from the strictly neurological point of view, some of these paraneoplastic conditions are exposing for the first time neuropathologic processes worthy of systemic investigation in their own right.

#### HYPERCALCEMIC STATES PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF 

###### CHARLES Y. C. PAK 

Hypercalcemia is being recognized with increasing frequency, in part because of the inclusion of serum calcium determinations in automated biochemical screening programs. The incidence of hypercalcemia in the general population has been estimated at 0.6 percent and in hospitalized patients at 2 to 3 percent. Two additional factors have contributed to the recent increase in research interest in this problem. One is the improved understanding of the hormonal control of calcium homeostasis. The other is the recognition that hypercalcemia in malignancy may result from the action of humoral factors secreted by tumors. 

Different factors are involved in the etiology of hypercalcemia in individual cases, including hormonal, nutritional, genetic, immunologic, and neoplastic causes. This heterogeneity of etiologies makes it critical to develop reliable diagnostic criteria for identification of the different causes of hypercalcemia and for the design of treatment programs tailored to correct specific underlying derangements. DEFINITION OF HYPERCALCEMIA Ideally, hypercalcemia should be defined in terms of the circulating concentration of ionized calcium and not of total calcium. It is the ionized calcium concentration that regulates the secretion of various hormones involved in calcium homeostasis. Under normal circumstances, the concentration of ionized calcium in serum is maintained within more narrow limits than that of total calcium. The total calcium in serum is the sum of ionized and nonionized (bound) calcium. The nonionized calcium is composed of protein- 

bound and complexed fractions. The proteinbound fraction is nondiffusible, whereas complexed calcium is diffusible. Under normal circumstances, the total serum calcium is composed of approximately 47 percent ionized calcium, 40 percent protein-bound calcium, and 13 percent complexed calcium. The relationship between these different states of calcium in serum obeys the general solubility equation. When the circulating concentration of total calcium is increased, the proportion of bound and free calcium remains essentially unchanged because the amount of available binding sites in serum protein is large. Thus, ionized calcium concentration rises by the same fraction as the total calcium. However, when the protein concentration alone is increased, the fraction of bound calcium rises and the ionized calcium fraction falls. The extent of protein binding is approximately 0.8 to 0.16 mg calcium for each gram of albumin or globulin per deciliter, respectively. 

In usual hypercalcemic states the circulating concentration of ionized calcium can be estimated from the total calcium using the above assumptions. However, this estimation is invalid in three situations: (1) in the presence of abnormal circulating proteins with a high affinity for calcium, as in some cases of multiple myeloma; (2) during changes in systemic pH that influence protein binding and formation of soluble complexes; and (3) with an abnormal circulating concentration of soluble ligands, such as sulfate, citrate, and phosphate, which can influence complex formation. In addition, in primary hyperparathyroidism the ionized calcium fraction may be increased independently of changes in protein concentration or pH. It is hoped that direct 

###### PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

measurements of ionized calcium will be available routinely for clinical use in the near future. CALCIUM HOMEOSTATIC MECHANISMS 

Under normal circumstances the circulating concentration of ionized calcium is maintained within a narrow range by three types of homeostatic mechanisms: one physicochemical, another physiological, and the third hormonal. In the physicochemical regulation, circulating concentrations of calcium and phosphate are believed to reflect the solubility of bone mineral and are maintained at a constant product representing saturation of a specific component of calcium phosphate in bone. According to this formulation, any alteration in serum calcium concentration outside the normal range would be met by an opposing change that would return the calcium concentration to normal to maintain the solubility product. Unfortunately, the particular phase of calcium phosphate with which serum calcium and phosphate might exist in a steady state has not been identified. Thus, physicochemical regulation may have a limited role in calcium homeostasis, except possibly in the presence of soft-tissue calcification. The physiological regulation constitutes a nonhormonal process by which renal excretion and intestinal secretion of calcium respond to changes in the calcium concentration in serum. Although the intestinal secretion of calcium may not be altered substantially by an increase in circulating calcium concentration, the renal excretion of calcium increases rapidly in response to such an increase. The kidneys may remove as much as 800 mg calcium per day, while maintaining serum calcium concentration in the normal range. The renal excretion of excess calcium is probably mediated by an increased filtered load of calcium and by impaired renal tubular reabsorption of calcium as a direct consequence of hypercalcemia. Conversely, the kidneys avidly conserve calcium by limiting calcium excretion when the circulating concentration of calcium is reduced. The renal response to changes in serum calcium concentration is also under hormonal control, which further refines it. Hormonal regulation exerts the most important influence on calcium homeostasis. The basis 

for this regulation is the influence of the serum concentration of calcium (ionized) on the secretion of certain hormones that affect bone and calcium metabolism. Such ‘‘calcium-regulatory”’ hormones include parathyroid hormone (PTH), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, calcitonin, and possibly 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The classic physiologic response to PTH and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is augmentation of serum calcium concentration, whereas the net effect of the action of calcitonin and 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is the reduction in circulating calcium concentration. The critical feature of calcium homeostasis is the suppression of the secretion or synthesis of PTH and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and the stimulation of the secretion or production of calcitonin and 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in hypercalcemia; the opposite situation occurs in hypocalcemia. Because of these appropriate changes in the secretion of calcium-regulatory hormones, marked fluctuations in the circulating concentration of calcium are avoided under ordinary physiologic conditions. 

Recent studies have shown that the circulating concentrations of calcium and immunoreactive PTH have an inverse, logarithmic rather than an inverse, linear relationship. This relationship indicates that wide fluctuations of PTH secretion occur Over narrow limits of calcium concentration near the normal range and that a basal rate of PTH secretion cannot be suppressed completely by hypercalcemia. Physiologic actions of calciumregulatory hormones 

To clarify the role of these hormones in calcium homeostasis, the physiologic actions of the calcium-regulatory hormones will be briefly reviewed: Parathyroid hormone promotes bone resorption, by stimulating skeletal adenyl cyclase and by activating osteoclasts. In addition, PTH may increase the osteoclast population by enhancing the transformation from precursor cells and decrease osteoblast activity by inhibiting proliferation of osteoblast precursors. PTH does not augment intestinal calcium absorption directly but does so indirectly by stimulating the synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in the kidney; PTH also enhances the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium. 

###### CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA 173 

In bone, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D potentiates the action of PTH on osteoclastic bone resorption but probably does not affect osteoclast number. Moreover, it has been suggested that this vitamin D metabolite stimulates osteocytic resorption and causes rapid skeletal mobilization of calcium. In the intestinal tract, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D probably provides the most potent stimulus to the absorption of calcium. Last, 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D augments the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium. However, this renal action of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is less effective than that of PTH and probably plays a minor role in calcium homeostasis. 

Calcitonin opposes the action of PTH by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption. Its effect on the intestinal absorption of calcium is uncertain, and its action on the renal handling of calcium varies with the species of origin of calcitonin and with the species tested. In humans, this hormone typically enhances renal excretion of calcium. Despite these actions, calcitonin probably plays a minor role in calcium homeostasis under normal physiologic circumstances, especially in adults. 

Recent preliminary evidence suggests that 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D may be the metabolite responsible for the stimulation of bone matrix synthesis and mineralization by osteoblasts. This metabolite is also capable of augmenting intestinal calcium absorption, although it is less effective than 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in this regard. It is not known whether 24,25dihydroxyvitamin D exerts any action on renal calcium transport. As with calcitonin, an important physiologic role of 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D on calcium homeostasis has not been established. Thus, the hormonal regulation of calcium homeostasis involves appropriate responses in three target organs: intestine, kidney, and bone. This concept may be illustrated by considering the sequelae of ingestion of a high-calcium diet. The ensuing increased absorption of calcium, if unabated, could cause hypercalcemia. However, hypercalcemia is normally averted by compensatory changes that occur as the result of reduced secretion of PTH and impaired PTH-dependent synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. In bone, less calcium is mobilized into the circulation because of reduced osteoclastic and osteocytic 

resorption. In the intestine, a lower fraction of calcium is absorbed because of a decreased availability of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. In the kidneys, more calcium is excreted following an oral calcium load, since the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium is reduced by the decreased availability of PTH (and to a lesser extent by the decreased amount of circulating 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D). PATHOGENESIS OF HYPERCALCEMIA 

Hypercalcemia results when homeostatic control of calcium metabolism is lost or impaired. For hypercalcemia to develop, there first must be a sufficient input of calcium into the extracellular fluid, as from a continued high rate of bone resorption or intestinal calcium absorption. Second, the extent of the input of calcium must exceed the capacity of the three organ systems to clear calcium from the circulation by means of formation and mineralization of bone, intestinal secretion, and renal excretion. An excessive calcium input into the circulation, if great enough, may itself cause hypercalcemia even when the calcium removal processes are adequate. On the other hand, it is uncommon for defects in the removal process alone to elicit hypercalcemia, unless there is a coexisting increase in the input of calcium into the circulation. 

###### CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA 

Hypercalcemia can be divided into two broad categories: hypercalcemia resulting from an enhanced calcium input into the circulation and hypercalcemia resulting from a reduced removal of calcium from the circulation (Table 1). The first category may be subdivided into conditions that stimulate bone resorption and conditions that enhance intestinal calcium absorption. The second category is composed of conditions that cause reduced renal excretion of calcium and those associated with impaired bone formation and mineralization. Certain disorders may cause hypercalcemia by several means; they are therefore included in several groups. For some conditions, the implicated defect alone may be insufficient to cause hypercalcemia but may exaggerate or elicit it in the setting of another derangement.
