A loss of calcium homeostatic control and hypercalcemia can also result from an abnormal production of humoral substances not involved in the physiologic regulation of calcium homeostasis. For example, hypercalcemia due to accelerated bone resorption may result not only from excessive synthesis of PTH or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D but also from abnormal production of prostaglandin or osteoclast-activating factor. Each condition associated with hypercalcemia will be discussed separately with respect to pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and specific therapy. Primary hyperparathyroidism and neoplasm constitute the most frequent causes for hypercalcemia, with an estimated incidence of 50 and 25 percent, respectively. 

###### Primary hyperparathyroidism 

Pathogenesis Primary hyperparathyroidism results from an excessive secretion of PTH by abnormal parathyroid tissue, usually adenoma 

but occasionally hyperplasia and rarely carcinoma. The critical determinant for the development of hypercalcemia is the secretion of PTH in amounts that are either absolutely increased or inappropriately high for the level of circulating calcium. This situation could occur if the PTH secretion were not suppressible by an increased serum concentration of calcium or when there is a normal suppressibility of PTH secretion by each cell, if the number of PTH-secreting cells is markedly enhanced. In the latter circumstance, the normal basal, nonsuppressible component of PTH secretion may be increased sufficiently to cause hypercalcemia. Contrary to the traditional view, PTH secretion in primary hyperparathyroidism is not completely free from control by the circulating concentration of calcium, even in patients with parathyroid adenoma. However, in comparison with normal subjects, the degree of suppressibility of PTH secretion that results from an increased serum concentration of calcium is not as marked, particularly in patients with parathyroid adenoma and carcinoma. This relative nonsuppressibility of PTH secretion in intact subjects can also be demonstrated with parathyroid cell preparations in vitro. The serum concentration of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is increased in primary hyperparathyroidism, probably as a consequence of the stimulation of the renal synthesis of this metabolite by PTH. The hypercalcemia of hyperparathyroidism is the consequence of enhanced action of PTH and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D on calcium transport in the three critical organ systems. In bone, osteoclastic bone resorption is stimulated by both hormones. In the kidneys, the tubular reabsorption of calcium is increased by the action of both hormones, particularly PTH. This action may be opposed by the suppressive effect of hypercalcemia on renal calcium reabsorption. The enhanced intestinal calcium absorption has been attributed to the action of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and not of PTH. However, there may be a component of increased intestinal calcium absorption not accounted for by increased 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D. Although serum 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D returns to the normal range following parathyroidectomy, the intestinal absorption of calcium remains high in some pa- 

###### CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA L75 

tients with primary hyperparathyroidism following surgery. Hypercalciuria is common. Even though PTH augments the renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, this action is usually insufficient to overcome the increased renal filtered load of calcium and the suppressive effect of hypercalcemia on calcium reabsorption. Serum phosphorus is usually low but may be within the normal range. Hypophosphatemia is the result of the phosphaturic response to PTH. Renal tubular acidosis may develop occasionally, as the result of the stimulation of the renal excretion of bicarbonate by PTH and hypophosphatemia, although this action may be opposed by hypercalcemia. 

Diagnosis Theoretically, the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism may be made most reliably and directly by the radioimmunoassay of serum PTH. The value of the radioimmunoassay depends on which portion of the PTH molecule is recognized by the antibody used in the assay system and on whether the assay is sensitive enough to detect the basal (nonsuppressible) PTH secretion in normal subjects. Assays that utilize antiserum directed against the carboxyterminal portion of the PTH molecule are generally more useful than assays that utilize antiserum directed at the amino-terminal portion of the molecule. This finding probably reflects the longer biological half-life of the PTH fragments containing the carboxy terminus. The presence of an increased serum PTH (above the absolute upper limit of normal) in the face of a high serum calcium suggests the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. Establishing the diagnosis is more difficult in patients with hypercalcemia when the serum immunoassayable PTH is detectable but is not increased above the absolute normal range. Such a situation can represent an inappropriately high PTH secretion if the value in the control subjects is lower or undetectable at a correspondingly high serum calcium concentration. On the other hand, a detectable but normal (relative to the corresponding value in control subjects) serum PTH may indicate a normally occurring, nonsuppressible component of PTH secretion. Consequently, additional discriminating tests may be required to establish the diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism. 

One such assessment involves the measurement of urinary cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP). This test is based on the fact that PTH is a potent stimulus for renal adenyl cyclase and that the cyclic AMP so formed is rapidly excreted in the urine, probably because of the permeability characteristics of the tubular membrane near the site of nucleotide synthesis. No other hormone system shares these features. The measurement of urinary cyclic AMP has certain advantages over the assay of serum immunoassayable PTH as a test of parathyroid function, since it reflects the biological activity of PTH and it represents an “integrated’’ measure of PTH level over the period of urine collection rather than a single moment of time. 

The total urinary cyclic AMP is the sum of a filtered component from plasma and a nephrogenous component produced within the kidney. Under normal circumstances, approximately 40 percent of total cyclic AMP consists of the nephrogenous fraction, most of which is produced under the influence of PTH. In conditions of PTH excess, the amount of filtered cyclic AMP is not altered, which indicates that any nucleotide produced outside the kidney under the influence of PTH does not contribute significantly to the urinary cyclic AMP. However, the PTH-dependent nephrogenous fraction is significantly increased in the hyperparathyroid state. Thus, assessment of nephrogenous cyclic AMP is superior to the total cyclic AMP in urine in providing a specific measure of parathyroid function, unaffected by other hormonal influences. However, because of the relative constancy of the filtered fraction when renal function is normal, measurement of total urinary cyclic AMP, expressed in relation to the glomerular filtration rate, yields qualitatively similar data to the nephrogenous cyclic AMP. 

When significant renal disease is present, the correction of urinary cyclic AMP for the glomerular filtration produces a more reliable measure of parathyroid status than the total excretion rate or the excretion rate relative to urinary creatinine. The urinary cyclic AMP may also show an inverse relationship with the serum calcium concentration under normal circumstances, as has been demonstrated for serum PTH. Consequently the diagnostic utility of the measurement 

###### 176 

###### PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

In some patients peptic ulcer disease may result from the stimulation of the secretion of gastrin and of hydrochloric acid by hypercalcemia. However, gastric acid secretion has been found to be normal in the vast majority of patients with primary hyperparathyroidism. Pancreatitis sometimes complicates the course of primary hyperparathyroidism, although it is uncommon in other causes of hypercalcemia. The reasons for peptic ulcer and pancreatitis in primary hyperparathyroidism remain to be elucidated. 

in primary hyperparathyroidism may be improved by comparing individual values for urinary cyclic AMP with the corresponding interpolated value for the control group at the same level of serum calcium. 

Measurement of nephrogenous cyclic AMP provides the most reliable and specific diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism, abnormal in about 97 percent of patients. Measurement of total urinary cyclic AMP expressed per 100 ml glomerular filtration is almost as reliable (increased in 94 percent of patients). The excretion of total urinary cyclic AMP corrected for urinary creatinine is elevated in 70 percent of patients with primary hyperparathyroidism whereas the total excretion rate of urinary cyclic AMP is increased in only 31 percent of patients. 

There is an apparent increase in hypertension. The cause of hypertension in primary hyperparathyroidism is not known; recent evidence suggests a pathogenetic role for the renin-angiotensin system. Some patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and hypertension may have an increased plasma renin activity. Following parathyroidectomy, blood pressure declines commensurate with the restoration of normal plasma renin activity. Although the triad of nephrolithiasis, bone disease, and peptic ulcer disease continues to comprise the principal symptomatology, there has been a major change in the clinical presentation of primary hyperparathyroidism during the past 10 to 15 years. This changing trend, resulting probably from an earlier detection through a routine analysis of serum calcium and from an availability of improved diagnostic techniques, consists of (1) increased frequency of diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism, (2) recognition of milder forms of bone disease, and (3) a larger fraction of patients who present with hypertension or without symptoms. 

Clinical presentation The major clinical presentations of primary hyperparathyroidism continue to be nephrolithiasis, bone disease, and peptic ulcer disease. Hypercalciuria is an important though not the sole factor concerned with renal stone disease. Hypercalciuria probably contributes to stone formation by rendering the urinary environment supersaturated with respect to brushite (CaHPO,-:2H.O) and calcium oxalate. (Many patients with primary hyperparathyroidism do not form stones despite hypercalciuria and the supersaturated state of the urine.) In patients who do form stones, there may be an increased renal excretion of certain noncrystalline substances that facilitate stone formation by enhancing spontaneous nucleation of calcium phosphate and calcium oxalate. This “promoter” of nucleation has not been characterized. There may be a deficiency of urinary inhibitors as well. A low pyrophosphate and citrate excretion has been reported in stone-forming patients with primary hyperparathyroidism. The severity or the type of bone disease probably depends to some extent on the degree of PTH secretion. Brown tumor, osteitis fibrosa cystica, or extensive subperiosteal resorption is usually associated with a high circulating concentration of PTH. Bone disease resembling osteoporosis may result from a mild to moderate stimulation of PTH secretion for a prolonged period, especially in white postmenopausal women. 

Treatment The increased frequency of diagnosis of asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism presents a new therapeutic challenge. Although the need for surgical parathyroidectomy in symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism is well recognized, the role of surgery in the asymptomatic form has not been established. A recent study indicates that a search for certain physiological derangements indicative of PTH excess may help to identify asymptomatic patients who might benefit from parathyroid surgery. These derangements may include hypercalciuria, negative calcium balance 

1/77 

###### CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA 

(e.g., a high fasting urinary calcium, urinary calcium exceeding absorbed calcium, and a low bone density), and reduced endogenous creatinine clearance of less than 65 ml/min. The above deleterious effects of PTH excess form the basis for the further separation of the asymptomatic group, since they are present in some but not all patients with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (Fig. 1). Parathyroidectomy is probably indicated in the subgroup with physiological derangements because these derangements may herald the eventual development of symptoms, are also present in the symptomatic group, and may be corrected largely by successful parathyroid surgery. The need for parathyroid exploration in the asymptomatic patients without physiological derangements is not established. The delineation of the natural history and clinical course of this form of primary hyperparathyroidism, especially whether the asymptomatic condition progresses to the development of physiological derangements or symptoms, is necessary before the indications for parathyroidectomy can be established. The medical management of primary hyperparathyroidism is generally disappointing. Estrogens may be effective in the control of hypercalcemia in mild to moderate cases of primary hyperparathyroidism, by inhibiting PTH-dependent bone resorption. Orthophosphate may reduce serum calcium concentration and retard stone formation; however, the complication of soft-tissue calcification limits its usefulness. Adrenal corticosteroids and inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis are ineffective in most patients. 

Association with other conditions Primary hyperparathyroidism may be associated with Paget’s disease of bone, carcinomatosis, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, medullary sponge kidney, sarcoidosis, thyrotoxicosis, and ankylosing spondylitis. No clear-cut etiologic relationship has been disclosed for these associations. Primary hyperparathyroidism may also occur as a part of multiple endocrine neoplasia, probably as the result of a genetically determined defect. No clear-cut etiologic relationship between parathyroid disease and other components of the syndrome has been established.

Classification of primary hyperparathyroidism. 

Primary hyperparathyroidism may also coexist with pheochromocytoma or acromegaly in the absence of apparent genetic transmission. The surgical correction of pheochromocytoma typically does not ameliorate the hyperparathyroid state. However, a reduction in the severity of hypercalcemia and hyperparathyroidism sometimes follows successful treatment of acromegaly. This finding suggests that acromegaly and hyperparathyroidism may be pathogenetically related. Hypercalcemia may also occur in pheochromocytoma and acromegaly in the absence of parathyroid stimulation; the exact mechanism has not been elucidated. 

Hypercalcemia of secondary hyperparathyroidism Hypercalcemia may develop after a prolonged stimulation of parathyroid glands by either of two mechanisms. Rarely, adenomatous transformation of hyperplastic parathyroid tissue may occur in_ hyperparathyroidism secondary to renal _hypercalciuria or intestinal malabsorption of calcium. Hypercalcemia is the result of the relative autonomy of PTH secretion. More commonly, hypercalcemia in chronic renal failure occurs because the basal (nonsuppressible) secretion of PTH is high due to the large glandular mass despite a normal suppressibility. The term sometimes used to describe this condition, tertiary hyperparathyroidism, is probably a misnomer, since it implies that autonomy of PTH secretion is present. Subtotal parathyroidectomy or a total parathyroidectomy with parathyroid autotransplantation in the forearm may be required. 

Successful renal transplantation may elicit or aggravate hypercalcemia in patients with renal osteodystrophy. The production of 1,25-dihy- 
###### PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

droxyvitamin D by the functioning transplanted kidney could best explain this development. The ensuing rise in the serum concentration of 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D from low or undetectable levels, superimposed upon a high circulating concentration of PTH from an incomplete resolution of parathyroid hyperplasia, probably contributes to hypercalcemia by actions on the three target organs previously described. Parathyroidectomy may sometimes be required to prevent destruction of the transplanted kidney. Oncogenic hypercalcemia Hypercalcemia is a common complication of malignancy, with an overall incidence of 10 to 20 percent. Virtually all forms of neoplasms are capable of causing hypercalcemia. However, hypercalcemia is relatively uncommon in myeloproliferative or lymphoproliferative disorders, with the exception of multiple myeloma, and is rare in primary bone cancers. The most common neoplasm associated with hypercalcemia in men is carcinoma of the lung, and the most common in women is breast carcinoma. The term oncogenic hypercalcemia is appropriate to describe the hypercalcemia of malignancy. Oncogenic hypercalcemia traditionally has been divided into two groups on the basis of whether it is associated with a malignant invasion of the skeleton. In most patients (80 to 85 percent), skeletal metastases can be demonstrated. Since malignant lesions are often osteolytic, the hypercalcemia has been explained on the basis of localized bone destruction by neoplasm. In some hypercalcemic patients (15 to 20 percent), however, no evidence for tumor can be found in bone. Hypercalcemia in this group is believed to result from the elaboration from the extraskeletal neoplasm of humoral substances that cause osteoclastic resorption. The concept of an ectopic production of “hypercalcemic humoral factors” has therefore been introduced. The above categorization of oncogenic hypercalcemia is arbitrary for the following reasons: (1) The methods of detection of bone metastases in living subjects are not sufficiently sensitive to detect all instances of skeletal invasion. (2) The presence of osteolytic metastasis or neoplasm in bone does not exclude the production by neo- 

plasm of hypercalcemic humoral factors. (3) The mechanism for local bone destruction by the metastases may partly involve the stimulation of osteoclastic resorption by humoral factors elaborated by neoplasm located in bone. It is recognized, however, that neoplasm may directly cause bone destruction independently of humoral factors. In this discussion, oncogenic hypercalcemia will be categorized according to the different forms of hypercalecmic factors elaborated. Such factors may be either humoral (extraskeletal) or local (skeletal) in origin. Evidence for a direct osteolysis by malignancy will then be presented. The relative frequency of the various causes of oncogenic hypercalcemia is not known. Production of PTH-like substance by neoplasm There is substantial evidence for the production of PTH-like substance by certain neoplasms of nonparathyroid origin and for the development of hypercalcemia from the action of such an agent. This substance will simply be referred to as PTH. 

The presence of PTH in certain malignant tumors has been demonstrated by immunofluorescent and immunoautoradiographic techniques, as well as by radioimmunoassay of tumor extracts. The content of the hormone in the neoplasm is generally less than 2 wg/g, whereas that in parathyroid adenoma is in the range of 20 to 280 ug/g. However, because of tumor mass the consequences of the abnormal production can nevertheless be severe. 

It has been established that such neoplastic tissues synthesize PTH, rather than serve simply as a Storage depot. Synthesis of the hormone has been shown by culture of tumor fragments in vitro. Moreover, selective catheterization studies have revealed a higher concentration of the hormone in the venous effluent than in the arterial blood supplying the neoplasm. The PTH produced by malignancy shares certain biological activities with the native hormone. The tumor extract can stimulate bone resorption in vitro and increase serum concentration of calcium in the in vivo assay system. Patients with hypercalcemia due to this mechanism may present with a high renal phosphate clearance, hypophosphatemia, and enhanced urinary cyclic 

CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA 179 

AMP, thus providing indirect evidence that the PTH of neoplastic origin can also cause phosphaturia and stimulation of renal adenyl cyclase. It is curious that the intestinal calcium absorption is apparently not increased, unlike the situation in primary hyperparathyroidism, which suggests that the PTH of neoplastic origin may be less effective than the native hormone in the stimulation of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis. Finally, successful treatment of the neoplasm, either by surgical or by medical means, has been found to restore normal serum calcium concentration and to reverse other biochemical abnormalities enumerated above. The fact that biochemical restoration may follow surgical resection of an extraskeletal neoplasm provides the best evidence that the disorder is the consequence of ectopically produced PTH. However, PTH can also be produced by neoplasm that has invaded bone. 

The chemical nature of PTH elaborated by nonparathyroid neoplasm is not known. On the basis of available data, it is not possible to determine whether the substance of neoplastic origin is different from the native hormone or whether it undergoes different metabolic transformation or degradation. It is apparent, however, that the serum from patients with neoplasm contains different immunoreactive components (to PTH antiserum) than does serum from patients with primary hyperparathyroidism. This phenomenon probably accounts for the varying results obtained with different assay systems for PTH in serum. The demonstration of either a relatively high or a relatively low immunoassayable PTH in the circulation of patients with neoplasm, as compared with those with primary hyperparathyroidism, probably reflects different antigenic recognition of various antiserums used in the assays. For any particular PTH assay system employed, its value in the diagnosis of neoplastic production of PTH requires comparison with the control group and with primary hyperparathyroidism at the same level of circulating calcium concentration. The production of PTH is more commonly encountered in “‘solid’’ tumors than in malignancies of the hematopoietic system. Malignancies of the kidney and the lung are most commonly involved. Though initially considered rare, 

breast carcinoma has also been implicated. Other associated solid neoplasms include carcinomas of the pancreas, colon, parotid gland, gallbladder, esophagus, bladder, and penis; hepatoma and hepatoblastoma; and melanoma and reticulum cell sarcoma. Recently, the production of PTH has been described in soft tumors, including acute lymphocytic leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, undifferentiated lymphoma, acute myeloblastic leukemia, and acute myelofibrosis. Diagnostically, the presentation of neoplastic hypercalcemia due to PTH secretion differs from that of primary hyperparathyroidism in the following general respects: (1) the onset of hypercalcemia is more sudden and more rapidly progressive; (2) the degree of hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria is more marked, often exceeding 14 mg/dl and 600 mg per day, respectively; (3) symptoms of peptic ulceration, skeletal fractures, and renal stones are usually absent; and (4) serum alkaline phosphatase is more frequently elevated. 

Antitumor therapy is the only specific treatment. 

Neoplastic production of prostaglandin The potentially important role of prostaglandin in the pathogenesis of oncogenic hypercalcemia was first suggested by studies in vitro and in experimental animals. Prostaglandins of the E series (PGE) stimulate skeletal adenyl cyclase and augment bone resorption in tissue culture, and certain malignancies of experimental animals that cause hypercalcemia (mouse fibrosarcoma and rabbit carcinoma) also produce PGE,,. Inhibition of PGE, synthesis in animals so affected by indomethacin restores normal serum calcium, commensurate with a reduction in serum PGE,. There is substantive evidence that prostaglandin may exert a similar role in the development of hypercalcemia in certain human neoplasms. Such malignancies contain PGE and synthesize it in tissue culture. Elevated circulating concentrations of PGE and high renal excretion of the PGE metabolite PGE-M have also been demonstrated. Treatment of such patients with indomethacin or aspirin may ameliorate the hypercalcemia commensurate with the decline in the circulating concentration of PGE and urinary 

180 PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

PGE-M. In one study PGE concentration was elevated in the venous effluent of the tumor. The above studies, however, do not prove that the ectopically produced prostaglandin is responsible for the hypercalcemia. Even if sufficient amounts of PGE were produced by an extraskeletal neoplasm, the rise in the circulating concentration of PGE may be limited because of the high rate of its clearance and metabolism, particularly by the lung. Even when an elevation in the circulating concentration of PGE occurs, the amount may be insufficient to influence bone resorption significantly and to cause hypercalcemia. It is theoretically possible that hypercalcemia results from the action of a metabolite of PGE, which attains a higher concentration in circulation and shares similar bone resorptive capacity with PGE. However, such a metabolite has not been found. Nevertheless, the response to treatment with indomethacin or aspirin in the absence of a malignant invasion of bone suggests a probable etiologic role of ectopically produced PGE. 

The evidence for the PGE-mediated hypercalcemia as the consequence of neoplastic invasion of bone is more secure. An increased PGE production has been demonstrated in skeletal metastases. A role for local PGE-mediated osteoclastic resorption obviates the problem of an inadequate concentration of the prostaglandin in the circulation that is inherent in the concept of ectopic PGE production. The neoplastic tissue in bone may also stimulate PGE production indirectly by eliciting local proliferation of macrophages and monocytes. The monocytes so formed have been shown to produce PGE. It is curious that treatment with indomethacin or aspirin ameliorates hypercalcemia less dramatically in the presence of bony metastasis than in its absence. The finding suggests that other factors are responsible for hypercalcemia when metastasis to bone has occurred or that prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors are less effective in bone. 

Associated neoplasms include carcinomas of the kidney, lung, breast, esophagus, parotid gland, ovary, penis, and tonsil; adenocarcinoma of the pancreas; hepatoma; and melanoma. The presentation of hypercalcemia associated with a neoplastic production of PGE resembles that of neoplastic synthesis of PTH with the fol- 

lowing exceptions: (1) serum immunoreactive PTH and urinary cyclic AMP are normal or low, which suggests that endogenous PTH secretion is suppressed by the hypercalcemia; (2) hypercalcemia secondary to PGE production is invariably caused by solid neoplasms; and (3) hypercalcemia may be responsive to treatment with indomethacin or aspirin. Although serum phosphorus concentration is usually: normal because of parathyroid suppression and increased bone resorption, hypophosphatemia has sometimes been found, which suggests that other influences may contribute to the excessive renal clearance of phosphate. 

Not all patients with neoplastic production of PGE have amelioration of hypercalcemia after treatment with indomethacin or aspirin therapy despite an inhibition of PGE synthesis. This suggests that PGE may not play an etiologic role in a particular situation or the presence of other hypercalcemic humoral factors. Since there is an overlap in the types of neoplasms associated with the production of PTH and PGE, certain tumors may elaborate both humoral factors. 

Neoplastic production of osteoclast-activating factor (OAF) The concept that OAF may be involved in the pathogenesis of hypercalcemia of malignancy emanated from studies of localized bone resorption in periodontal disease. Lymphocytes, upon stimulation by antigens to which the donor has developed cellular immunity or by nonspecific mitogens (solubilized dental plaque or phytohemagglutinin), secrete a soluble substance that stimulates bone resorption in organ culture. The substance was called osteoclast-activating factor because the treated bone showed numerous active osteoclasts. OAF can be distinguished from PTH, PGE, and 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D, and its action is inhibited by cortisol. 

Although its molecular structure has not been elucidated, the biological activity is probably due to a peptide component, since a loss of activity ensues upon treatment with trypsin or pronase. It occurs in two forms, “big OAF”’ (12,500 to 25,000 daltons) and “‘small OAF” (1330 to 3500 daltons). Both forms produce bone resorbing activity. 

The major drawback to the study of OAF in oncogenic hypercalcemia has been inadequate

The work with OAF in human malignancy has, therefore, required the use of a bioassay based on bone resorptive capacity. Cultures of malignant cell lines from multiple myeloma, Burkitt’s lymphoma, malignant lymphoma, and lymphosarcoma cell leukemia elaborate OAF. The stimulation of bone resorption by OAF derived from these cell lines can be inhibited by cortisol in vitro. The fact that mononuclear cell lines from peripheral blood synthesize OAF indicates that OAF may be produced extraskeletally. Moreover, OAF may be produced by neoplasm indirectly by means of immunologic or inflammatory stimulation of monocytes and macrophages. The above findings suggest, but do not prove, an important role of OAF in the pathogenesis of hypercalcemia of malignancy. Documentation of such a role must await the demonstration of OAF in circulation, in venous effluent of tumor, and in the extract of noncultured tumor, as well as demonstration that successful treatment of the hypercalcemia with antitumor therapy coincides with a decline in OAF production. OAF-mediated hypercalcemia has been described only in neoplasms of lymphoid origin. As in the malignant production of PGE, serum PTH and urinary cyclic AMP are normal or low. 

However, unlike the situation in neoplastic production of PTH or PGE, a favorable response to steroids (e.g., 30 to 60 mg prednisone per day) may be obtained. Specific antitumor therapy is expected to be effective in the control of hypercalcemia as well. Table 2 compares pertinent features in OAF production, primary hyperparathyroidism, and neoplastic production of PTH or PGE. 

Neoplastic production of other hypercalcemic humoral factors Hypercalcemia has been described in the watery diarrheal syndrome associated with an excessive secretion of vasoactive intestinal peptide. It has been suggested that vasoactive intestinal peptide may induce hypercalcemia by way of stimulation of bone resorption; this contention lacks experimental verification. 

Besides the synthesis of PTH and PGE as described, breast cancer was thought to produce vitamin D-like sterols that stimulate bone resorption. However, equivalent circulating concentrations of such sterols are found in normal women and patients with breast cancer and in hypercalcemic patients and normocalcemic patients with breast cancer. Thus, such sterols are unlikely to play an important role in the pathogenesis of hypercalcemia in breast cancer. Nevertheless, the possibility that vitamin D may be involved in oncogenic hypercalcemia was suggested by a 

182 PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

recent preliminary study reporting the production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D by a histiocytic lymphoma. 

Recently, it has been speculated that certain patients with oncogenic hypercalcemia may elaborate a “‘non-PTH renotropic factor” that stimulates phosphaturia and renal adenyl cyclase but does not enhance synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Serum immunoreactive PTH in such patients is detectable but lower than in primary hyperparathyroidism. This situation resembles that found in ectopic PTH production in which the “hormone” produced may not be immunologically as reactive as the native hormone by the particular assay system used. As already discussed, synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D may be impaired in neoplastic production of PTH. Thus, non-PTH renotropic factor need not be considered as a separate hypercalcemic humoral factor until further evidence is provided. 

Direct osteolysis In oncogenic hypercalcemia associated with a neoplastic production of PTH, PGE, or OAF, the hypercalcemia has been attributed to the increased bone resorption induced by osteoclasts. However, it is apparent that in some situations of malignant invasion of bone there may be excessive bone destruction without osteoclastic stimulation. Tumor-mediated bone resorption independent of participation of osteoclasts could ensue through one or two mechanisms: (1) Malignant tissue in bone may stimulate local concentration of monocytes and macrophages, which can cause a direct resorption of bone. Monocytes are known to be capable of stimulating the release of bone mineral and matrix from “‘killed”’ bones devoid of live cellular components. (2) Neoplastic tissue may elaborate a substance that resorbs bone direcily without osteoclastic participation. Preliminary data support this view. The supernatant fluid from a cultured cell line of breast cancer can resorb dead bone in organ culture. 

Direct osteolysis should be suspected in the presence of osteolytic metastases, when the production of PTH, PGE, or OAF can be excluded. The hypercalcemia of osteolytic metastases is more responsive to treatment with adrenal corticosteroids (with a reported 30 percent responsiveness) than is the oncogenic hypercalcemia of 

PTH or PGE production without obvious malignant invasion of bone. This finding may reflect the inhibitory effect of steroids on the local inflammation and on the consequent induction of direct osteolysis by inflammatory cells. Hypercalcemia of thyrotoxicosis 

Hypercalcemia is a frequent complication of thyrotoxicosis, occurring in approximately a fifth of thyrotoxic patients. Of those with hypercalcemia, 15 percent may have coexisting primary hyperparathyroidism. The association of thyrotoxicosis and primary hyperparathyroidism is believed to be coincidental. There is no substantive evidence that the thyrotoxic state can induce hyperparathyroidism (or vice versa). It may be argued that certain influences in thyrotoxicosis could cause parathyroid stimulation. The intestinal calcium absorption is typically low, and urinary calcium is high. These changes could stimulate parathyroid hormone secretion. Moreover, B- adrenergic receptor responses may be enhanced in hyperthyroidism, and increased adrenergic activity could stimulate PTH secretion, as is suggested by enhancement of PTH secretion following epinephrine infusion. However, there is an increased turnover of bone, with an accelerated mobilization of calcium into the circulation. This effect probably tends to overcome the potentially stimulatory influences on PTH secretion mentioned above. As a result, parathyroid function is normal or suppressed in thyrotoxicosis in the absence of a coexisting primary hyperparathyroidism. The cause for the hypercalcemia of thyrotoxicosis in the absence of primary hyperparathyroidism is also obscure. It must ultimately be the result of increased skeletal mobilization of calcium, since opposing influences prevail in other critical organ systems, i.e., decreased calcium absorption and high renal calcium excretion. It has been suggested that thyroid hormone may increase the sensitivity of bone to the action of PTH or vitamin D. However, the circulating levels of PTH and 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D are low in this condition. An absolute or relative deficiency of calcitonin has also been postulated. This idea is supported by the facts that calcitonin inhibits thyroid hor- 

###### CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA 183 

The thyrotoxic state may be characterized by an increased skeletal sensitivity to adrenergic stimuli. Bone resorption may then be increased by the ensuing rise in the skeletal content of cyclic AMP. This hypothesis is supported by the correction of hypercalemia of thyrotoxicosis following propranolol treatment. However, it has not been proved that catecholamines and PTH share the same receptor for the stimulation of skeletal adenyl cyclase. mone-mediated bone resorption in tissue culture and that thyroid hormone excess potentiates “hypocalcemic”’ action of calcitonin. However, a decrease in the circulating concentration of calcitonin has not been found in thyrotoxicosis. 

The most likely explanation for the increased skeletal mobilization of calcium is the role of thyroid hormones on bone cell metabolism. Both thyroxine and triiodothyronine stimulate bone resorption directly in tissue culture. The effective concentrations of thyroid hormones approach those that occur in thyrotoxicosis. Propranolol inhibits the bone resorption stimulated nonspecifically by thyroid hormones in vitro, a finding that may explain the effectiveness of the drug in the management of thyrotoxic hypercalcemia without implicating its effect on the B-adrenergic system. The biochemical presentation of hypercalcemia of thyrotoxicosis depends on whether primary hyperparathyroidism coexists with it. The association of primary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by an increased serum immunoreactive PTH and nephrogenous cyclic AMP, lower values for serum phosphorus, and higher values for serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Symptomatically, there may be a greater frequency of bony abnormalities and renal calculi. The treatment of the hypercalcemia may require parathyroid surgery. 

In thyrotoxic hypercalcemia without primary hyperparathyroidism, parathyroid function is typically suppressed. Urinary cyclic AMP, expressed in relation to urinary creatinine, may be high because of a low urinary creatinine associated with the catabolic state, but nephrogenous cyclic AMP is not increased. Serum phosphorus concentration is normal or slightly increased. As previously mentioned, hypercalciuria and low intestinal calcium absorption are often found. An amelioration of hypercalcemia usually follows 

antithyroid therapy. Adrenal corticosteroids have also been reported as useful; the mechanism of their action has not been defined. 

###### Vitamin D toxicity 

Hypercalcemia is common during the course of treatment with exogenous vitamin D, a term used here to refer to all vitamin D preparations, including vitamin D,, vitamin D,, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The putative vitamin D metabolite responsible for the toxicity depends on the form of vitamin D preparation used. When complications develop following ingestion of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or 25hydroxyvitamin D, hypercalcemia must largely result from the action of the particular metabolite administered. However, in hypercalcemia developing from treatment with vitamin D, or vitamin D,, the circulating concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D is increased but that of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is normal or low. Hypercalcemia is therefore the result of an increased activity of 25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The apparent lack of the stimulation of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis is not surprising, since vitamin D toxicity is often accompanied by suppressed parathyroid function, hyperphosphatemia, and a renal functional impairment, factors that inhibit the production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Vitamin D intoxication, manifested by an increased circulating concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, contributes to the development of hypercalcemia by stimulating intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption. The importance of an increased bone resorption is emphasized by the failure of rigid dietary restriction of calcium to correct the hypercalcemia in some situations. The ability of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D to stimulate osteocytic resorption and to potentiate the effect of PTH on osteoclastic resorption has been discussed’ previously. This action is probably shared by 25dihydroxyvitamin D, albeit to a lesser degree. The appearance of vitamin D intoxication is often unpredictable, especially for parent compounds. It may develop suddenly after a long period of good control in patients maintained on the same treatment program. This unpredictability may reflect variable fat storage, binding by circulating proteins, or inactivation or meta- 
###### PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

bolic degradation of the vitamin. Moreover, there is a discordance between plasma half-life and the physiological half-life of vitamin D metabolites. For example, an increased calcium absorption may persist after the circulating concentrations of vitamin D and its metabolites have returned to normal. In addition, it may take longer to restore plasma calcium to normal than would be expected from the plasma half-lives of the vitamin. The physiological half-lives for reversal of hypercalcemia are around | to 2 days (sometimes longer) for 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, 1 week for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and 1 month for vitamin D, or vitamin D3. Biochemical manifestations of vitamin D toxicity include hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, suppressed parathyroid function, hypercalciuria, and renal impairment. Clinical manifestations of the disorder include symptoms of hypercalcemia, polyuria, nephrocalcinosis, and nephrolithiasis. Treatment should be directed toward withdrawal of vitamin D, restriction of calcium intake, and institution of a high fluid intake. Glucocorticoid therapy may be required if conservative measures are ineffective; the therapeutic action of this steroid probably results from direct inhibition of vitamin D-stimulated bone resorption and from inhibition of the synthesis or increased metabolic degradation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D. The possibility that steroids reduce the sensitivity of the intestinal tract to vitamin D action is less secure. 

###### Sarcoidosis and tuberculosis 

Sarcoidosis may be considered as an endogenous counterpart of vitamin D intoxication. The hypercalcemia that occurs in 10 to 30 percent of patients with sarcoidosis results from increased endogenous synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The site of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production is not known. Sarcoid tissue itself may be the locale of 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D synthesis, or the granulomas may elaborate a humoral factor that stimulates the renal synthesis of 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D. 

Because of the increased synthetic machinery for 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, hypercalcemia may develop as the consequence of an endogenous load of vitamin D, (from sunlight exposure) or from the exogenous administration of 

arelatively low dose of vitamin D, or vitamin D, that normally would not cause hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia is probably the consequence of stimulation of intestinal calcium absorption and of bone resorption. In some patients normal serum calcium may be restored by alow calcium diet or by an inhibition of calcium absorption with sodium cellulose phosphate, indicating that intestinal hyperabsorption of calcium may primarily account for the hypercalcemia. In others, hypercalcemia may occur in the presence of normal calcium absorption, indicating the importance of increased skeletal mobilization of calcium in its pathogenesis. 

Biochemical presentations include hypercalcemia, normal or high serum phosphorus levels, high intestinal absorption and renal excretion of calcium, and suppressed parathyroid function. Avoidance of sunlight and a low-calcium diet may avert or ameliorate the hypercalcemia. When this conservative regimen fails, administration of glucocorticoids (e.g., 20 to 50 mg prednisone per day) is effective. Restoration of normal serum concentration of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D ensues following steroid therapy (due to an uncertain mechanism). Hypercalcemia may also complicate the course of tuberculosis. Certain features of the hypercalcemia resemble those found in sarcoidosis. The majority of patients have a history of ingesting small amounts of parent vitamin D (400 to 3000 USP units per day), and short-term corticosteroid treatment causes a prompt decline in serum calcium concentration, which indicates the presence of increased sensitivity to vitamin D. This hypothesis awaits documentation by measurements of circulating vitamin D metabolites and of intestinal calcium absorption. The Kveim test has been shown to be positive in some patients. However, the restoration of normocalcemia with antituberculous therapy alone makes the coexistence of sarcoidosis unlikely. 

###### Milk-alkali syndrome 

The milk-alkali syndrome consists of hypercalcemia and alkalosis that develop after prolonged ingestion of milk and absorbable alkali. Hypercalcemia results from a disturbance in calcium transport in the intestinal tract and the kidneys. The primary pathogenetic event is the absorp- 

###### CAUSES OF HYPERCALCEMIA 185 

tion of large amounts of alkali as well as calcium (from milk). The ensuing alkalosis promotes renal tubular reabsorption of calcium. Renal insufficiency further limits calcium excretion, and hypercalcemia ensues. It may be speculated that patients who develop milk-alkali syndrome are those who had an increased intestinal absorption of calcium to begin with. Under normal circumstances the amount of calcium absorbed is limited even during a large calcium intake because of the intestinal adaptation process discussed previously. The content of vitamin D in milk is probably insufficient to modify this process. Preexisting intestinal hyperabsorption of calcium could explain the purported lack of intestinal adaptation, as well as the development of the syndrome only in a minority of individuals exposed to milk and alkali ingestion. 

The situation in milk-alkali syndrome contrasts strikingly with that of absorptive hypercalciuria, in which hypercalcemia rarely develops despite intestinal hyperabsorption of calcium. This suggests that in the absence of stimuli for enhanced renal tubular reabsorption of calcium, the increased delivery of calcium from the intestinal tract may be handled adequately by compensatory mechanisms. 

Biochemical manifestations of the milk-alkali syndrome include hypercalcemia, normal or high serum phosphorus, metabolic alkalosis, low urinary calcium, parathyroid suppression, normal serum alkaline phosphatase, and renal insufficiency. Extraskeletal calcification may be present. This condition has become less frequent with decreasing use of absorbable antacids and wider use of nonabsorbable alkali. Improvement usually ensues upon withdrawal of milk and alkali therapy. 

###### Phosphorus depletion syndrome 

Though uncommon, mild hypercalcemia may ensue from the ingestion of nonabsorbable antacids that bind phosphate. Hypercalcemia is probably the consequence of an increased intestinal absorption and skeletal mobilization of calcium. Ingestion of phosphorus-binding antacids, especially when dietary phosphate is low, may cause development of hypophosphatemia. Hypophosphatemia in turn stimulates the synthesis of 1 ,25- 

dihydroxyvitamin D, and the ensuing rise in serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D stimulates intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption. If hypophosphatemia inhibits matrix synthesis in bone, the net calcium mobilization from bone becomes exaggerated. The ingestion of phosphorus-binding antacids may also increase the absorption-of calcium directly by increasing the intraluminal pool of calcium available for absorption secondary to the reduction in availability of phosphate that normally binds calcium. Nevertheless, increased calcium absorption has not been found consistently. 

This condition is characterized by mild hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, a high serum alkaline phosphatase activity, hypercalciuria, and suppressed parathyroid function. Treatment consists of a cessation of antacids and of a lowphosphorus diet and oral administration of orthophosphate supplements when necessary. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia 

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is a hereditary disorder with an autosomal dominant mode of transmission, and it is typified by hypercalcemia, hypermagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypocalciuria. Parathyroid hyperplasia may occur. However, several features distinguish this condition from primary hyperparathyroidism. Serum immunoreactive PTH and urinary cyclic AMP are increased in only a minority of patients. Glomerular filtration rate is normal. At comparable levels of serum calcium, urinary calcium is substantially lower in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia than in primary hyperparathyroidism. The clinical course is more benign. Bone disease, nephrolithiasis, and peptic ulcer are uncommon. This condition may represent the prototype for the development of hypercalcemia from an avid renal conservation of calcium. Hypercalcemia in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia cannot be accounted for by an abnormal protein binding of calcium. The rise in total serum calcium concentration is associated with an equivalent increase in ultrafiltrable and ionized calcium. The findings therefore suggest that hypercalcemia may have developed from an enhanced renal tubular reabsorption of calcium. The role of 

186 PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

PTH is uncertain, although the findings could be explained if the hyperplastic parathyroid tissue produces an abnormal hormone or a factor with a selective effect on renal transport of divalent cations. However, the possibility that this condition is a manifestation of a primary renal disease characterized by an enhanced renal reabsorption of calcium is supported by the marginal response to parathyroidectomy. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia resembles asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism. However, in the latter condition, no familial transmission can be documented and hypermagnesemia is absent. 

###### Extracellular volume depletion 

Hypercalcemia may be found in patients with severe contraction of extracellular fluid volume. The underlying defect is the marked increase in the renal (proximal) tubular reabsorption of calcium secondary to the reduction in the effective circulatory volume. This disturbance alone is unlikely to cause significant hypercalcemia during the usual short duration of the disorder. However, it may cause or exaggerate hypercalcemia when there is a concurrent enhancement of skeletal mobilization or of intestinal absorption of calcium. Volume expansion typically corrects or ameliorates the hypercalcemia. 

###### Thiazide therapy 

An increased serum concentration of total calcium occurs in about 2 percent of patients receiving thiazide diuretics. In normal subjects a true hypercalcemia, reflected by arise in the circulating concentration of ionized calcium, is usually absent. In these individuals, high serum concentration of total calcium can be accounted for by hemoconcentration and ensuing increased protein binding of calcium. Moreover, the degree of hypercalcemia is not marked (<11 mg/dl) and typically abates within a month following withdrawal of thiazide therapy. However, true hypercalcemia may develop during thiazide therapy in states characterized by a high turnover of bone and an increased mobilization of calcium, such as primary hyperparathyroidism, secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic renal failure, vitamin D-treated hypoparathyroidism, and juvenile osteoporosis. 

The etiology for the hypercalcemia is multifactorial and has not been fully clarified. Direct stimulation of intestinal calcium absorption by thiazide has not yet been shown experimentally. It has also not been possible to demonstrate that serum PTH or urinary cyclic AMP is increased during thiazide therapy. Although primary hyperparathyroidism is occasionally diagnosed in patients treated with thiazide, there is no evidence that this condition is caused by thiazide. The “hypocalciuric” action of thiazide has often been invoked for the development of hypercalcemia. Indeed, thiazides are unique among diuretics in their ability to reduce renal excretion of calcium. This action of thiazide has been attributed to the induction of extracellular volume depletion and consequent augmentation of proximal tubular reabsorption of calcium, as well as to a direct enhancement of distal tubular reabsorption of calcium. This hypothesis may partly account for the development of hypercalcemia in conditions with a high skeletal resorption, such as primary hyperparathyroidism. In such conditions, hypercalcemia may ensue since the reduction in urinary calcium by thiazide is not likely to be accompanied by a compensatory inhibition of bone resorption. The inability of thiazide to cause hypercalcemia in patients with renal hypercalciuria and in normal subjects is not inconsistent with this hypothesis. In renal hypercalciuria, thiazide treatment corrects the renal leak of calcium, restores normal parathyroid function, and decreases the synthesis of 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D. Thus, the decline in urinary calcium produced by thiazide is compensated by a commensurate reduction in intestinal calcium absorption, and hypercalcemia is prevented. Although it has not been proved, a similar mechanism could prevail in normal subjects. However, this hypothesis is not supported by responses to administration of thiazide in patients with hypoparathyroidism or chronic renal failure. In both conditions, hypercalcemia may develop even though thiazide causes a small or negligible decline in urinary calcium. Thiazide might potentiate the action of PTH on bone. This hypothesis is supported by a thiazide-induced increment in serum calcium in secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic renal failure and by the exaggeration of hypercalcemia that follows administration of thiazides to pa- 

###### GENERAL DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC CONSIDERATIONS 

tients with primary hyperparathyroidism. The lack of the development of hypercalcemia in normal subjects could be due to the compensatory suppression of PTH secretion resulting from an increased skeletal mobilization of calcium. However, this hypothesis is not supported by the development of hypercalcemia during thiazide therapy in vitamin D-treated hypoparathyroidism. The result could be explained if the accentuation of bone resorption by thiazide were assumed to be more generalized, to include not only the action of PTH but that of vitamin D as well. Restoration of normal serum calcium usually ensues following cessation of thiazide therapy. If hypercalcemia persists, search for another cause should be made. 

been determined. Nevertheless, the results suggest that immobilization hypercalcemia is a sequel of the combined influence of reduced bone formation and increased bone resorption. Associated features include hypercalciuria and reduced bone density in the affected skeleton. Complications of nephrolithiasis and osteoporosis may ensue. Hypercalcemia typically improves following active mobilization. GENERAL DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC CONSIDERATIONS The previous discussion has considered not only the pathogenetic mechanisms but also specific diagnostic criteria and treatment programs for different causes of hypercalcemia. This section will consider diagnosis and management in an overall context. 

###### Immobilization hypercalcemia 

Hypercalcemia of immobilization typically occurs in states of high bone turnover, such as Paget’s disease, primary hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, and thyrotoxicosis. Although rare in normal adults, it is sometimes encountered in normal children who may have a high rate of bone turnover. 

In the general approach to hypercalcemia, it is critical to demonstrate that a true hypercalcemia, reflected by a rise in ionized calcium concentration, is indeed present. A familiarity with the state of calcium in serum should allow an estimation of ionized calcium fraction even when a direct assay is not available. 

The exact cause for immobilization hypercalcemia is not known. The traditional view attributed it to the inhibition of bone formation (and hence of mineralization) from the effect of the lack of stress on osteoblast function. The unopposed bone resorption would be suffcient to cause hypercalcemia. This hypothesis is supported by the demonstration of reduced bone formation during immobilization, from direct histomorphometric analysis of bone, and from the decline in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. The predilection of hypercalcemia to develop in states of high bone turnover further supports this view. 

Once a diagnosis of hypercalcemia is established, additional diagnostic tests are required to assess the specific cause for the hypercalcemia. Because of the heterogeneity of etiologies, it is impractical to design a diagnostic program applicable to all causes. Thus, certain tests are selected to clarify the existence of a particular suspected cause. This selection is obviously guided by the index of suspicion, which is formulated from knowledge concerning pathogenesis and clinical presentation, as well as from a careful history and physical examination. The nature and complexity of evaluation depend largely on the exact cause of the hypercalcemia. The evaluation may entail a simple procedure, e.g., withdrawal of thiazide and reassessment of serum calcium concentration. However, the assessment may sometimes be complex, involving, for example, an extensive search for a malignancy. 

However, bone resorption has also been shown to be increased during immobilization, and there is some evidence that parathyroid stimulation may be responsible for increased bone resorption. In experimental animals, the development of osteoporosis of immobilization may be prevented by prior parathyroidectomy. Although assays for PTH in serum have provided conflicting results, increased values have been shown using reliable methods. The cause for a parathyroid stimulation when present has not

Furosemide is then given in a dosage of 80 to 100 mg every 1 to 2 h, with appropriate replacement of losses of water, sodium, and potassium. The basis for the “hypocalcemic” action of furosemide-induced natriuresis is the promotion of the renal loss of calcium. Other tests include serum calcium, phosphorus, albumin, total protein, electrolytes, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, and 24-h urinary calcium and creatinine. Management depends on whether the hypercalcemia presents as an emergency and on whether the treatment is directed at correcting the underlying cause or at nonspecifically ameliorating hypercalcemia. 

###### General conservative measures 

These nonspecific measures, applicable in all situations, include (1) an adequate fluid intake to avoid dehydration and to ensure good urine output, (2) withdrawal, when possible, of drugs that cause hypercalcemia, such as thiazide, vitamin D preparations, and antacids, (3) restriction of dietary calcium, and (4) avoidance of protracted immobilization and encouragement of mobilization whenever possible. The rationale for the above recommendations is obvious. 

When the above approach is ineffective or contraindicated, second-line measures, including administration of mithramycin and calcitonin, may be instituted. Mithramycin, an antibiotic related to actinomycin D, inhibits DN A-directed RNA synthesis. Osteoclasts are apparently particularly sensitive to this antibiotic, since osteoclastic resorption is markedly inhibited by amounts of mithramycin that are suboptimal for chemotherapy of tumors. This action most likely accounts for the hypocalcemic effect of mithramycin. Other postulated mechanisms of mithramycin action such as the induction of refractoriness to vitamin D_ have not been substantiated. Following the intravenous administration of mithramycin (25 uwg/kg over 3 to 8 h), serum calcium decreases within | day and reaches a nadir in 3 to 4 days. The drug may be given again when the effect is dissipated. The decrement in serum calcium may be substantial; it averages 3 mg/dl and may be as high as 7 mg/dl. Associated biochemical findings include decline in serum phosphorus and urinary calcium and stimulation of endogenous PTH secretion. Mithramycin is usually effective in hypercalcemia that is primarily the result of increased bone resorption, such as oncogenic hypercalcemia and hyperparathyroidism. Although this drug has been associated with hemorrhagic disorders, hepatic toxicity, and renal impairment, few documented complications have been reported during its use in hypercalcemia, a finding that is probably attributable to the low dose 

###### Emergency measures 

Hypercalcemia may present as a_ medical emergency, usually when the circulating concentration of calcium increases abruptly to high levels. Hypercalcemic crisis is characterized by a semicomatose or comatose state that may be accompanied by rapidly deteriorating renal function. In such a situation, a quick correction of hypercalcemia may be life-saving. It may also be advantageous to institute emergency measures directed at rapidly lowering serum calcium in any situation of severe hypercalcemia, irrespective of the state of consciousness, and in acute complications of hypercalcemia (e.g., soft-tissue calcification) even when the serum calcium concentration is only moderately elevated. Such regimens are often nonspecific; i.e., they are not necessarily directed at correcting the underlying cause of hypercalcemia. 

In the absence of renal failure, an intravenous administration of furosemide and saline may constitute the first-line emergency measure, applicable to all forms of hypercalcemia. Typically, 1 to 2 liters of physiologic saline are given intravenously to overcome dehydration. This is impor- 

###### GENERAL DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC CONSIDERATIONS 

utilized. However, mithramycin should be used with caution in patients with renal impairment. Calcitonin has certain advantages over mithramycin, since it does not have the above side effects and it may produce a more rapid decline in serum calcium concentration (within 2 h). Salmon calcitonin is commonly used, because it is the most potent and has the longest duration of action among the available calcitonins. The customary dose is 4 MRC units per kilogram given subcutaneously every 12 h. The hypocalcemic action is attributed mainly to the inhibition of bone resorption. As with mithramycin, a decline in serum phosphorus and a stimulation of parathyroid function are encountered during calcitonin therapy. Calcitonin is useful in the control of hypercalcemia of excessive bone resorption, such as oncogenic hypercalcemia, hyperparathyroidism associated with parathyroid adenoma or carcinoma, and vitamin D intoxication. However, the decrement in serum calcium produced by calcitonin is generally slight (1 to 2 mg/dl) and is sometimes not sustained. The apparent loss of activity with continued use has been attributed to secondary stimulation of PTH secretion, formation of neutralizing antibodies, and development of cellular refrac- 

toriness. Nevertheless, calcitonin is useful in the short-term control of hypercalcemia of certain disorders. Severe hypercalcemia is unlikely to develop solely from increased calcium absorption or from defective renal excretion of calcium. Thus, the above emergency measures are effective in most situations of hypercalcemic crisis. Intravenous orthophosphate and ethylenediaminetetraacetate have also been employed as emergency measures. However, their use should be discouraged because of the serious hazards of soft-tissue calcification and nephrotoxicity. Intravenous sodium sulfate offers no advantage over furosemide and saline infusion. Adrenal corticosteroids (e.g., 40 to 80 mg prednisone per day) may be employed in severe hypercalcemia of lymphoid origin, vitamin D toxicity, thyrotoxicosis, or osteolytic metastasis. The use of the inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis must be on a putative basis since the diagnosis of PGE-induced hypercalcemia is usually made retrospectively. 

Hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis may rapidly lower serum calcium and may be useful in patients with congestive heart failure and oliguric renal failure.

190 PATHOGENESIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERCALCEMIC STATES 

###### Specific measures 

The emergency measures described above are generally directed at a short-term control of hypercalcemia and are not intended for longterm use. During their institution, diagnostic evaluation should be pursued. Attempts should be made to replace emergency measures with more specific treatment programs directed at the underlying cause. 

The specific measures for the various causes of hypercalcemia have been discussed in earlier sections. 

###### Rational approach to hypercalcemia 

In an earlier discussion of pathogenic mechanisms, hypercalcemia was attributed to disturbances in three organ systems: increased resorption and/or impaired formation and mineralization of bone; excessive calcium absorption in the intestine; and impaired renal excretion of calcium. Control of hypercalcemia 

may be achieved by opposing these influences at the three target organs. This concept forms the basis for the functional classification of therapeutic modalities for the hypercalcemia described in Table 3. Certain of the maneuvers exert more than one opposing action. Some of the opposing effects may be of major importance, whereas others may be of minor significance in the control of hypercalcemia. A full appreciation and continued refinement of this classification will facilitate the selection of specific treatment regimens.

##### PROSTAGLANDINS, THROMBOXANES, AND EICOSANOIDS: ARACHIDONIC ACID METABOLITES RELEVANT TO MEDICINE 

###### R. PAUL ROBERTSON 

Arachidonic acid is a precursor of several physiologically active compounds, many only recently discovered. The precise role of these various metabolites in health and disease is currently under intense scrutiny. In such a rapidly moving area some current hypotheses may be disproved in the future, and other hypotheses not mentioned here may develop into important concepts. 

This chapter is organized into areas of pharmacology, physiology, and pathophysiology. The pharmacology section will describe the synthetic and catabolic pathways of the arachidonic acid metabolites, the methods for measurement, and possible mechanisms of action. The physiology section will focus on the biological phenomena in which various arachidonic acid metabolites appear to play a role. The pathophysiology section will describe the pathologic processes in which these substances may play a role. 

###### PHARMACOLOGY OF THE PROSTANOIDS AND EICOSANOIDS 

Prostaglandins were so named in the 1930s because they originally were thought to be made exclusively in the prostate gland. This misnomer persists despite subsequent findings that prostaglandins are made by all tissues. The metabolic pathway by which arachidonic acid is converted to prostanoids and eicosanoids is summarized schematically in Fig. 1. 

The term prostanoid is derived from a theoretical substance, prostanoic acid, and refers to the products of the cyclooxygenase pathway, the prostaglandins and the thromboxanes. The term eicosanoids refers to the products of the lipoxygenase pathway. 

The initial synthetic step involves the cleav- 

age by a phospholipase of arachidonic acid from phospholipid, which is in the plasma membrane of all cells. Arachidonic acid can then be shunted into two separate metabolic pathways to form the cyclic endoperoxide PGG, by the cyclooxygenase system or to form the hydroperoxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HPETE) by lipoxygenase. PGG, can be converted to PGH, through a peroxidase step. PGG, and PGH, are key intermediates in the formation of the classical prostaglandins (PGA,, PGD,, PGE,, and PGF,.), prostacyclin (PGI,), and thromboxane A, (TXA,). HPETE can be converted to either hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (HETE) or the leukotrienes (LTA, LTB, LTC, and LTD). 

All cells have the necessary substrate and enzymes to form at least some of the metabolites of arachidonic acid. However, these enzymatic reactions have not been studied exhaustively in many tissues. Therefore, while it is essential to describe a general synthetic pathway for the metabolites, these generalizations may not be applicable to all cells. Additionally, two substrates [3,11,14-eicosatrienoic acid (dihomo-y-linolenic acid) and 5,8,11,14,17-eicosapentaenoic acid] other than arachidonic acid can be converted to closely related metabolites. Products of the former substrate carry the subscript 1, whereas those from the latter have the subscript 3. The subscripts designate the number of double bonds between carbon atoms in the side chains. Arachidonic acid is 5,8,11,14-eicosatetraenoic acid and forms products with the subscript 2, as shown in Fig. 1. These compounds appear to be the ones that are preferentially synthesized in humans. All arachidonic acid metabolites are made by cells according to need and are not stored for later release.

The overall scheme of arachidonic acid metabolism. Phospholipase cleaves arachidonic acid from phospholipid. Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid to the cyclic endoperoxides, and lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid to 5-HPETE. The drugs in- 

dicated at each of these enzymatic steps act to inhibit the reaction. Five major groups of arachidonic acid metabolites are formed: the classical prostaglandins, prostacyclins, and thromboxanes, via the cyclooxygenase pathways, and 5-HETE and the leukotrienes via the lipoxygenase pathway. 

###### The classical prostaglandins 

Prostaglandins (named by letters of the alphabet) are formed when the cyclic endoperoxides are acted upon by the enzyme endoperoxide isomerase. Of these, PGE, and PGF, appear to be important in normal physiology (Fig. 2). PGA, is a degradation product of PGE... It has strong vasodepressor actions, but its exact role is uncertain. PGD, may play a role in platelet function. 

###### Prostacyclin (PGI.,) 

Formation of PGI, from arachidonic acid by the enzyme prostacyclin synthetase (Fig. 3) appears to be a dominant pathway in the endothelial cells 

of vessel walls. Prostacyclin functions to mediate vasodilatation and prevent platelet aggregation on the vessel wall. Nonvascular tissues also synthesize PGI,. 

###### Thromboxanes 

The thromboxanes differ from prostaglandins in their lack of the cyclopentane ring (Fig. 4). Thromboxane synthetase acts on endoperoxides to incorporate an oxygen atom into the ring, thus making it six-membered. TXA, is formed by platelets and plays an important role in platelet aggregation. It is uncertain whether TXA, has physiologic roles unrelated to platelet function.

###### Drugs that inhibit synthesis of prostanoids and eicosanoids 

Many commonly used drugs inhibit the synthesis of arachidonic acid metabolites. Glucocorticoids and several antimalarial drugs interfere with the phospholipase-regulated cleavage of arachidonic acid from phospholipids (Fig. 1). The cyclooxygenase-mediated reaction that forms cyclic endoperoxides from arachidonic acid is inhibited by a variety of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs including the salicylates, indomethacin, and ibuprofen. However, all three drugs also inhibit the peroxidase-mediated step that converts HPETE to HETE (Fig. 5). One drug known to inhibit the lipoxygenase-mediated conversion of arachidonic acid to HPETE is benoxaprofen. An arachidonic acid analogue, 15-hydroperoxyarachidonic acid (15-HPAA) and tranycypromine, an antidepressive, both inhibit the conversion of cyclic endoperoxides to PGI, (Fig. 3). Imidazole inhibits thromboxane synthetase (Fig. 4) and consequently prevents the conversion of cyclic endoperoxides to thromboxane A,,. Although these drugs can inhibit the formation of arachidonic acid and its metabolites, most of them act so early in the synthetic pathways that they inhibit the formation of many products rather than of any specific one. Imidazole and 15S-HPAA, although apparently specific for 

TXA, and PGI,, respectively, cannot be used in humans. No specific inhibitors that prevent the conversion of HPETE to the leukotrienes have been identified. 

###### Major problem: a lack of antagonists 

No specific antagonists have been identified that prevent specific actions of individual arachidonic acid metabolites. The lack of such antagonists is a major barrier to understanding the role of the arachidonic acid metabolites in physiologic and pathophysiologic processes. The availability of specific inhibitors of prostanoid and eicosanoid synthesis and action would greatly enhance our understanding of the function of the arachidonic acid metabolites. 

The fact that effects are produced by drugs known to inhibit the synthesis of prostanoids does not necessarily mean that the observed phenomena result solely from such inhibition. For example, indomethacin not only inhibits formation of cyclic endoperoxides by cyclooxygenase but also disrupts calcium flux across membranes, inhibits cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase and phosphodiesterase, and inhibits one of the enzymes responsible for degradation of PGE,. Structurally unrelated drugs that inhibit a given enzymatic step must be tested to determine 

PHARMACOLOGY OF THE PROSTANOIDS AND EICOSANOIDS 195 

Metabolism of prostanoids and eicosanoids whether inhibition of that enzyme is responsible for the observed effects. 

Arachidonic acid metabolites turn over rapidly in vivo. For example, prostaglandins of the E and F series are chemically stable at physiologic pH but are approximately 90 percent degraded during a single passage through the liver and the lung (Fig. 7). A variety of products are formed during metabolism of PGE and PGF. 13,14-Dihydro15-keto derivatives can be measured in the circulation; the final derivative is excreted in the urine. Nonmetabolized PGE in urine is the result of synthesis in kidneys and seminal vesicles, whereas metabolites of prostaglandins in urine represent the amount synthesized by other organs. PGI,, TXA,, and the leukotrienes are chemically unstable and also have short halflives in the circulation. PGI, is converted to 6- keto-PGF,., and thromboxane A, is converted to thromboxane B,. Since both PGI, and TXA, are short-lived in vivo, measurement of inactive metabolites is commonly used as a measure of the rates of formation. The degradative pathways for HETE and the leukotrienes have not been characterized in detail. 

###### Methods of measurement 

Five methods are currently used to quantify arachidonic acid metabolites in physiologic fluids: bioassay, immunoassay, chromatography, receptor assay, and mass spectrometry. Bioassay was developed first, but the major problem is lack of specificity. Many of the measurements of different prostaglandins in physiologic fluids have been generated using the radioimmunoassay. Immunoassay is more sensitive than bioassay, but great care must be taken to ensure specificity. A closely related method, the receptor assay, uses a cell component such as the plasma membrane that binds prostaglandins with high affinity to establish a standard curve. The unknown competes for the binding site, and the standard curve is used to calculate the amount of PGE in the sample. This method (and the radioimmunoassay) requires prior extraction and chromatography of the sample. Mass spectrometry is the most accurate method of assessment. It requires preparation
