No method circumvents the major difficulty of handling samples during and after collection. Under certain circumstances prostaglandin synthesis in biological samples is induced by manipulating tissue or physiologic fluid during the collection procedure. For example, platelets synthesize and release PGE and thromboxanes, and, if blood is allowed to clot or if platelets are not carefully and gently separated from the plasma, large amounts of these substances may be generated during processing and lead to erroneous results. Use of an inhibitor of prostaglandin synthesis in the collection tube may minimize this problem. 

196 PROSTAGLANDINS, THROMBOXANES, AND EICOSANOIDS 

###### Mechanism of action 

Prostaglandins have binding sites exclusively on the plasma membranes of many cells. Most binding experiments have been performed with prostaglandins of the E and F series, but more recently binding sites for PGI, have been demonstrated. Sites for various prostaglandins are found in liver, corpus luteum, adrenal gland, fat cells, thymocytes, uterus, and platelets. Prostaglandin receptors are specific in that they preferentially bind prostaglandins and not other endogenous substances. Moreover, most of these binding sites are specific for prostaglandins of a given type. For example, the binding site in the liver plasma membrane for prostaglandins of the E series binds PGE, and PGE, with high affinity but not prostaglandins of the A, F, and I configurations. The PGE binding site in platelets appears to recognize PGI, as well as PGE,. However, platelets have a separate binding site for PGD, that does not readily recognize either PGE, or PGI,. Thus, it is necessary to study a particular tissue to draw conclusions about receptors. The arachidonic acid metabolites are believed to act directly on cells rather than through enhancement of the formation of so-called second messengers. Antagonists to a variety of recognized neurotransmitters and hormones do not prevent the actions of these metabolites. Instead, intracellular mechanisms such as adenylate cyclase stimulation and alterations in calcium flux appear to be involved in their action. A major question is whether competition per se for these intracellular processes (hence blocking of stimulation by other agonists) represents a fundamental mechanism of action that results in modulation of signals reaching the cell from extracellular sources. PHYSIOLOGY Arachidonic acid metabolites: Hormones or modulators? 

The conventional definition of a hormone is a substance that is formed in one tissue, enters the circulation, and travels to another tissue to exert its effects. By this definition, arachidonic acid metabolites are not hormones. Instead they may exert paracrine functions or act as local intracellular modulators of biochemical activity in 

the tissues in which they are formed. Most are short-lived in the circulation either because of chemical instability or because of rapid degradation by organs such as the lungs and the liver. Considerable effort has been expended to measure circulating levels of these substances, but no convincing evidence has been demonstrated of biologically meaningful changes in circulating prostanoid or eicosanoid levels in response to endogenous substances known to stimulate the formation of arachidonic acid metabolites in vitro. Thus, prostanoids and eicosanoids probably act as intracellular modulators of signals received from the cell’s environment. 

###### Lipolysis 

Except for insulin, most endogenous substances that affect lipolysis are stimulatory in nature. Recently, PGE, has been shown to be synthesized by fat cells and to be a potent endogenous inhibitor of lipolysis. This interpretation is based on both in vitro studies of the effects of PGE and in vivo studies of the effects of 16,16-dimethylPGE;, an analogue not catabolized by the lung. Since the formation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP) by the enzyme adenylate cyclase is involved in the activation of lipolysis by hormones, the interactions between PGE and adenylate cyclase in the fat cell have been examined in considerable detail. PGE inhibits lipolysis by decreasing the amount of cyclic AMP formed in response to epinephrine, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), glucagon, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). However, PGE itself is also a weak stimulator of adenylate cyclase in the fat cell. Thus, PGE may act as an endogenous antilipolytic substance because it interferes with the stimulation of cyclic AMP formation by hormones. 

Whether insulin and PGE interact during their antilipolytic actions on the fat cell remains to be determined. For example, insulin but not PGE inhibits the stimulation of lipolysis by exogenous cyclic AMP in isolated fat cells, but both agents inhibit hormone-stimulated generation of cyclic AMP. This suggests a site of action for insulin distal to the stimulation of adenylate cyclase. In chicken fat cells, which are not responsive to insulin, PGE inhibits glucagon-induced lipolysis (Fig. 8) whereas insulin does not.

###### Luteolysis 

Hysterectomy in sheep during the luteal phase results in luteal maintenance, which suggests that the uterus produces a luteolytic substance. Since PGF, can cause luteal regression, experiments were designed to assess whether PGF, in uterine venous drainage might reach the ovary without passing through the systemic and pulmonary circulations where it would be degraded. Following infusion of radiolabeled PGF,,. into the uterine vein of sheep, the amount of radioactivity was many times higher in the ovarian arterial plasma than in the iliac arterial plasma. Consequently, the hypothesis has been advanced that a countercurrent phenomenon between the uterine vein and ovarian artery may allow PGF,. from the uterus to reach the ovary and induce luteolysis without passing into the systemic circulation.

###### Piatelet aggregation 

PGE,, PGD.,, and thromboxane A, are synthesized by platelets. Although a physiologic role has not been established for PGE, and PGD, in platelet function, thromboxane A, is a potent stimulator of platelet aggregation; in contrast PGI,, formed by the endothelial cells of blood vessel walls, is probably the most potent endogenous antagonist of platelet aggregation known and is now being tested as an anticoagulant in a variety of clinical disorders (Fig. 10). It has been postulated that TXA, and PGI, exercise their opposite effects by affecting the generation of cyclic AMP by platelets. Decreases in cyclic AMP are associated with aggregation of platelets. 

sterone axis is the major regulator of salt metabolism, and the vasopressin or antidiuretic hormone system exerts the principal control over water balance. Arachidonic acid metabolites influence both systems and may play a physiological role in the overall regulation. For example, PGE, and PGI, stimulate renin secretion whereas inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis have the opposite effect. PGI, decreases renal vein resistance and increases blood flow, which results in redistribution of blood from the outer renal cortex to the juxtamedullary cortex. Conversely, two inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis, indomethacin and meclofenamate, decrease total renal blood flow and shunt the remaining flow to the outer cortex. PGE, also causes a decrease in net sodium ion transport in isolated, perfused rabbit collecting tubules and induces natriuresis in intact subjects. Furthermore, indomethacin increases sensitivity to exogenous vasopressin in dogs. Treated animals concentrate urine more effectively in response to the hormone. Conversely, PGE, decreases vasopressin-stimulated water transport. These two findings suggest that PGE, exerts a negative modulating effect on the antidiuretic properties of vasopressin. In addition, 

Inhibitors of endogenous prostaglandin synthesis have potent effects on platelet aggregation. For example, a single dose of acetylsalicylic acid can interfere with normal platelet aggregation for 48 h. Since these drugs inhibit cyclooxygenase and thereby inhibit formation of TXA, by the platelets, the suppression of thromboxane synthesis is presumed to be the mechanism by which they interfere with platelet aggregation. Inhibition of cyclooxygenase lasts longer in platelets than in other tissues, possibly because the platelet does not have the necessary machinery to form new enzymes in contrast to nucleated cells that can synthesize new protein. Consequently, new platelets may have to be formed before the

The ability of endothelial cells to recover after treatment with prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors by forming new enzymes for PGI, synthesis may explain why patients who take these drugs do not clot excessively. Another postulated explanation is that the platelet is more sensitive than the endothelial cell to drugs that inhibit cyclooxygenase. Endothelial damage may lead to platelet aggregates along the blood vessel wall (Fig. 10) by causing a local absence of PGI, synthesis, thereby allowing unbridled platelet aggregation at the site of vessel wall damage. Such a platelet clot might then serve as a nidus for formation of atherosclerotic plaques. 

###### Vascular effects 

The vasoactive properties of arachidonic acid metabolites are among the most important actions. For example, prostaglandins of the E and A series and PGI, are vasodilators (Fig. 11) where PGF,, and TXA, are vasoconstrictors. 

These effects appear to be the result of direct action on the smooth muscles of the vessel wall. Provided that sufficient systemic blood pressure is maintained, the vasodilatory arachidonic acid metabolites act to increase blood flow. If the blood pressure falls, however, blood flow decreases even though the arterial bed is dilated. Furthermore, systemic hypotension causes catecholamine release, which in turn superimposes vasoconstriction. Where the predominant effect is alpha-adrenergic, vasoconstriction, although serving to elevate the blood pressure, may further decrease the amount of blood flow to tissues. Thus, significant alterations in systemic blood pressure must be excluded when evaluating the effects of arachidonic acid metabolites on organ blood flow. 

Arachidonic acid metabolites may participate in coronary artery spasm and shock of various etiologies. The implications of these findings for medicine await human investigation because virtually all data to date have been collected in animal models.

Oral PGE also protects the mucosa of the gastrointestinal tract from several forms of injury. Since oral PGE, does not invariably decrease gastric acid output, this protection of the mucosa may be due to direct actions rather than inhibition of gastric acid secretion. In in vitro experiments prostaglandins stimulate gastrointestinal smooth muscle and thereby increase motility, but it has not been established whether these actions are physiologically important. A role has been postulated for arachidonic acid metabolites in the gastrointestinal symptoms associated with certain tumors, such as carcinoid, but the evidence is not conclusive. 

###### Neurotransmission in the autonomic nervous system 

Most studies suggesting that arachidonic acid metabolites modulate autonomic transmission 

have been performed in animal species using in vitro and in vivo methodologies, and it is difficult to project the applicability of the animal data to human neurophysiology. Nevertheless, several findings warrant attention. PGE inhibits egress of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals such as norepinephrine release from the perfused cat spleen after nerve stimulation (Fig. 13). Moreover, PGE, synthesis is increased by nerve stimulation, thus providing a counterregulatory system. The PGE effect on norepinephrine secretion appears to be prejunctional, i.e., at a site on the nerve before the terminal reaches the synaptic cleft. Inhibitors of PGE, synthesis also augment norepinephrine release in response to stimulation of adrenergic nerves, and this inhibitory action of PGE, can be reversed by increases in calcium concentration in the perfusing medium. Therefore, PGE, may act to inhibit norepinephrine release by blocking calcium influx. In contrast, catecholamines can release PGE, from a variety of tissues, probably by effects on alpha-adrenergic activity. For example, in innervated tissues such as the spleen, nerve stimulation or injection of norepinephrine causes release of PGE,. This release is blocked after denervation or use of drugs that provide alpha-adrenergic blockade, which suggests that PGE, serves as a local counterregulator of norepinephrine release

###### PATHOPHYSIOLOGY 

A problem in defining the pathophysiologic role of arachidonic acid metabolites in disease states resides in definition of the manner in which abnormal amounts of the metabolites gain access to cells. As stated above, prostaglandins do not behave as hormones in physiologic situations. That is not to say, however, that elevations of these substances in the systemic circulation might not occur in pathophysiologic states. For example, although lung and liver normally degrade circulating PGE, in the presence of arteriovenous shunts or disease of the lung or liver, excessive amounts of PGE or PGF might gain access to the systemic circulation. In addition, prostaglandin synthesis might be stimulated to such an extent in pathological states as to overwhelm the various degradative mechanisms and allow significant amounts to escape into the arterial circulation. Likewise, therapy with agents that inhibit the synthetic pathways for some arachidonic acid metabolites may shunt substrate to other pathways and thereby increase formation of different metabolites. However, it is not essential to demonstrate increases in circulating prostaglandins to document their postulated roles in pathophysiologic processes since the source of such metabolites could be intracellular. 

Most postulated roles for these metabolites in disease involve excessive production, but a few pathophysiologic states may be the result of deficiency, for example, from diets deficient in arachidonic acid (an essential fatty acid). Likewise, deficiency could result from damage to a tissue required for prostaglandin synthesis, such as endothelial cells, the site of production of PGI, to prevent platelet aggregation on the vessel wall. Alternatively, therapy with drugs that inhibit synthesis of arachidonic acid metabolites could be a cause of prostaglandin deficiency. 

###### Bone resorption: hypercalcemia of malignancy 

Hypercalcemia occurs in association with nonparathyroid malignancies of many different types. Parathyroid hormone excess, as the result either of inappropriate production by parathyroid tissue or ectopic formation by the tumor itself, is the basis for a portion of these cases. However, most patients with hypercalcemia of malignancy do not have elevated plasma levels of biologically active fragments of parathyroid hormone, and the etiology of the disorder has been the subject of considerable interest. Prostaglandin E, is a potent inducer of bone resorption and calcium release from bone. Furthermore, PGE, production is elevated in certain hypercalcemic animals with metastatic transplantable tumors. Treatment of these animals with inhibitors of endogenous PGE synthesis results in reduction of PGE synthesis and a concomitant decrease in hypercalcemia. Likewise, some cancer patients with hypercalcemia and malignancy have excessive amounts of PGE in plasma and of PGE metabolites in urine (Fig. 14), whereas elevated levels have not been observed in normocalcemic patients with otherwise similar malignancies. to ascertain whether agents that inhibit endogenous prostaglandin synthesis also decrease circulating calcium levels. Such drugs were effective in some but not all patients. It is important, however, that patients whose plasma calcium respond to the drugs all have evidence of elevated prostaglandin E production. Patients who have no evidence for elevated PGE production fail to respond by lowering their circulating calcium levels. Thus, a small subset of patients with hypercalcemia and malignancy, perhaps 10 to 15 percent, have elevated PGE production and can be treated with drugs that inhibit prostaglandin synthesis. An unresolved problem with this postulated pathophysiologic mechanism is the source of the excess PGE. Increased liver and lung degradation of PGE would be expected if large amounts of PGE were present in the circulation. It is possible, of course, that PGE release by a tumor into the venous circulation is so large that liver and lung degradation cannot handle the load. Alternatively, if lung metastases are present, the venous drainage from the tumors arrive at bone directly. A third possible mechanism involves metastatic seeding of bone. Tumor cells synthesize PGE in culture; it is possible that metastatic 

tumor cells in bone synthesize PGE that acts locally to cause bone resorption. Hypercalcemia of malignancy can occur in the absence of documented bony metastases, but the clinical tools for the documentation of such metastases, such as radioisotope scans, may not be sensitive enough to detect many small lesions. Bone resorption: Rheumatoid arthritis and dental cysts 

One manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis is juxtaarticular osteoporosis and bony erosions, and PGE, has been postulated as a cause. Rheumatoid synovia in tissue culture synthesize PGE, (Fig. 15), and media from these cultures promote bone resorption. The addition of indomethacin to such cultures blocks the capacity of the ultrafiltrates in this regard. Thus, PGE, produced by the synovia may be responsible for bone resorption. Indomethacin does not prevent bone resorption due to bone-resorbing agents including PGE, itself. Glucocorticoids such as dexamethasone and hydrocortisone used to treat rheumatoid arthritis can also inhibit PGE, production by rheumatoid synovia. Cells from benign dental cysts also cause bone resorption and synthesize PGE, in tissue culture. Again, bone resorption caused by the culture medium can be diminished if indomethacin is added prior to the incubation. A related problem is that of alveolar bone resorption in patients with periodontal disease, a common inflammatory disease of the gums. PGE, levels in inflamed gingiva are greater than in healthy gingival tissue. Thus, it is possible that alveolar resorption might be due in part at least to overproduction of these local metabolites. 

###### Bartter’s syndrome 

Bartter’s syndrome is characterized by elevated levels of plasma renin, aldosterone, and bradykinin; resistance to the pressor effect of angiotensin infusion; hypokalemic alkalosis; and renal potassium wasting in the presence of normal blood pressure. The basis for the postulated role of prostaglandins in Bartter’s syndrome is that PGE, and PGI, can stimulate the release of renin and that the pressor response to infused angiotensin can be blunted by their vasodilator effects. In addition, synthesis of arachidonic acid

Conversely, arachidonic acid metabolites can promote renin release, in turn leading to increased aldosterone secretion, which can increase urinary kallikrein activity. In keeping with this postulate, elevated levels of PGE, and 6-keto-PGF,, have been documented in urine from patients with the syndrome. Hyperplasia of renal medullary interstitial cells (which synthesize PGE in culture) has also been demonstrated. 

These findings led to therapeutic trials of prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors. Indomethacin reversed virtually all the abnormalities except for hypokalemia (Fig. 16). Other inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis have also been used successfully in this disorder. Thus, a prostaglandin, probably PGE, or PGI,, appears to be responsible for mediating many but not all of the manifestations of Bartter’s syndrome. Diabetes mellitus Within minutes of glucose administration to a normal individual, an acute or first-phase increase in secretion of insulin into plasma can be demonstrated, and this is followed by a slower, more prolonged response termed second-phase insulin secretion. Patients with non-insulindependent, adult-onset diabetes mellitus have subnormal first-phase insulin release in response to glucose administration, and the second phase of insulin secretion is variably diminished in such 

patients. Insulin response to other secretagogues, such as arginine, isoproterenol, glucagon, and secretin, is present in adult-onset diabetes mellitus. Thus, diabetics appear to have a specific defect that interferes with normal perception of glucose signals (the glucoreceptor hypothesis). The fact that diabetic subjects fail to respond appropriately to other glucose signals such as glucagon release in response to hypoglycemia, suppression of growth hormone secretion by glucose administration, and taste threshold for the glucose molecule supports this hypothesis. As with insulin secretion, these processes remain responsive to signals other than that of glucose. Since PGE inhibits insulin secretion in vivo in animals and in humans (Fig. 17), inhibitors of endogenous prostaglandin synthesis have been given to patients with adult-onset diabetes mellitus to ascertain whether insulin secretion can be improved. Intravenous administration of sodium salicylate partially restores the acute insulin response and improves glucose disposal (Fig. 17). Whether this effect is due to inhibition of prostaglandin E synthesis or to some other property of the drug has not been completely established.

204 PROSTAGLANDINS, THROMBOXANES, AND EICOSANOIDS 

Acetylsalicylic acid, which has a different mechanism of action from sodium salicylate, also improves insulin secretioa **n** d glucose tolerance in diabetics, which suggests that endogenous PGE production may contribute to defective insulin secretion in patients with adult-onset diabetes mellitus. In keeping with this idea, PGE inhibits glucose-induced acute insulin responses but not acute insulin responses to arginine in normal humans; conversely, sodium salicylate improves acute insulin responses to glucose but does not affect acute insulin responses to arginine in normal subjects. The role of prostaglandins in patients with insulin-dependent or juvenile-onset diabetes mellitus has not been studied extensively. However, platelets from patients with juvenile-onset diabetes produce more PGE and TXB, than do platelets from nondiabetics. Although PGE, is not thought to play an important role in platelet physiology, the finding of enhanced production of TXB, (and presumably TXA,) by platelets from diabetics is of interest. An intrinsic defect in diabetes might promote excessive TXA, production by platelets and enhance platelet aggregation, thus increasing the tendency to atherosclerosis in the disease. Additional possiblities include TXA, and PGI, involvement in microangiopathy and in peripheral arterial disease in diabetics. 

###### Essential hypertension 

Shortly after the vasodilator roles of PGA and PGE were characterized, it was suggested that a deficiency of one or the other might be involved in the pathogenesis of essential hypertension; the rationale for this is that such a deficiency could be responsible for failure to compensate for endogenous vasoconstrictive forces. Some early studies reported subnormal amounts of circulating PGA in this disease. However, subsequent work using mass spectrometry failed to find measurable levels of PGA in the plasma of normal subjects. More recently, patients with essential hypertension have been reported to excrete subnormal amounts of PGE in urine. Urinary PGE levels in patients with essential hypertension are also lower than in subjects with renovascular hypertension or primary aldosteronism. PGE in human urine is normally ascribed to renal pro- 

duction. Consequently, the hypothesis has been advanced that essential hypertension in some people may be due to a deficiency of renal production of PGE. The rationale for this hypothesis involves the requirement that PGE is normally produced by the human kidney to offset the effect of vasoconstrictive substances on the renal circulation. However, much more information is needed before this hypothesis can be evaluated. 

###### Patent ductus arteriosus 

The ductus arteriosus in sheep is very sensitive to the vasodilatory properties of PGE, and PGElike material has been demonstrated in ductal tissue. This has led to the idea that enhanced endogenous PGE might maintain prenatal patency of the ductus. Furthermore, since administration of inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis cause constriction of the ductus of fetal lambs, similar trials were undertaken in premature human infants with persistent ductus arteriosus. Treatment for several days is followed by closure of the vessel in the majority of patients, although many require a second course of therapy and a minority of patients eventually require surgical ligation. Infants under 35 weeks of age are most likely to respond, and the failure rate is higher in older infants. Indomethacin is the agent tested most extensively to date. Since large doses can cause renal failure, it is critical to use the smallest dose possible and to monitor renal function carefully. 

Some types of congenital heart disease require a patent ductus arteriosus to preserve life. This has given rise to the concept of ““ductus-dependent pulmonary blood flow” in circumstances in which the ductus is the major channel by which nonoxygenated blood reaches the lungs from the aortic arch, for example, in pulmonary atresia and tricuspid atresia. Since PGE relaxes the smooth muscle in the lamb ductus arteriosus, clinical trials involving intravenous infusion of PGE were undertaken to attempt to maintain patency of the ductus as an alternative to emergency surgery in such patients. PGE infusions for a short time cause increased blood flow to the lungs and improve arterial oxygen saturation until the patient is stabilized so that the necessary corrective heart surgery can be per-

###### Dysmenorrhea 

The cause of dysmenorrhea is not known, but the disorder is usually associated with increased uterine contractions. The fact that some analgesics that are effective in the disorder also inhibit prostaglandin synthesis led to the suggestion that arachidonic acid metabolites might play a role in its pathogenesis. Prostaglandins of the E and F series are present in human endometrium, and intravenous infusion of either produces uterine contractions. In addition, both have effects on blood vessels and can potentially alter blood flow to the uterus. Several controlled trials using prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors have been performed in subjects with dysmenorrhea. Improvement appears to be greater with the prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors than with a placebo. Furthermore, PGF and PGE levels in menstrual blood can be decreased by inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis. However, a causeand-effect relationship has not been established between uterine production of prostaglandins and development of dysmenorrhea because of the complex nature of pain perception, the different phenomena that may be altered during menstruation (blood flow, muscle contraction, 

nerve discharge, etc.), and the problem of what physiologic fluid to sample for measurements of arachidonic acid metabolites. 

###### Asthma 

Arachidonic acid metabolites may play a role in the clinical manifestations of allergic and drugassociated asthma. PGF,, is a potent bronchoconstrictor, whereas PGE, is a potent bronchodilator. The effect of PGF,, is antagonized by PGE, and by catecholamines but not by atropine, antihistamines, serotonin antagonists, or alpha-adrenergic antagonists. In some studies TXA, is even more potent as a bronchoconstrictor than is PGF,,. Furthermore, nearly all known arachidonic acid metabolites can be formed by lung tissue, and many of these have significant effects on the lung. Patients with asthma have increased sensitivity to inhalation of PGF,,, whereas inhalation of PGE, causes comparable bronchodilation in asthmatics and in healthy subjects. Perhaps the most convincing evidence for a role for PGF in asthma has been obtained in studies involving administration of allergens to asthmatic patients. Increases in the plasma levels 

206 PROSTAGLANDINS, THROMBOXANES, AND EICOSANOIDS 

of PGF metabolite have been documented following induction of asthmatic symptoms by allergens. Negative results have also been obtained under circumstances in which PGF was measured in peripheral plasma and might have been normal because of degradation of PGF by the lung. Failure of prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors to alter the clinical course of allergic asthma have also been reported, but this does not exclude a role of PGF in the pathogenesis of asthma since no inhibitors are specific for PGF formation or action. An interesting subset of asthmatic patients have symptoms precipitated by drugs such as aspirin, indomethacin, and mefenamic acid — the syndrome of aspirin-sensitive asthma. If arachidonic acid metabolites play a role in this particular syndrome, it might involve selective inhibition of arachidonic acid metabolism such that substrate is shunted to the leukotriene pathway, thereby inducing formation of large amounts of bronchoconstrictor substances. Inflammatory response and immune response 

Drugs such as acetylsalicylic acid have long been used as antipyretics and anti-inflammatory agents as well as analgesics. The fact that structurally unrelated drugs, such as indomethacin and sodium salicylate, inhibit prostaglandin production in humans has lent strength to the idea that therapeutic doses of these drugs interfere with the inflammatory responses by inhibiting arachidonic acid metabolism. Many arguments have been marshaled to support this theory: (1) Several inflammatory stimuli such as histamine and bradykinin release endogenous prostaglandins in parallel. (2) Several arachidonic acid metabolites cause vasodilatation and hyperalgesia. (3) Prostaglandins are present in areas of inflammation, polymorphonuclear cells release PGE during phagocytosis, and PGE is chemotactic for leukocytes. (4) Some arachidonic metabolites cause increased vascular permeability, a feature of the inflammatory response that gives rise to local edema. (5) Vasodilatation induced by PGE is not abolished by atropine, propranolol, methysergide, or antihistamines, which are known antagonists of other possible mediators of the inflammatory 

response. Thus, PGE may have a direct inflammatory effect, and some potential mediators of inflammation act by influencing PGE release. (6) Various arachidonic acid metabolites can cause pain in appropriate animal models and hyperalgesia or an increased sensitivity to pain in humans. (7) PGE can cause fever, usually after injection into the cerebral ventricles or into the hypothalamus of experimental animals. (8) Pyrogens cause increased concentrations of prostaglandins in cerebrospinal fluid, whereas prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors decrease fever and decrease release of prostaglandin into cerebrospinal fluid. However, a definite cause-and-effect relationship has not been established between these metabolites and inflammation. Much of the investigative work has involved experimental animals, and subjective symptoms such as pain are difficult to quantify and can develop in response to many agents. The question is whether the amount of arachidonic acid metabolites that produce pain when injected locally are the same as the amounts normally formed during inflammation. Moreover, for valid interpretation of these studies, it is essential that both arachidonic acid metabolites and inhibitors of their synthesis be administered to determine whether the inflammatory response can be simulated. Otherwise, generation of arachidonic acid metabolites may be unrelated to the development of the inflammatory response. An alternative possibility is that prostanoids and eicosanoids are as yet unappreciated counterregulatory agents directed against the inflammatory response. Arachidonic acid metabolites have also been postulated to play a role in the immune response. Smali amounts of PGE can suppress stimulation of human lymphocytes by mitogens such as phytohemagglutinin. This observation and the fact that the inflammatory response is associated with the local release of arachidonic acid metabolites have led to the hypothesis that these substances act as negative modulators of lymphocyte function. The release of PGE by mitogen-stimulated lymphocytes may constitute a portion of a negative feedback control mechanism wherein lymphocyte activity is regulated. Sensitivity of lymphocytes to the inhibiting effects of PGE, has been reported to increase with age. Moreover, indomethacin augments lymphocyte responsiveness to mitogens to a greater degree in the el- 

###### REFERENCES 207 

derly. Lymphocytes cultured from patients with Hodgkin’s disease release more PGE, after the addition of phytohemagglutinin, and cellular responsiveness is enhanced by indomethacin in lymphocytes obtained from patients with Hodgkin’s disease. When suppressor cells were removed from the cultures, the amount of PGE, synthesized was diminished, and the responsiveness of the lymphocytes from the Hodgkin’s patients and controls was no longer different. These observations may explain the depressed cellular immunity in Hodgkin’s disease. 

###### CONCLUDING REMARKS 

The medical relevance of the arachidonic acid metabolites is burgeoning. We are only at the dawn of understanding their roles in human biology; certain of the best developed functions have been described in this chapter. Still other areas hold promise for the future. The most important message is that the evidence is overwhelming that these metabolites play vital roles in many aspects of physiology and pathophysiology. Consequently, it is essential that physicians become familiar with their known functions and postulated roles in health and disease.

#### SYNDROMES INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL 

###### CHARLES C. J. CARPENTER and R. BRADLEY SACK 

Infectious diarrheal disease remains one of the major health problems throughout the world. Diarrheal disease is both the leading cause of death among children throughout the developing world and a major contributing factor to the malnutrition that is rampant in large segments of Asia and Africa. Acute diarrheal illnesses continue to cause significant morbidity rates among small children even in the more industrially developed areas of Europe and North America. 

During the past decade, there has been an explosion of information concerning the infectious agents responsible for diarrhea, their pathogenetic mechanisms, the physiologic mechanisms by which the host responds to these microorganisms, and immunologic mechanisms that may provide a basis for prophylaxis against these illnesses. In 1967, a recognized enteropathogen could be identified in no more than 20 percent of patients with acute infectious diarrheal illness in most regions of the world. Today the recognized enteric pathogens listed in Table 1 are known to account for 75 to 85 percent of cases of acute diarrheal diseases in such geographically separate areas as Bangladesh and Costa Rica. Although each of the agents listed plays a significant and epidemiologically distinctive role in acute diarrheal illnesses, enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli and rotavirus have proved to be, on a worldwide basis, the most common causes of acute diarrheal disease. It is uncertain whether the small remaining group of diarrheal illnesses of unknown etiology reflect as yet unidentified pathogens or the insensitivity of current techniques<sup>fordefiningknownagents.</sup>

because of their relatively new recognition as enteropathogens (e.g., enterotoxigenic E. coli, rotavirus, Campylobacter jejuni) or because of significant new information about certain aspects of the illnesses they cause (e.g., Vibrio cholerae). Long-recognized pathogens such as Shigella and Salmonella will be mentioned only briefly in the light of new information about the illnesses they cause.

membrane translocation, and effect on adenylate cyclase, have provided insight into how other bacterial enterotoxins exert their pathophysiologic effects. Current data indicate that a large proportion of life-threatening acute diarrheal illnesses result from stimulation of electrolyte secretion in the small intestine by bacterial enterotoxins. 

Physiologic studies of normal intestinal absorption and secretion, and its alteration by bacterial enterotoxins, have provided the basis for important developments in therapy. Of greatest significance has been the recognition that the addition of glucose to orally administered electrolyte solutions makes it possible to replace adequately most diarrheal fluid losses by the oral route. 

In the late 1960s, the period immediately preceding the rapid advances in our understanding of new etiologic organisms, a sound method of treating diarrheal diseases by the oral route was developed on the basis of studies of cholera. During the past decade, essentially the same oral fluid repletion regimen has proved to be effective in all acute infectious diarrheal diseases in all age groups. This therapeutic approach, which was an example of the rapid application of a basic scientific observation to a major group of clinical illnesses, provides the cornerstone for treatment of acute diarrheal disease today. Understanding of the gut secretory mechanisms has also stimulated a realistic search for antisecretory drugs which may be safe and effective in patients. One such drug, chlorpromazine, appears promising; results with this agent have stimulated efforts to find similar antisecretory agents with even fewer potentially untoward side effects. 

The role of plasmids in the genetic control of the virulence of some of these organisms has been delineated. These developments will be discussed, particularly as they relate to the production of enterotoxins, colonization factors (fimbria), and invasiveness. The rapid advances in recombinant DNA technology have made the study of plasmids one of the most exciting and productive areas in our understanding of bacterial virulence. 

When pertinent, new information on the local secretory immune system of the host, and the op- 

timal means of stimulating this system by antigenic challenge, will be outlined. The combination of new antigens and different routes and timing of their administration may eventually bring about novel ways to control diarrheal disease through oral vaccines. This discussion will attempt to summarize as much of this information as is clinically relevant to an understanding and treatment of these diseases, particularly in adults. GENERAL CONCEPTS OF THE PATHOGENESIS AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF ACUTE DIARRHEAL ILLNESSES 

A general review of pathogenesis and pathophysiology will first be presented, as this provides the basis for the categorization of the agents listed in Table 1. Specific mechanisms will be presented, when appropriate, in the more detailed discussion of individual etiologic agents. 

###### Ingestion and colonization 

All the diarrheagenic agents must be ingested by mouth. Normally, the low pH of the stomach, the rapid transit time of the small bowel, and the antibody-producing cells in the lamina propria of the small bowel are adequate to keep the jejunum and proximal ileum relatively free of microorganisms (though not sterile). Furthermore, the ileocecal valve partially prevents the proximal migration of the huge numbers of bacteria in the large bowel, which are well adapted to the colonic ecological niche and are a relatively stable, slow-growing population. The diarrheagenic organisms are able to pass through the hostile environment of the stomach, because (1) they are acid-resistant (e.g., Shigella), (2) they are ingested in huge numbers that allow for a few survivors (e.g., V. cholerae or E. coli), or (3) they are ingested with food and therefore partially protected in their neutralized environments. Persons with decreased gastric acidity, either natural or surgically induced, are at an increased risk to develop acute diarrheal disease. 

Once in the small bowel, the organisms must either colonize (e.g., V. cholerae, E. coli) and/or 

###### PATHOGENESIS AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF ACUTE DIARRHEAL ILLNESSES 

invade (e.g., rotavirus, Norwalk agent) the mucosa there, or pass through into the terminal ileum (Salmonella) or colon (Shigella) to colonize and invade the mucosa there. The active peristalsis of the small bowel is an effective deterrent to the successful colonization of most organisms entering from the stomach. The organisms (V. cholerae, E. coli) that are able to colonize this area have developed special colonization factors such as the fimbria (hairlike projections from the bacterial cell wall surface) or lectins (special proteins that attach to specific carbohydrate-binding sites), which allow them to associate intimately with the mucosal cell surface and not be washed downstream by periStalsis.

The electrolyte pattern in the stool is remarkably constant whenever voluminous diarrhea is caused by any of the enterotoxigenic pathogens. The mean stool electrolyte concentrations, as shown in Table 2, can therefore serve as a guide to fluid repletion needs in all the enterotoxigenic diarrheal illnesses. 

The diarrheagenic organisms that do not have those special colonization factors pass into the terminal ileum and colon, and must compete there with the established flora for an ecological niche in which they can grow and invade the mucosa. Members of the fecal flora are known to produce substances (Bacteroides produce fatty acids; other enteric bacteria produce specific colicins) which serve to prevent newly introduced bacterial species from proliferating. It is probably the ability of these organisms to invade intestinal mucosa that allows them to multiply preferentially. 

In certain of the enterotoxigenic or secretory diarrheas, caused characteristically by V. cholerae and E. coli enterotoxins, the intestinal fluid losses may be massive, exceeding | liter per hour in adults. In the diarrheal illnesses caused by certain other bacterial enterotoxins (e.g., staphylococcal, clostridial), just as in diarrheal diseases caused by viruses and protozoa, the fluid losses seldom exceed 750 ml per day in adults. There are three well-recognized exceptions to the above scheme of enterotoxigenic diarrheas. In each of these exceptions, the culpable enterotoxin exerts its effect by some means other than stimulation of one of the known secretory mechanisms of the small bowel mucosa, and the resulting fluid losses are seldom voluminous: (1) Enterotoxins may be ingested directly in food, as with staphylococcal or Bacillus cereus food poisoning. These organisms make the.enterotoxins while they are growing to high concentrations in the food, rather than in the small intestine, (2) The Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin, which is produced by ingested bacilli in the small bowel, clearly damages the gut mucosa and produces a short-lived diarrhea in which the volume is characteristically small and the protein content high. (3) Clostridium difficile heavily colonizes the large bowel, rather than the small bowel, and 

###### Enterotoxigenic diarrheas 

Most bacteria that have colonized the small bowel do not invade mucosal cells, but grow to large numbers (10° to 108 organisms per milliliter of fluid) and produce enterotoxins which are ultimately the cause of the diarrhea. The enterotoxins bind to the mucosal cells and cause hypersecretion of isotonic fluid at a rate which overwhelms the reabsorptive capacity of the colon. Effortless diarrhea results. In this type of diarrhea, there is almost no inflammatory response by the host, and the patient has little or no fever or other systemic symptoms. The diarrhea that results is watery, often voluminous, with an electrolyte content that reflects its source of production, and without protein or inflammatory cells. The loss of this diarrheal fluid results in predictable saline depletion, base-deficit acidosis, and potassium deficiency. The amount and

produces its enterotoxins(s) which is cytotoxic. The enterotoxins(s) in turn causes severe mucosal damage to the colon and may produce lesions similar to those produced by Shigella. Although the lesions are similar to those in shigellosis, C. difficile is not invasive per se. 

###### Invasive diarrheas 

Some bacateria (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni) can also invade the upper small bowel and produce an inflammatory diarrhea by this mechanism. Most organisms in this category, however, invade primarily the lower ileum (e.g., Salmonella) or the large bowel (e.g., Shigella, Yersinia enterocolitica, and usually C. jejuni). The organisms that invade the colon may cause changes which are indistinguishable on sigmoidoscopy from ulcerative colitis. They may also, rarely, invade the bloodstream (Salmonella, Shigella, and C. jejuni ), and they occasionally produce mesenteric lymphadenitis, which simulates acute appendicitis (C. jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica). There is a marked inflammatory response to these invasive organisms, and the stool contains pus cells, large amounts of protein, and often gross blood. Usually, frequent small amounts of stool are passed, accompanied by abdominal cramps, tenesmus, and fever. Significant dehydration rarely results from this kind of diarrhea, because the diarrheal fluid volume is relatively small compared with that caused by the secretory enterotoxins. 

Viruses must of necessity grow in host cells, and by definition both the rotavirus and the Norwalk agent produce invasive diarrheal disease. Both the rotavirus and the Norwalk agent

characteristically damage the villous epithelial cells, the degree of damage ranging from modest distortion of epithelial cells to sloughing of villi. Presumably both the rotavirus and the Norwalk agent cause diarrhea by interfering with the absorption of normal intestinal secretions by the small bowel villi. The stool is usually watery and is more characteristic of a noninvasive process, with few inflammatory cells. Large amounts of reducing substances are found in the stool, resulting from malabsorption of carbohydrates. Patients may have some degree of fever and mild abdominal complaints. Although most diarrheagenic agents produce either invasive or enterotoxic disease, there are probably situations in which a combination of both processes contributes to the diarrheal illness. Certain strains of Shigella, nontyphoidal Salmonella, Y. enterocolitica, and C. jejuni have the capacity to produce enterotoxins in vitro. Such enterotoxins may play a contributory role in the disease process. However, from evidence now available, the invasive capacity of these organisms is of paramount importance in their ability to produce disease. 

###### Natural course of disease 

All the acute infectious diarrheal diseases (with the exception of pseudomembranous enterocolitis), are generally self-limiting with adequate fluid repletion therapy, and each has a clinical course which lasts 1 to 9 days. Recovery is thought to be mediated, at least in part, through the local secretory immune system. In some illnesses, antibiotics are clearly of value in shortening the course of the illness (V. cholerae, Shigella) (Table 3). In others, there has been little or no satisfactory demonstration of the value of antimicrobials. During recovery, the patients develop an antibody response to certain antigens from the responsible microbial agents. In some cases, this can be measured in serum and is of diagnostic usefulness (rotavirus, Norwalk agent, V. cholerae). In other cases, though serum antibodies develop, they are type-specific and therefore of use only where the serotype of the infecting organism is known (e.g., C. jejuni). In still others, the immunologic response is not uniformly reflected in serum antibody levels, and

###### GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS OF EPIDEMIOLOGY 

Since simple, sensitive techniques for establishing the diagnosis of certain of the newly recognized etiologic agents (e.g., rotavirus, enterotoxigenic E. coli) are not yet generally available, relevant epidemiological information about the diseases they produce is still meager. A few major observations have emerged, however, that will help to give a general overview. 

Newborn infants arrive in a world full of hostile microorganisms and are transiently and partially protected by placentally transferred serum antibody (largely IgG) and, in the case of nursing infants, by passively transferred antibodies contained in breast milk (largely IgA). Both types and amounts of antibodies reflect the immunologic experience of the mother. Subsequent exposure to, and development of immunity against, specific enteric pathogens will depend on the geographic area in which the child is raised. In the developing countries, where sanitation is generally inadequate, young children develop multiple episodes of diarrhea (often four to eight per year) during the first 2 to 3 years of life, during which they presumably develop intestinal immunity to the majority of enteropathogens in their immediate environment. Most of these diarrheal episodes are mild, but some are lifethreatening. All probably contribute negatively to the nutritional development of the child. In these areas, enterotoxigenic E. coli and rotavirus are the most common etiologic agents in the first 2 years of life, producing the large majority of diarrheal illnesses. Shigella infections are far less common during this period. 

By way of contrast, in the developed world, infants and small children have many fewer episodes of diarrhea, and the most common etiologic agent is the rotavirus. Enterotoxigenic E. coli and Shigella are infrequently seen except in a few poorly developed geographic areas. Most episodes are mild and probably have little or no impact on the nutritional health of the children. On the other hand, in adults throughout the world, clinically significant diarrhea is a rela- 

tively infrequent event, outside of specific epidemics, such as cholera, or common-source outbreaks due to contaminated food or water. This is probably due to the acquired protective immunity of the adult living in the developing world and to the lack of exposure in the adult living in the developed world. 

The same etiologic agents are, however, responsible for the diarrheas of both adults and children. This is probably best demonstrated in the immunologically inexperienced tourists from the developed world who visit the developing countries. They have an extremely high incidence of diarrheal disease, and the organisms responsible are the same ones that cause a major portion of the diarrhea in children of the specific country visited. 

###### Association between diarrheal disease in humans and animals 

The association between the diarrheal illnesses of humans and domestic animals is an intriguing one. Both animal and human rotaviruses are common causes of diarrhea in newborns of the various species; yet the viruses seem to be species-specific in that animal rotaviruses are not known to cause disease in humans. Likewise, enterotoxigenic E. coli strains are a common cause of diarrhea in young calves, pigs, and sheep, just as they are in young children in the developing countries; yet the serotypes and colonization factors seem to be species-specific. Since the enterotoxins themselves are, however, closely related structurally and immunologically, it is possible that plasmids containing enterotoxigenic genes are exchanged between animal and human strains. No definitive evidence for this has yet been produced. Other enteric pathogens, such as Salmonella, have well-established animal-to-human transmission patterns. Two of the newly recognized enteric pathogens. C. jejuni and Y. enterocolitica, are commonly carried in domestic animals in which they may cause diarrheal disease. The extent to which animal-to-human transmission contributes to disease caused by these pathogens has not yet been established. 

Still other diarrheagenic agents (e.g., Shigella, V. cholerae) have no known mammalian reservoirs other than humans.

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

###### GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF MANAGEMENT Electrolyte repletion therapy 

Intravenous fluids The therapeutic approach to fluid replacement which emanated from studies of cholera has resulted in the definition of intravenous fluid regimens that can be equally well applied to other acute diarrheal illnesses. Whenever voluminous infectious diarrhea occurs in adults, the same characteristic pattern of electrolyte loss is observed. With relatively small volumes of diarrheal fluid loss, the stool potassium concentration increases, probably as a result of more prolonged action of aldosterone on sodiumpotassium exchange during passage through the large bowel. However, when large quantities of fluid are lost, the electrolyte content remains remarkably constant. The electrolyte characteristics are somewhat altered in diarrhea in young children in that the mean sodium and chloride concentrations are 15 to 20 meq per liter less than that observed in adults. With diarrheal disease of viral etiology, sodium and chloride concentrations are even further reduced. Since all pathophysiologic manifestations of the noninvasive secretory diarrheas are due to the intestinal fluid loss, these abnormalities can rapidly be corrected by intravenous infusion of isotonic fluids approximating those lost via the intestinal tract. A uniformly effective solution can be prepared simply by the addition of 5 g sodium chloride, 4 g sodium bicarbonate, and 1 g potassium chloride to a liter of pyrogen-free water. Other fluid preparations, such as lactated Ringer’s solution, can likewise be used with uniformly good results. With the severely ill, hypotensive patient, the intravenous fluids are initially infused rapidly, at a rate of up to 100 ml/ min, until a strong radial pulse is restored; fluids are then infused at a less rapid rate until skin turgor has returned to normal. Subsequent maintenance intravenous fluid administration can be guided by the clinical appearance of the patient, including vital signs, appearance of neck veins, and skin turgor. Alternatively, intestinal fluid output, when measurable, can be replaced by equal quantities of intravenous fluid. It is important to emphasize that clinical evaluation alone can provide an adequate guide to fluid replace- 

ment in toxigenic diarrheal illnesses. If the approach of matching stool volume with intravenous fluids is used, this should always be combined with the more consistently reliable clinical evaluation. The same principles of intravenous fluid therapy are applicable to patients with dehydrating diarrheas caused by other microbiological agents. If intravenous fluids are administered in adequate quantities throughout the diarrheal illness, virtually every patient with secretory diarrhea caused by toxigenic bacteria should be restored to health. Complications, such as acute renal failure secondary to renal hypoperfusion, are exceedingly rare if intravenous fluid balance is rapidly restored and maintained throughout the course of the illness. 

Orai fluid therapy A major advance in the treatment of diarrheal illnesses occurred during the late 1960s, when field studies clearly demonstrated that fluid and electrolytes could be adequately restored, by the oral route, to actively purging cholera patients. This development resulted from the basic observation that intraluminal glucose enhances sodium absorption by the mammalian small bowel. This observation, coupled with the demonstrations that there is no disruption in the gut mucosal architecture and that intraluminal glucose is absorbed normally during cholera, led to a trial of oral glucose-containing electrolyte solutions in the treatment of cholera. A series of studies demonstrated clearly that even actively purging cholera patients can be maintained in fluid balance by the administration of isotonic glucose-containing electrolyte solutions. The optimal concentration of glucose in such solutions is roughly 20 g per liter; a uniformly effective solution can be prepared by the addition of 20 g glucose, 3.5 g sodium chloride, 2.5 g sodium bicarbonate, and 1.5 g potassium chloride to a liter of drinking water (Table 4). Such fluids are administered initially in large quantities, 250 ml every 15 min in adults, until fluid balance has been restored, as gauged by clinical observations. The fluids are thereafter administered in quantities sufficient to maintain normal fluid balance; if stool output is measured, roughly 1.5 liters of oral glucose-electrolyte solution should be given orally for each liter of stool. It is impor-

Most patients with cholera can be treated adequately by oral fluids from the time of onset of illness. A few patients, who are already in hypovolemic shock when first seen by the physician, will require an initial infusion of intravenous fluids in quantities sufficient to restore an adequate circulating blood volume before they can retain orally administered fluids. The development of an effective oral fluid repletion regimen has made a major impact on treatment of cholera in those endemic areas where sterile intravenous fluids are in very short supply. 

Since the effects of the E. coli enterotoxins are similar to those of cholera enterotoxin, patients with diarrhea caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli likewise respond well to oral glucose-electrolyte solutions. 

Furthermore, since a similar pattern of fluid loss occurs in diarrheal illnesses caused by other intestinal pathogens, patients with fluid depletion caused by other microbial agents (e.g., rotavirus, Salmonella) have likewise responded well to oral glucose-electrolyte therapy. Although the pathogenesis of diarrheal disease caused by the rotavirus is quite different from that caused by enterotoxigenic bacteria, and structural damage to the small bowel mucosa is a consistent finding in rotavirus diarrheas, children with rotavirus illness have consistently responded well to oral glucose-electrolyte replacement. So it now appears that individuals in all age groups, with acute infectious diarrheal disease of any etiology, 

may be treated by a single oral fluid replacement regimen, which can be readily obtained in almost all areas of the world. A modest modification of the fluid replacement regimen, for use in areas where glucose is not available, involves the substitution of 40 g sucrose for 20 g glucose in each liter of oral replacement fluid. The sucrose is metabolized by intestinal sucrase to glucose and fructose, and therefore appears to work as well as equimolar amounts of glucose in the oralelectrolyte solution. 

###### NEWER ASPECTS OF RECOGNIZED AGENTS OF ACUTE DIARRHEAL DISEASE 

This section deals only with new information bearing upon previously described, recognized enteropathogens. Therefore, the discussion will deal only with those aspects of the illnesses to which the new information is relevant. 

###### Vibrio cholerae, O group 1 

New developments of major importance have occurred in regard to epidemiology, pathophysiologic mechanisms, and potential therapeutic approaches. 

Epidemiology Vibrio cholerae, O group 1, whichis the only one of the enterotoxigenic bacteria that has the capacity to cause pandemic disease, has been found to exhibit epidemiologic properties not previously suspected. A limited cholera outbreak, secondary to contaminated seafood, occurred in Louisiana near the Gulf of Mexico in 1978. This was the first time that cholera had appeared de novo in the United States since World War I, except for a single case in 1973 in Port Lavaca, Texas. Examination of the strains involved in the Louisiana epidemic indicated that they were different from the pandemic strain being isolated from the rest of the world, but were identical to the strain isolated previously in Texas. This suggests that the organism was able to survive this 5-year period in salt water or associated with the plant or animal life in these waters. This is the first time that V. cholerae, O group 1, has been suspected of having its own free-living cycle in water. Our understanding of 

###### 216 

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

the epidemiology of the organisms and their reservoirs may need revising, as additional studies are being done to confirm these speculations. 

Pathophysiology Cholera is the prototype of the noninvasive secretory bacterial diarrheas, as the bacterium neither invades nor damages the gut mucosa, and all pathophysiologic effects are mediated by a single enterotoxin which acts only on the small bowel mucosal cell. Recent studies have further defined the molecular mechanisms by which cholera enterotoxin causes gut fluid loss. The importance of these observations transcends their relevance to cholera in that one of the two E. coli enterotoxins has been shown to act by the same molecular pathways, and there is suggestive evidence that similar enterotoxins may occasionally be produced by other enteric bacteria. 

In the pathogenesis of cholera, those ingested microorganisms that survive passage through the gastric acid barrier multiply rapidly in the small intestine and produce an enterotoxin. The same protein enterotoxin, with a molecular weight of 84,000 daltons, is produced by all toxigenic strains of V. cholerae. This enterotoxin is composed of two moieties: a binding (B) moiety which consists of five identical subunits of approximately 11,500 daltons; and an activating (A) moiety which is composed of two unequal subunits, linked through a single disulfide bond. The A, subunit (~ 5000 daltons) probably serves only to connect the A, subunit (~ 23,000 daltons) to the binding moiety. The amino acid sequences of the binding subunits have been determined; the terminal sequences share considerable homology with the binding units of certain peptide hormones [e.g., thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)]. Each of the B subunits of the cholera toxin has the ability to bind to a Gy, monosialoganglioside molecule in the small intestinal mucosal cell wall. This binding occurs very rapidly and becomes irreversible within minutes after the initial contact of the binding subunits with the G,,, monosialogangliosides. Following the rapid binding of the B subunits to the cell wall, the A, subunit, which contains adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-ribosyltransferase activity, migrates through the epithelial cell; it then stimulates, by a catalytic process, the transfer of ADP-ribose from nicotinamide-adenine dinu- 

cleotide (NAD) to a guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-binding protein that regulates adenylate cyclase activity. This ADP-ribosylation of the GTP-binding protein inhibits the GTP “turnoff” reaction and causes a sustained increase in adenylate cyclic activity. The resultant increase in intracellular levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cyclic AMP) leads to rapid secretion of electrolytes into the small bowel lumen. The putative mechanism of action of the cholera enterotoxin is illustrated diagrammatically in Fig. 1. The G,,, monosialoganglioside receptors are present in the wall of virtually ali mammalian cells and occur in high concentration in the gut mucosal cell wall. There are roughly 1 million potential binding sites per gut mucosal cell, and the occupation of only 50,000 such binding sites by the cholera enterotoxin appears to cause maximum stimulation of cellular adenylate cyclase and maximum gut fluid secretion. The rapid cellular binding of the toxin is followed by a lag period which has been shown, in vitro, to be dependent upon temperature, the concentration of enterotoxin, and the density of Gy ganglioside receptors in the cell wall. The lag period presumably reflects the time required for the A subunit to penetrate the lipid bilayer and become reduced to the catalytic A, peptide. The lag period is followed by a gradual increase in adenylate cyclase activity and gut fluid secretion. In the mammalian gut at body temperature, the lag period varies from 10 to 30 min, and adenylate cyclase activity and fluid production generally reach maximum levels within 3 to 4h after the binding event. Adenylate cyclase activity and fluid production then persist at a maximum level for a period of 8 to 12 h, following which fluid production gradually subsides. The intestinal fluid transport is generally back to normal levels within 36 h after a single exposure to toxin, which probably reflects the fact that the cells originally exposed to toxin have been shed in the normal turnover of gut mucosa epithelial cells. 

Current evidence indicates that the increased cyclic AMP causes increased sodium-dependent chloride secretion; the increased intracellular cyclic AMP also prevents sodium and chloride absorption via the sodium chloride cotransport mechanism across the brush border. Current data support the concept that the cyclic AMP 

###### NEWER ASPECTS OF RECOGNIZED AGENTS OF ACUTE DIARRHEAL DISEASE 

exerts its direct chloride secretory action primarily on crypt cells and its inhibition of neutral sodium chloride absorption primarily on villous cells. The net effect of the increased intracellular cyclic AMP is to cause secretion of an isotonic fluid throughout the entire small bowel. The cholera toxin does not cause fluid secretion by the stomach, and its effects on fluid movement in the human colon are minimal. The cholera stool, essentially the sum of the fluids produced by each of the small bowel segments, slightly modified by the colon, is an isotonic fluid, with a bicarbonate concentration twice that of normal plasma and a mean potassium concentration five times that of plasma (Table 2). The rate of intestinal fluid loss by the adult cholera patient may reach | liter per hour. The duration of the diarrheal disease, if untreated by antimicrobials, may exceed 5 days. All pathophysiologic effects of cholera can be readily reversed by the administration of appropriate replacement fluids by either the intravenous or the oral route, as discussed above.

In light of the increased understanding of the pathogenetic mechanisms in cholera, a large number of potential antisecretory agents have been evaluated. Of these, only three have shown potential therapeutic usefulness, since they can reverse the secretory process after the enterotoxin has been bound to the intestinal mucosa. These substances are chlorpromazine, nicotinic acid, and berberine. Of these, only chlorpromazine has been studied in humans, under controlled conditions, as an antisecretory agent. It is promising in that it rapidly decreases the rate of intestinal fluid loss, but it has the significant disadvantage of causing drowsiness in patients. Neither of the other two agents has been evaluated in a controlled field trial.

###### Vibrio cholerae, non-O group 1 

Previously called noncholera vibrios or nonagglutinating vibrios (NAGs), these organisms are now being recognized increasingly as a cause of acute diarrheal disease. Such vibrios may cause up to 5 percent of acute diarrheal illness in cholera-endemic areas and have occasionally been incriminated in waterborne microepidemics of diarrheal disease. These organisms are known to be associated with aquatic environments, but 

their ecological niche has not been studied extensively. A large number (approximately 50) of different serotypes have been identified. This group of vibrios is pathogenetically heterogeneous. Some of these strains produce an enterotoxin indistinguishable from cholera enterotoxin, whereas other strains produce an enterotoxin similar to the heat-stable E. coli enterotoxin. 

###### 217 

###### 218 

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

###### Shigella 

Shigella organisms have been found to produce an enterotoxin which is cytotoxic to tissue culture cells and is capable of causing isotonic fluid secretion by the small intestine of experimental animals. The role of the enterotoxin in disease production is not certain, but it may be responsible for the initial watery diarrhea which sometimes occurs during the first 24 to 36 h of illness in patients with shigellosis. 

###### Vibrio parahemolyticus 

This organism continues to be isolated primarily from patients with diarrhea (often in outbreaks) secondary to ingestion of contaminated seafood. Its ecological niche is being intensively studied; it is now known to be a common inhabitant of the waters of Chesapeake Bay, as well as other coastal waters. 

The exact mechanisms of virulence of V. parahemolyticus has still not been defined. Although occasional strains have been shown to produce an enterotoxin, this organism appears to cause illness primarily on the basis of its ability to invade the terminal ileum and colon. The hemolysin produced by the organism, which is characteristic of isolates from diseased persons, does not seem to be a virulence factor. 

###### Nontyphoidal Sa/monella 

There has been much concern recently over the possibility that widespread use of antibiotics in the feed of domestic animals may lead to a major public health problem in humans because of the selection of R factor-carrying fecal organisms, particularly Salmonella, which could then be transmitted to humans. Although this scenario has not yet been unequivocally demonstrated, there has been a concerted effort to alter the animal feeding practices in order to minimize this potential problem. 

Certain strains of Salmonella typhimurium have been reported to produce cholera-like enterotoxins, although the role of such enterotoxins in disease production is not understood. Invasiveness, as with Shigella, seems to be a prerequisite for the initiation of diarrheal disease. There is no new information that would alter the recommendation of not using antibiotics in 

uncomplicated acute diarrheal disease caused by Salmonella. Such use has been shown not to shorten the clinical disease, but only to prolong the carrier state following recovery. 

###### Norwaik agent (parvovirus-like agent) 

This group of parvovirus-like agents, shown to be responsible for acute diarrheal disease in humans, usually in outbreak situations, has not yet been cultivated in vitro. The Norwalk agent has, however, been studied, as has the rotavirus, by making purified preparations from diarrheal stool. 

The virus can be detected in stool by means of electron microscopy and radioimmunoassay techniques. Antibodies can also be assayed using a radioimmunoassay method. Using these methods, Norwalk agent has been found to account fer up to 10 percent of cases of traveler’s diarrhea and to be a common cause of infection in young children in the tropics. The epidemiology of the disease has been studied in only a limited way because of the difficulties of recognizing the agent and the disease it causes. 

###### Entamoeba histolytica 

This organism has been found to produce a cytotoxic enterotoxin in axenic culture filtrates. The role of this enterotoxin in disease production is being evaluated. 

###### Giardia lamblia 

Epidemiologic studies have demonstrated that this protozoan is a far more common cause of acute diarrheal disease in adults than was formerly appreciated. In 2 of the last 5 years, G. lamblia has been the most frequently recognized cause of waterborne outbreaks of diarrheal disease in the United States; 23 epidemics in the past 10 years have been associated with breakdowns in municipal water purification systems. Although it is most prevalent in the Rocky Mountain states, several surveys have indicated that 2 to 10 percent of North Americans are asymptomatic excretors of Giardia cysts. Recent circumstantial evidence has suggested that beavers may serve as animal reservoirs.

The clinical course timicrobial but metronidazole has drochloride; relapse rates of roughly 10 percent with either of these agents. 

The identification of several new enteric pathogens, and the definition of the clinical syndromes they produce, have been exciting developments of the past decade. Whenever possible, the characteristics of the new etiologic agents will be described in the traditional sequence (i.e., epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnostic techniques, and management). In several instances, however, available information is too scanty to permit so complete a description. Enterotoxigenic E. coli 

Epidemiology Although so-called enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) strains have previously been incriminated in limited outbreaks of infantile diarrheal disease, especially in nurseries, it was not until the late 1960s that enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) strains were first recognized as etiologic agents of diarrheal disease in humans. At this time, they were shown to be responsible for severe cholera-like disease in adults in Calcutta. Enterotoxigenic E. coli strains have subsequently been shown to be worldwide in distribution. In most of the developing countries, they have been incriminated as the most common cause of acute diarrhea in small children, and they have clearly been identified as the most common etiologic agent in traveler’s diarrhea. They are also an occasional cause of hospital nursery outbreaks of diarrhea, as well as of common-source (food or water) outbreaks in the developed nations. 

At present, serotyping of ETEC strains is most valuable as an epidemiologic tool for identifying transmission of organisms. Serotyping may eventually be more useful as a diagnostic test, when pools of appropriate antiserum be- 

come available. Serotyping of EPEC, when done correctly, is of use in identifying outbreaks of diarrhea in nurseries, but it is of equivocal value in assigning pathogenic significance to isolates of E. coli from sporadic cases of diarrhea. 

Pathogenesis Diarrheal disease caused by E. coli is far more variable than that caused by cholera, because of the multiple pathogenetic mechanisms which may be involved. As with cholera, a true secretory diarrhea is caused by ETEC, and at least two distinct toxins, a heatlabile toxin (LT) and a heat-stable toxin (ST), may be produced by E. coli strains which have colonized the small bowel. Unlike cholera, in which the ability to produce enterotoxin is chromosomally mediated and a single toxin is produced by all pathogenic strains, the ability of E. coli to produce enterotoxins is plasmid-mediated, and specific plasmids code for the production of LT and ST. Genes for either or both of these toxins may be on a single plasmid. The E. coli LT has a molecular weight of approximately 83,000 daltons and is structurally similar to, but not identical with, the cholera toxin. As in the case of cholera enterotoxin, the primary binding site for the E. coli LT is the Gy, monosialoganglioside. Having bound to the gut mucosal cell, the E. coli LT also stimulates adenylate cyclase via ADP-ribosylation, with kinetics similar to those of cholera toxin, causing delayed secretion of isotonic fluid which persists for many hours after binding of the toxin. Like the cholera enterotoxin, the E. coli LT also has binding and activating moieties. The binding subunits are antigenically similar, but not identical, to those of the cholera toxin. The activating, or A,, subunit of the E. coli LT is also similar, but not identical, to the A, subunit of the cholera enterotoxin. Although the LT may be produced by a large number of E. coli serotypes, current data suggest that an identical LT molecule is produced by all such strains. 

The E. coli ST is quite different from LT in that it exhibits a rapid onset of action, does not bind to gangliosides of the mucosal cell wall, and is of low molecular weight—less than 2000 daltons. It is not antigenic in its natural state. The ST appears to act by stimulation of guanylate cyclase with resultant cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cyclic GMP) accumulation in muco-
