Isolate of enterotoxigenic E. coli demonstrating pili, hairlike projections designated colonization factor antigens (CFA). The CFA appear to be critical virulence factors in causing adherence of the E. coli to the small bowel mucosa. (From Evans et al.) 

sal cells. The kinetics of ST action are strikingly different from those of LT in that ST causes an almost immediate increase in gut fluid secretion after exposure to the gut mucosa, and its secretory effect rapidly disappears when ST is washed out of the gut lumen. The increased levels of intracellular guanylate cyclase cause chloride secretion by gut mucosal epithelial cells, in a manner similar to that seen with the cholera enterotoxin, but the ST does not alter neutral sodium chloride absorption by the brush border cotransport route. Although the binding properties have not yet been established, the binding appears to be specific for small bowel mucosal cells. In certain experimental animals, the E. coli ST has no detectable effect on duodenal mucosa, although it exhibits its characteristic effect on jejunal and ileal mucosa. Unlike the cholera enterotoxin and E. coli LT, the E. coli ST does not exhibit its characteristic effect on cyclase activation in nonintestinal tissues. Despite the different kinetics, the major physiologic effect of ST is also to increase net movement of isotonic fluid from blood to gut, resulting in a watery diarrhea which may be indistinguishable from cholera. An E. coli strain may produce LT, ST, or both enterotoxins, depending upon the plasmids it carries. The enterotoxin types may vary with the geographic location and serotype. In certain geographic areas, diarrheal disease is more commonly caused by E. coli strains which produce 

both ST and LT; in other regions, E. coli strains which produce ST alone predominate. The plasmids carrying the genetic material controlling enterotoxin production have been well characterized. These are for the most part transferable plasmids (like R factors) and can be transferred among strains through bacterial conjugation. The plasmid DNA sequences controlling exterotoxin production have now been studied extensively by investigators using recombinant DNA technology. The LT and ST genes have been cloned; the ST gene has been shown to be a transposon (a DNA replicon that can insert itself into the chromosome as well as onto different areas of the plasmid). Methods are being developed using DNA probes for the direct recognition of the gene sequences in the bacteria as a diagnostic tool; such methodology could replace the current techniques for identifying the LT and ST themselves. Furthermore, DNA responsible for the production of only the A or the B subunits can be placed on separate plasmids, which may be useful in eventual vaccine production. Enterotoxigenic E. coli strains also produce colonization factors that allow them to adhere to the small bowel mucosa rather than to be washed through the intestinal lumen. Some of these factors have been identified as fimbria or pili (hairlike projections of protein material extending from the cell surface) and designated as colonization factor antigens (CFA I and II) (Fig. 2). These occur, however, only on certain ETEC strains and are related to the serotype of the organism; it is suspected that other colonization factors will be found to account for the remainder of the strains. Colonization factors are also plasmid-mediated, and indeed a single plasmid may carry genes for both enterotoxin and CFA production. Although enterotoxin and CFA production are mediated by transferable plasmids, and therefore one may postulate that any E. coli strain could harbor them, in nature this does not seem to occur. Certain serotypes of E. coli seem to be especially adept at carrying these plasmids, although the reasons for this are not known. Furthermore, it seems that there must be a combination of O, K, and H antigens (as well as often a certain characteristic fermentation pattern, or biotype) in order for enterotoxin plasmids to be harbored successfully. Some serotypes more 

NEWER ETIOLOGIC AGENTS OF ACUTE DIARRHEA PPA | 

often produce both LT and ST, such as O6:K15:H16, and others ST only, such as O128:H (antigens variable). Likewise some serotypes carry CFA I, such as O78:H11, and others CFA II, such as 06:K15:H16. A summary of some characteristic associations is given in Table 5. Some enterotoxigenic serotypes are found worldwide, whereas others aré more localized in distribution. In fact, each geographic area studied appears to have a characteristic spectrum of typical ETEC serotypes. The ETEC serotypes, with a few exceptions, are different from the enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) serotypes previously described as the cause of nursery outbreaks of diarrhea; the EPEC serotypes do not produce LT or ST. Recent information from adult volunteer challenge experiments and from animal models suggests, however, that at least some of the epidemic-associated EPEC strains are enterotoxigenic, although the enterotoxins they produce are different from the LT and ST of ETEC strains. Clinical features The clinical features of ETEC-mediated diarrhea are characteristic of a small bowel secretory diarrhea. The stool is watery and contains little or no inflammatory exudate. The patient is usually afebrile but may have moderate abdominal cramping sensations. Although the average patient with ETEC-associated diarrhea is less ill than the average patient with cholera, patients more severely ill with ETEC may be clinically indistinguishable from cholera patients. The relationship of the clinical symptoms to the enterotoxin type produced by the etiologic agent has been studied in one area of the developing world. Patients with ETEC producing both LT and ST had disease which was more severe and longer lasting than patients with ETEC producing only ST. The differences were not great enough to be of any diagnostic value in a single patient, but they were statistically significant between the two groups of patients. 

Diagnostic techniques Enterotoxigenic E. coli strains appear, on primary isolation plates, as all other E. coli strains, and therefore their ability to make enterotoxin must be demonstrated. This is done presently by randomly picking approximately 5 to 10 typical E. coli colonies

Although animal models were originally used for the demonstration of enterotoxins, at present the methods of choice are the following: (1) For LT, the use of a tissue culture system, such as the mouse Y 1 adrenal cell, or the Chinese hamster ovary cells. These cells respond morphologically to stimulation of their adenylate cyclase systems by the LT. A newer method, which will probably largely replace the tissue culture assays, involves the use of an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method in which either Gy, ganglioside or specific antibody is used to bind the LT as the initial step in the assay. (2) Unfortunately, an animal model, the infant mouse, is still the most useful assay for ST. Once methods for producing an antiserum to ST are successful, an immunologic test, such as the ELISA, should replace this cumbersome test. 

Once ETEC strains are recognized, they can be characterized further according to serotype, ability to produce colonization factor, and antibiotic sensitivities. 

The determination of anti-LT in acute and convalescent serums is not generally helpful as a diagnostic procedure, except in highly endemic areas. 

Since ETEC strains are rarely isolated in the United States, except for such areas as the reservations of American Indians, where water supply and sewage disposal may be suboptimal, one could argue against setting up the presently known diagnostic techniques in domestic laboratories except reference laboratories. Clearly, the laboratories in which ETEC would be seen frequently are those of the developing world. Fur- 

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

ther simplification of diagnostic tests will be required before the recognition of ETEC becomes a routine diagnostic event. Management Replacement of fluid and electrolytes lost in the stool by either the intravenous or oral route is the mainstay of therapy. Since most ETEC diarrhea is mild to moderate, oral therapy alone is almost always adequate. Oral therapy packets, as used in the rest of the world, are not yet commercially available in the United States, but they probably will be shortly. Fluids, such as juices containing some sugar and salt, are probably adequate for most adults in the developed world since the disease is relatively mild in these individuals. 

Enterotoxigenic FE. coli strains in many parts of the world are unusually sensitive to antibiotics. This is thought to be due to the observation that plasmids of similar types (incompatibility groups) cannot be harbored by the same bacteria. Thus, E. coli strains which harbor an enterotoxin plasmid cannot also carry a similar R-factor plasmid. In spite of this, there are yet no published data which indicate a clear effectiveness of antibiotics in treatment. In the one published controlled study, done in Bangladesh, the natural course of the illness was short, so that a clinical effect of antibiotics could not be measured clearly. In other parts of the world, however, where the disease often lasts longer than 2 days, it is probable that antibiotics would be effective in reducing the length of illness, as is the case with cholera. If this proves to be the case, tetracycline would seem to be the drug of choice in these areas. In some areas of the world ETEC strains, like non-ETEC strains, are often antibiotic-resistant. It is postulated that, in these strains, the enterotoxin plasmids and the R factors are of different plasmid types and can therefore be harbored by a single E. coli host. Indeed, in rare instances, the genes for enterotoxin production and antibiotic resistance reside in the same plasmid. In summary, ETEC strains are now recognized as one of the most significant causes of diarrhea in the developing world. They are of particular interest because of the enterotoxins they produce and the plasmid DNA which controls their production. Immunologic control may eventually be possible through the use of live 

Other enteric bacilli oral vaccines, utilizing live E. coli strains containing appropriate nontoxic virulence antigens which have been developed through recombinant DNA technology.

Certain E. coli strains, closely related taxonomically to Shigella species, may produce invasive diarrhea similar to shigellosis. These strains appear to belong to a limited number of serotypes, generally different from ETEC and EPEC. Invasive E. coli strains are recognized as rare causes of acute diarrheal disease in Southeast Asia and North America, but are somewhat more frequently implicated in clinical illness in Eastern Europe. Thus far, no clinical isolates of invasive E. coli have been found to produce enterotoxin. Non-enterotoxin-producing, noninvasive E. coli It is clear that some factors in addition to the ST and LT may play a pathogenetic role in diarrheal illnesses caused by E. coli, in that commonly associated features such as malaise, abdominal pain, and myalgias cannot be attributed to either of these two enterotoxins. Recent studies have indicated that diarrheal disease may be associated with E. coli strains which produce neither enterotoxin, either in vitro or in anima! models, and which do not demonstrate the capacity to invade, although they heavily colonize the small bowel and cause demonstrable damage to the intestinal microvilli. Possibly other enteropathogens may also produce diarrheal disease without producing any of the currently recognized enterotoxins and without invading

###### Campylobacter jejuni 

Campylobacter jejuni was first etiologically associated with acute diarrheal disease in humans in 1972. By 1979, C. jejuni was second only to Giardia as a recognized cause of waterborne outbreaks of acute diarrheal disease in the United States. This organism was previously called “related vibrios” and was included in the species Vibrio fetus and Campylobacter fetus. Campylobacter jejuni is the only one of this group of organisms that is clearly related to acute diarrheal disease. 

Epidemiology Although it is suspected that C. jejuni has a worldwide distribution, and that the usual mode of human infection is from animals, i.€., aS a zoonotic disease, adequate epidemiologic support for this hypothesis is not yet available. Campylobacter jejuni has been found in the intestinal flora of many animal species, including birds (particularly poultry), cows, dogs, and sheep. Organisms can be transmitted to humans by the infected carcasses of poultry and cows or by milk and water polluted with animal feces. Campylobacter jejuni accounts for from 5 to 14 percent of acute diarrhea cases in the few areas it has been searched for, largely countries in temperate climates. Fewer than | percent of asymptomatic persons excrete the organism. Only limited data are available from tropical areas, but they suggest that the organism is responsible for roughly the same proportion of acute diarrheal illnesses as in the industrialized parts of the world. Pathogenesis This organism is primarily an invasive one, although a few strains have been reported to produce an ST-like enterotoxin, the significance of which is unknown. The organism causes patchy destruction of the mucosa of both the small intestine, particularly the distal ileum, and the colon; the stools therefore contain inflammatory exudate and frequently blood. Occasionally the bloodstream is invaded, and transiently positive blood cultures result. 

Clinical features Following an incubation period of 3 to 5 days, which is slightly longer 

than for most bacterial diarrheal pathogens, fever develops, followed by abdominal cramping pain and diarrhea. The diarrhea is initially watery but later may contain blood and mucus. The acute diarrhea lasts for 2 to 3 days, without specific antimicrobial therapy. Even following recovery, however, the C. jejuni may be isolated in the stool for periods of 2 to 5 weeks. The spectrum of the disease may range from asymptomatic infection to severe diarrhea, as is true of all diarrheal pathogens. Most patients identified with C. jejuni diarrhea have not required hospitalization. 

Young children, in whom this illness is most common, usually have blood in the stools, fever, and abdominal pain. In some older children and young adults, a clinical picture simulating acute appendicitis is seen. In such cases, laparotomy has revealed patchy inflammation of the small bowel as well as inflamed mesenteric lymph nodes. 

Diagnostic techniques The diagnosis depends on isolating the organism from stool or demonstrating specific antibodies against the homologous organisms. Since the organism, a gram-negative, curved, motile bacillus, does not compete well for growth on the media used by most laboratories for identification of enteric pathogens, it will rarely be isolated from stool unless special techniques are used. These include using an agar containing blood to which a number of antimicrobials have been added, and incubating the inoculated media at 42°C. Growth at 42°C distinguishes C. jejuni from the morphologically similar C. fetus. 

At the present time, these culture techniques are not widely utilized, although several suitable media are now commercially available. It is hoped that further simplification of the media will result in the ability of more laboratories to isolate this relatively common enteric pathogen. Since C. jejuni can occasionally be grown from blood, blood cultures should be obtained in severely ill patients. 

Serological diagnosis is only possible if the homologous organism is used as the antigen. There are many different serotypes of C. jejuni, but these are not cross-reacting, so that antibodies are type-specific. Agglutination tests utilizing formalinized suspensions of organisms are the most widely used.

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

Management Since this is a nonsecretory diarrhea which rarely produces a significant degree of saline depletion, rehydration therapy is seldom needed. Furthermore, the disease is selflimited, and the associated mortality rate is low. Antimicrobial therapy, therefore, is not an essential part of management. There is anecdotal information that erythromycin will shorten the course of disease, but the effectiveness of antibiotics has not been demonstrated by controlled trials. The organisms are usually sensitive to erythromycin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, the aminoglycosides, and furazolidone; they are usually resistant to the penicillins, cephalosporins, and polymyxins. Yersinia enterocolitica 

Yersinia enterocolitica, like C. jejuni, has been causally associated with diarrheal disease in humans only since the early 1970s. 

Epidemiology The prevalence of this organism has been studied in only a few parts of the world, generally in temperate regions. Laboratories have reported isolation in about | to 3 percent of acute diarrheal cases studied. 

Yersinia enterocolitica is also a common inhabitant of the intestinal tract of animals, particularly pigs, dogs, and cats, and there is some suggestion that direct transmission to humans occurs. Outbreaks due to contaminated milk have been reported, and household spread from an index case to other family members has occasionally been demonstrated. The disease seems to be primarily one of children, but community incidence data have not been collected. There is a relationship between the O serogroups and certain geographical areas. O groups 3 and 9 are mostly seen in Europe, whereas group O8 isolates are most common in the United States and Canada. Pathogenesis The organisms are primarily invasive, but most strains also produce an ST enterotoxin when grown at 25°C, although not at 37°C. The role of this enterotoxin in pathogenesis, if any, is not presently known. The invasive property of Y. enterocolitica has been shown to be mediated by a plasmid, which is unique among members of the Enterobacteriaceae. Strains 

must have this plasmid in order to invade tissue, as measured by the Sereney test, the in vivo model of tissue invasion which utilizes the conjunctiva of the guinea pig. During infection, the organisms primarily invade the terminal ileum and may cause microabscesses and mesenteric adenitis. 

Clinical features Yersinia enterocolitica causes a more variable clinical illness than that caused by the other invasive enteropathogens. In infants and young children, the predominant symptom is acute watery diarrhea, accompanied by abdominal pain and fever, which may persist as long as 2 weeks; blood is observed in the stools in fewer than half the patients. In older children and young adults, right lower quadrant abdominal pain is the most common symptom, usually accompanied by fever and leukocytosis; diarrhea is not a prominent feature. The clinical picture may be sufficiently similar to acute appendicitis that surgery may be undertaken. In one well-studied group of patients in Scandinavia, 5 percent of cases diagnosed as acute appendicitis were shown to be related to Y. enterocolitica enteritis. Another unusual feature of this illness is that erythema nodosum and/or acute arthritis may occur 1 week to several months after the acute illness has subsided. Erythema nodosum and arthritis generally occur in patients older than the age of 40, and the arthritis may persist for several months. The majority of patients developing the post- Yersinia arthritis belong to the histocompatibility group HLA-B27, suggesting a pathogenetic mechanism similar to that seen in Reiter’s syndrome. Again, the molecular mechanism by which Yersinia invades the small bowel is not known. Although the clinical picture is that of nonsecretory diarrhea, it is possible that an as yet unidentified enterotoxin may be responsible for the watery diarrhea so frequently seen in small children with this illness. 

Diagnosis The diagnosis is made by isolating the organism from acute stool specimens or by the demonstration of rising serum antibodies to the homologous serogroups. Isolation and identification of Y. enterocolitica can be done by any microbial laboratory, since no special media or growth conditions are 

###### NEWER ETIOLOGIC AGENTS OF ACUTE DIARRHEA 

required. This gram-negative bacillus is a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family, which grows slowly as a lactose-negative organism on usual media used for the identification of enteric enteric pathogens. The organism grows well at lower temperatures, however, unlike other enteric organisms, and this is useful in its primary isolation. The laboratory should therefore be notified when this organism is suspected, so that a lower incubation temperature can be used. An additional plate of MacConkey’s agar can be included at 22 to 25°C for 48 h when when these organisms are being looked for. In cases in which low numbers of Y. enterocolitica are expected, selective enrichment can be achieved by keeping the stool swab in phosphate-buffered saline in the refrigerator (S°C) for several days prior to streaking it onto the usual media. Since the antibody response is serogroupspecific, the serogroup of the isolated organism must be known. Bacterial agglutination, using killed suspensions of organisms, is most widely used for determining the antibody response.

There is some evidence now, from both animal studies and hospital outbreaks of disease, that C. difficile can be passed from person to person, and should therefore be treated as a nosocomial organism. Patients with disease who are excreting large numbers of organisms should be isolated from other patients who may be susceptible to this disease. 

Susceptibility factors include, in addition to antibiotic administration and surgical procedures, advanced age and general debility. Although many patients taking antibiotics experience mild diarrhea, most such episodes are not due to C. difficile. The cause of this mild antibiotic-associated diarrhea is at present unknown. 

Management Rehydration therapy is_ indicated in the small minority of patients who show significant evidence of saline depletion. The disease is self-limited, and usually recovery is uneventful. There have been no controlled studies on the effects of antimicrobial therapy on the course of this disease or its sequelae. In vitro testing of clinical isolates has indicated that the microorganisms are usually sensitive to tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, chloramphenicol, and gentamicin, but are resistant to most penicillins and cephalosporins. Clostridium difficile Clostridium difficile was shown only in 1978 to be the major cause of antibiotic-associated enterocolitis. This discovery was made possible by a series of experiments in animal models (primarily the hamster) in which the disease could be reproduced and therefore studied etiologically and therapeutically. This organism is an anaerobic spore-forming gram-positive bacillus that produces enterotoxin(s) that are also cytotoxins, which are responsible for the clinical manifestations of disease. 

Pathogenesis With the unexplained exception of the neonatal period, these organisms are not often part of the recognized normal fecal flora. In patients taking antibiotics, particularly clindamycin, however, the organisms may grow to large concentrations in the colon and release the enterotoxin(s) which cause marked mucosal damage. The enterotoxins are present in large amounts in the colon and are found in the diarrheal stool as well. The organisms are therefore not invasive, but produce a disease which in many respects (such as sigmoidoscopic and histologic appearance) simulates severe shigellosis. The growth of the organisms is limited to the colon; no small bowel pathology is known to occur. The enterotoxins of C. difficile are being characterized and purified. There seems to be more than a single toxin, and each has different biological effects. The cytotoxic response is probably a 

###### 225 

###### 226 

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

###### result of these several toxins being produced by the organism. 

Clinical features The diarrheal disease these organisms produce is generally seen only in persons receiving antibiotics or in persons who have had abdominal surgery and in whom the normal fecal flora has been drastically altered by preoperative procedures. The most common antibiotic associated with this disease is clindamycin, although practically all known antibiotics have been associated with some cases. The disease begins within a few days to as many as several weeks from the onset of antibiotic administration or in the postoperative period. The disease may occur up to 2 weeks after the antibiotic has been stopped. The disease is characterized initially by diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. As it progresses, the stools may become grossly bloody and contain large numbers of inflammatory cells, and the patient becomes progressively more toxic. Sigmoidoscopy usually shows evidence of colitis, which may be severe. Untreated, the disease is frequently fatal. Mortality rates between 40 and 80 percent have been reported. 

Diagnosis The diagnosis can be made by (1) demonstrating the toxin in the stool of such a patient, (2) culturing the organism from the stool, and (3) the characteristic sigmoidoscopic appearance. 

The toxin can be demonstrated in stool by the use of several tissue culture assays, which reflect the cytotoxicity of the material. Usually, stool can be diluted many times (often 1:100,000) and still produce the toxic effect in tissue culture; these toxic effects can be neutralized by specific antiserums. Whereas not all persons with a positive stool assay have the disease, since toxin has been noted to occur following the use of antibiotics in the absence of illness, all persons with the clinical picture described above and toxin in the stool can be presumed to have the disease. (Occasionally Staphylococcus aureus will produce a similar clinical picture due to bacterial overgrowth and tissue invasion in the colon; dilutions of stool will also cause toxicity in tissue culture assays, but the toxicity will not be neutralized by specific antiserums. Furthermore, a Gram stain of stool will show large numbers of staphylo- 

cocci. Why Staph. aureus was a major cause of antibiotic-associated enterocolitis in the 1950s and is rarely seen now is not understood.) Only a few laboratories perform these C. difficile toxicity tests at the present time. 

The organism is relatively easy to grow under standard anaerobic procedures. Quantitative counts will demonstrate large numbers of organisms (often > 10° per gram of stool). Virtually all isolates of C. difficile are toxigenic. At sigmoidoscopy, a marked inflammatory response is seen, often with pseudomembrane formation. However, in some patients in whom the disease involves only the more proximal areas of the large intestine, sigmoidoscopy may be normal. No serologic tests are of value in making the diagnosis. Management This is a highly fatal disease if untreated. Therefore, every effort should be made to diagnose it rapidly so that treatment may be started as soon as possible. The antibiotic should be stopped, if the patient is receiving one. If antibiotic therapy is crucial for treatment of another disease, an alternative drug should be chosen. The patient should be started on oral vancomycin 500 mg every 6 h. Parenteral antibiotic is not indicated in this disease, since the organisms are not invasive but are growing within the lumen of the colon. 

There should be a prompt response to therapy. Diarrhea should decrease and the fever and abdominal pain lessen within 1 to 2 days of beginning therapy. The recovery rate should be nearly 100 percent, as long as therapy is begun before the patient is in extremis. Another drug, oral cholestyramine, has also been used successfully in the treatment of this disease. This drug is an anion-exchange resin which binds the toxin in the colon. It has no direct antibacterial action. It would seem to be an alternative possibility for treatment but not the method of first choice. It should be realized that patients can have a relapse of their disease following cessation of therapy; this may even occur more than once. It is postulated that C. difficile spores, which are not killed by antibiotics, germinate following cessation of therapy and initiate the disease process once again. Similar repeat therapy with van- 

ETIOLOGIC DEFINITION OF A FAMILIAR SYNDROME—TRAVELER’S DIARRHEA 

###### aay, 

comycin is the preferred method of treating relapses. 

###### Rotavirus 

Rotavirus was first established as an etiology of infantile diarrhea in 1973 in Australia. Since then it has been found to have a worldwide distribution and to be one of the most common causes of ° severe diarrhea in children between the ages of 6 to 18 months. The virus originally went under several names, including orbivirus and reoviruslike agent. It is called rotavirus because its appearance resembles that of a spoked wheel. Until very recently, the human rotavirus could not be grown in tissue culture, and it was studied primarily by extracting it from diarrheal stool and purifying it. 

Epidemiology Rotaviruses are known to exist in two antigenic forms. Most children have exposure (infection with or without disease) before the age of 2 or 3 years. This is true in all parts of the world, both in the developed and the developing countries. Therefore, by adulthood virtually everyone has antibodies against this agent. This probably explains why adults develop only mild disease with reinfection. 

The disease occurs primarily during the cooler months of the year, but its exact mode of transmission is not known. 

Rotaviruses are also major causes of diarrheal disease in the young of a large number of animal species. Most of these can readily be grown in tissue culture, and many share common antigens (such as the Nebraska calf virus which was first used as a substitute antigen in detecting human rotavirus). However, they seem to be speciesspecific in their ability to cause disease. There is the possibility that these cross-reacting animal rotaviruses may be useful in the development of a hybrid stain that could produce immunity in humans when given orally. 

The virus primarily invades and destroys the cells from the upper small bowel. Virus excretion can be demonstrated also for several days after recovery from symptoms. The diarrhea is thought to be secondary to the mucosal damage, with resultant impaired sodium chloride absorption by the villi. Malabsorption of carbohydrates (particularly lactose) and fats appears to occur 

during this infection to a greater extent than in other acute infectious diarrheal illnesses. 

Clinical features Although rotavirus disease is primarily a childhood disease, infections do occur in adults as well. In particular, parents of children with rotavirus diarrhea may develop clinical diarrheal symptoms associated with rotavirus particles in their stool. Travelers to the developing world may develop diarrhea secondary to rotavirus, although the frequency with which this occurs has not been established. The diarrhea in adults is a mild one, rarely requiring any form of therapy. 

Diagnosis The diagnosis of rotavirus diarrhea is made by demonstrating the antigen in the stool or demonstrating a rise in serum antibody to rotavirus. The former is done most readily by the use of an ELISA assay, the latter either by a complement-fixation assay or an ELISA assay. Rotavirus can also be identified morphologically in stool by electron microscopy (as it was originally discovered), but this technique has largely been replaced by the simpler assay. 

Management The replacement of fluids and electrolytes lost in the diarrheal stool can be done almost exclusively with oral glucoseelectrolyte solutions. Although vomiting may be one of the presenting features of this illness, it is generally mild, subsides during the first 12 h of illness, and is not a major deterrent to oral therapy. Only rarely does intravenous therapy need to be given; this measure generally only needs to be used occasionally in infants. In adults, the disease is mild and replacement solutions are not necessary. No specific measures other than replacement therapy are known to be of value. ETIOLOGIC DEFINITION OF A FAMILIAR SYNDROME — TRAVELER’S DIARRHEA 

The definition of newly recognized enteropathogens during the past decade has resulted in a clear etiologic definition of the wellknown syndrome of “‘traveler’s diarrhea.”’ The acute diarrheal illness experienced by 

###### 228 

###### INFECTIOUS DIARRHEAL SYNDROMES 

travelers from the developed, sanitized world who visit the developing, relatively unsanitized world is an example of a disease of medical (social?) progress, a stark indication of the disparities between these two worlds, and at best an intimate cross-cultural experience. The disease is the most common one experienced by tourists (and a major reason why some countries are not visited) and is thus of major economic importance to developing countries who wish to promote an influx of tourists. 

Extensive studies done in the early 1960s failed to reveal an etiologic organism in the vast majority of cases, although the illness could be partially prevented with antibacterial agents, thereby suggesting a bacterial etiology. 

Following the recognition of enterotoxigenic E. coli as an etiologic agent in human diarrhea, studies were again mounted to see whether this organism could be responsible for part of the syndrome. Studies done first in Mexico, and then in Kenya, Morocco, and many other parts of the world revealed that ETEC strains were the single major cause of traveler’s diarrhea. Incidence figures indicate that from 30 to 70 percent of episodes are caused by ETEC, and it is postulated that this is a minimum figure because of the relative insensitivity of the presently available culture techniques and the inadequacy of serum antibody testing. Other organisms may also be responsible for this syndrome, including Shigella (S to 10 percent), rotavirus and Norwalk agent (S to 10 percent), and Salmonella (rarety). Campylobacter have not yet been extensively looked for in this syndrome; in one study, C. jejuni were isolated from about 10 percent of cases. Thus traveler’s diarrhea is indeed a disease of multiple etiologies, of which by far the most common is ETEC. As mentioned earlier, the serotypes and enterotoxin types of the ETEC organisms vary from one geographical area to another, as do the antibiotic sensitivity patterns. In those areas of the world in which ETEC strains are known to be multiply sensitive to antibiotics, two studies have shown that doxycycline, taken as 100-mg capsules once a day for a 3-week period, is 85 to 90 percent protective against the traveler’s developing diarrheal illness. Since this protection is greater than one would predict if only ETECmediated disease were being prevented, it is 

postulated that other doxycycline-sensitive organisms, such as Shigella (and probably others not yet identified) are also being killed by the prophylactic therapy. In another study in which the doxycycline dose was reduced to twice a week, there was a significant (50 percent) reduction in the number of episodes experienced, but not in the number of persons developing at least one episode of disease. Furthermore, this latter study was done in an area where 40 percent of ETEC were resistant to doxycycline. Additional investigations are now in progress to evaluate the effect of daily doxycycline in areas of the world (Thailand, Philippines, Honduras) known to have a relatively large percentage of doxycycline-resistant strains. Since the small bowel concentrations of doxycycline are much greater than serum levels (the drug is secreted through the small bowel mucosa as well as in the bile) and since subinhibitory levels of antibiotics, including tetracyclines, have been shown to interfere with the expression of fimbria and thus colonization, there is reason to believe that doxycycline may be effective even in these areas. 

The only other agent that has been studied recently for the prevention of traveler’s diarrhea is Peptobismol. This agent was tried clinically because of the known action of its active ingredient, bismuth subsalicylate, in preventing the secretory response to E. coli LT in the rabbit ileal loop model. Peptobismol, 2 oz taken four times a day, provided 60 percent protection against diarrhea in short-term travelers to Mexico. 

The antibiotic therapy of traveler’s diarrhea has not yet been extensively studied. Oral replacement of stool losses is obviously indicated in those persons with severe diarrhea. Peptobismol has also been shown to be of benefit in reducing the length of disease and stool output. Studies of antibiotic therapy are still in progress. Based on data from Bangladesh, it would be expected that the duration of diarrhea should be shortened to not more than 24 to 36 h by antibiotics; thus those persons destined to have a more prolonged course would be benefited. Probably either doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole would be effective in this regard, but data are not yet sufficient to support routine antimicrobial therapy in this illness which is generally more annoying than life-threatening. 

###### REFERENCES 229 

###### SUMMARY 

Two major recent developments have been the identification of the agents responsible for 75 to 85 percent of all cases of acute diarrheal disease throughout the world and the description of a simple, orally administered sugar-electrolyte solution that is effective in the rehydration of both adults and children with infectious diarrheas of all etiologies. This latter development should have a major impact in decreasing both mortality and morbidity rates of diarrheal diseases, and especially in alleviating the malnutrition which is associated with recurrent childhood diarrheas throughout the developing world. Our knowledge is still fragmentary in two other major areas: epidemiology and _ immunology. More detailed knowledge in these areas will be critical to the ultimate control of infectious diarrheal illnesses. A more thorough knowledge of the distinct epidemiologic patterns of the culpable microorganisms should lead to more effective means of preventing their transmission. More effective immunologic control of this group of illnesses now appears possible through the use of live oral vaccines that can selectively stimulate the gastrointestinal secretory immune system. New developments in recombinant DNA technology should lead to the generation of candidate vaccines for this purpose. The ultimate beneficiaries of such control measures will be the children of the developing world, who remain the most vulnerable targets of infectious diarrheal agents.

###### MARVIN TURCK 

###### HISTORY OF DEVELOPMENT 

One of the truly remarkable developments in contemporary science is the discovery, synthesis, and clinical application of the B-lactam antibiotics. This story began in 1928 when Fleming observed the lytic properties of the mold Penicillium on cultures of staphylococci. A full 12 years elapsed, however, before the group of workers at Oxford, headed by Chain, Florey, and Abraham, appreciated and demonstrated the chemotherapeutic properties of penicillin in 1940. Following their discovery, a search for other antibiotic-producing organisms was _ initiated on a worldwide basis. In 1945, Professor Giuseppe Brotzu in Sardinia isolated a fungus which he concluded was _ similar to Cephalosporium acremonium. When grown on solid medium, this fungus secreted material that inhibited the growth of a number of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Subsequently, a strain of fungus which produced considerable amounts of antibiotic material when grown in broth was isolated, and both culture filtrates and active concentrates from the Cephalosporium species were tested in patients by injecting the filtrates directly into staphylococcal and streptococcal cutaneous lesions. Concentrates of the fungus also were administered both intravenously and intramuscularly to patients with typhoid fever, paratyphoid infections, and brucellosis. It was not until 20 years later, however, that the cephalosporin antibiotics came into widespread clinical use. 

Since these early beginnings, progress in the cephalosporin field has been rapid, and in historical terms four generations of these drugs have appeared. 

- I Initially, these drugs were limited to two parenteral dosage forms, cephalothin and cephaloridine. 

- 2 This was followed by the development of oral formulations, as well as other parenteral ones which had the same general spectrum as cephalothin but were less painful to administer, had a longer half-life, and were capable of achieving higher blood levels. 

- 3 The third generation emphasized extension of the antibacterial spectrum to include Haemophilus influenzae and anaerobic organisms, notably Bacteroides fragilis. 

- 4 A fourth generation of these and related agents is aimed at including antipseudomonas activity, a characteristic lacking in all previous and presently available cephalosporins. 

There are now 11 cephalosporin drugs available in this country, and close to another half a dozen are under investigation. Commercial competition is steep, and every new product is being touted as superior to its predecessor. In general, it is necessary to become familiar with only one formulation that can be given parenterally and one that is available for oral use. Occasionally, there is need to use one of the extended-spectrum cephalosporins, but these tend to be very expensive and should be employed only when specifically indicated. As will be discussed in more detail, cephalosporins are rarely the drug of first choice for any infection, and when they are used in this frame of reference they should be much less costly items than they are at present. Equally important is the concept that oral cephalosporins are rarely necessary because equally effective and less expensive alternatives are 

###### Pak

usually available. Entering the ‘world of cephalosporins” with this philosophy will limit the profligate use of these drugs, which has become such a dominant feature of hospital practice. CHEMISTRY Experiments with Brotzu’s isolate resulted in the identification of three active antibacterial substances. Attention was first given to a substance called cephalosporin P which could be extracted in organic solvents. This substance, however, showed activity only against certain gram-positive organisms. In 1949, a second substance, which remained in the aqueous phase after the extraction of cephalosporin P, was named cephalosporin N. This product was active against gram-negative as well as gram-positive bacteria and appeared to be the substance responsible for the antibacterial activity originally observed in Sardinia. Additional studies showed that cephalosporin N was actually a penicillin with an aminocarboxybutyl side chain linked to the nucleus of the penicillin molecule. It was, therefore, renamed penicillin N. Subsequently, in 1953, another hydrophilic substance was discovered among the metabolic products of Brotzu’s Cephalosporium species. This substance was named cephalosporin C, and is the forerunner of the cephalosporin antibiotics. 

Cephalosporin C was found to inhibit a wide variety of microorganisms, although its activity was only about 10 percent of that of penicillin N. However, cephalosporin C was resistant to hydrolysis by penicillinase from Bacillus subtilis; this suggested that cephalosporin C contained a modification of the classic penicillin ring system. In 1957, a mutant strain of the Cephalosporium species was found which yielded sufficient amounts of cephalosporin C to enable its chemical structure to be determined. Cephalosporin C resembles a penicillin but has a six-member dihydrothiazine ring rather than a five-member thiazolidine ring. The relative stability of the cephalosporin C ring system eventually led to the isolation of 7-aminocephalosporanic acid in 1959 (Fig. 1). However, not much could be done clinically with this substance until the discovery of a method for the production of 7-

Cefoxitin, an agent that resembles cephalothin, is actually a member of the cephamycin group of antibiotics. Cefoxitin is derived from products of Streptomyces lactamdurans and differs chemically from cephalothin primarily because it has a methoxy group at position 7 of the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid nucleus. More recently, a novel B-lactam antibiotic, moxalactam, has been developed by Shinogi Research Laboratories in Japan. Moxalactam possesses a unique chemical structure in that the 1-oxa-lactam nucleus is referenced by 7a-methoxy and phenylmalonyl groups. 

###### MECHANISM OF ACTION AND RESISTANCE 

Most of the work of investigating the mechanism of action of B-lactam antibiotics has been performed with benzylpenicillin (penicillin G). This work has been extended to other penicillins and to the cephalosporins. Penicillins and cephalosporins specifically inhibit the third and final stage of cell wall synthesis in susceptible bacteria. This stage of cell wall synthesis involves cross-linking of linear peptidoglycan strands on the outside of the cell membrane. The cross-linking occurs by means of a transpeptidation reaction in which two linear peptidoglycan strands interact with each other, forming a peptide bridge with the elimination of D-alanine. This influence on cell wall synthesis results in the production of aberrant bacterial forms and their subsequent lysis and death. In addition to inhibiting the transpeptidase responsible for cell wall biosynthesis, e.g., acting as antimetabolites, B-lactam antibiotics have other modes of action. For example, proteins which bind £-lactam antibiotics have been isolated from bacterial cells, and there appears to be a close correlation between the avidity of the binding with a penicillin or a cephalosporin and the degree of antimicrobial action that these drugs can exert. The binding pattern 

between different 8-lactam antibiotics and bacterial cells varies and might explain why certain 6- lactam antibiotics induce spheroplast formation, others produce primarily filamentous forms, and still others cause lysis. 

Permeability of bacterial cell walls to certain cephalosporins may also affect the sensitivity of bacteria. For example, treatment of cells with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) can enhance the activity of cephalexin against Escherichia coli, presumably by chelation of magnesium, which makes the bacterial cells more permeable to the #-lactam antibiotic. Moreover, correlations have been made between the lipophilic character of certain cephalosporins and their ability to inhibit certain bacterial species. Resistance of bacteria to the cephalosporin antibiotics may involve several mechanisms. The first is the relative stability or instability of these antibiotics to certain B-lactam-inactivating enzymes. Following the discovery that some strains of Staphylococcus, Bacillus species, and Escherichia were resistant to benzylpenicillin because they were able to destroy the antibacterial activity of the molecule, considerable work was done with enzymes from these bacteria and, subsequently, from members of nearly all bacteria. Initially, these enzymes were called penicillinases because their only known substrates were penicillins. Eventually, these same enzymes were shown to hydrolyze some cephalosporins as well. Since they destroy both penicillins and cephalosporins, the name B-lactamases is more appropriate. Different enzymes can be distinguished by their differing abilities to hydrolyze a range of penicillin or cephalosporin substrates; some bacteria can make more than one f-lactamase, which differ from each other in chemical, physical, and enzymological properties. Cephalosporin antibiotics are resistant to B- lactamases produced by staphylococci. However, even with staphylococci, the various cephalosporins are not inactivated to the same degree. For example, cephalothin is very resistant to degradation by staphylococcal {-lactamase, whereas cephaloridine and cefazolin are inactivated in vitro to a much greater extent by some strains of Staphylococcus aureus. A\lthough it is difficult to relate the in vivo effec- 

234 CEPHALOSPORINS AND RELATED £-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS 

tiveness of cephalosporins in the treatment of staphylococcal infections to» B-lactamase stability per se, failures in the treatment of staphylococcal endocarditis with cefazolin have been ascribed to this mechanism. Of more probable clinical relevance is the role of B-lactamases in the management of patients with gram-negative infections. Many gram-negative organisms can produce one or more B-lactamases. These enzymes appear to be very specific, and it has been suggested that they may be of value in differentiating various genera of bacteria taxonomically. On the other hand, there are also B-lactamases mediated by transferable R factors which are common to many different species. Although the relationship between structure and ability of a B- lactam antibiotic to resist B-lactamases is unclear, the idea of constructing antibiotics along these lines is an exciting recent development and accounts for the plethora of new B-lactam antibiotics. 

Many organisms become resistant to B-lactam antibiotics by mechanisms other than the possession of a B-lactamase. A second form of resistance, referred to as intrinsic resistance, may be induced by repeated exposure to sublethal concentrations of antibiotic. This maneuver will increase the intrinsic resistance of most bacteria, unaccompanied by an increase in, or the acquisition of, a f-lactamase. A_ striking clinical example of an infection related to intrinsic resistance to #-lactam antibiotics is that of penicillinase-negative segregants of methicillin-resistant Staph. aureus; these organisms are highly resistant to all the penicillins and cephalosporins but produce no B-lactamase at all. A third form of resistance to B-lactams is known as tolerance. This form of resistance is ascribed to a decrease in the autolytic activity of the bacterial cells in the presence of the antibiotics, which, in turn, results in a marked disparity between the minimal inhibitory and minimal bactericidal concentrations of antibiotic required to kill susceptible isolates. Specifically, a ‘‘tolerant”’ organism is one that is inhibited but not killed by a given concentration of an antibiotic. Although the clinical significance of tolerance is still undefined, tolerance may play a role in certain infections in which bactericidal therapy is deemed to be essential, such as infective endocarditis.

These authors concluded that enzymatic inactivation of the drug may play a role in vivo in the outcome of staphylococcal infection treated with cephalosporin antibiotics. Cephaloridine, a semisynthetic derivative of cephalosporin C, has virtually the same antibacterial spectrum and clinical efficacy as cephalothin. It enjoyed temporary vogue because it was better tolerated intramuscularly and gave higher and more sustained blood levels than did cephalothin. When the acetoxy group of cephalothin is replaced with pyridine, the resulting compound, cephaloridine, is more stable both in vitro and in vivo. The drug is bound to protein to a much lesser extent than is cephalothin and is excreted in the urine unchanged, with no known metabolites of lesser activity. Cephaloridine has several drawbacks not shared by cephalothin or the other cephalosporin antibiotics. Cephaloridine is potentially nephrotoxic, and the daily dose should not exceed 4 g, especially in patients with azotemia, in whom serum levels must be monitored and renal function appraised serially. Cephaloridine is less active in vitro against B-lactamase-producing staphylococci than is cephalothin. This difference becomes apparent only with a large inoculum of microorganisms, and has been related to the greater susceptibility of cephaloridine to inactivation by staphylococcal B-lactamase. Clinically, cephaloridine has been used successfully in the treatment of many patients with serious staphylococcal infection. However, because of the availability of other cephalosporins, there is little, if any, need for cephaloridine, and the use of this compound is no longer recommended. Cephapirin is a derivative of cephalosporin C that is available for parenteral use only. For clinical purposes, it should be regarded as identical to cephalothin. Although results of early clinical trials indicated that cephapirin was better tolerated intramuscularly and associated with less thrombophlebitis than cephalothin, results of other trials have refuted this observation. Cefazolin, a derivative of cephalosporin C, also is available only for intramuscular or intravenous. administration. Although cefazolin shares the basic structure of cephalothin, it differs considerably by having both a tetrazolylacetyl side chain on the amino group and a 5- 

methylthiadiazolylthiomethyl group on position 3 of 7-aminocephalosporanic acid. These modifications account for some differences in activity, tolerance, and pharmacology in comparison with cephalothin. In vitro studies with cefazolin show increased activity against Escherichia coli and Klebsiella. Like cephalothin, cefazolin shows little activity against most isolates of indole-positive Proteus, Enterobacter, and enterococci. Strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa have been very resistant to cefazolin, as they have been to other commercially available cephalosporins. Like cephaloridine, cefazolin appears more susceptible than cephalothin to inactivation by B- lactamase elaborated by some strains of Staph. aureus. Because of this susceptiblity, some workers in the field feel that cefazolin is inferior to cephalothin as an antistaphylococcal drug. On the other hand, the effectiveness of cefazolin as an antistaphylococcal drug has been demonstrated by the successful treatment of many patients with endocarditis in whom sustained bactericidal concentrations are important for cure. The usual adult dose of cefazolin is 0.25 to 1 g every 6 to 8 h. Serum concentrations after comparable doses administered intramuscularly are about twice those reached with cephaloridine and four times those achieved with cephalothin. This is related in part to both a smaller volume of distribution and a longer half-life with cefazolin. Peak levels above 25 yg antibiotic per milliliter are readily achieved with a 0.5-g intramuscular dose. Like cephalothin, cefazolin enters joint fluid very readily, and synovial concentrations are equivalent to those in the serum. Cefazolin is metabolized to an insignificant degree, and nearly 100 percent of an administered dose appears unchanged in the urine. Cefazolin is bound to protein to a greater degree than are other available cephalosporins. However, the clinical significance of protein binding remains to be determined. Cefazolin also appears to cause less pain than cephalothin after intramuscular administration. Cephaloglycin is derived from 7-(D-aaminophenylacetamido)cephalosporanic acid. Structurally, this antibiotic is the phenylglycine analogue of cephalothin. Cephaloglycin can be administered only orally, and because serum levels are poor it is restricted to treating bacterial 

###### CEPHALOSPORINS AND RELATED £-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS 

infections of the urinary tract. However, since cephalexin and cephradine are absorbed better, cephaloglycin has become outmoded and has been superseded by these newer agents. Cephalexin differs in structure from cephaloglycin by substitution of the acetoxy group witha hydrogen atom. Both cephaloglycin and cephalexin are absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, but the slight change in structure apparently accounts for the difference in pharmacological properties of the two antibiotics. Cephaloglycin is metabolized mostly to desacetylcephaloglycin in humans. Cephalexin is excreted in the urine unchanged. Although the antibacterial spectrum of cephalexin is similar to that of cephalothin, cephalexin is less active, and more antibiotic is required for in vitro inhibition of susceptible organisms. However, the drug is extremely well absorbed, and peak serum levels of 18 yg antibiotic per milliliter are readily achieved following a 500-mg oral dose. Cephradine is the only semisynthetic cephalosporin available in both parenteral and oral forms. Cephradine differs from cephalexin structurally in that it possesses two double bonds in the aromatic ring rather than three. The oral formulation is very similar in activity and pharmacology to cephalexin. The usual dose of cephradine by mouth is 0.25 to 0.5 g every 6 h. The parenteral forms offers no advantage over cephalothin or cephapirin; it should be _ prescribed in the same dosage. Unlike cephalothin or cephapirin, cephradine and cephalexin are excreted unchanged in the urine and accumulate in serum when renal function is severely impaired. 

Cefadroxil is the parahydroxy analogue of cephalexin. It is available for oral administration, and its antimicrobial spectrum is similar to those of cephalexin and cephradine. Although peak serum levels after a 0.5-g oral dose are comparable to those achieved with cephalexin and cephradine, cefadroxil achieves more sustained serum and urine levels because of its longer serum half-life. Because of the prolonged excretion of cefadroxil, the drug may be administered only once or twice a day for the treatment of certain infections. Following a single oral dose, cefadroxil can be detected in the serum for 12 h and in the urine for even longer. Cefaclor has the same basic structure as ceph- 

alexin except for the substitution of a chloride for a methyl group. Although peak serum concentrations achieved with cefaclor are appreciably lower than those reached with a comparable dose of cephalexin, cefaclor is more active in vitro against many microorganisms, including both -lactamase-positive and {-lactamasenegative strains of H. influenzae. Cefamandole is a parenterally administered semisynthetic cephalosporin which is more active than cephalothin in vitro against a number of gram-negative bacilli. Because of its instability, this compound has been formulated as the nafate derivative. After administration, cefamandole nafate is hydrolyzed rapidly to cefamandole. The enhanced in vitro activity against certain gramnegative bacilli, including H. influenzae, is partly due to the resistance of cefamandole to B-lactamase enzymes. However, some strains that hydrolyze cefamandole are also susceptible to it in vitro, and it has been postulated that the drug may be able to penetrate the cell envelope of certain gram-negative bacilli more effectively than other cephalosporins. Compared with cephalothin, cefamandole blood levels are higher, whereas serum half-life and protein binding are similar. Cefamandole is excreted in the urine unchanged. The drug is generally well tolerated and has been approved for pediatric as well as for adult use. Cefamandole inhibits most Enterobacteriaceae to an equal or greater degree than cephalothin. However, strains of Klebsiella which are resistant to cephalothin usually are also resistant to cefamandole. Isolates of Enterobacter species frequently are resistant to cefamandole in vitro when tested against a large inoculum size of bacterial cells. Cefoxitin is a member of the cephamycin group of antibiotics and differs chemically from cephalothin primarily by having a methoxy group at position 7 of the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid nucleus. This alteration in structure somewhat diminishes its activity in vitro against common gram-positive cocci but enhances its activity against many gram-negative bacilli, including indole-positive Proteus species as well as strains of Bacteroides fragilis and Serratia. Acinetobacter and Enterobacter species generally are resistant. its enhanced spectrum is explained, in part, by cefoxitin’s resistance to hydrolysis by B-lactamases. Pain at the site of intramuscular injec- 

EXTENDED-SPECTRUM CEPHALOSPORINS AND NEW £B-LACTAMS 237, 

tion is common with cefoxitin, and, for this reason, the drug is administered primarily by the intravenous route. The half-life of cefoxitin is approximately 45 min, compared with 25 min for cephalothin, and the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine. 

very active against H. influenzae, including ampicillin-resistant strains. The drug is not significantly metabolized, and its biological activity in the urine is unchanged. Pharmacokinetic studies show that peak levels achieved in serum following administration of cefuroxime are slightly higher than those achieved with comparable doses of cefamandole, but not as high or as sustained as with ceforanide. Cefotaxime is a methoxyimino derivative of 7- aminocephalosporanic acid. This parenteral drug also demonstrates relative resistance to B-lactamases of certain gram-negative bacilli. A particularly interesting aspect of the spectrum of cefotaxime is its in vitro activity against isolates of P. aeruginosa. Some investigators have reported that median minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) for isolates of P. aeruginosa were 8 and 6 wg cefotaxime per milliliter. In some studies, however, a rather marked inoculum effect was noted, which showed that the MIC increased as the inoculum was enlarged. This may modify the clinical usefulness of this drug. Similar observations have been made with strains of Serratia marcescens tested with cefotaxime, i.e., the activity demonstrated by the antibiotic was confined to studies done with lower inoculum sizes of bacterial cells. 

Cephacetrile is a parenteral cephalosporin derived from 7-aminocephalosporanic acid which is not marketed in the United States. It has an antibacterial spectrum similar to cephalothin, but is more active in vitro against many organisms. The metabolism of the drug appears to be negligible, and it is bound less to serum than is cephalothin. Although both cefamandole and cefoxitin have a spectrum somewhat greater than that of the initial cephalosporins, there still are notable gaps in their pharmacology and the scope of their antimicrobial activity. Recently a number of modified B-lactam antibiotics, some with unique antimicrobial activity, have been developed and are undergoing extensive evaluation in the the laboratory and clinic. Ceforanide is a parenteral cephalosporin antibiotic with a spectrum of activity against some gram-negative bacilli that are not inhibited by cephalothin. against P. aeruginosa, and its protective effect in experimental infections in mice was more potent than that of carbenicillin. Cefsulodin, however, shows negligible activity against other gramnegative bacilli and is only partially effective against gram-positive bacteria in vitro. Thienamycin is an experimental B-lactam antibiotic produced by Streptomyces cattleya. It differs structurally from the penicillins and cephalosporins because it lacks a sulfur in the secondary ring. The drug resembles clavulanic acid, but thienamycin possesses a broad antimicrobial spectrum as well as 8-lactam-inhibiting properties. The compound also is active in vitro against anaerobes including B. fragilis and shows potent activity against P. aeruginosa. The parent compound is fairly unstable in aqueous solution. Congeners of thienamycin may soon come to clinical trial. 

Moxalactam is a novel B-lactam antibiotic for parenteral use which possesses a unique chemical structure, namely, the 1l-oxa-6-lactam nucleus substituted by 7a-methoxy and phenylmal- 

onyl groups. The spectrum of antibacterial activity is similar to that of thienamycin. The drug is undergoing extensive in vitro and clinical trials and appears to be more resistant to B-lactamases, including the R plasmid-mediated and cephalosporinase types, than other extendedspectrum G-lactams. 

###### ANTIBACTERIAL SPECTRUM AND CLINICAL APPLICATION (Tables 1 and 2) 

Because of their broad antibacterial activity, the cephalosporins have challenged the penicillins as the major class of compounds for use against most common infections caused by gram-positive cocci and gram-negative bacilli. Nevertheless, the cephalosporins are not the drugs of primary choice against any particular pathogen. tible organisms who were allergic to the penicillins. Recently, however, because of their broad spectrum and relative safety coupled with extensive promotion, this class of compounds has been used widely for both the treatment and prophylaxis of infection, regardless of whether the patient has a history of penicillin allergy. Presently, the cephalosporins are among the most frequently prescribed antibiotics both in and out of hospitals. Unfortunately, selection of these drugs frequently is made indiscriminately, without regard to the specific etiologic agent responsible for the infection or to the cost of the drugs. 

###### Skin and soft-tissue infection 

Cephalosporins are effective in the treatment of Staph. aureus or group A streptococcal cellulitis, abscesses, or wound infection. However, a penicillin clearly is the preferred drug in such situations, and erythromycin can be used for the outpatient management of the great majority of individuals with skin and soft-tissue infections who are allergic to penicillin. A small number of isolates of Staph. aureus may be resistant to erythromycin, and a cephalosporin is recommended in the treatment of severe staphylococcal infection in the patient who is allergic to penicillin, especially if results of in vitro susceptibility tests are not available. 

###### Upper respiratory infection 

Acute bacterial pharyngitis caused by group A streptococci, and otitis and sinusitis associated with group A streptococci, Strep. pneumoniae (diplococcus pneumoniae), and H. influenzae are included among the infections responsive to treatment with the cephalosporins. Again, one of the penicillins generally is preferred in these situations except in the patient who is allergic to penicillin. Although the increased activity against H. influenzae demonstrated by cefamandole may be useful for treating some penicillinresistant respiratory infections, this drug cannot be administered orally to outpatients. And although cefaclor is absorbed when taken by mouth, some strains of H. influenzae are resistant to this drug. Although precise treatment of otitis media, especially in children, is unclear because of emerging resistance of H. influenzae to ampicillin and amoxicillin, the cephalosporins are not the best alternatives even in patients allergic to penicillin. 

###### Lower respiratory infection 

In pneumococcal infections, cephalosporins appear comparable to penicillin. Cephalosporin therapy would be anticipated to be effective in pneumonia when Klebsiella or Staph. aureus are 

240 CEPHALOSPORINS AND RELATED £-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS 

the likely pathogens. However, routine use of cephalosporins rather than a penicillin in these patients appears to be associated with a higher risk of pulmonary superinfections, related to a more pronounced alteration in the normal flora ascribed to the broad antibacterial activity of cephalosporins, especially in debilitated patients requiring endotracheal intubation and respiratory support. Perhaps the main reason for the popularity and frequent use of cephalosporins in the management of pneumonia has been the feeling of security it gives physicians when treating patients before a precise pathogen has been identified. Certainly, erythromycin appears equally effective against pneumococci and, because of its activity against Mycoplasma pneumoniae, is favored over cephalosporins in the management of pneumonia in ambulatory patients. Moreover, although H. influenzae frequently is recovered from the sputum of patients with chronic purulent bronchitis and pneumonia, rarely have B-lactamase-producing strains been incriminated in causing these infections in adults. It does not seem reasonable, therefore, to employ cefamandole routinely in these situations. 

###### Urinary tract infections 

Although the cephalosporins are effective against the majority of strains associated with bacteriuria, a number of other agents appear to be equally effective, especially in acute, uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Because of the prolonged excretion of cefadroxil, this drug may be taken only once a day for the treatment of urinary tract infections. However, even if taken only once a day, cefadroxil is very expensive compared with other drugs that are capable of eradicating bacteriuria. None of the clinically available cephalosporins is effective against enterococci or pseudomonas, which are frequent pathogens in recurrent and complicated infections of the urinary tract. Unlike other available cephalosporins, cefoxitin appears active against indole-positive Proteus species encountered in patients with complicated infections. In contrast to cefoxitin, the primary in vitro advantage of cefamandole in urinary tract infections appears to be its activity against some strains of Enterobacter. Even then, this advantage may be vitiated in vivo because of cefamandole’s de- 

creased activity in the face of large inocula of Enterobacter. An interesting, and as yet unresolved, issue is whether ampicillin-resistant E. coli, particularly those strains in which resistance is due to the triethylenemelamine B-lactamase (about 20 percent of all isolates), should be treated with a cephalosporin against which they test as susceptible or intermediate but to which they are resistant when heavy inocula are employed. Cefamandole or cefoxitin may be _ particularly effective in this situation. 

###### Sexualiy transmitted infections 

Even among penicillin-allergic patients there are more suitable alternatives to the cephalosporins in the treatment of syphilis and gonorrhea. However, 2 g cefoxitin administered intramuscularly along with 1 g probenecid appears effective in anogenital and urethral gonococcal infection associated with penicillinase-producing strains. Even then, spectinomycin is the preferred alternative to penicillin. Meningitis The lack of efficacy of cephalothin in the treatment of bacterial meningitis due to Strep. pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis has been applied to all cephalosporins. However, if the high failure rate observed with cephalothin can be attributed to high concentrations of the less active desacetyl metabolite in the spinal fluid, other cephalosporins might be effective. For example, cephaloridine does penetrate the central nervous system and is not metabolized to an inactive form. Unfortunately, the nephrotoxic potential of this drug has precluded its use in the doses necessary for the treatment of meningitis. It is conceivable that structural modifications in some of the newer cephalosporins will result in compounds that penetrate into the cerebrospinal fluid in adequate concentrations. This may be especially important in the treatment of gram-negative baciillary meningitis, since other available drugs have only limited clinical activity. An example of a drug that will turn out to be very effective in gram-negative bacterial meningitis is moxalactam, which appears to penetrate into the cerebrospinal fluid in sufficient concentration to 

###### PHARMACOLOGY AND PHARMACOKINETICS 241 

achieve bactericidal levels of 1:4 to 1:256. For the time being, however, none of the available cephalosporins can be recommended for the treatment of meningitis. 

###### Endocarditis 

The cephalosporins have been employed successfully in endocarditis associated with the viridans group of streptococci, Staph. aureus and Staph. epidermidis. There has been an inordinately high relapse rate when cephalosporins have been substituted for penicillins in the treatment of enterococcal endocarditis, and their use in this infection is contraindicated. Although many isolates of Staph. epidermidis, a significant pathogen in patients with prosthetic heart valves, appear sensitive to cephalosporins in vitro, many question their utilization and favor vancomycin. Vancomycin also is recommended in the management of enterococcal endocarditis in the penicillin-allergic patient. Some authors favor cephalothin as the best alternative to penicillin in the management of Staph. aureus endocarditis because of its stability to B-lactamase. Cephalosporins are used along with aminoglycosides in the management of gram-negative bacillary endocarditis. However, the results of treatment in these infections frequently are unsatisfactory, and surgical intervention is usually required. 

###### Septicemia without obvious portal of entry 

Because of their broad antibacterial spectrum, cephalosporins frequently are prescribed as initial antibiotic therapy in hospitalized patients with presumed sepsis. This course of action may be quite appropriate before the results of culture and in vitro susceptibility tests are available, because none of the available penicillins is effective against the majority of Staph. aureus as well as against common Enterobacteriaceae. Whether the increased in vitro activity and slightly expanded spectrum of cefamandole and cefoxitin against certain gram-negative bacilli justify their routine use in place of other cephalosporins is difficult to determine on the basis of the available evidence. In fact, most gram-positive cocci are less susceptible in vitro to cefamandole and cefoxitin than to other parenterally administered 

cephalosporins. None of the cephalosporins are effective against methicillin-resistant Staph. aureus. Anaerobic and polymicrobial infection 

Infections emanating from intraabdominal and intrauterine sites frequently involve a polymicrobial flora with anaerobes as well as various coliforms. Of the available cephalosporins, cefoxitin is the most active against anaerobes, including B. fragilis. However, cefoxitin is not uniformly active against all strains, and its activity is diminished in vitro when tested against a large inoculum of bacterial cells. Its role as a single agent in the therapy of serious polymicrobial infection involving anaerobes remains to be determined. AlIthough cefamandole also has been purported to be effective in polymicrobial infection, it has no greater activity in vitro against anaerobes than cephalothin. Moreover, the majority of isolates of B. fragilis are not readily inhibited by cefamandole. 

###### Prophylaxis 

Cephalosporin antibiotics are widely used for prophylaxis of a variety of infections. Examples include attempts to prevent Staph. aureus and Staph. epidermidis infections associated with the insertion of prosthetic heart valves and total hip replacement, and enteric gram-negative infections associated with biliary tract, intestinal, and pelvic surgery. A single 1-g intramuscular dose of cefazolin administered shortly before the surgical procedure has been recommended for most instances in which prophylaxis is thought to be necessary. Although both cefamandole and cefoxitin have a broader spectrum of activity against gram-negative bacilli than previously available cephalosporins, whether these drugs would be more effective for surgical prophylaxis than other regimens, such as the combination of a B-lactamase-resistant penicillin plus an aminoglycoside, remains to be determined.
