table differences in their absorption, distribution, and excretion. Absorption 

Cephalothin, cephaloridine, cephapirin, cefazolin, cefamandole, and cefoxitin are absorbed poorly from the gastrointestinal tract and must be administered parenterally. Cephradine is the only cephalosporin clinically available for both oral and parenteral use. Cephalothin, cephapirin, and cefoxitin appear to be less well tolerated intramuscularly than the other parenteral agents. After 500-mg oral doses of cefadroxil, cephalexin, and cephradine, serum concentrations are comparable, but both serum and urine concentrations are more sustained with cefadroxil; serum levels of cefadroxil can be detected for 12 h following a single oral dose and urine levels for even longer. Peak serum concentrations of cefaclor are only about 65 percent of those achieved with the other oral agents. 

###### Excretion 

The primary path of excretion for all these agents is renal, and there should be a modification of dosage in patients with renal insufficiency. However, with the exception of cephaloridine, which has a high potential for nephrotoxicity, generally only moderate modification is required for this class of compounds, even in patients with severe impairment in renal clearance. Both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion are involved in the excretion of these drugs. Except for cephaloridine, the administration of probenecid results in an increase in the serum levels and serum half- 

life. Those compounds that contain an acetyl group at the R, side chain (cephalothin, cephapirin, and cephaloglycin) undergo metabolism to the desacetyl forms, which have less biological activity than the parent compounds against certain organisms. None of the other cephalosporins or cephamycins undergoes appreciable alteration in the host, although a small amount of cefoxitin is metabolized to the descarbamyl! form. 

###### Distribution 

The various cephalosporins are widely distributed and penetrate well into pleural, synovial, and pericardial spaces. Their penetration, however, into the central nervous system is insufficient for management of bacterial meningitis. Biliary levels are usually adequate and parallel serum levels; hence the highest biliary levels are achieved with cefazolin. Cefazolin also is the most highly protein-bound of the cephalosporins. Protein binding appears to affect the serum level, duration, and the elimination of the antibiotic as well as its tissue penetration. However, the clinical relevance of protein binding is unclear, and even large differences in the percentage of protein-bound antibiotic do not seem to make any difference in drug distribution. 

###### ADVERSE REACTIONS 

The cephalosporins in clinical use are relatively nontoxic for mammalian tissues. Most of the untoward reactions to this group of antibiotics are not toxic but are related to hypersensitivity, and usually are characterized by urticaria or other 

###### ADVERSE REACTIONS 243 

erythematous skin eruptions. Although most of these cutaneous manifestations of hypersensitivity are relatively mild, some progress to severe exfoliative dermatitis. Less frequently, the cephalosporins cause fever and arthralgias that resemble serum sickness. Most of these hypersensitivity reactions are more of a nuisance than a hazard. However, at times an individual may develop severe, and even fatal, anaphylaxis. The question of cross sensitization between the penicillins and cephalosporins remain to be resolved fully. Although the magnitude and severity of this problem remains to be defined, extensive clinical experience over a period approaching 20 years has demonstrated that the great majority of patients with a history of penicillin allergy can be given cephalosporins without risk of serious reactions. In animal experiments, antibodies produced against cephalothin bovine gamma-globulin conjugates cross reacted with penicillin G. The 6-lactam ring of penicillin is also capable of inducing antibodies which will cross react, although not extensively, with the ,- lactam ring of some of the cephalosporin antibiotics. Finally, anaphylactic shock has been induced in guinea pigs sensitized to penicillin G by the intravenous injection of a cephalothinpolylysine conjugate. However, there is little clinical evidence that the phenomenon of crossreactivity is the same as cross-allergenicity. The results of skin tests indicate that only a small number of individuals with penicillin hypersensitivity are also allergic to the cephalosporins. Some patients develop a positive direct Coombs reaction during therapy with cephalothin and other cephalosporins. This is usually associated with large doses and appears to be especially prevalent in patients with poor renal function who attain high levels of antibiotic. In these circumstances, a cephalothin globulin complex coats the red blood cells and, in turn, reacts with anti-human globulin serum. However, the positive direct Coombs test found in these patients rarely, if ever, produces a hemolytic state, and red cell survival studies have shown no change from patients who are receiving other antibiotics. In general, the positive Coombs test appears to be more of a nuisance in cross matching blood or in determining the Rh factor status of pregnant women than a hazard to patients treated with cephalosporin antibiotics. Although in humans true toxicity is uncom- 

mon during therapy with recommended doses of cephalosporin antibiotics, various degrees of nephrotoxicity have been observed in certain laboratory animals. For example, rabbits appear especially susceptible to the nephrotoxic effect of cephaloridine and develop a dose-dependent lesion of the second segment of the renal proximal tubule that results in early disruption of the structure and function of the cell membrane. Among the cephalosporins, deterioration of renal function and the development of acute tubular necrosis in humans has been reported primarily in patients treated with cephaloridine. Unlike cephaloridine, its congener cephalothin is not believed to be nephrotoxic when employed alone. The structures of the two antibiotics differ primarily in that at position 3 of cephalothin there is an acetoxy group, whereas in cephaloridine a pyridine ring occupies this position. It has been suggested that the pyridine moiety or a metabolite of it, and not the cephalosporin itself, is responsible for the renal injury. Pyridine has been shown to cause renal tubular damage in rats after 2 to 4 weeks of oral administration, although the doses far exceeded the amounts conceivably received by patients during therapy with cephaloridine. An ability to split off the pyridine moiety from cephaloridine has been demonstrated in certain species. For example, free pyridine has been detected in the urine of dogs given cephaloridine, and small residues of the pyridine component have been found in the liver of rats for up to 24 h following administration of the antibiotic. Rabbits, however, appear more sensitive to the nephrotoxic effects of cephaloridine than other species and may metabolize the drug differently from humans. Specifically, in humans, 80 percent of an injected dose of cephaloridine is excreted unchanged in the urine within 24 h, but only 50 percent can be recovered from the urine of rabbits. This finding suggests that the greater susceptibility of these animals to cephalosporin toxicity may be due to increased or altered metabolism of cephaloridine. Although cephalothin alone does not appear to be nephrotoxic, well-controlled studies have demonstrated that concomitant administration of cephalothin enhances the risk of aminoglycoside toxicity. Animal studies have indicated that cephalosporins do not potentiate and, indeed, may protect against aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, 

244 CEPHALOSPORINS AND RELATED B-LACTAM ANTIBIOTICS 

but these results have proved misleading in humans. In humans, concomitant use of cephalothin increases the risk of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity. Whether other cephalosporins also potentiate the nephrotoxicity of aminoglycosides is not known, but all have been presumed to do so. On the other hand, synergistic nephrotoxicity has not been observed when various semisynthetic penicillins have been used with aminoglycosides.

##### DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

###### ELLIOT D. WEITZMAN 

Sleep disorders can occur at any time in the life span of humans, from infancy to senescence. Some sleep disorders are peculiar to specific age groups, such as nocturnal enuresis, night terrors, and somnambulism in childhood and adolescence, and insomnia and hypersomnia in middle and old age. Others, such as the narcolepsycataplexy syndrome, may begin in childhood and persist throughout life. 

Although data on the prevalence of sleep disorders is fragmentary, it appears that between 8 and 15 percent of the adult population in the United States has frequent and chronic complaints about the quality and amount of their sleep. Several studies have shown an increased mortality ratio for men and women who sleep less than 4h or more than 10h per night. From 3 to 11 percent of adults use sedative-hypnotic drugs, and the percentage increases with age. Furthermore, the mortality rate for persons who use sedative drugs frequently is 1.5 times higher than the mortality rate for those who never use sedative drugs. Therefore, not only is the prevalence of sleep disorders a major problem in terms of frequency of complaint, excessive drug usage, and financial cost, but, more important, there is evidence for increased risk of mortality for persons with a chronic sleep disorder. 

The use of continuous recordings of the electroencephalographic, electromyographic, and eye movement activity, together with measurement of heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rhythm (polysomnograph) has provided new data on the patterns of responses and activity that occur during a normal period of night sleep. In addition, these objective measurements of physiological and autonomic changes in patients have guided the clinical observer to new catego- 

ries of sleep disturbance and to the recognition of new syndromes. Since the field is new, the clinical descriptions remain largely descriptive, and much remains to be done to define the underlying pathophysiology. 

With few exceptions, there is an absence of tissue pathology to support the description of specific sleep disorders. It is necessary, therefore, to rely on the natural clustering of clinical signs and symptoms to classify the sleep disorder syndromes and disease entities. Recently, a committee of the Association of Sleep Disorders Centers classified sleep disorders on the basis of clinical symptomatology (Table 1). 

In this review only selected disorders will be described, with the emphasis on common syndromes and those for which new information or treatment regimens are available (Table 2). Fora more complete review of all the sleep disorders outlined, the reader is referred to the special issue of Sleep (Association of Sleep Disorders Centers). 

###### STAGES OF SLEEP 

There are two distinct phases of sleep: nonrapid eye movement sleep (non-REM sleep), and rapid eye movement sleep (REM sleep). Non-REM sleep consists of four stages, designated as stages 1h 2 Sand 4: 

Three major physiologic parameters are commonly used in the polygraphic measurement of sleep stages: (1) the electroencephalogram (EEG), (2) the electrooculogram (EOG), and (3) the mentalis electromyogram (EMG). EEG electrodes are attached to the scalp at the C3 and C4 locations (international classification) with the reference electrode over the mastoids. EOG 
###### 246 DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

electrodes are applied to the skin at the outer canthus of both eyes and are also referred to the mastoids (to measure lateral eye movements). EMG electrodes are attached to the skin overlying the chin muscles (mentalis). 

Stage 1 sleep is characterized by low-voltage mixed-frequency EEG activity, associated with slow rolling eye movements recorded on the EOG channel. The chin EMG is typically of moderately high amplitude but is decreased from

that of the waking state. Stage 2 sleep is represented by a moderately low-voltage background EEG, interspersed with brief (0.2 to 0.75 s) highvoltage discharges (K complexes) and 12 to 15 Hz low to moderate amplitude coherent discharges (spindles). Stage 3 sleep consists of highamplitude background activity of theta (5S to 7 Hz) and delta (1 to 3 Hz) waves, as well as K complexes and spindle activity. This high-voltage slow-wave activity is present for between 20 and 50 percent of the epoch (one page of polygraph recording). Stage 4 sleep consists of highvoltage delta waves (75V or greater) with a frequency of 0.5 to 3.0 Hz. Spindles may or may not be present. This delta wave activity is 

present for 50 percent or more of the epoch. Tonic chin muscle potentials are usually present during these non-REM sleep stages. Electrical activity seen on the EOG channels represents the EEG transmitted from the frontal and anterior temporal regions of the brain. 

REM sleep consists of low-voltage mixed-frequency EEG activity which resembles that seen during stage 1 sleep; however, saw-tooth waves are often seen. These are moderately high-amplitude, 3 to 5 Hz triangular-shaped waveforms. The EOG shows groupings of conjugate eye movements in all directions of gaze (rapid eye movements). Tonic EMG activity from the chin is either totally absent or markedly suppressed. 

248 DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

Phasic muscle potential discharges, however, are prominent and irregularly present. REM sleep alternates with non-REM sleep approximately every 90 to 100 min, the first REM period occurring about 90 to 100 min after the onset of sleep. The sequence of stages 1, 2, 3, and 4 typically occurs at the time of going to sleep. The sequence is then reversed (stages 4, 3, and 2), and REM sleep ensues. The normal sleep pattern of the night consists of three to five such short-term sleep cycles, with an increasing duration and percentage of the REM-sleep period during the latter half of the sleep period. Stages 3 and 4 occur predominantly during the first onethird of the sleep period. Stage 1 sleep occupies approximately 5 to 10 percent, stage 2 about 50 percent, stage 3 approximately 15 percent, stage 4 about 10 percent, and REM sleep approximately 20 percent of the average of 450 min of total sleep. 

Continuous or frequent sampling of blood during the 24-h sleep-wake cycle has demonstrated alterations in the temporal pattern of pituitary hormones during the night’s sleep. Sleep synchronizes several hormonal rhythms. A major surge of growth hormone secretion occurs after sleep onset, during the first 2 h of sleep that is commonly, but not exclusively, associated with stages 3 and 4 sleep. Adenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-cortisol secretion is not secreted just before and for several hours after sleep onset. During the latter half of the night’s sleep, ACTH-cortisol secretion occurs as a series of individual episodes, the accumulation of which produces the high concentrations on awakening that are characteristic of the circadian rhythm. Cortisol secretion, stimulated by ACTH, follows a similar pattern with five to seven individual episodes readily identified. Prolactin secretion in men and women increases during the night, with highest concentrations just after sleep onset, and continues in an episodic manner until immediately before awakening. The prolactin concentration falls very rapidly after awakening to normal daytime levels. Serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels are also secreted in episodic bursts, approximately 1 h apart throughout the day and night. In women, during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, a 2- to 3-h decrease in LH concentration occurs just after sleep onset. In- 

creased sleep-associated LH secretion has been shown to occur selectively during puberty in boys and girls. Thyrotropin is secreted only minimally during the waking day but has a secretory surge just before sleep onset in the evening. Sleep appears to inhibit thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) secretion throughout the night. 

###### DISORDERS OF SLEEP Disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep (insomnias) 

Insomnia may occur with affective disorders, the use of drugs and alcohol, sleep apnea and hypoventilation syndromes, nocturnal myoclonus (periodic movements during sleep and “restless legs” syndrome), and the delayed sleep phase syndrome. The last entity will be described in more detail under “‘Disorders of the Sleep-Wake Schedule,” below. 

Insomnia associated with the affective psychiatric disorders The major sleep abnormalities found in the affective disorders consist of a chronic and recurrent inability to maintain sleep through the expected sleep period, early morning (i.e., ““~premature’’) arousal, and, to a lesser degree, difficulty initiating sleep at the expected time at night. The affective disorders have been divided into major depressive and bipolar disorders (recurrent depression, manic-hypomanic episodes, or both) and secondary depression (see Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders IIT). 

The sleep disturbances associated with the affective disorders characteristically involve different degrees of intrusive wakefulness occurring during the course of the daily sleep period. The patients typically complain of severe and persistent restlessness at night, and a tired, disinterested, ““‘washed out” feeling during the day. It is very unusual for most depressed patients to complain of true sleepiness or actually to sleep recurrently (i.e., take naps) during the day. Indeed, there is not only the complaint of nocturnal but often of daytime insomnia. The older individual with an affective disorder characteristically suffers from an abbreviated nocturnal sleep with a premature early morning arousal pattern. 

###### DISORDERS OF SLEEP 249 

Patients with bipolar depression have different amounts and organization of sleep stages from those with nonbipolar depressions. The nonbipolar depressives have repeated awakenings with a premature nocturnal arousal, a shortened REM latency, and reduced stages 3 and 4 non-REM sleep. On some nights there is an associated increase in REM sleep. It is well known that REM sleep deprivation can lead to a REM rebound on recovery nights. Although this has been suggested as a possible explanation for the increased amounts of REM sleep, changes in the quantity and timing of REM sleep may be a primary feature of the sleep disturbance in depression. 

By contrast, patients with bipolar depression often have excessive daytime sleepiness (naps) and extended sleep periods at night. Although sleep periods lasting 5 to 6 h have been confirmed by polygraph recordings, these patients commonly awaken feeling unrefreshed. During times of mania or hypomania, total or partial sleeplessness may be present in association with inappropriate and excessive agitated behavior. Polysomnographic recordings demonstrate that bipolar and unipolar depressed patients show a shortened REM sleep latency and reduced stages 3 and 4 sleep. 

Patients who have secondary depression or personality disorders (generalized anxiety, neurotic phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorders, and “‘neurotic’’ personality disorders) and moderate to severe insomnia do not generally demonstrate a shortened REM latency. They do, however, have fragmented sleep with a reduction in stages 3 and 4 sleep and often an associative reduction in REM sleep. These patients may also have a concomitant circadian rhythm disturbance, especially associated with sleep onset insomnia (see “Disorders of the Sleep-Wake Schedule,’ below). 

In patients with the complaint of chronic insomnia, several additional abnormal patterns of the polygraphic sleep recording have been identified. These include the presence of coherent alpha activity of 9 to 11 Hz “riding” on the sleep EEG (alpha-delta activity), and the simultaneous occurrence of rapid eye movements and 12- to 14-Hz sleep spindles in the EEG (REM-spindle activity). These indications of temporal disorganization in the EEG pattern are characteristic of 

chronic insomnia and are almost never seen during normal sleep. They are probably related to the observation that certain insomniac patients, upon awakening in the morning after sustained periods of 6 to 7 h of polygraphically defined sleep, insist that they either have not slept at all or have slept for only a few hours (‘‘pseudo-insomnia syndrome’’). In order to understand the nature of the sleep disturbances in the insomnias, it is important to study the sleep-wake biological rhythm of the patient. Several new nondrug treatments for depression are currently under study. These use the manipulation of the timing of sleep within the circadian rhythm or of specific sleep stages. Both total sleep deprivation and specific deprivation of REM sleep for limited time periods have been reported to reverse the symptoms of depression. A progressive phase advance (timing of the onset of sleep) within the patient’s circadian biological day has also been reported to reverse acutely the depressive phase in bipolar depression. Insomnias associated with the use of drugs and alcohol The widespread use and abuse of central nervous system depressants (hypnotic and sedative drugs, tranquilizers, bedtime use of alcohol) without a rational pharmacological basis is well documented. Psychopathology is present in most insomniac patients, and most fail to respond to hypnotics for more than a short period of time. The effectiveness of long-term use (greater than 30 days) of any hypnotic drug has not been established. Flurazepam, which is now the most frequently used “‘sleeping pill” in the United States, has not been studied in sleep laboratories with polysomnographic recording beyond 1 month of continuous use. In addition, although approximately one-third of all sedative drugs are used by people over the age of 60, there have been few objective studies of the effectiveness of hypnotic drugs in this aging population. The use of alcohol as a sedative drug is common but, again, its effectiveness over the long term has not been demonstrated. 

Tolerance to or withdrawal from central nervous system depressants may produce drug dependency insomnia. The short-term sleep-inducing and sleep-maintaining effects are lost, and the patient and the physician often increase the dos- 

250 DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

age or combine it with other drugs. Specific sleep-disturbing symptoms due to partial withdrawal can develop even though administration of the drugs is continued. The symptoms are often misinterpreted as evidence of persistence of the underlying insomniac syndrome. When the drugs are acutely withdrawn, a severe sleep disturbance occurs with marked sleeplessness again misinterpreted as the return of the underlying “insomnia.” 

Sleep studies in patients who regularly and chronically use hypnotic agents, demonstrate that sleep is interrupted by frequent awakenings lasting more than 5 min, especially during the second half of the night. As the drug’s effectiveness decreases, partial withdrawal occurs each night and contributes to the early morning arousal. Polysomnographic recordings have demonstrated that stages 3 and 4 and REM sleep are decreased, and sleep stage demarcations are less clear. Frequent stage transitions, sleep spindles, K complexes, delta waves, and REM sleep eye movementsare decreased, and 14- to 18Hz “pseudospindles” and beta frequencies (20 to 30 Hz) are present during all sleep stages. These observations point to a considerable degree of sleep disorganization. 

The sleep pattern is very disrupted following rapid or acute withdrawal from hypnotic agents (especially barbiturates) that have been used chronically in high daily doses. A high percentage of REM sleep appears, presumably due toa compensatory REM rebound. Sleep-related periodic movements (nocturnal myoclonus) may also occur during the withdrawal period. In addition, daytime symptoms appear, including restlessness, nervousness, generalized muscle aches and, in severe cases, drug withdrawal symptoms, confusion, hallucinations, and grand mal convulsions. These complications are most common after barbiturate and glutethimide (Doriden) withdrawal. It is important in patients who are chronic high-dose and multiple hypnotic drug users that withdrawal be gradual with direct clinical supervision after withdrawal. Many patients show remarkable improvement in both objective and subjective sleep patterns, although they may not return immediately to a fully normal sleep pattern. 

The sleep disturbance that occurs in chronic alcoholism should be differentiated from the 

nightly sedative use of alcoholic beverages. With heavy and sustained ingestion of alcohol, the sleep stage organization is severely disrupted. REM sleep periods are abbreviated, and associated intrusive awakenings occur. Acute withdrawal from alcohol in the chronic alcoholic leads to a lengthening of the sleep onset time, a decrease in non-REM sleep, and an increase in REM sleep. The REM latency shortens and changes qualitatively as well. If severe, the acute toxic withdrawal syndrome (delerium tremens) will develop. In the chronic “‘dried out’’ alcoholic, an abnormal sleep pattern may persist for many weeks, although most show a return to normal sleep within 2 weeks. 

Insomnia associated with sleep-induced respiratory impairment Patients who complain of frequent awakenings and restless, unrefreshing sleep associated with excessive daytime somnolence may have either sleep apnea or hypoventilation. Cessation of breathing during sleep (sleep apnea) is the predominant respiratory abnormality, although in some cases a sleeprelated mixed upper airway obstruction may also be present. Apneic episodes often end with a gasping for air or choking, and arousal occurs during or at the termination of an episode. Major apneic episodes coincide with periods of REM sleep. The pathophysiology of sleep apnea will be described under “Syndromes of Excessive Daytime Somnolence.” In the central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome, sleep-related central apnea and hypopnea are clearly present and associated with recurrent hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and a decreased tidal and minute volume. The syndrome occurs in association with certain specific conditions, which include massive obesity, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic residual poliomyelitis, muscle diseases (e.g., myotonic dystrophy), impairments of thoracic cage bellows action and/or diaphragmatic muscle weakness, high spinal cord cordotomy, and brainstem lesions involving structures that control ventilation. 

Sleep-related (nocturnal) myoclonus (periodic movements during sleep, PMS) In some patients with a primary complaint of chronic disturbed sleep, a highly periodic movement of one or both legs and feet may be present

###### FIGURE | 

Nocturnal myoclonus in a 52-year-old woman with the chief complaint of insomnia for 20 years, which had increased during the past 3 years. She reported great difficulty falling asleep upon retiring at 10 P.M., and she would often lie awake in bed for 3 to 4 h. She would then sleep for 1 to 2h and awaken again, having trouble returning to sleep for the rest of the night. She denied any history of restless leg syndrome and was 

not aware of abnormal movements during sleep. She had not taken any medication for this problem for many years. The patient says that she also is unable to nap during the day. Polysomnography during two consecutive nights demonstrated severe nocturnal myoclonus occurring in prolonged episodes that lasted several hours each. The myoclonus was synchronous in both legs. 

during sleep. These periodic movements in sleep (PMS) are stereotyped, repetitive, and nonepileptiform; they occur primarily in non-REM sleep (Fig. 1). The basic movement consists of a dorsiflexion of the foot and toes, and often flexion of the lower leg at the knee and hip. The movement lasts 1.5 to 2.5 s. Although historically called myoclonic by Sir Charles Symonds (1953), PMS do not occur in an isolated muscle and are not as brief as true myoclonic contractions. They are remarkably periodic (occurring approximately every 20 to 30 s), and characteristically continue for many minutes and at times for hours. Unlike most movement disorders (e.g., parkinsonism, chorea, hemiballismus, dystonia, etc.), PMS are initiatea rather than inhibited by sleep. PMS are to be differentiated from “‘sleep starts” (hypnic jerks) which are nonperiodic myoclonic movements, generally of the trunk and all extremities simultaneously, that occur at sleep onset and are 

frequently associated with the perception of falling. Sleep starts can be considered normal since most normal children and adults have experienced them, usually on several occasions. Periodic movements during sleep occur in association with a wide variety of sleep disorders. In a study of 409 sleep disorder patients by means of all-night polysomnographic recording, 53 (13 percent) had PMS (Coleman et al.).. PMS occurred in almost all diagnostic categories of sleep disorders, including narcolepsy-cataplexy, sleep apnea, drug-dependency insomnia, and restless legs syndrome. These findings suggest that a chronic sleep-wake disturbance may give rise to PMS rather than PMS being a primary cause of insomnia. PMS may also develop in patients treated with tricyclic antidepressants and during withdrawal from a variety of drugs including anticonvulsants, benzadiazepines, barbiturates, and other hypnotic agents. They have also been 

252 DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

described with chronic uremia. Movements during sleep similar to PMS have been observed in patients with Parkinson’s disease receiving high dosages of L-dopa and in patients with narcolepsy on high doses of chlorimipramine for the treatment of cataplexy. Although a wide variety of drugs has been tried in clinical and experimental treatment trials, none has been clearly effective in eliminating PMS. The neurophysiological mechanisms responsible for PMS are unknown, but the remarkable periodicity found in all studies suggests that there is an underlying central nervous system pacemaker that is “‘disinhibited” by a chronic disturbance of the temporal organization of the daily sleep-wake schedule and specific sleep stages. 

Restless legs syndrome is a disorder in which the afflicted individual feels an irresistible urge to move the legs, generally when sitting or lying down, and especially in bed, at night, just prior to getting to sleep. The patient has an extremely unpleasant deep discomfort inside the calfs, which, although not truly painful, is perceived as a “‘dysease,” requiring that the legs be moved. This interferes with sleep onset but may also recur during the night. Usually by morning the restless legs symptoms have either disappeared or become considerably attenuated, and the patient is able to fall asleep more easily. PMS is present in all cases of restless legs syndrome studied polygraphically. 

###### Disorders of excessive somnolence 

The chief symptoms of this category of sleep disorders are undesirable and inappropriate sleepiness leading to actual sleep during a time of day when the patient wishes to be awake. Characteristic complaints include an_ increased amount of unavoidable napping, increase in total sleep during the 24 h, and difficulty achieving full alertness upon awakening at the end of the daily sleep period. These complaints should be differentiated from abnormalities of the sleep-wake schedule (see “Disorders of the Sleep-Wake Schedule,’ below) and should not be confused with complaints of tiredness, lack of energy, decreased alertness, and lack of motivation, interest or “drive.” These latter complaints may accompany sleepiness, but they are actually alterations in mood and affect during the waking 

state. A diagnosis of excessive somnolence presupposes a regular (i.e., entrained) 24-h sleepwake cycle. Somnolence occurring on a transient basis is a common experience and should be present for weeks to years in order to be considered pathological. The Multiple Sleep Latency Test developed at the Stanford Sleep-Disorders Center is a useful diagnostic tool. When done during an 8-h “‘waking”’ period, the test differentiates normal individuals, who rarely fall asleep when conducive conditions are present, from patients who demonstrate recurrent sleep episodes during the test. The latter complain of excessive daytime sleepiness and fall into a clear diagnostic category on the basis of clinical history and polysomnography. A complete classification of disorders of excessive daytime somnolence should include a large list of conditions (Table 1). In clinical practice, however, two major syndromes account for approximately 80 percent of patients seen in sleep disorders centers with the complaint. These are sleep-induced respiratory impairment and narcolepsy. Sleep-induced respiratory impairment (the hypersomnia sleep-apnea syndrome, HSA) Excessive daytime somnolence is the primary complaint. In addition to severe daytime sleepiness, there are also nighttime symptoms that can be very disturbing to the patient and to the bedpartner. Almost all patients have loud intermittent snoring upon inspiration, which increases in severity with each breath during a period of approximately 20 to 50 s, culminating in a series of loud partially obstructive gasps. The episode is terminated by a brief arousal with body and head movements, typically followed by a variable period of apnea. Episodes recur in a cyclic pattern. The patient often talks during sleep (somniloquy). Occasionally nocturnal enuresis or falling out of bed during sleep occurs. The patient awakens in the morning unrefreshed, tired, and very sleepy —often with a generalized severe headache. In adults, the ratio of men to women with HSA is 15:1 to 25:1, and the age range is the fourth to sixth decade. Approximately two-thirds of the patients are obese. A rapid weight gain will increase the severity of the symptoms. HSA occurs in women but predominantly after the

Mixed obstructive sleep apneic episodes in a 49-yearold man with a 10-year history of increasingly severe daytime sleepiness and systemic hypertension. The polysomnograph demonstrates the marked alternating

Radiographic and direct fiberoptic endoscopic observations of the upper airway during the apnea process have shown that the site of functional airway obstruction during sleep is in the oral pharynx at the level of the velopharyngeal sphincter (Fig. 2). The mechanism of obstruction involves a recurrent apposition of the lateral pharyngeal walls and a posterior movement of the base of the tongue. All night polysomnographic recordings are useful in diagnosing the condition and in establishing the frequency, severity, and type of sleep apnea. Nonobstructive sleep apnea is the cessation of all respiratory movements (diaphragmatic arrest). Obstructive apnea is the absence of airflow (from nose or mouth) in association with 

respiratory effort. Mixed apnea consists of initial nonobstructive followed by obstructive apnea. A partial decrease of respiratory effect and airflow by greater than 50 percent is termed hypopnea; subobstructive apnea is a partial decrease of airflow in the presence of increased respiratory effect (indicating a partial functional obstruction of the pharyngeal airway). All the above types of apnea patterns can be present in an individual patient. However, the obstructive, mixed, and subobstructive types are most common in patients with the HSA syndrome. A characteristic abnormal respiratory and sleep pattern occurs during polygraphic sleep recording of patients with HSA. This consists of recurrent apnea (ranging from 20 to 120 s, with an average of 38 s), oxygen desaturation (often below 50 percent), and a bradycardia (< 50 beats

per minute) alternating with a tachycardia (> 120 beats per minute) (Fig. 3). The patient with severe sleep apnea has little if any stage 3 or 4 sleep but normal REM sleep. Apnea may occur either during non-REM or REM sleep, but the duration of apneic episodes increases and the extent of oxygen desaturation is greater with apnea occurring during REM sleep. A wide range of cardiac arrhythmias is seen in these patients, often present only during sleep. On occasion these may be quite severe (with cardiac arrest lasting 5 to 7 s). Bradycardia and transient episodes of asystole typically occur at the end of an apnea prior to the resumption of breathing (loud snores). Since the heart rate pattern can be blocked by atropine, the episodes presumably represent excessive vagal activity. The cause of the respiratory abnormality during sleep is not known. However, it is evident that it occurs in a wide range of conditions associated with narrowing of the upper airway. These include nasal passage deformities, enlarged tonsils and adenoids, mandibular shortening, and 

temporomandibular joint abnormalities, pharyngeal soft-tissue disturbances such as occur in hypothyroid myxedema or acromegaly, congenital palatopharyngeal abnormalities, and following velopalatal reconstructive surgery for cleft palate. In addition, conditions with respiratory muscle weakness have been associated with nonobstructive apnea and hypopnea types of sleep apnea. These include chronic poliomyelitis, myotonic dystrophy, and cervical spinal cord disease. Studies of high-altitude (hypoxic) respiratory patterns during sleep have also demonstrated the sleep apnea syndrome to be present. A link between sleep-related apnea and the sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) has been postulated on the basis of studies “of near misses” for SIDS infants. Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease also demonstrate sleep apnea episodes with significant oxygen desaturation. Studies in humans and experimental animals on the control of breathing during sleep have shown that the ventilatory response to CO, is 

DISORDERS OF SLEEP oo: 

much decreased during REM sleep, specifically during phasic REM events, compared with tonic REM sleep, non-REM sleep, and waking. In contrast, the response to hypoxia remains intact during REM sleep despite a delayed waking response. Elimination of vagal respiratory control in dogs leads to a profound slowing of respiration during non-REM sleep but not during wakefulness or REM sleep. There is a 29 percent higher upper airway resistance in REM than in non-REM sleep in normal cats and a marked reduction of both tonic and inspiratory-related intercostal muscle activity during REM sleep similar to the REM-related inhibition of other skeletal muscles. These changes are associated with decreased expansion (in adults) and even a paradoxical motion of the rib cage (in infants). The diaphragm muscle, driven by alpha motor neurons, is apparently not affected normally in REM sleep. However, with clinical disease of anterior horn cells, phrenic motor nerves, the neuromuscular junction (myasthenia), or the diaphragm muscle itself (polymyopathy), the patient can be at special risk during REM sleep. In addition, diminished ventilatory response to a respiratory “load” (airway occlusion or inspiration from a rigid container) in REM sleep adds to the risk factor of patients with low hypoxic sensitivity. 

The most effective treatment of severe HSA is to provide the patient with an open tracheal airway (tracheostomy) during the night’s sleep (Table 3). Tracheostomy results in marked re- 

duction in daytime sleepiness and improvement in mood, a decrease in systemic hypertension, a fall in an abnormally high hematocrit, elimination of the bradycardia-tachycardia pattern, a return to maintained high values of oxygen saturation during sleep, and in most cases a marked decrease in the frequency of sleep-related cardiac arrhythmias. Other treatments reported for mild to moderate forms of HSA, using tricyclic drugs, progesterone, and weight loss, have resulted in only limited long-term success. 

Narcolepsy-cataplexy syndrome The zarcolepsy-cataplexy syndrome is a distinct clinical entity with well-defined symptoms, age of onset, and natural history. The most characteristic symptom is recurrent episodes of excessive daytime sleepiness and daily sleep attacks. It is characteristic for the sleep periods to occur episodically and irresistibly; commonly the patient also complains of sleepiness and decreased vigilance between sleep attacks. Cataplexy developing at some point in the history of the illness in approximately 80 percent of all cases is characterized by brief sudden episodes of muscle weakness, without loss of consciousness. These episodes may be marked with flaccid paralysis of all somatic musculature (except diaphragmatic and extraocular muscle movements), resulting in collapse to the floor if the individual is standing, or they may be characterized by various degrees of isolated muscle weakness. If a thorough history is taken, episodes of head or jaw dropping,

dysarthric speech, facial muscle weakness, or weakening about the knees or hands, which last only seconds or minutes, are frequently described. Cataplectic episodes are almost always triggered by a sudden emotion such as happiness, anger, excitement, surprise, or even sadness and crying. In most instances, sleepiness and sleep episodes and cataplectic attacks occur independently, but they may occur in combination or in rapid succession. A conscious cataplectic episode can immediately develop into a sleep episode (REM sleep onset) with characteristic sleep onset hallucinations (hypnogogic), or conversely an episode of sudden overwhelming sleepiness may be associated with or followed by muscle paralysis. These episodes of sleepiness or cataplexy often occur more than once a day, although in some patients they may be less frequent, occurring at weekly or longer intervals. Other associated symptoms are hallucinations at the end of sleep (hypnopompic), sleep paralysis, brief lapses of memory, and automatic behavior episodes. The significance of these symptoms, often described in a bizarre manner by the patient, is often not appreciated by physicians. The narcolepsy-cataplexy syndrome usually begins at the end of puberty or during early adulthood and is then a lifelong illness. The nature of the symptoms produces serious social, familial, educational, and economic consequences for the patient. Clinical studies have shown that patients with the syndrome often fail to achieve their intellectual potential and are likely to experience marital, occupational, and educational failures. Family members, friends, and even the patient often interpret the symptoms as indicating nonmotivation, “laziness,” and/or depression. It is estimated that the narcolepsy-cataplexy syndrome occurs with a prevalence of 40 per 100,000 population and affects men and women equally. For example, in the city of New York, with a population of approximately 8 million, there should be approximately 3000 patients with the syndrome. Although firm statistics are not available, it is probable that much fewer than half the cases are identified. The daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, and hypnogogic hallucinations are manifestations and fragments of the REM sleep process. The occurrence of REM periods at the onset of sleep during an afternoon nap or at night is character- 

istic and is used to establish the clinical diagnosis. Narcolepsy-cataplexy is known to occur in dogs and other animals and can be transmitted genetically as an autosomal recessive trait. Relatives of index cases of narcolepsy are estimated to have a 60 times greater risk for the condition than the general population. The most effective treatment for narcolepsy is the use of “stimulant” drugs (methylphenidate, amphetamines, pemoline, etc.) for the sleepiness and sleep attacks and tricyclic compounds (imipramine, chlorimpramine, etc.) for cataplexy. y- Hydroxybutyrate given nightly and propranolol given during the day have also been reported to be effective in preventing sleep episodes. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as phenelzine sulfate (Nardil) have been shown to totally suppress REM sleep in patients with narcolepsy, but because of serious side effects these drugs are not used clinically. 

The etiology and central nervous system localization of narcolepsy has not been established. A few cases of structural central nervous system disease with classic narcoleptic symptoms have been reported. Lesions were found in the brainstem in the area of the pontomesencephalic reticular formation. Evidence that there is aloss of monosynaptic reflex activity (deep-tendon reflexes and H reflex) during REM sleep and in cataplexy and sleep paralysis in humans and in dogs points to a similar neurophysiological mechanism for both conditions. In addition, when carefully recorded, the narcoleptic has a periodic (120- to 200-min) pattern of recurrent REM sleep episodes during 24-h periods. Present evidence strongly supports the concept that the narcolepsy-cataplexy syndrome is a genetically transmitted organic disease of the central nervous system and that the control of the normal recurrent REM sleep episodes is abnormal. At the present time, it is not clear whether the syndrome is due to an increased “drive” for REM sleep or whether the abnormal timing of REM sleep during the waking day is a manifestation of a disinhibition of neural control of REM sleep. Other conditions associated with excessive daytime somnolence A less common but clinically recognized condition is the KleineLevin syndrome (periodic hypersomnia), which 

###### DISORDERS OF SLEEP 297 

begins between the ages of 10 and 21. It occurs more often in males and is characterized by recurrent periods lasting for days to weeks of very prolonged sleep alternating with wakefulness. During a bout of periodic hypersomnolence, the patient develops a voracious appetite and may exhibit serious disturbances in social interaction, sexual hyperactivity and exhibitionism, behavioral excitation, depression, and even frank delusions, hallucinations, disorientation, and memory deficits. During the intervening (nonhypersomniac) sleep-wake periods, the patient is usually “normal,” although some cases of a persistent personality disorder have been observed. The frequency of hypersomnia attacks is quite variable but usually is self-limited, rarely occurring beyond the fourth or fifth decade. The course is unknown, and no specific neuropathology has been reported, although it has been postulated to be a dysfunction of limbic and hypothalamic regions. Rare cases have shown cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis, which suggests that an episode of encephalitis may underlie the disorder. Excessive somnolence is a feature of many endocrine and metabolic disorders, including uremia, liver failure, hypothyroidism (severe with myxedema), chronic pulmonary disease (with hypercapnia), and diabetes mellitus with incipient coma or with severe hypoglycemia. In addition, hypersomnolence may occur in other central nervous system disorders, such as a tumor in the area of the third ventricle (glioma, pinealoma, dysgerminoma, craniopharyngioma, pituitary adenomas), obstructive hydrocephalus, viral encephalitis, and other infections of the brain and its surrounding membranes. Although relatively uncommon, excessive daytime somnolence also can occur in various degenerative diseases of the brain, including dementia of the Alzheimer type, multiple sclerosis, and cerebrovascular disease. The postconcussion syndrome has been associated with increased sleepiness. In all the above conditions, it is important to distinguish complaints of tiredness, fatigue, depression, lack of interest, malaise, and lethargy associated with metabolic, endocrine, neurologic, and psychiatric disease from sleepiness per se. In addition, it is often clinically difficult to distinguish an abnormality of disordered consciousness, such as occurs in stupor, obtundation, and degrees of coma, from excessive sleepiness. 

###### Disorders of the sleep-wake schedule 

Recent developments in our understanding of the physiology of human sleep and its disorders derive from studies of human circadian (circa, approximately; dian, day), time-keeping systems. The observation that organisms, when not entrained by 24-h cues or zeitgebers, develop daily cycles that have periods greater or less than 24 h, has now been documented in normal humans. Studies carried out for weeks to months in both cave and controlled laboratory conditions have consistently demonstrated that the preferred length of the ‘‘free-running”’ period for humans is approximately 25 h. Measurements of body temperature, urinary electrolytes, plasma and urine hormones, psychological and performance measures, and recently sleep duration and sleep stage organization have been carried out in humans in time-isolated laboratory environments. These studies have shown that consistent changes of timing relationships between body temperature and rest (sleep) time occur and that different physiological rhythmic variables develop independent cycle lengths under such time-isolated conditions. This has led to the hypothesis that multiple oscillators exist that are normally synchronized with each other but can become desynchronized under free-running conditions, which indicates the importance of “‘social’ and other entraining signals to humans. In the human, the length of the sleep episode under free-running conditions is correlated with the phase of the circadian core temperature rhythm and not with the duration of prior wakefulness. Prolonged sleep lengths of up to 18 h frequently occur, with the sleep length depending on the self-selected bedtime in relation to the phase of the temperature cycle; long sleep lengths (12 to 16 h) occur when one chooses to sleep at the peak of the temperature cycle and shorter sleep lengths (6 to 8 h) when one sleeps at the nadir. There is an associated “phase advance” of REM sleep relative to sleep onset and the temperature cycle, giving rise to a significant shortening of the REM latency, an increase in REM sleep amounts, and commonly a sleep onset REM period during the first third of the sleep episode. A phase shift of stages 3 and 4 sleep, however, does not occur during free run- 

DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

###### 258 

ning. Rather, the timing and amount of stages 3 and 4 are linked to the initiation and course of the sleep process and do not appear to be dependent on the total duration of sleep. There are no differences in the REM-non-REM cycle length under entrained and free-running conditions. Measurements of plasma cortisol throughout entrained and free-running conditions have demonstrated that one component of the circadian rhythm has a phase advance (6 to 8 h) relative to sleep onset, whereas a second component clearly follows sleep onset. The temporal pattern of growth hormone secretion, on the other hand, is directly related to the first 2 h after sleep onset. A major episode of hormonal secretion occurs just after sleep onset for almost all sleep periods during both entrained and free-running conditions. 

Studies of phase shifts of the sleep-wake cycles under laboratory conditions or after transmeridian air flights demonstrate that the daily sleep episode is disturbed after east-west or west-east shifts as well as after 180° acute inversion. Under these conditions, REM sleep also phase advances relative to sleep onset, but the adaptation occurs more rapidly with a phase delay (east to west) than with a phase advance (west to east). These findings are relevant to a condition called a delayed sleep phase syndrome and to chronotherapy treatment regimens. Disorders of the circadian sleep-wake cycle are classified under two major categories: (1) transient and (2) persistent. In the transient category, the dyssomnia of a rapid time-zone change (“jet lag’’) is very similar to that found in an acute work-shift change. The sleep disturbance that results is due to both sleep deprivation and the circadian phase-shift change. The symptoms vary considerably from subject to subject, but generally consists of a deficiency in the sustained sleep period, with frequent arousals that occur primarily at the end of the sleep episode associated with excessive daytime sleepiness and falling asleep at inappropriate times in relation to social or economic requirements. For varying periods of time (usually several days to 2 weeks), the person affected is intermittently sleepy, fatigued, and inattentive during the waking period, with partial insomnia during the sleep period. The persistent category of the sleep-wake cycle disorders is divided into five subcategories: 

(1) frequently changing sleep-wake schedules, (2) delayed sleep phase syndrome, (3) advanced sleep phase syndrome, (4) non-24-h sleep-wake syndrome, and (5) irregular sleep-wake pattern. The subject with a frequently changing sleepwake schedule characteristically has a mixed pattern of altered excessive sleepiness alternating with periods of arousal, often at inopportune and inappropriate times during the day. Sleep is usually shortened and disrupted and waking is associated with decrements in performance and vigilance. The syndrome characteristically disrupts social and family life and often becomes intolerable, as in the case of the chronic shift worker. Through the process of self-selection, some shift workers prefer or at least adapt readily to night work and rotating shift schedules. The delayed sleep phase syndrome (DSPS) is a chronobiological sleep disorder that can be differentiated from other forms of insomnia. The patient with DSPS reports a chronic inability to fall asleep at a desired clock time required to meet work or study schedules, typically being unable to fall asleep until 2 to 6 a.m. However, when not required to maintain a strict schedule (e.g., weekends, holidays, and vacation periods), the patient will sleep without difficulty and after a sleep period of normal length will awaken spontaneously, feeling refreshed. A polysomnogram will demonstrate that the sleep length and internal organization is normal. For normal sleep to occur, the patient’s choice of the clock time of sleep onset should coincide with the time the patient usually falls asleep (e.g., 4 to 5 a.M.). If sleep is attempted at a time considerably earlier (e.g., midnight), a long latency until sleep onset usually occurs. These patients have a long history of many unsuccessful attempts to fall asleep at an earlier time, i.e., to phase advance their sleep onset times. They score high as “night persons” on a standard questionnaire. Such patients have been previously considered to have “‘sleeponset insomnia.” Attempts to phase advance the time of going to sleep to an earlier time fails repeatedly in these patients. Such attempts have included the use of hypnotic drugs, alcohol, behavior modification techniques, sleep hypnosis, psychotherapy, and a variety of home remedies. A successful phase shift of the time of the daily sleep episode has been achieved in such patients by a progressive phase delay of the sleep 

DISORDERS OF SLEEP 259 

time (chronotherapy). That is, by delaying the time of going to sleep by 3 h each day (i.e., a 27-h sleep-wake cycle) the patient’s sleep timing can be “reset” to occur at the clock time preferred by the patient. Since chronotherapy can clearly be effected by a phase delay but not by a phase advance, it has been postulated that differences in the shape of the phase-response curve may underlie these patients’ chronobiological problems. The phase advance portion of the curve may be much less prominent than in normal subjects, whereas the phase delay portion is quite intact. This concept implies that each day normal individuals phase advance their sleep time by | hin order to hold to a 24-h day. Since the nonentrained biological day length is approximately 25 h, the daily entrainment process requires a well-functioning advance portion of the phase response curve with a range of entrainment sufficiently broad on both sides of 24 h to enable normal individuals to adjust to variations in bedtime and time of arising in order to maintain an appropriately phased sleep time with a period of 24 h. 

There is no clear evidence as yet that there is an advanced sleep phase syndrome; however, it has been suggested that individuals who have chronic sleep onset and wake times that are undesirably early but who have no disturbance of the sleep process itself might fall into this category. Since the “early to bed—early to rise’?! rhythm conforms very well with our socialeconomic and solar-day timing system, these individuals probably do not seek medical or psychological help. However, it has been well documented that the process of aging leads to a characteristic change in the timing of sleep such that the older individual spontaneously awakens earlier in the morning and becomes sleepy and goes to sleep earlier in the evening. It is possible 

1 Different points of view regarding this maxim are well expressed in the following three quotations: Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise. [Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanac, 1735) I have, all my life long been lying till noon; yet I tell all young men, and tell them with great sincerity, that nobody who does not rise early will ever do any good. [Samuel Johnson, from Boswell, Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, 1785) Early to rise and early to bed makes a man healthy and wealthy and dead. [James Thurber, Fables of Our Time, 1940] 

that maturational alterations in the shape of the phase-response curve may underlie these aging changes and that many older individuals do, in fact, have an advanced sleep phase syndrome. However, it is also clear that other biological rhythm changes of the endogenous circadian oscillators occur as a function of aging, including intrusive nocturnal awakenings, fragmentation of the sleep pattern, and repeated brief daytime sleep periods (i.e., naps). 

The non-24-h — sleep-wake (hypernychthemeral) syndrome is characterized by an inability to be entrained to society’s 24-h day. These individuals develop a 25- to 27-h biological day length in spite of all attempts to do otherwise. Blindness or a personality disorder may predispose to this condition. No individual has been described who has developed a consistent sleep-wake rhythm with a consistent period of less than 24 h. Repeated attempts to hold to a normal 24-h sleep-wake schedule by patients with a day length greater than 24-h can lead to cyclic periods of nonsynchronization with society’s rhythm as well as to cyclic (3 to 4 weeks) disrupted and delayed sleep with associative daytime sleepiness. Since patients with the delayed sleep phase syndrome also demonstrate a consistent tendency toward a progressive phase delay of their sleep time, it is postulated that the two syndromes may only differ in degree, the difference being that the patient with the non-24-h sleep-wake syndrome has an even further altered phase response curve with essentially no phase advance capability. 

Large individual differences in regard to a phase advance capability have been demonstrated in studies of phase shift after transmeridian air flight and adaptation after phase shifts in the laboratory. It was found that an eastward flight (phase advance of 6 h) and a laboratory advance of 8 h took much longer in some subjects than others, whereas a phase delay (westward flight) occurred more rapidly. 

The syndrome of irregular sleep-wake pattern is marked by a considerable irregularity without an identifiable persistent circadian sleep-wake rhythm. The condition is presumed to be associated with frequent daytime naps at irregular times associated with a disturbed nocturnal sleep pattern. A similar pattern can be produced in animals (rats, hamsters, monkeys, etc.) by bilat- 

260 DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

eral destruction of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). It has been shown that the sleep-wake (activity-rest) cycle of these animals no longer demonstrates a circadian rhythm under free-running conditions. The retinohypothalamic tract to the SCN is the presumed pathway mediating light-dark entrainment in animals. Many studies have demonstrated the importance of SCN in the control of timing of mammalian circadian rhythms, and it has been proposed that the SCN is an endogenous central nervous system pacemaker. Dysfunctions associated with sleep, sleep stages, or partial arousals (parasomnias) 

It is well recognized that there is a group of clinical conditions in which an undesirable behavioral and physiological event occurs in association with or during sleep but in which the sleep and waking process per se is not abnormal. The disturbing symptom specifically affects either motor behavior, autonomic dysfunction, psychological state, or a combination of the three. The range of abnormalities is very broad and occurs in all age groups. There may be considerable overlap with previously discussed nosological entities such as nocturnal myoclonus, sleep apnea, or sleep paralysis—narcolepsy, or the abnormalities may occur as independent clinical entities (somnambulism, night terrors, cluster headaches, gastroesophageal reflux. In the present state of our knowledge, it seems best to use clinical descriptions, although an attempt has been made to organize several of these around the concept of “disorders of the state of partial arousal” (sleep terror, sleep-related enuresis, and sleepwalking). A sleep stage relationship has been defined for several entities—somnambulism, enuresis, and night terrors (stages 3 and 4), sleep-related painful penile erections (REM sleep), and cluster headaches (REM sleep)— whereas others occur in several sleep stages (bruxism, somniloquy). The present list of parasomnias will certainly be added to during the next few years as a larger number of patients with sleep dysfunctions are referred to sleep disorders centers. 

Somnambulism episodes occur normally in children and adolescents; 15 percent of all children have one or more episodes. However, in a small percent of children (1 to 6 percent) these will occur frequently (at times, nightly). If the episodes persist into adulthood or begin in adulthood, there is a high association with serious psychopathology. nambulism characteristically occurs during nonREM sleep, usually in stage 3 or 4. The complex purposeful motor acts such as dressing, walking, On occasion patients will carry out an act that during the episode and typically will strongly a spontaneous arousal, returning to the bed, or or only a dim, fragmented recollection of the epiduring the episode, the patient usually will not report hallucinatory imagery or strong emotions or report thoughts. This condition consists of a sudden behavioral sequence that interrupts sleep and that consists of either sitting up in bed or leaving the bed and walking about. Full consciousness does not occur. Sombehavior includes repetitive automatic and semimay be harmful to themselves, such as climbing out a window. Patients are not easily arousable resist being aroused. The episode generally lasts no more than 15 min and is terminated by either going to sleep in another place. Patients are then surprised to find themselves in another place in the morning and commonly have no recollection sode. Dreaming is not prominent, and, if aroused will only brief and nonsustained Sleepwalking (somnambulism) Opening and closing doors, and climbing stairs. 

Polysomnographic studies have demonstrated that a somnambulism episode is preceded by high-amplitude delta waves during stage 3 and 4 sleep and that there is no evidence of any change in heart rate or respiration just before the onset of motor behavior. There is also no evidence of seizure activity either preceding or during the episode, although clinically it must be distinguished from a nocturnal seizure disorder originating in the temporal lobes. There is an association of somnambulism with other episodic sleep disorders including nocturnal enuresis and night terror attacks. Sleep terror (pavor nocturnus, incubus) A sleep terror episode is a sudden arousal during 

DISORDERS OF SLEEP 261 

stages 3 and 4 sleep (first third of the night) initiated by a sudden loud, high-pitched scream, sitting up in bed, and agitated, frightened, and panicked behavior. Although not present during sleep just before the attack, after the onset major autonomic changes appear including sweating, tachycardia, and hypopnea and pupillary dilatation (the pupils are normally meiotic during nonREM sleep). Sleep terror occurs primarily in children, although it may persist or begin in adults. The attacks last 5 to 15 min, during which the individual is usually inconsolable and may repeat the name of a family member such as “mama” or “‘grandma.’’ Complex dream imagery is not obtainable at the end of the event, and this differentiates it from a nightmare. Typically, the patient returns quickly to sleep after the episode and has amnesia concerning the event the next morning. Like somnambulism, sleep terrors can occasionally occur in children under normal circumstances, but, if they are frequent or especially if they are present in adults, they may indicate an underlying psychological disturbance. It is important that sleep terrors be differentiated from recurrent nightmares (dream anxiety attacks). Nightmares occur during REM sleep, during the middle and latter third of the nocturnal sleep period, and can usually be recounted in a detailed, vivid, and emotion-filled story which has personal fear and threats as prominent features. A terrified scream is uncommon in a nightmare. 

Sleep-related enuresis The clinical entity of nocturnal sleep-related bed wetting has characteristics similar to those found for somnambulism and night terrors. It occurs during stages 3 and 4 of non-REM sleep, during the first third of the night, and is associated with a brief arousal. Usually the individual is confused and disoriented and does not describe a characteristic dream sequence nor a feeling of terror or anxiety. The condition is divided into “primary” enuresis, which is the persistence of sleeprelated bed wetting from infancy to childhood, and ‘“‘secondary”’ enuresis, the appearance of bed wetting after a time of successful toilet training. Both “primary” and ‘‘secondary”’ (idiopathic) bed wetting must be distinguished from symptomatic enuresis, which is caused by a known 

organic condition. Most children with idiopathic enuresis stop having the episodes by puberty, although emotional stress can reactivate the problem. There is often a family history of nocturnal enuresis which may be related to somnambulism and night terrors. There is no evidence that idiopathic enuresis is associated with epileptic discharge. Clinically, it must be distinguished from sleep-related seizures which may result in urinary incontinence. Polysomnographic and electroencephalographic recordings are useful in identifying this and other parasomnias. 

Other parasomnias_ There is a growing list of other pathophysiological sleep-disturbing events. These include dream anxiety attacks (nightmares), sleep-related epileptic seizures, bruxism (clenching of the jaw and grinding of the teeth), sleep-related head banging and rocking (jactatio capitis nocturnus), familial sleep paralysis, impaired sleep-related penile tumescence, sleeprelated painful erections, sleep-related cluster headaches, chronic paroxysmal hemicrania, abnormal swallowing syndrome, _ sleep-related asthma, sleep-related cardiovascular symptoms, sleep-related gastroesophageal reflux, and sleeprelated hemolysis (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria). The reader is referred to the Diagnostic Classification of Sleep and Arousal Disorders (Association of Sleep Disorders Centers) and other selected references for more complete information regarding the above disorders. In this article, three of these parasomnias will be described briefly because of special pathophysiological relevance. IMPAIRED SLEEP-RELATED PENILE TUMESCENCE Penile erections occur normally during 80 to 90 percent of all REM periods in males in every age group from premature infants to the aged (eighth and ninth decade). Tumescence occurs in non-REM sleep as well, but it is much less frequent and, when present, is not well sustained. The amount of nocturnal penile tumescence (NPT) per night decreases with age. In the 20- to 30-year-old age group, it is present for an average of 200 min of sleep, and in the 70- to 80year-old age group for approximately 100 min. The presence of a highly predictable recurrent REM-related cycle of NPT distinguishes 

DISORDERS OF SLEEP AND THE SLEEP-WAKE CYCLE 

###### 262 

organic from psychogenic impotence. In organic disease, which affects waking erectile potency, NPT is either totally absent or markedly diminished. These organic diseases include diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular syndromes (e.g., hypertension), neurological diseases (e.g., multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury), and endocrine and urogenital diseases (e.g., Peyronie’s disease). Many pharmacological substances (tricyclic, antidepressants, and adrenergic blockers) also inhibit NPT. In patients with psychogenic impotence, NPT measurements show no or little reduction compared with normal age-related standards. Sleep disorder centers therefore use the measurement of NPT to assist in the differential diagnosis between organic and psychogenic causes of impotence. 

SLEEP-RELATED CLUSTER HEADACHES AND CHRONIC PAROXYSMAL HEMICRANIA Many patients with cluster headaches, migraine, and chronic paroxysmal hemicrania have an attack during sleep. The cluster headache attack and the paroxysmal hemicrania awakens the patient with severe pain either directly out of REM sleep or in the immediate post-REM period. Phase shifts of the daily sleep time demonstrate that the headache follows REM sleep. Cluster headaches are characterized by the rapid development of severe unilateral eye and upper facial pain in association with tearing, rhinorrhea, and conjunctival redness. An ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome may be present. Nausea and anorexia may also occur. The pain awakens the patient. The attack may last for 30 min to several hours. Many patients have several episodes during the night, each associated with a REM sleep period. Attacks of chronic paroxysmal hemicrania occur more frequently —at times there may be up to 24 episodes per day —are short lasting (5 to 15 min), and have no special nocturnal predominance. However, when they occur during sleep, they are ‘“‘time-locked”’ to REM sleep. Since it has been well established that marked autonomic nervous system changes occur (“‘autonomic storm’’), the triggering of these headache attacks may be related to altered autonomic functions. 

SLEEP-RELATED GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX The clinical symptoms of sleep-related gastroesophageal reflux are recurrent awakening 

from sleep with a burning substernal pain (heartburn), associated with a sour taste, coughing, choking, and respiratory discomfort. These symptoms are often associated with postprandial regurgitation, dysphagia, esophagitis, laryngopharyngitis, and heartburn during the waking state. It has been shown that there is decreased acid clearance in the lower esophagus during sleep in association with recurrent reflux of gastric juice up into the esophagus. This in turn leads to a progressive esophagitis and, in serious cases, to esophageal stricture, aspiration pneumonia, bronchiectasis, and laryngopharyngitis. Recent studies during sleep have demonstrated that gastric acid will reflux up the lower esophagus and that a decreased clearing mechanism is present. A specific sleep-stage relationship has not been established as yet. 

###### SUMMARY 

Recent advances in research on sleep and biological rhythms have led to specific recommendations for the clinical diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders. A new clinical specialty has developed with the establishment of sleep disorder centers and a diagnostic classification of sleep and arousal disorders. This new nosological approach has evolved from an extensive base of new scientific information concerning descriptive polygraphic and analysis of clinical cases. Four major categories have been defined: (1) disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep (insomnias), (2) disorders of excessive somnolence, (3) disorders of the sleep-wake schedule, and (4) dysfunctions associated with sleep. Within this comprehensive classification, certain major pathophysiologic advances are described for the “‘insomnias.”” These include polysomnographic identification of altered sleep stage patterns in the major affective illnesses, insomnias related to hypnotic drugs and alcohol, sleep disturbances associated with sleep-induced respiratory impairment, and sleep-related periodic movements during sleep (nocturnal myoclonus). Excessive daytime somnolence is primarily associated with the hypersomnia sleep-apnea syndrome and with narcolepsy. The interface between basic research in biological rhythms (chronobiology) and disorders of the human sleep-wake schedules is a recent but rapidly ex- 

###### REFERENCES 263 

panding area of investigation. The importance of sleep length, internal organization, and timing within neurophysiological circadian time-keeping systems has been recognized in the diagnosis of these sleep-wake disorders and has led to new chronotherapeutic regimens. Finally, increasing identification and description of parasomnias, i.e., dysfunctions associated with sleep, have led sleep research into important new areas that interface with a very broad spectrum of general integrative physiological and pathological entities. It is now clear that sleep research and sleep disorders medicine have progressed from a field of interdisciplinary relationships to a new scientific and clinical discipline in their own right.

###### INTRODUCTION SSS 

The general educational objective of any carefully planned program of continuing medical education (CME) must be to encourage physician mastery of a finite body of medical knowledge. The specific educational objective of this program, sponsored by the University of Texas Health Science Center at Dallas, is to ensure that general internists, family practitioners, and other physicians understand recent advances in internal medicine that are necessary to ensure good clinical practice. 

Update I: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition, is an educational program divided into three parts: 

- 1 Study materials: Update I: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition, or other appropriate readings 

- 2 Formal examination: a 109-question, multiple-choice test in national board format 

- 3 Specific feedback: an individualized, computer-generated printout that reports raw score, percent correct, and the specific number of questions that an individual has failed to answer correctly 

Participants who submit the computer answer sheet for scoring and achieve a minimum of 60 percent correct can earn 25 hours of category 1 CME credit. The charge for the CME program is 

SSS SSS 

$25.00 (a check payable to McGraw-Hill Book Company must accompany the scoring sheet). 

Participants who do not choose to return their computer answer sheets for scoring may claim up to 22 credit hours in category S(a) (on the basis of hour-for-hour participation). Participants who submit their computer answer sheets but do not receive a passing score and do not choose to retake the examination also can claim up to 22 credit hours in category 5(a), on the basis of hour-for-hour use of Update I: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition, and up to 22 credit hours in category 5(d), on the basis of hour-for-hour use of this examination. 

The examination that follows in this booklet consists of 109 multiple-choice questions that are representative of the major areas covered in Update I: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition. The material in both the review book and the examination was prepared by physicians representing the subspecialties of internal medicine, under the aegis of Harrison’s editorial board—Kurt J. Isselbacher, M.D.; Raymond D. Adams, M.D.; Eugene Braunwald, M.D.; Joseph B. Martin, M.D.; Robert G. Petersdorf, M.D.; and Jean D. Wilson, M.D. After studying Update I: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition, or completing other appropriate readings, participants should be prepared to pass this examination.
