###### CME EXAMINATION CME 5 

###### Time allotment 

This examination has no set time limit, and participants are allowed—in fact, encouraged—to spend time verifying their answers. Should participants wish to treat this program as a preparation for a certification or recertification examination, however, they should allow themselves no more than two and one-half minutes per question. Additionally, there is no immediate time limit in which your computer answer sheet must be returned for scoring. The program will be scored for a minimum of 6 months after it has been replaced by a new edition or is no longer current enough to warrant publication. 

###### Returning your program for scoring 

When you open your CME package, please remove the folded, preaddressed envelope; this is the envelope you will use to return your answer sheet. When you have finished the examination, place your completed answer sheet and a check for $25.00, payable to McGraw-Hill Book Company, in the preaddressed envelope. 

###### Scoring 

The score for this test is determined strictly by the number of questions answered correctly, and there is no penalty for wrong answers. Questions that have been marked with more than one response will be scored as incorrect, as will questions that have no responses. Scores are confidential and will be reported only to you; they will go on file at the University of Texas only if you achieve a passing score on the examination. 

Computer scoring of completed and returned CME programs will take place at least once a month. When your program has been scored, and if you have answered at least 60 percent of the questions correctly, you will receive your individualized computer scoring, a set of complete explanations and references, and a ceitificate from the University of Texas attesting to your participation in the program. If, on the other hand, you do not achieve a passing score, you will receive only your individualized computer scoring and a new copy of the computer answer 

sheet. You will be given only one opportunity to retake the examination. 

###### CONCLUSION 

We believe that the Updates to Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition, together with the accompanying CME examinations and computer-scored evaluations comprise a stimulating educational program. We hope that you will find the CME program valuable in expanding your knowledge, enhancing your ability to provide quality medical care, and augmenting your own efforts to remain well educated in the field of internal medicine. 

This program has been conceived in accordance with the objectives of the University of Texas Health Science Center at Dallas. The major aims of the continuing medical education division of the University of Texas include (1) the presentation, auditing, and evaluation of quality, structured educational programs based on proven needs, (2) the granting of CME units to qualifying programs according to American Medical Association guidelines, with maintenance of permanent cross-referenced records for each participating physician, and (3) the broad support of a commitment to lifelong learning. 

###### PHYSICIAN’S RECOGNITION AWARD 

As an organization accredited for continuing medical evaluation, the University of Texas Health Science Center at Dallas designates this continuing medical education activity as meeting the criteria for 25 hours’ credit in category 1 for educational materials for the Physician’s Recognition Award of the American Medical Association, provided it has been successfully completed (at least 60 percent correct). Participants who do not achieve a passing score are eligible for up to 22 credit hours in category 5(a) for hour-for-hour use of Update 1: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ninth Edition, and up to 22 credit hours in category 5(d) for hour-for-hour use of this examination.

###### Questions 1 to 3 

A 78-year-old man is admitted to the hosital because of gradually deepening jaundice. The man’s medical history includes two myocardial infarctions complicated by congestive heart failure, stable angina provoked by minimal exertion, and very severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from heavy cigarette smoking. A cholecystectomy was performed 14 years ago. In the 6 months prior to admission, the man noticed an increase in chronic midback pain, had a poor appetite and a 30- to 40-lb weight loss, and began passing four to seven foul-smelling, loose yellow stools daily. Current medications include digoxin, a thiazide diuretic, and a nitrate preparation. 

On physical examination, the man is afebrile and has stable vital signs. He is dyspneic at rest and cachectic in appearance. Marked icterus is present but without either the peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease or a palpably enlarged liver or other abdominal mass. Total serum bilirubin concentration: 15 mg per 100 ml
